en: The First Fascicle of the Commentary on the Contemplation of the Mind in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Definitive Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Composed by the Tiantai Bhikṣu Lingyao, resident at Lianhua Monastery in Jiahe.

Following the comprehensive classification established by Miti Gao, all sutras are divided into three parts according to their textual structure. In this sutra, the section from the beginning up to the Buddha’s arrival constitutes the Introduction (Nidāna);
the section from Āḷavaka’s vision of the Buddha until his lack of attachment to the triple world constitutes the Main Body (Śarīra);

and everything following this constitutes the Dissemination (Pariṇāmanā). Within the Introduction, there is first the General Introduction, followed by the Specific Introduction; herein is the text of the General Introduction.

The principle is universal while the meaning is specific; this is because the specific [details] pertain to the present sutra. While the events of the specific introduction (nidāna) are distinct, their underlying meaning is universal, for all such introductions share commonalities.

Furthermore, in the present universal introduction, the virtues of the śrāvakas are praised by way of the "opening and revealing" (kai-xian), whereas the bodhisattvas are listed from the point of the *svairacaryā* (self-indulgence).
This is particularly distinct from other sutras, and thus represents the specific within the universal. These are the five matters preceding the sutra.
Now, there are six kinds of accomplishment. First is the accomplishment of faith.
"Thus" (evam) and "thus" (evam) are terms used to point toward a phenomenon; they refer to what is called this matter, this person, or this object. Now...
This refers to the method expounded in this sutra for initially contemplating the single mind with right observation, followed by specifically clarifying the perfect understanding, practice,
and realization through the retribution of karmic invitations, proceeding until the ultimate fulfillment of Bodhi and the return to the state of non-attainment.
This one kind of secret causal rule for cultivation and realization was personally inquired about and respectfully received by me, Ānanda, from the Buddha.

This was obtained through hearing. Now, relying once more upon the established models of a single school, I shall explain the text by means of causes and conditions (*nidāna*) and the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*).

First, regarding the explanation according to the four *siddhāntas*: the sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods all begin with "Thus" (*evam*). That the Way of all Buddhas is identical and does not contend with the world is the *loka-siddhānta*.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Citing time, place, and person serves to inspire faith in people."

This is the *puruṣa-saṃvṛti-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for the sake of people). Furthermore, it is intended to refute the two characters *a* and *ou* used by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"A" signifies non-existence (*abhāva*), and "ou" signifies existence (*bhāva*). These two are the tenets held by the outsiders.

Now, establishing [the term] "thus" (*evam*) serves as a remedial standpoint (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*) to refute those [tenets], showing that they are neither superior nor correct. Moreover, "thus" is a word of faith and compliance; when one has faith, then...
Upon hearing this, one understands it. When things proceed according to principle, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected; this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).

Next, regarding the explanation by means of the classification of teachings (*yōkyō-shaku*): because the Buddha has already spoken [of this] previously and now recounts it again, he says "Thus" (*evam*).

Regarding this from the perspective of the words, they are "thus"; regarding this from the perspective of the principle, they are "correct. Since the words are a reiteration, "thus" is discussed in terms of the expressive medium (*vyañjana*), while "correct" refers to the principle (*artha*).
Since there is fundamentally no difference, this is discussed in terms of what is expressed (*vācya*). Regarding the teachings, there are four aspects. The Buddha said:

"All mundane and supramundane phenomena arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Because of afflictions (*kleśa*), there is birth and death (*saṃsāra*); if one is free from afflictions, there is no birth and death.
Afflictions are the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); birth and death are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); freedom from afflictions is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)."

The absence of birth and death is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Because Ānanda transmitted this to the Buddha and it did not differ from what the Buddha had taught, he said, "Thus" (*evam*).
This is the opening formula "Thus" at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras. The Buddha said: "Dharmas born of causes and conditions are empty in their very substance.
When they come, they do not come from self, other, both, or neither; when they go, they do not go toward the east, west, south, or north. This is existence itself.
Furthermore, emptiness is not the emptiness resulting from the extinction of form. Ānanda’s transmission of this text is in accordance with the truth;

thus it is the opening of the Sūtras of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). The Buddha said that the phenomena of birth and death are all like flowers in the sky, while true emptiness and nirvāṇa are also like illusions and transformations.
Buddha-nature is like the moon beyond the clouds, transcending both extremes. Ānanda transmitted this as being the Buddha’s teaching.
They are not different. Thus it is at the beginning of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) sūtras. The Buddha said: "Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself the Middle Way;
how much more so is Nirvāṇa—how could it not be the Middle Way? Earth, water, fire, wind, space, views, and consciousness are of one single nature and all fully possess [it]."
The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is both with and apart from characteristics; though empty, it is endowed [with all], and though endowed, it is empty.

Ānanda transmitted this to the Buddha, who said it was not different from what he had taught: "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the fact that the principle is fundamentally non-erroneous, hence "is" (*iti*). Thus, the opening of the Perfect Teaching Sūtras begins with "Thus.
Since the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was preached during the Vaipulya period, it should possess the four kinds of "Thus"; furthermore, it has undergone further revelation and clarification.

Thus, the complete realization of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is established in this manner. Although the sutra reveals [the ultimate truth] and belongs to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) division, it nonetheless sets forth the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested.
Since the main body of this sutra fully elucidates the contemplation of the mind (xin-guan), there is no discussion of contemplating the mind within the introductory section. II.
Accomplishment through Hearing.
"I have heard.
This refers to Ānanda himself. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* clarifies that there were three Ānandas:
Ānanda (translated as "Joy") held the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; Ānandabhadra (translated as "Virtuous Joy") received and upheld the *Miśraka* [piṭaka];...
*Zang* (藏). Ānanda Sāgara—here translated as "Ocean of Joy"—upholds the *Buddha-piṭaka*. In the *Āgama-sūtras*, there is mention of the "Dharmagupta Ānanda" who upholds the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka*.

This likely refers to one individual possessing four virtues who transmits four Dharma-gates: the *Hīnayāna* is the *Piṭaka* of the Teaching (*Śāsana*); the *Miśra-piṭaka* is the *Piṭaka* of the Common Teaching (*Pāryāya*);
the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka* is the *Piṭaka* of the Distinct Teaching (*Vibhinna*); and the *Buddha-piṭaka* is... [the *Piṭaka* of the Perfect Teaching (*Ekayāna*)].

The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Therefore, the beginning of the *Shiqian* states: "As fully explained in the *Shu*, there are four kinds of Ānanda. However, within the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no self and no hearing;
that which is now called "self" refers to the three kinds of selfhood of ordinary beings—namely, the self of views, the self of pride, and [the self of ignorance].
The "self" is a mere name. There are two kinds of practitioners: those who have not yet seen the selflessness of the self, yet can subdue the conceit of self but have not yet severed it;
and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who are of one kind. For them, there is no fault in using the conventional name "self" in accordance with worldly usage.
As the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states: "The learned Ānanda knows that 'self' and 'selflessness' are non-dual; therefore, he is able to transmit and uphold the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom."

This refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding "I have heard" (*śruta*): the *Mahā-śāstra* states that when the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within range of being heard, and one directs the mind with the desire to hear—because these various conditions harmonize, it is said, "I have heard.
The *Mahā-nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: there is that which is not-hearing yet hearing; there is that which is not-hearing and not-hearing;

there is that which is hearing yet not-hearing; and there is that which is hearing and hearing. One school employs these to correlate with the Four Teachings. If one maintains the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) Teaching...
The Vaipulya (Vaipulya) is the transmission of hearing what has not been heard. The Prajñāpāramitā (Prajñā) is the transmission of not hearing what has been heard.
The Ekayāna (Ekayāna) is the transmission of neither hearing nor not hearing what has been heard. This present sutra contains all four of these meanings.
Some sutras say "Thus have I heard," which is merely a difference in phrasing between the beginning and the end. Furthermore, there are many... [text continues].
An explanation cannot be fully set forth here. ○ Three times of accomplishment:

First, at the time when the Dharma King inaugurates his mandate and a sublime assembly gathers, the Way is realized through the mutual resonance of cause and response, attaining enlightenment according to one's capacity, neither too late nor too early.
The preceding is called "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*). Therefore, it does not specify spring, summer, autumn, winter, day, month, year, or season.
○ Fourth, the principal achiever is the Buddha.

"Buddha" is fully called *Buddha*. This means "the Awakened One. Under the tree at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he realized and awakened to the general and specific characteristics of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Among the six stages of being a Buddha, this refers to ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*). Furthermore, he is able to awaken all sentient beings;
therefore, it is said: "How marvelous! Sentient beings all possess the wisdom and virtues of the Tathāgata."

One merely fails to realize the marks due to false conceptualization and attachment. The Buddha is unmoving and unemerging within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), yet he enables sentient beings to perceive movement and emergence.
His body is sixteen feet tall, manifesting the appearance of an eighty-year-old bhikṣu;
beneath the Bodhi tree, having reached the thirty-four moments of mind, both active defilements and residual habits are exhausted—this is the Tripiṭaka Buddha who has attained self-awakening.

This is the characteristic of awakening others. If one manifests in the form of a *bhikṣu* while appearing in the *viśeṣa-kāya* (exalted body), attaining correspondence in a single thought beneath a tree and severing all remaining residual habits, this is the characteristic of self-awakening and awakening others of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) Buddha.

If one manifests solely in the *viśeṣa-kāya*, sitting upon a lotus pedestal to receive the office of a Buddha, this is the characteristic of self-awakening and awakening others of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching). If one manifests...

The inconceivable body, which has the characteristic of being like empty space and pervades the dharma-realm, is precisely the aspect of the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) who awakens both himself and others.

Since this sutra contains the four teachings, it contains the four Buddhas; yet, when explained according to the opening and merging [of these teachings], there is only the single Buddha of the Perfect Teaching.
Thus, the aforementioned body is the eternally perfect body, and the aforementioned Buddha is the eternally perfect Buddha. ○
The accomplishment of the five locations.
[The Buddha] was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Śrāvastī is also called Śāvatthī; it is newly translated as "Abundant Virtue" (Puṇyavat), because the kingdom abounds in four virtues: first, wealth and goods.

Second, the objects of desire; third, extensive learning; fourth, liberation. *Ji* (祇) is a phonetic transcription for *Jita*; the correct form is *Śītavana*. This translates as "Victorious in Battle.
It is the name of the prince who, at the time of his birth, was given this auspicious title because his father, the King, had been victorious in battle against foreign nations.
It was for him that Sudatta purchased the grove and built the vihāra to offer to the Buddha. *Huan* (桓) is... [text fragment].
"Forest. As for "vihāra" (jing-she): it is so named because it is the dwelling place of śramaṇas of refined conduct—consisting of winter houses, summer halls, monastic quarters, and meditation caves.
Because the Buddha dwells internally in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and is able to establish the Great Dharma, he manifests his presence in a vihāra to benefit all sentient beings.
[Section on the Achievement of the Six Multitudes, Part Three: The Multitude of Śrāvakas, Section One: Clarification]
"Classified as such.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
"Together with" means that Ānanda is cited because he was among those one thousand two hundred and fifty people who were the audience for the teaching.
This is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s *Śraddhā-prasāda-nidāna* (Preface of Testimony and Faith). Furthermore, it shares this same meaning [with other versions].

Some say that when the Buddha and the bhikṣus dwell in the same place, the Buddha is the principal (*nāyaka*) and the bhikṣus are his companions (*parivāra*); this interpretation is also valid. If one relies on the testimony of faith, the account of Ānanda being with the assembly is superior.
If one relies on the relationship of principal and companion, the case of the Buddha and the bhikṣus is appropriate. Now, based on this...
To testify to the faith is the primary intent. The Sanskrit term *mahā* now possesses three meanings: great (*mahat*), many (*bahu*), and excellent (*viśiṣṭa*).

Because his capacity and dignity are such that he is revered by great beings such as celestial kings, he is called "Great. Because he has universally mastered both internal and external scriptures, he is called "Many.
Because he excels the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths, he is called "Excellent. This is the name for a *bhikṣu*.
It contains three meanings: the mendicant (bhikṣu), the terrifier of Māra, and the destroyer of evil. Regarding the mendicant, there are four kinds of sustenance:
cultivating medicine and planting fields and gardens is called downward-facing sustenance; gazing upward at the stars and constellations is called upward-facing sustenance;
using clever speech in the four directions is called horizontal-mouth sustenance; and incantations, sorcery, and divination are called corner-mouth sustenance. A bhikṣu does not engage in these four.

He is called a "Pure Mendicant" (*śramaṇa*) because, upon attaining the fruit, he achieves the virtue of being worthy of offerings (*arhat*). Regarding "Frightening Māra": having himself left the household life, he further transforms others so that they all depart from the triple world.
This opposes the intent of Māra; though Māra exerts his power to restrain him, he is instead bound by the five fetters and is left only with sorrow and fear.
Thus, he is called "Frightener of Māra. Upon attaining the fruit, he achieves the virtue of non-arising (*anutpāda*). [He is also] the "Destroyer of Evil."

"Those who can destroy" refers to those who have severed all ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) that afflict the mind; thus they are called "destroyers of evil. Upon reaching the fruit [of Arhatship], they achieve the virtue of being "slayers of thieves.

"A community" (*saṃgha*) refers to four or more individuals, up to hundreds, thousands, or even immeasurable numbers, performing the ritual of *karmavācanā* (formal act) in one place, conducting the counting of votes (*śalākā*), and observing the *poṣadha*.
When both the matter and the principle are in harmony and no conflict or dispute exists, it is called a "harmonious community" (*saṃgha-samagra*). ○
Second, the indication of the number:
"accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he converted the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya; subsequently, he converted the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their disciples.
One thousand [monks]. Next, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with a retinue of one hundred.
Next, he converted the householder Yaśas and others, fifty people in total. Although the scriptures cite a large number, they simply state "one thousand two hundred and fifty.

All of these had previously served non-Buddhist teachers for many kalpas, undergoing diligent hardship without attaining anything; yet, upon encountering the Buddha's Dharma, they immediately attained [realization].
The supreme fruit: having deeply felt the Buddha’s grace, they became his constant retinue. ○ Third, the manifestation of their status:
they are all untainted (*anāsrava*) Great Arhats. Guishan says:
"Untainted" means that internally they are in harmony with the Middle Way and do not leak into or fall into the two extremes. Arhat.

The name contains three meanings: slayer of thieves (*arhat*), worthy of offerings (*arhat*), and one who is non-arising (*an-utpāda*). According to the fourth reliance in the "Chapter on the Four Reliances" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is designated as an Arhat.
As for the conventional explanation regarding the three outflows (*āsrava*):

first, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), which refers to all afflictions of the desire realm with the exception of ignorance; second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), which refers to [the afflictions] of the two upper realms... one.
All afflictions are eliminated except for ignorance; there are three outflows of ignorance, namely the ignorance of the three realms.

However, delusion and karma are the causes of the various outflows, while birth and death are the fruits of those outflows. Now, "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the absence of both the segmented and transformational types of outflows within the three realms.
Therefore, Guishan identifies this as the tenth stage (bhūmi). This is based on the perspective of the ultimate revelation [of the One Vehicle].
This is the explanation. ○ Fourth, praising his virtues:
"The Son of the Buddha abides in the maintenance of the Dharma, skillfully transcending all realms of existence. He is able to perfect dignified deportment within the lands;

he turns the wheel of the Dharma following the Buddha and is most worthy of receiving his final entrustment. He strictly purifies the Vinaya, establishing a grand model for the three worlds; with infinite response-bodies, he delivers and liberates sentient beings."
"Delivering [beings] from the future and transcending all worldly entanglements.
This clarifies that all the great disciples abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

According to ancient interpretations, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is the manifestation of various dignified demeanors while remaining unmoved within the extinction samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Here, the first four lines indicate that they abide in this very samādhi. [They] are...
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that one who receives the family inheritance is a son of the Buddha;

dwelling in the realm of the Buddha and upholding the True Dharma, they likewise abide within the Great Samādhi, and thus are called "abiding and maintaining. When it says "all existences," it refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
To transcend existence while remaining within it is called "skillfully transcending. Is this not precisely abiding in the Mahāyāna extinction samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?

Having already transcended all realms of existence (*bhava*) and attained the fundamental realm of serene light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), he is thus able to respond to the three lower lands, manifesting a dignified countenance to awaken sentient beings;

is this not the manifestation of various majestic demeanors (*īryāpatha*)? From here, the text explains the preceding four lines. Regarding the first two lines, "The Buddha-son maintains and sustains":

"Turning the wheel following the Buddha" means that the Buddha possesses both sudden and gradual wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), all of which [the Bodhisattva] is fully capable of turning in accordance with them.
The *Fahua shu* states: "Now, the various manifestations of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi adapt to the capacities of sentient beings, leaving nothing undone.

When the Wheel of Dharma is first turned and the Gate of Ambrosia is opened, if the conditions for transformation of the great beings (*mahāsattva*) have not yet matured, they manifest as deaf or mute, remaining entirely like milk.
However, when those to be transformed have matured, it is as easy to dye white silk as it is for lotuses to bloom early in a pond."

They opened [the gates of liberation], transforming the ordinary into the holy and turning milk into curd. As the foremost disciples of the Master, each was preeminent in wisdom, supernatural powers, eloquence, and samādhi.
Together they assisted the Dharma King to further deliver those not yet delivered and to bring to full maturity those already matured.
At the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, hearing of the inconceivable merit of the Bodhisattvas, they felt ashamed of their own limited views.
Aspiring to the Great [Vehicle] is like transforming fresh milk into *maṇḍa* (curd-butter). Next, one hears the gate of the Prajñā Mahāyāna.

Beginning with the investigation of form and mind and culminating in the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it encompasses and contains both the Small and the Great, involving taking in and giving out, or internalizing and externalizing.

Whether shared or distinct, partial or perfect, by receiving these instructions and attaining realization, the mind gradually becomes open and expansive, like transforming *maṇḍa* into *ghṛta* (clarified butter). Next, one hears...

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the innate nature of the father and son is determined, and they receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and the entrustment of the Mahāyāna, wherein the three vehicles are set aside to return to the One.
This is like the other four flavors being identical to the single *tīmana* (clarified butter). All the great Arhats, from the ground of the Dharma-body, cast their reflections and follow conditions;
their traces appear upon the ten thousand waters. Such is the power of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). (Text) Indeed, this proceeds from the Buddha.

The turning of the wheel of Dharma in five stages, manifesting as provisional means to bring about the realization of practice and the benefits of the five flavors, is the meaning of the Buddha’s turning of the wheel.
While the Buddha was in the world, he turned the wheel of Dharma accordingly;

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is the task of the sons of the Buddha to skillfully carry out his final instructions. Just as a father, when approaching death, must certainly leave a testament, so too did the Buddha.

Entrusting the teachings to disciples is also termed a "final testament. One must understand that *śrāvakas* are unfit for such entrustment, just as an old or sick person is unfit to be entrusted with gold.
The unsurpassed Buddha-dharma should be entrusted to Bodhisattvas, just as one might entrust a hundred pieces of gold to twenty-five capable men.
Because Bodhisattvas are skilled in inquiry and response, they enable the Buddha-dharma to endure for a long time.
In the world, one is called "Subhūti" (妙堪) only when one increases, intensifies, and brings benefit and peace to sentient beings.
In this sutra, Ānanda’s ability to ask the Buddha various questions that elucidate the profound meaning is the characteristic of being "Subhūti.

Furthermore, engaging in various question-and-answer sessions at the time of death is called "Subhūti," and ensuring that the Buddha-dharma remains long after one's passing is also called "Subhūti. Therefore...
The first two lines explain "the Buddha-sons who maintain [the Dharma]. The following two lines explain "excellently transcending all realms of existence" (*bhava*).

*Vinaya* is translated as "extinction" (*mie*), because it extinguishes all non-virtues of body and speech. Alternatively, it is said that this is not the primary translation; the correct translation is *lü* (vinaya). *Lü* means "to weigh.

It refers to weighing the gravity [of offenses], distinguishing between what constitutes a transgression and what does not. [The phrase] "excellently transcending all realms of existence" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The power of concentration and wisdom is derived from precepts. If one possesses the ten Mahāyāna precepts, then concentration and wisdom are also contained therein.
Therefore, it is said that only the Buddha alone maintains pure precepts, while all others are termed those who defile the precepts.
Now, regarding the aspect of partial realization of truth, that which is realized shares in commonality with the Buddha and may be termed "adorned and pure.

In this way, it serves extensively as a model for the triple world. If it were not transcendent of all realms of existence (*bhava*), how could it serve as the teacher and model for the two kinds of triple worlds?

Regarding the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the subsequent commentary explains its ability to achieve majestic deportment within lands; it has long been the foundation of the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya.

One should descend into the three lower lands; only by manifesting bodies within the ten realms can it be called "immeasurable. This refers to teaching the nine realms of sentient beings so that they take refuge in the Buddha-realm.
Furthermore, one delivers future sentient beings, causing them to transcend the defilements of the three realms.

This reveals that one has already attained the eternally abiding Dharma-body, which is not comparable to those who extinguish their wisdom through the annihilation of the physical body. Whether for oneself or others, such is the majestic deportment.
Because they are all fully endowed [with these qualities], this explains the accomplishment of majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).

This passage first presents the headings and subsequently provides the explanations, clarifying that the great disciples have already abided in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and are endowed with two kinds of meanings for revealing and manifesting.

First is "revealing the provisional to manifest the real" (*kaiquan xianshi*): this means opening up the provisional of the Hīnayāna to reveal the reality of the Mahāyāna. Second is "revealing the traces... [to manifest the source].
"Fundamental" means that while outwardly manifesting the traces of a *śrāvaka*, one inwardly harbors the essence of a bodhisattva.

This principle of the revelation and manifestation in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is clarified at the very beginning of that scripture; thus, it is evident that this present sutra must share the same "ghee-like" flavor (*tiktaka*) as the *Lotus Sutra*.
Nevertheless, the claim that this present sutra was preached after the *Lotus Sutra* is not necessarily certain. At the beginning of this present sutra...

Regarding the fact that the passages in the first assembly concerning the investigation of the mind and the discernment of vision (*citta-vicāra-dṛṣṭi-vibhaṅga*) actually precede the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet their praise of virtues surpasses that of the *Lotus Sūtra*:
this is because this scripture was spoken by the Buddha for the sake of the compilers (*saṃgītikāra*) and was only completed as a single work after twenty years had passed.
Although the teachings of the first assembly were indeed prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, four or five fascicles [of this scripture] follow after that *Lotus Sūtra*.
It is said: "Ānanda personally recorded what he had heard; the gateways of realization from beginning to end are all contained within this present sutra.

If the principle of revealing the provisional to manifest the real and revealing the traces to manifest the fundamental were not elucidated at the very beginning of the sutra, where else would this intent be revealed?
For the general introduction (sūtra-pūrva-vastu) serves as the preface to the sutra and stands at its head; it is also called [the *nidāna*].
Because this postscript to the sutra was composed by those who performed the compilation (*saṃgīti*), the compilers were able to clarify their own intentions.

This can be understood by analogy with other sutras as well. Since the compilers personally recounted what they knew to elucidate the meaning of the teaching, their words of praise for its virtues surpass even those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, among the five titles of the compiled sutra...
It is also titled *The King of the Great Vaipulya Lotus*. The meaning of its revelation and manifestation is clarified at the beginning of the sutra.
V. Listing the Names: Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, and Pūrṇa.
Nandimitra-putra, Subhūti, Upānanda, and others were their leaders. Śāriputra—his full name is Śāriputra; this translates as "Son of Śārī.
Because his mother possessed a beautiful form and he was born from her body, he is called "Son of Śārī.
He is also called "Son of Śāri" (Śāri-putra), for his mother was the most intelligent among women.
His marks of intelligence reside in his eyes; because the black and white of his eyes were clearly distinguished and their movement was as fluid as that of a *śāli* bird, he is named Śāriputra.
Furthermore, he is called Śāriputra because it manifests both his father’s name, Śāri, and his mother’s name, Putrikā.
He is called "Son" (*putra*) because his father’s name was Upatiṣya. As for the title "Great Wise One," it refers to his wisdom among the assembly of śrāvakas.
First: Because Mañjuśrī is among the assembly of bodhisattvas, he is called the Second World-Honored One.

When the Buddha spoke a single phrase, Śāriputra took that single phrase as his foundation and, for seven days and seven nights, let out a lion’s roar, producing ever-new phrases and meanings without end.
How much more so when the Buddha speaks extensively—how could the wisdom and eloquence of Śāriputra possibly be exhausted?
"Jin" (盡) is the clan name of Mahāmaudgalyāyana; it is translated as "Praise and Recitation. In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is translated as "radish";
Paramārtha states that this is translated as "mung bean. Because these two things were favored by ancient seers, they used them to name their clans.
"Kulada" (拘律陀) means "knotless tree. The *Śāstra* refers to Śāriputra as the "right-hand disciple. Great...

Maudgalyāyana was the left-hand disciple; he was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). These powers arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); thus, concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*) form a pair.
He is called "Great" (*Mahā*) to distinguish him from other Maudgalyāyanas who were skilled in calculation.

Mahākauṣṭhila is translated as "Great Thigh"; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. He constantly excelled his sister in debate, but when she was pregnant with Śāradvatīputra, he could no longer defeat her in discussion.
[The Master] was victorious. Knowing that the wise man harbored [this resolve], he entrusted his eloquence to the mouth of his mother and departed for South India to study the eighteen scriptures.

The people of the time mocked him, saying, "To master these over several generations is difficult; to hope for it in a single lifetime is impossible. He sighed deeply and said, "At home I was surpassed by my sister; on the road I am held in contempt by others.
He vowed to read without ceasing, having no leisure even to trim his nails; at that time he was called "Long-Nails" (Chángzhǐ).
The Brahmin Cūḍapanthaka, having completed his studies, returned home and asked where his nephew was. People told him that he had become a disciple of the Buddha.

He immediately became greatly arrogant, thinking, "My nephew was eight years old when his fame shook the five regions; what kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to have enticed my sister's son?
He went straight to where the Buddha was staying and reflected for a long time, yet not a single dharma entered his mind. He then spoke to the Buddha:
To say "I do not tolerate all phenomena" means that "tolerance" (*kṣānti*) has the sense of being at ease. This statement means: "I am able to refute all phenomena so that they cannot remain at ease.
Therefore, it is said, "I do not tolerate all phenomena. When the Buddha asked, "Do you tolerate this view?

the Brahmin reflected to himself: "I have fallen into a position of double defeat. If I tolerate this view, it contradicts my previous claim that 'I do not tolerate all phenomena. If [I do not tolerate it]..."
Unable to bear the thought that this man could surpass the Buddha in view, he immediately bowed his head; thereupon, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

When Śāriputra fanned the Buddha, he heard his uncle’s discourse and attained arhatship. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and was foremost among those who could answer difficult challenges, such as Kautūhala.
Pūrṇa’s father was named Maitreya (translated here as "Full"), and his mother, Mitrā, was named... [text fragment].
He is called Maitreya; now, as he is associated with his parents' names, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Among those who preach the Dharma, he is the foremost.

The Madhyama Āgama states that monks dwelling in retreat praised Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra for having few desires and being content, for his diligence and solitary abiding, and for his single-mindedness, right mindfulness, and untainted wisdom; he was also praised as the foremost in exhorting others to the Dharma.

At that time, Śāriputra heard this and thought, "When shall I meet this person? Another pointed out to him, saying, "The one with the white complexion, the dragon-like nose, and the parrot-like beak—that is his likeness.
Later, in the Andhavana forest, he saw Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Śāriputra asked, "Venerable sir, do you practice the holy life under Gautama? He replied, "It is so. Śāriputra asked again, "Is it for the sake of purifying the precepts?"

"Does one practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of purity of mind, purity of view, purity through overcoming doubt, purity regarding what is and is not the path, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the path, and purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment through the realization of the path? "No. Again he asked:
"Previously you said 'yes,' but now you say 'no. How is this to be understood? He replied: "It is for the sake of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa)."
"Therefore, one cultivates the holy life. He asked again: "Is it because of the purity of morality that one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder? He replied: "No. [He asked this] even up to:

"Is it because of the purity of the knowledge of the path and the abandonment [of defilements] that one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder? He replied: "No. He asked again: "What is the meaning of this? He replied:
"If one were to say that *nirvāṇa* without remainder is attained through the purity of morality, this would be calling 'with remainder' what is 'without remainder. This applies even up to..."
Even if the purity of the knowledge and abandonment of the path-traces (*mārgākārajñatā*) were not yet complete, it would still be called "complete" [in name].
If one were free from these seven, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would attain parinirvāṇa; for an ordinary person is free from these seven.

Because they are not [yet] free from them, [the practitioner proceeds] from the purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*) up to the purity of mind (*cittaviśuddhi*), and so on until the purity of the knowledge and abandonment of the path-traces. Listen, O Venerable One, as I speak an analogy. It is like...
King Prasenajit wished to travel from Kauśala to Vājīmatī. Along the way, he arranged seven carriages;
he left the first to take the second, and so on, until he left the sixth to take the seventh. When the people of Vājīmatī asked him, "Did you come by the first carriage? he replied, "No.

[They continued asking about each carriage] until they asked, "Did you come by the seventh carriage? to which he replied, "No. The meaning can be understood through this analogy. Śāriputra then asked, "Venerable one..."
"What is your name? How do fellow practitioners of the holy life address you? He replied, "My father's name is Pūrṇa and my mother's name is Maitrāyaṇī.
Fellow practitioners of the holy life address me as Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Śāriputra praised him, saying, "Excellent, worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"
He is a disciple of the Tathāgata, possessed of wisdom and eloquence, intelligent, resolute, secure, and fearless.
He has attained great辩才 (eloquence/patience), obtained the banner of the Deathless (amṛta-dhvaja), and personally realized the Deathless for himself. Those who encounter him obtain great benefit.

Fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) should wrap their robes around his neck and bear him upon their heads like a crown. The son of Pūrṇa asked: "Venerable one, what is your name? The fellow practitioner replied: [He is called] Mahākātyāyana.
"What is your name? He replied, "My father’s name was Upatiṣya and my mother’s name was Śārī; therefore, I am called Śāriputra.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra sighed and said, "Now, while debating with the disciples of the World-Honored One, I have failed to recognize him."
He conversed with the second Buddha and did not know [the answer]; he conversed with the General of the Dharma and did not know;
he conversed with the Disciple who turns the Wheel of Dharma again and did not know.
If I knew that the Venerable One could not answer even a single phrase, how much less a profound discourse? Excellent, excellent! You are a disciple of the Tathāgata... even unto [your] entanglement.
He wears [the robe] upon his head... (and so forth). Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra form a pair as eloquent preachers of the Dharma.
Subhūti is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kūṅ-shēng); when he was born, the storehouses and utensils were all empty, and the diviners declared it auspicious.
Because he was born from emptiness, he was named Kūṭadanta (Born of Emptiness). Because those who make offerings to him obtain immediate retribution, he is called Śubhūti (Good Fortune).

When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, people from all over the land flocked together, vying with one another to prostrate in worship. The Venerable One sat upright in his stone chamber, contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas:
form is not the Buddha; even consciousness is not the Buddha; the eye is not the Buddha; even the mind is not the Buddha.
The Buddha suddenly and completely awakened to the Way. The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇī Padmā: "It was not to you that I previously prostrated;
you were prostrating to the form-body (rūpakāya). Subhūti sat in tranquil meditation within a cave and first beheld the dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Upānisa, translated here as 'the nature of dust,' attained the Way by contemplating that the nature of dust is empty. Since emptiness gives rise to the nature of dust, this is called the union of emptiness and existence."
This constitutes one pair. As for the other individuals, they are referred to as "and others" (*ādi*) because their names are not fully recorded in the sutra.
These are all prominent *śrāvakas* who serve as teachers and guides to the assembly; thus, they are called "foremost. Guishan says: "The listing of names varies across the various sutras."
If seniority by years of ordination is emphasized, then Cūḍapanthaka is mentioned first; if renown and virtue are emphasized, then Śāriputra is mentioned first.
Here, we follow the precedent of emphasizing virtue. Second, the assembly of pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning, together with those at the initial stage of their resolve, all coming together at the Buddha’s dwelling.

In the Sanskrit language, *pratyekabuddha* is translated as "Pratyekajina," which means "Solitary Realizer. They are so called because they awaken to the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
It is also translated as "Solitary Realizer" (*pratyekabuddha*) because they awaken by themselves in a world where no Buddha exists. The *Jingde* [Chronicle] states:
"The Sanskrit term is *vivekacārin*, which means 'each wandering alone. The *Yinyi* [Dictionary] notes that "Solitary Realizer" correctly captures the meaning.
Changshui says: "This category is divided into two types. Those of sharp faculties are called 'Rhinoceros-like' (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*), for the rhinoceros has a single horn."

Those who appear in a world without a Buddha observe the transformation of phenomena and realize for themselves that they are unborn; those of duller faculties are called *vargacārin* (group-practitioners).
They also appear in a world without a Buddha and proceed in groups to instruct and transform their disciples. As it says in the *Zhongjing*:

"The scripture already states 'together with those of initial resolve,' which clearly suggests that master and disciples gathered together; thus, even in the era of a Buddha, there were *vargacārin* practitioners. However...
Those who follow the group-practice (vargacārin) are not necessarily entirely dull-witted. One who acts as a teacher and has attained self-awakening is like a *qilin* (a mythical unicorn);
those disciples who follow him may be termed "dull," which refers to the group-practitioners. Regarding the term "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), the *Xiyuan* (Analyzing the Profound) states:

"In this stage, the four wisdoms are already perfected, and there is no further dharma to be learned; therefore, it is called 'beyond training. There are four types of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*): first..."
1. "My births have been exhausted" is the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). 2. "There is no further existence" is the knowledge of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

3. "The holy life has been established" is the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). 4. "What was to be done has been accomplished" is the knowledge of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The "beginner" refers to one who has first resolved to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha. The *Miaoxuan* states: "This person possesses sharp faculties and does not require the formal restriction of the fruit."
Furthermore, they are able to suppress habitual tendencies. For example, their bodies are robust and they proceed directly to wherever they go without stopping or resting;

thus, they do not produce karmic results. Although they do not produce such results, how could there not be those who possess the initial resolve? There are various distinctions regarding pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*), which I shall not describe at length here.
As for why their names are not listed and their virtues not extolled: it is because they weary of clamor and delight in tranquility, spending most of their time in secluded, empty places.

This is merely because they are well-known to the multitude. If one follows the perspective of the revealed teaching (*kaixian*), then the stage of the Arhat is likewise situated within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

However, since we are naming them according to their original status and providing an explanation based on the Hīnayāna—given that there is no text extolling their virtues—the assembly of Bodhisattvas [is discussed here].
This passage should have been placed in the separate introduction (*prastāvanā*) as part of the introductory sequence of the narrative (*nirdeśa-prastāva*).
Regarding the term "initiation" (*samutthāna*): when the Tathāgata was about to proclaim the precepts, Ānanda was on the verge of violating the essence of the precepts;

because their minds were necessarily interconnected, it is called "initiation. However, since the listing of the assembly in the general introduction (*pūrvayoga*) had not yet been completed, it is for the time being categorized under the general introduction.
Furthermore, by resorting to causes and conditions, the Bodhisattvas are enumerated to demonstrate how this sutra is skillful and subtle.
It was during the period when the bhikṣus concluded their summer retreat and held the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Bodhisattvas from the ten directions consulted the Buddha to resolve their doubts;

reverently honoring his compassionate yet majestic presence, they sought its profound meaning. Thereupon, the Tathāgata prepared a seat and sat in tranquil composure, proclaiming the deep and esoteric teachings for the assembly.
The assembly at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before. The kalaviṅka-like voices of the sages resounded throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī serving as their leader.

"Belonging to" (*shǔ*) means "appropriate. Because one rests during this period in the summer, it is called "resting in summer" (*xiūxià*). Guishan said: "The *Vinaya* permits three days for the *pravāraṇā*:

the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month. 'Self-indulgence' (*zìzì*) refers to freely allowing oneself to confess whatever transgressions have been committed, permitting the Sangha to raise them, so that one may repent and become pure;
thus it is called *pravāraṇā*. 'Bodhisattva' is translated in full as *bodhisattva*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:"
"Bodhi" refers to the Buddha-way; "sattva" refers to the accomplishment of sentient beings, because one uses the Buddha-way of all Buddhas to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
Furthermore, bodhi is self-cultivation, while sattva is the transformation of others.

Regarding the phrase "the ten directions," Bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla were natives of this land and served as leaders among the assembly of bodhisattvas; the other bodhisattvas [were from elsewhere].
Many come from the ten directions. The Master of the Zuo Tradition says: "To seek out what is good is called *zī* (consultation).

Those who harbor doubts do so because the dust-like sands of ignorance have not yet been exhausted. Because the Tathāgata’s great compassion dictates that it is now time to proclaim the precepts, he is called "Compassionate and Reverent" (*Cíyán*).

"Reverently following" manifests the mind of a Bodhisattva; "Compassionate and Reverent" manifests the virtue of the Tathāgata. For ninety days, one restrains the feet [observing the *kaṭhina* retreat].
Having no means to see the Buddha, he went to pay his respects at the end of the summer retreat.

Regarding the pursuit of the profound meaning (*guhyārtha*), if discussed in terms of time, it refers to the desire to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras during the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

If discussed in terms of teaching, it refers to the Buddha’s pointing of the finger to explain the profound samādhi and wisdom of the Mahāyāna as the profound meaning. This immediately clarifies the preaching of the Dharma in response to the capacities of sentient beings.
Tranquil composure belongs to concentration (*samādhi*); the proclamation of this is wisdom (*prajñā*). Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; one must first enter meditative absorption.

In the degenerate age, many who possess wild wisdom do not attain it through samādhi. Since the Sage responded to beings by establishing a model within a single text that encompasses the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), how could one fail to follow them?
Regarding the profound and abstruse: a great sūtra states that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the *sūtra*...
The subtle meaning is taught for Bodhisattvas; the shallow and proximate meaning is taught for Śrāvakas.

That is to say, "impermanence" and "non-self" are the shallow and proximate; whereas within impermanence there is permanence, and within the dharma of non-self there is the true self—is this not the subtle?
What is now called the "profound and esoteric" meaning is likewise so. *Kalingabinga* is translated as [the kalaviṅka bird].
The *Miaosheng* (Wondrous-Voiced) bird emerges from the Snowy Mountains; while still within its shell, it can already sing, surpassing all other birds.

Its voice is harmonious and elegant, such that listeners never tire of hearing it. The Buddha’s voice is like this, pervading the worlds of the ten directions; this is the Buddha’s perfect sound (*pariśuddha-svara*).
As recorded in secular texts, during the time of Sun Xiu of the Wu state, there was a person who could produce "echo-words" (*xiangyan*): speaking here, they were heard there. From [this account...].
Those who listen to it do not perceive the magnitude of its sound. Listening from afar, it is like someone speaking face-to-face; one does not perceive the sound as coming from a distance.
Wherever the sound travels, it follows the direction in which it is aimed. For those far away, it reaches across ten or more *li*.
If even the retributive phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are such as this, how much more so must be the celestial voice of the Tathāgata? Is it not indeed so?
It reaches everywhere. That is to say, the perfect voice (pariṣvaṇa) is vast and pervasive, encompassing ten lands all at once; how could it be something that even Maudgalyāyana could fathom?
The Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are not necessarily the same as the assembly from the ten directions mentioned previously;

they have gathered here because they heard the celestial voice. Thus, the mutual resonance between cause and response gave rise to this Dharma-gate. Mañjuśrī—this is translated as [the Youth of Wisdom].

Wondrous Virtue (Miaode): Because he had realized the three virtues of the Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation, and served as the "eye for discerning dharmas" at the assembly on Mount Lúăng-yán, he occupied the position of the foremost disciple.

II. The Specific Preface, in two parts: 1. The King and Ministers Prepare the Feast; 2. Ānanda is Captured. The first part is further divided into two: 1. [Ānanda’s] Initial Inquiry; 2. [His] Subsequent Realization.
The Buddha was to visit the royal palace.
At that time, King Prasenajit was holding a memorial feast for his deceased father’s anniversary;

he invited the Buddha to the inner quarters of the palace to welcome the Tathāgata in person, providing an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, while also personally extending invitations to the great Bodhisattvas.
"Pusini" (波斯匿) here means "Harmonious and Joyful. It is also translated as "Victorious Army" (Shengjun).

In the *Renwang Jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), the name Pusini is rendered as "Moonlight," which refers to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) of virtuous conduct. Regarding the "day of the taboo" (*huìrì*): the *Qu Lǐ* (Book of Rites) states, "One observes the taboo after the final wailing.

This means that for feudal lords, seven months after the burial, there is a sacrifice in the courtyard or the ancestral temple called the "final wailing. Thereupon, an order is issued from the central palace to cease [the use of the deceased's personal name].

For this reason, the new reign name was avoided and no one dared to utter it. Thus, on that day, King Aniruddha established a fast and reverently invited the assembly of holy ones to provide spiritual sustenance for the spirit of his late predecessor.
Furthermore, the day of avoidance is also called the "day of taboo" (*jìrì*). As the *Jìyì* (Meaning of Sacrifices) states:
On the anniversary of a death, one must certainly mourn and pronounce the taboo name as if seeing the person in person. Regarding the term "gongye" (宮掖):

according to the *Tang Zhi* (History of the Tang) and the *Song-Yuan Gongdian Lu* (Records of the Palaces of the Song and Yuan), "ye" (掖) refers to the *yeyuan* (掖垣) or *yemen* (掖門), and not the inner court;

it refers to the palace city (*gongcheng*). For instance, Ban Gu’s *Xi-du fu* (Rhapsody on the Western Metropolis) states: "The rear palace includes the Yeting and Jiaofang. Lü Xiang’s commentary on Yeting explains: [The remainder of the passage would follow here.]
"Palace" (*gong*) refers to the name for the area on either side of the Son of Heaven, like the armpits (*zouye*).

In this text, following the invitation of the Buddha, there are five successive layers demonstrating the height of his reverence: the reception was personal; the arrangements were extensive; the delicacies were rare; the flavors were unsurpassed;
and the companions were the various Great Beings (*mahāsattva*). To invite the Buddha to the palace armpits is precisely the Middle Way. [The *zhai* (fast/retreat)]...
"Zhè (者)" means "to fasten" (*zhì*). It refers to not exceeding the midday meal. The *Fāngyán* states that "xiū" means "cooked"; it refers to cooked food.
Alternatively, it is said that "xiū" means "to present. ○ Second, Sengyingchen-shè.
Furthermore, within the city there were elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously providing meals for the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival to accept their offerings.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the Bodhisattvas and Arhats to attend to the various hosts of the feast-givers.
In India, those who possess billions in accumulated wealth are called *śreṣṭhin* (elders); those who preserve the Way and abide in rectitude are called *gṛhapati* (lay practitioners).
The *Hanzi* says: "One who dwells in gravity and sincerity is called an elder. The *Yuzao* states: "The *gṛhapati* wears a brocade sash," with the commentary noting:
"A *gṛhapati* is a practitioner of the Way or an *achu-shi* (recluse). II. Ānanda is Summoned 2-1. Walking Alone Without Provisions
Regarding the first of the two introductory sections on encountering [obstacles] while begging for food: it excludes Ānanda’s other travels;
rather, it concerns how Ānanda alone had previously accepted a separate invitation and, having traveled far and not yet returned, was unable to attend to the sequence of the Saṃgha.

This refers to having previously accepted a separate invitation (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*) or being engaged in other matters such that one is not observing the fast (*upoṣadha*). Changshui says: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that Ānanda did not accept separate invitations;
this likely means he did not follow the Buddha in accepting them. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies that there are two types of invitations for the Saṃgha:
namely, the sequential invitation (*saṃgha-paryāya-āmantraṇa*) and the separate invitation. Although the Vinaya permits separate invitations, in various texts...
He frequently criticized individual invitations and praised invitations by the monastic order’s turn. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"An individual invitation to the Buddha and five hundred arhats is not as meritorious as an invitation by the monastic order’s turn to even a single semblance of a bhikṣu who is extremely wicked. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Inviting the Sangha by the monastic order’s turn is like drinking seawater; one thereby drinks all the rivers. The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* also makes this statement. (2)
Mingdu returned alone without offerings.
Since there was neither an *upādhyāya* nor an *ācārya*, he returned home by himself that day without provisions.
"Up" (*shang*) refers to no one else being designated as an *upādhyāya*; *ācārya* is translated here as "preceptor" (*guifanshi*). According to the Vinaya regulations, monks must travel in groups.
A traveling party must consist of at least three people: one senior elder (sthavira) and one preceptor (ācārya). This is to ensure that conduct is dignified and to prevent errors or omissions.
Since there is currently no senior elder or ācārya, I am returning alone; as I have not been able to join the formal monastic procession, there is no offering.
This is the occasion for encountering those who obstruct one while begging for food. II. Encountering Obstructions While Begging for Food.
A. The Mental Application of the Beggar. 1. Applying Equal Compassion.
At that time, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl and went through the city he was visiting, begging from house to house in due order. From the very beginning, he sought within his mind...

Finally, the donor acts as the presiding host of the *śrāddha* feast. Without distinguishing between the pure and the impure, whether they be of the noble Kṣatriya caste or the lowly Caṇḍāla, one practices impartial compassion, making no selection among the humble or the base.
By thus resolving the mind, one brings to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.

Because alms were easily obtained at the first watch of the day, it is called "immediately. *Pātra* refers to the "receptacle for offerings," as its substance, color, and size all accord with the Dharma.
*Xunwen* states: "The Vinaya clarifies that there are essentially two types of *pātra* substances: clay and iron.
As for the color, it is to be blackened by fumigation, or red, or the color of a peacock’s throat, or the color of a pigeon, and so forth."
Regarding the measurements: the large bowl holds three *dou*; the small holds one and a half *dou*; the medium may be inferred accordingly.
Mount Nan said that this refers to the *dou* of the Western Zhou dynasty; according to the Tang *dou*, the upper bowl holds one *dou* and the lower holds five *sheng*.
"City" refers to Śrāvastī. "Dānapati" is translated here as "donor. In view of the preceding sequence of monks, this constitutes the very last. That is to say—
The middle section states: "The 'final donor' refers to one who provides the last meal for the Sangha.
Seeking out such a person is called the 'first seeking,' and this does not mean that Ānanda was the first to conceive this thought. Is Mātaṅgī not such a person?
Among those sought as *śrāddhadeva* (host of the feast), purity and impurity form a pair, and nobility and lowliness form a pair. A Kṣatriya king is of noble lineage."
Furthermore, "Caṇḍāla" refers to those of a low caste, meaning "killers. "Method" (fang-fa) means "rule" or "standard"; it signifies that the Tathāgata practices impartial compassion.
The term "lowly and base" (wei-jian) encompasses both the impure and the Caṇḍālas. Since it is said that he makes no distinctions, how could he fail to include Mātaṅga?
Because he desires to lead both the pure and the impure toward Bodhi, it is said that he "perfectly accomplishes the immeasurable."
Regarding merit: the practice of a Mahāsattva relies entirely upon their original vow.

That the Bhikṣuṇī Śīghra later attained the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and would surely return to the fruit of Buddhahood can also be said to have accomplished immeasurable merit. II. Respectfully Adhering to the Admonitions.
Ānanda already understood that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for having minds that were not impartial despite being arhats;
he now reverently looked up to the Tathāgata to expound the unobstructed Dharma and resolve all doubts and slanders.
Regarding the phrase "already known": Ānanda had not yet realized arhatship, yet he already knew that there were those who were partial toward arhats;
therefore, he looked up solely to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, because this was after the period of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras, it is said that he "already knew.

Subhūti abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor; one was for the sake of making giving easy for the rich, and the other was for the sake of the poor.
This refers to the planting of causes. The Tathāgata’s censure of this was to clarify the impartial and unobstructed compassion that transcends unequal suspicion and slander.
As for the phrase "reverently admiring," Ānanda was merely reverently admiring the Tathāgata’s supreme instruction.
Third, he solemnized his demeanor according to the Dharma.

Passing through the city moat, he proceeded slowly toward the outer gate, maintaining a dignified and orderly bearing with reverent gravity in accordance with the rules of the *zhāifǎ* (fasting ritual).
A moat is called a *huáng*; the *zhāifǎ* refers to the practice of begging for alms in a disciplined, orderly, and solemn sequence.
Furthermore, the *Piṇḍapāta Sūtra* clarifies that all worthies and sages enter the villages for the purpose of relieving the suffering of the poor.
At the time of begging for food, they should even maintain the perception of there being no city and the perception of there being no people.

Ānanda, having already perfected his majestic deportment and solemnly observed the rules of purification, these modes of mental application and conduct are all instances of being encompassed by [the practice]. II. 2.
Regarding the experience of being captured: once, while Ānanda was on his alms-round, he passed by a brothel.

There, he was seized by the great sorceress Mātangī, who used the *sāvikāra* mantra of the ancient Brahmā to draw him into her bedchamber. As she physically caressed him, he was on the verge of violating his precepts.
Changshui said: "The meaning of 'Mātanga' is translated as 'original nature' (*prakṛti*); this refers to the 'naturally ordained bhikṣuṇī' mentioned in the text below.
Gushan said: "The *Mātanga Sūtra* states that in five hundred past lives, Ānanda had been her husband;
because the habitual tendencies of their attachment had not yet been forgotten, this incident occurred. Zizhong said: "Śākyamuni is..."
The Immortal Golden Head was a non-Buddhist practitioner who ate from the center of rice grains. He served Brahmā and obtained this dhāraṇī. Youxi said:

"The essence of the precepts is precisely the essence of the unmanifest (avijñapti) precepts. This means that at the time of receiving the precepts—through the three 'whites' and four 'bindings'—the body and speech receive them while the mind does not diverge toward other objects.

Because of these actions, one attains the precepts and gives rise to the unmanifest precepts. As for 'unmanifest,' [it refers to the moral quality that continues to exist even when the manifest action has ceased]."

The essence of the precepts (śīla-ātman) exists eternally and is spontaneously accomplished; because it does not depend upon the physical or vocal acts of creation, it is called "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*).
As stated in the Commentary: "If it does not arise, that is that; if it arises, its nature is unmanifest and is a 'fictive color' (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*).

One must understand that when one violates the precepts, one is actually violating this very essence. The subsequent statement, "Because the mind is pure, one has not yet sunk into [suffering]," implies that even while on the verge of violation—
[End. The practitioner of the initial fruit has already severed sexual misconduct; because he does not enter the flow of desire, he does not sink into it.
II. The Tathāgata’s Compassionate Rescue: 1. Knowing in Secret while in the Palace.
The Tathāgata knew that he had been subjected to the arts of seduction.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "When the Buddha sought an attendant, his mind was fixed upon Ānanda, like the sun shining from the east onto a western wall.

How could he have remained unaware while being thus ensnared? The text refers here to Ānanda; the practice of using incantations to lead one into lust is termed "the arts of seduction" (*yinshu*). [End of] Obscure [passage].

Xī said: "The Tathāgata’s knowledge of the application of that licentious art clearly demonstrates the arising of the capacity within the Buddha-realm and the mutual resonance of the path of response.
The single word 'knows' is the Tathāgata’s wisdom that reflects capacities—tranquil yet ever-illuminating—and is the essence of unconditioned compassion.
2. Returning to the Garden to Expound the Dharma.

When the fast was concluded and they had returned, the king, along with the great ministers, elders, and lay devotees, all came to follow the Buddha, desiring to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, from the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, there issued forth a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness; from within this light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged.
There is a transformation body of the Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture, proclaiming a divine mantra.

It is the Tathāgata’s constant custom that upon receiving an invitation for a meal, he preaches the Dharma once the feast is concluded. Since he has now returned so quickly, there must surely be a special reason;
therefore, the king, his ministers, and the great assembly have followed him here. At such a time as this, one is on the verge of destroying the essence of the precepts.
At that time, his crown was the mark of the invisible crown (anavalokitamūrdhatā). The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Immediately upon birth, he was swiftly held up;
though observed closely, his crown could not be seen. Thus we know this crown is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, it does not merely manifest from the crown but radiates light;
it does not merely radiate light but surges forth as a thousand-petaled jewel lotus. Therefore, we know that the Buddha of the unconditioned mind is... [unconditioned].

The Supreme Honored One of Divine Mantras is the ultimate. Because he possesses every virtue, he is called "Hundred Treasures" (Śatadhāraṇī). Because he crushes every evil, he is called "Fearless" (Abhaya).
Because cause and effect are fully perfected, he manifests as a thousand-petaled precious lotus. Transformation Buddhas appear from his crown and sit upon the thousand-petaled precious lotus;
this is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya). Therefore, within this passage, all three bodies are fully present. Thus it is explained.
The *kāya* is the *nirmāṇakāya*; the crown is the *dharmakāya*. The manifestation of the Buddha upon the flower pedestal to preach the mantra is entirely the light of wisdom.

There is a specific reason for the special decree addressed to Mañjuśrī. Question: Since the Tathāgata already knew of the urgent distress, why did he not provide rescue within the royal palace, but instead wait until [the king] returned to the vihāra?
Answer: The Buddha knew that those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) do not commit wrongs.
"Indulgence in lust may be slightly relaxed for now. Furthermore, it would not be appropriate for Tāraka to be brought back to the royal palace while being exhorted and encouraged.
[The opponent] asks: 'Why did the Buddha not himself recite the mantra against Tāraka’s minor arts? Instead, he relied on an emanation Buddha and specifically dispatched the Greatly Wise Mañjuśrī.
What use is an ox-sword for such a trivial evil spell? [The Master] answers: 'It is because we have now encountered a rare opportunity.'"
Thus, he bestowed the inconceivable Dharma upon those who encountered such difficulties. Regarding this rare occurrence, the text states that she encountered the great illusionist Mātaṅgī;
how could it have been merely a minor art? Therefore, there are three wonders: first, that one of lowly status sought Prince Ānanda as her husband;
second, that she used the heterodox to gather the orthodox; and third, that she matched a worldling with a sage. [This refers to] the first fruit.

When the precept-body of a sage is about to be destroyed, how could there not be lingering attachments? This is truly because throughout five hundred lifetimes they have constantly been husband and wife;
their affection is already so deep that it cannot be a minor matter. The power of the Three Bodies cannot shatter the delusion of attachment to forms unless it is a response to unrighteousness.
Without the great wisdom of Mañjuśrī, one is unworthy to receive this command; how much more so in the case of lustful desire!
Obstructions are the root of birth and death. Now, by employing Ānanda as a catalyst, [the Buddha] rescues sentient beings of the final age;
this is what is called the inconceivable Dharma. According to the *Mātanga Sūtra*, it merely records the Tathāgata himself reciting a single mantra to dissolve that erotic spell.
Question: When others commit sexual misconduct, the Tathāgata does not necessarily rescue them immediately; why then does he rescue Ānanda now?

"How is it that there is such commotion? He replied, "The Dharma of the first fruit does not lead to falling into sexual misconduct; that the Buddha now provides salvation is precisely the proof of this.

In the final age, those who realize the first fruit experience a similar resonance. As for those who have not yet realized the stage of *srotāpanna*, they are originally ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
How can one blame the Tathāgata for his lack of response? If one is merely negligent and lacks self-restraint..."
They merely emerge from and submerge back into the ocean of birth and death. ○ Third, Mañjuśrī protects them and returns them.
The Buddha commands Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect them, so that the evil spell is extinguished; he then leads Ānanda and Mātanga back to the place where the Buddha is.
The emanated Buddha atop the crown (uṣṇīṣa) possesses a majestic and dignified form.
The divine mantra he proclaimed is such that even those of small wisdom cannot understand it, let alone go forth to save others. It is not that Mañjuśrī could not receive the command;

rather, Mañjuśrī secretly expounded the subtle interpretation of the evil mantra, and Ānanda did not hear it openly. Therefore, the subsequent text says [as follows]. "Tiewei" (提謂) means "to uplift" (提拔). "Jiang" (獎) means to encourage.
"Assistant" (*zhu*) means to lend assistance; it is also to borrow power. Regarding "those who return together with Dengga," as stated in the five titles of the sutra's preface:
"To rescue and protect his kinsmen and causes, and to deliver Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati.
Dengga not only left the household life but also realized the fruits of sainthood. As the subsequent text states: "The fire of lust suddenly ceased, and she attained the fruit of Anāgāmin."
This point is included herein, though it has not yet been specifically mentioned. When Mañjuśrī concluded his selection of the perfect organ of penetration, Ānanda became an Arhat.
According to the *Dengqie jing*, it was not stated that he gained benefit at the time of hearing the mantra;
rather, he sought out the Buddha himself and returned without being exhorted by Mañjuśrī. It was only upon hearing the Dharma exposition that he realized the fourth fruit. Thus, then—
In both sutras, one attains arhatship through hearing the Dharma; however, the capacities and perspectives of those in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ. An ancient commentary states:

"If we speak in terms of actual practice (*satya-pratipatti*), it refers to the time when the capacity has matured and one attains the Way; yet Ānanda subsequently draws them in with the hook of desire to lead them later into the Buddha-way.
If, however, they are of great transformative power (*mahopāya-kauśalya*), then they act together with Ānanda to initiate this teaching."
This concludes the Separate Preface, which serves to benefit those with various capacities.

The Main Body of the Teaching consists of two chapters. From "Ānanda’s Request for the Sublime Śamatha" up to "Inquiring about the Name of the Sūtra," this section establishes the general principle of ignorance through the mind, thereby clarifying cultivation and realization. From "Ānanda’s Question on the Seven [States of Mind]... [the second chapter begins].

Regarding the various destinies and births, one reaches the point of no longer longing for the triple world. This is explained in terms of cultivation and realization based on the specific mind that can attract retribution.
Generally speaking, for a practitioner, the most precious thing in their cultivation is first attaining its fundamental basis.

From the very moment a single thought fails to awaken, all sentient beings give rise to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), which obstructs original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*). Yet, even while being thus obstructed, the mind of original enlightenment itself remains immutable.

Following conditions, it becomes the single thought-moment of the *vijñāna-skandha*. That which is called the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) together with ignorance universally creating all manner of evils is termed "defilement.
This results in the manifestation of active conduct and the production of karmic retributions as secondary branches.

Yet one does not know that although the substance of this single thought-moment of the *vijñāna-skandha* is illusory, it is nonetheless the true and eternal. As the Sūtra says: "All floating dust and various illusions..."
The manifestations arise at their respective locations and perish at those very locations; their nature is truly the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true Suchness-nature.
Furthermore, it is said: "That which causes you to transmigrate through birth and death—the root of these fetters—is none other than your six sense faculties;
that which brings you ultimate peace, bliss, and wondrous permanence is likewise your six sense faculties and nothing else. Know this.
To perceive that which is established as "knowing" is the very root of ignorance (*avidyā*). To know that seeing is itself non-seeing is *nirvāṇa*. Through delusion and falsehood there is ignorance;
through the manifestation of clarity there is liberation. Therefore, it is sufficient simply to observe this mind of universal ignorance;

then, of its own accord, the false will depart and the true will manifest. When defilement is exhausted, clarity arises. This is the essential path for treating illness by cauterizing the correct point, or for felling the branches by cutting the root.

Now, the Tathāgata opens his mouth to interrogate this very mind; he does so precisely to provide the sublime teaching for observing and shattering this single thought-moment of the *skandha*-mind so that the true mind may manifest of itself.

The present school’s selection of the object and cultivation of contemplation—observing the single thought-moment before one to reveal the inconceivable and wondrous realm—is entirely in accord with the fundamental intent of the Master [Zhiyi].
As for the subsequent sections on the seven destinies and the five *skandhas*, these are the five...

The five consciousnesses, the three mental factors of sensation, perception, and formations, and their active manifestations—whether they arise within meditative concentration or not—are capable of inviting retribution;
these are all secondary afflictions associated with the branches and subordinates.
Therefore, by briefly distinguishing and weighing these, one prevents the practitioner from becoming attached, thereby revealing the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha.
As stated in the Great Outline (*Dagang*), this [section] now consists of two chapters: first, the formal exposition of cultivation and realization;

second, the conclusion that reveals the title of the sutra. Within the first chapter, there are three major sections: first, opening up the perfect understanding by means of refutation and manifestation;

second, demonstrating the primary and auxiliary practices to cultivate perfect conduct; third, clarifying delusion and awakening to realize the perfect stages. Within the first section, "Opening the Understanding," there is one pair concerning the Arhat...

The first section explains the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) by means of the difficult-to-pair sequence and non-sequence; the second section further examines the removal of subtle afflictions in response to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The first [section] is further divided into three parts: first, Ānanda’s repentance and request.
Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief. He lamented that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning without fully perfecting his power of the Way.
With earnest sincerity, he entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* through which they attained Bodhi.
Regarding the initial expedient means:
Ānanda, as a person who upholds the Dharma-treasury, manifested signs of being constantly harassed by Māra. His solitary weeping arose from grief born of self-reproach.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In the past, in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja, he together with the Tathāgata..."

The Buddha attained Bodhi because he was constantly diligent and energetic. Ānanda, though he always delighted in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

Based on this, it is evident that he has consistently been devoted to extensive learning since beginningless time. At this point, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, his true origins (*yiqie*) had not yet been revealed.
Yet, how could one who occupies a noble stage (*ārya-avasthā*) fail to know their own habitual tendencies from many lifetimes? This is the Way.
"Essence" refers to the substance; "power" refers to the function. Only after there is the Way is there power; only after there is the essence is there function.
Since he had already reproached himself for his extensive learning and meager wisdom, he proceeded to describe his earnest entreaties and so forth.
