It means that the clarity of external seeing is itself the obscurity of internal correspondence. Nevertheless, the phrase "external seeing" may also signify the obscurity of external seeing;

by setting aside this external obscurity and adopting the obscurity that faces one through reflexive observation, it is said to be "accomplished by internal correspondence. This is another path for supplementation. ○
2. Refuting the internal correspondence. 2.1. The actual refutation:

When the eyes are closed and one sees darkness, this is called being "within the body. When the eyes are open and one sees light, why does one not see one's own face? If one does not see one's face, the theory of internal correspondence is not established.
Closing the eyes and looking into the body is also a form of mental calculation. Opening the eyes and looking down corresponds to destroying the external to penetrate the internal.
Since closing the eyes enables one to reflect back upon the body within, one escapes the previous charge of not seeing the "burning palace" (the internal organs).

Now, according to this principle, when opening the eyes, one should likewise reflect back upon one's own face; therefore, it is asked: why do you not see your face? If, upon opening the eyes, one cannot reflect back...
If one observes one's own face, the principle of internal reflection cannot be established; and if the eyes are closed, how could one possibly turn back to observe within the body?
(2) Second, the refutation by concession:
If seeing the face were established, then this cognizing mind and the eye-faculty would reside in empty space; how then could they be said to be "within"?
If it were located in empty space, then since that space is not your own body, the Tathāgata seeing your face now would also be your body.
Your eyes already perceive this; therefore, your body should lack sensation. If you insist that both body and eyes perceive, then there ought to be two distinct cognitions.
Then your single body would have to become two Buddhas.
This passage contains three layers of hypothetical arguments (*yuanji*). The first layer refutes [the opponent's view] by taking it for granted:

"If the 'seeing the face' were established, then let us grant that the principle of 'seeing the face' is established. Since Ānanda maintains that the nature of seeing is present as soon as the eyes are opened...
If the external object is the original source of the eye’s light, which can exist externally and yet turn back to look inward, it must necessarily constitute the potential for seeing.
To refute this: if that were so, then both the mind and the eye would both reside in empty space. For the eye does not know, and the mental faculty (manas) does not see;
only when these two combine can seeing occur. Now, if both are in empty space, how could such a thing be possible?
Indeed. Not only does this [position] not exist, but Ānanda’s frequent assumption that the mind is located within also falls into error.
Next, regarding the section "If it were in empty space," the self and the other are refuted. Since Ānanda perceives the nature of seeing as being external, he can also look back [at himself].
Furthermore, there is the implication that the mind and eyes would be situated within space; therefore, the refutation is now turned toward its location in space. This assumption has three parts.

A further refutation: First, if [the mind] were in space, it would not be your own substance. Second, since you have no body, the face of the Tathāgata that you now see would, conversely, be your own body.
Third, if both your eyes and the conscious mind were outside the body, how could the body still possess sensation?
These three points together refute the second position—that the eyes and mind are in space.

This is a further argument. [I shall] necessarily refute both of your two perceptions. If you insist on establishing the principle that one turns back to observe external seeing, what harm is there in maintaining the two perceptions of body and eye? Therefore, I shall refute them together.

That is to say, if you maintain that the perception of the eye perceives light and darkness while mental cognition arises attached to the visual ray, and the perception of the body perceives pain and itch while mental cognition...

Furthermore, since it also arises from the contact of the body and touch, it is called "two perceptions" or "two cognitions. Thus, it is evident that a single body would necessarily become two Buddhas.
Reaching this point, the [opponent's] calculations are utterly destroyed and exhausted. This concludes the refutation. ○ Third, the conclusion of the refutation.
Those who have traditionally interpreted this all claim that closing one's eyes to see within constitutes the fallacy of asserting that the mind exists internally;
therefore, [the text] uniquely refutes this. However, the intended meaning within this passage, based on the explicit wording, is simply to refute the notion of darkness as an internal object.
Therefore, you should know this: your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal" is untenable.
Just as opening one's eyes to see the external prevents one from looking back [within], so too, closing one's eyes to see darkness does not constitute seeing the internal.
This merely refutes the notion of "seeing the internal," while the text incidentally refutes "seeing the external," as in the case where the mind-organ is said to reside in space. ○ Five: Refutation.
Accordingly, he established a calculation based on the Three-in-One.
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise;
and because dharmas arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now contemplate, this very essence of contemplation is my own true mind-nature. Following this...
Wherever there is a conjunction, the mind exists accordingly; yet it is not located in any of the three places—internal, external, or in between.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"When the mind arises, phenomena arise; the objective realm originates from the mind. When phenomena arise, the mind arises;
the mind follows the shifting of the objective realm. 即中 (Jizhong) says: "Since the four previous positions have already been exhausted through refutation, we now turn to investigate the mind."
Regarding the source of arising: the reason for citing the words of the "Exposition" (Kāśyapaparivarta) is that all phenomena (*dharmas*) originally do not exist, but exist because of the mind;
the mind also originally does not exist, but exists because of phenomena. This is the intended meaning of the cited passage. Although two phrases are cited, the emphasis lies on the latter phrase:
"the arising of phenomena and the arising of the mind," as well as the two characters "various" (*nānāvidha*). As for "I now," etc., this is the definitive [conclusion].

One contemplates this mind. This was likely Ānanda’s original intention; in the preceding text, "seeing" (*darśana*) was frequently identified as the mind, whereas here it specifically expresses that the mind is merely this mind itself.
Regarding the statement that it "conjoins with whatever it follows": if one binds the mind within the body, it conjoins with the internal;
if one directs the mind a thousand *li* away, it conjoins with the external. Because it does not remain fixed in a single location, it is said to be "not internal."
"External" and "intermediate. In reality, these encompass all three locations. "Intermediate" refers to the hidden root. 2. The Buddha Refutes the Two [Positions] A.
Restating the Adherence:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Now you say that because of dharmas, various minds arise, according to the place with which they correspond."
Regarding "the mind follows existence":
Ānanda wished to calculate that the arising of dharmas is the arising of the mind; therefore, he cited both phrases together. This is because the Buddha frequently makes such statements.
In reality, however, the calculation is based solely on the latter phrase; thus, when the Buddha refutes him, he cites only that latter phrase.
II. The Proper Refutation, in two parts: A. Directly clarifying that there is no substance.

If this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it could conjoin. If it were possible for something to conjoin while lacking substance, then the nineteen realms would conjoin with the seven objects; this principle is not tenable.

Since the mind exists only through conjunction with objects, it would seem that the substance of the mind did not previously exist and only comes into being through such conjunction. Therefore, the following refutation is now stated:
If the mind has no substantial nature, then this conjunction itself does not exist. This is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*).

If a mind lacking a substantial nature could conjoin with objects, then by analogy, the nineteen realms (*dhātu*) should conjoin with the seven sense-objects (*viṣaya*). Yet, the realms are limited to ten.
8. Now, regarding the statement that there are nineteen: this is by adding a seventh object, which lacks substantiality, to form the nineteen realms.
Since there is no object that lacks substantiality, how could there be a mind that lacks substantiality? The *Buyi* (Supplement) says:
"Just as fire in the world possesses its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), it subsequently relies upon the magnifying lens (*ādityakānta*) as a condition to become manifest."

It emits flames. If one says that the mind itself has no intrinsic substance and can only combine with conditions, this would be like fire having no intrinsic substance and only combining with a sunstone (*sūryakānta*).
2. A detailed refutation of the existence of intrinsic substance: 2-1. Refutation by means of the internal and external, and entering and exiting:
2-1-1. The refutation.
If it possesses a physical substance, then as you now strike your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within or enter from without?
If it emerges from within, it should see what is inside the body; if it comes from without, it should first see your face.

Since the non-existence [of the self] has already been refuted, one will inevitably reckon that it possesses existence; therefore, the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) are used to refute the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).

This clarifies that the mind comes from nowhere. *Zhi* (挃) is pronounced *zhi*; the ancient commentary states that *zhi* means "to touch. ○ Second, the rescue [of the opponent's position], which is further divided into two parts.
First, the rescue.
Ānanda said: "I see with my eyes, but the mind knows; it is not the eyes that see. This would mean that seeing is not the function of the mind.
Yet, from the very beginning of the inquiry, the Buddha has treated seeing as the mind. Ānanda, for his part, has temporarily conformed to the Buddha’s words.
However, according to what Ānanda previously stated—that "by personally beholding the Tathāgata’s sublime marks, a heart of love and joy arose"—then...
How could Ānanda’s original intention have been to take seeing as the mind?

Therefore, he now challenges the Tathāgata in reverse, asserting that seeing belongs to the faculty of sight and can only know [objects], whereas the mind is not the eye; thus, his claim that it performs seeing is logically untenable.
This question had not arisen previously; it emerges here for the first time as Ānanda’s underlying intent, which is the very root of his affliction.
2. Refutation.
The Buddha said: "If the eye were able to see, would you be able to see while inside a room through the door?
In that case, all those who have already died and still possess eyes should be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"
The first phrase restates your position. You will explain the difficulty below. The Buddha said to you: "The eye can see, but the mind cannot see.
For example, when you are inside a room, you must see what is outside; this is only possible after the door has been opened."

The eye is merely like a door, while the mind is like the person. It is because the mind relies on the opening of the eye that it is able to see, just as a person relies on the opening of a door to see what is outside the room.
If one were to claim that the eye sees while the mind does not, could one then say that the door sees while the person does not?
Therefore, by this analogy, although the door provides access for seeing, there must necessarily be a person within the room.

Only then does one see; thus, it is the person who sees, not the gate. In the analogy provided, although the eye has the capacity for vision, seeing necessarily occurs only when there is a mind within the eye;
thus, it is the mind that sees, not the eye. Regarding the further citation of the example of the deceased, Wēnlíng says:
"Citing the gate as a metaphor clarifies that the capacity to see resides in the mind; citing the dead makes clear that [the senses] are merely..."
"It is not seen by the eye; this statement is correct. Since it is the mind that sees at the time of birth and not the eye, after death the eye alone is useless for seeing.
Even if one were to see [with the eyes], this would further be refuted. Such clear texts all state that the mental consciousness is primary."

This refutes [the opponent's view] to reveal that there is only mind (*cittamātra*). The sense organs (*indriya*) are merely like gates; entering and exiting through these gates is simply a skillful means (*upāya*).

Why then do those who cling to [external objects] claim that it is the organs that function, rather than consciousness? 2. Refutation based on the one and the many, and the pervasive and the localized. 2.1. Refutation regarding the determination of the one.
Ānanda, furthermore, if this mind of yours that is capable of awakening and cognizing must have a substantial body, does it consist of a single entity or of many entities?
Is it currently located within your body, or does it pervade the entire body? Or does it not pervade the body?
In this context, pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness appear as if they were distinguished from within a single entity.
Here, "single entity" and "multiple entities" refer to the mind as the substance; "pervasive" and "non-pervasive" refer to the body as the substance.
When encountering an object, does the cognition pervade the entire body, or does it reside in only one place such that cognition cannot be pervasive? ○ Second, the refutation.
If [the body] were a single entity, then when you touch one limb with your hand, all four limbs should feel it. If they all felt it, there would be no specific location for the touch;
yet if the touch has a specific location, your "single entity" cannot be established. If [the body] were multiple entities, then you would become many people—of which entity would you be?
If [the body] were pervasive throughout all parts, it would be the same as the case of being touched previously. If it were not pervasive, [it would be fragmented].
"When you touch your head and also touch your feet, if the head has sensation, the feet should be without consciousness.

Yet this is not the case for you. This passage is divided into four parts; the first refutes the theory of a single substance. The first phrase restates the position, while the section beginning with "Then you" presents the objection.

If you were a single substance yet possessed two distinct perceptions, you would not be a single substance. To have both perception and non-perception constitutes two distinct characteristics; therefore, the objection is raised.
The four limbs should be perceived as a single entity; this is the characteristic of their unified nature.

If you were to establish the lower [position] and refute it, and if you were to say that one perceives both pain and itch simultaneously, then it would be like wanting to strike your head but striking your feet instead, or wanting to strike your left side but striking your right—does such a principle exist?
To "prick" (or touch) should mean there is no fixed location, implying it is not restricted to a single limb. If one pricks the lower [limb], [the sensation is felt elsewhere].

Refutation of the Composite: If [the object] has a fixed location, it necessarily constitutes two cognitions—one of conjunction and one of disjunction—which means they possess two distinct characteristics and are not a single entity.
Second, refuting the multiple entities: Since the unity of the entity has been refuted, one might alternatively argue that cognition possesses multiple entities.

However, if a single person possesses only one cognition, then having multiple cognitions would entail being multiple persons. Within this, there must be a distinction between self and other; by which cognition...?
Is it the whole body that constitutes "you"? Third, the refutation of the pervasive whole: "Pervasive" means that sentience pervades the entire body;
when one limb is pricked, [the sensation] should pervade all parts where there is sentience. This is identical in meaning to the previous point regarding the four limbs being capable of sensation.
Although the wording of the objection is the same, the intended meaning differs. "A single body" means the absence of two distinct forms; as for "a pervasive body,"...
Awareness pervades all locations. There are four ways in which it would fail to do so. "Failing to pervade" means that awareness does not extend throughout the entire body.
If you maintain that the mind does not pervade [the body], then when both the head and the feet are touched, since one part has awareness, the other part should be devoid of cognition.
Now, if this is not your position—that is, if both parts are touched and both have awareness—then it is not the case that awareness fails to pervade. ○ Third, the conclusion of the refutation.
Therefore, one should know this: it is impossible for the mind to exist wherever it is joined with something.
As stated above, since the existence of a substantial entity is untenable, its non-existence is likewise erroneous.
If the mind itself cannot even be established, how can one speak of its existence following whatever it is joined with? 6. Refuting the Intermediate [State], Part One: Establishing the Hypothesis.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have also heard the World-Honored One conversing with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One also said: 'The mind is neither within nor without.

As I contemplate this, there is nothing seen within, and there is no mutual cognition without. Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established. [Yet] body and mind cognize one another..."
The external is not the object. Since they are now perceived as mutually cognizant, yet there is no seeing within, it must be in between.
This calculation arises from the fifth [position]. Because the previous Buddha, in refuting the existence of a substantial entity, said:

"If it were emitted from within, one would see what is inside the body; if it came from without, one should first see the face. Since both the internal and external have been refuted, he again calculates [it to be in between].
This is the intermediate section. Within it, the initial passage concerning the Buddha’s discourse with Mañjuśrī on the true reality (*dharmatā*) is as follows:

True reality is precisely the mind. The mind does not exist within, for it is not among the six internal sense organs (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātma-indriya*); nor does it exist without, for it is not among the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhya-viṣaya*).

This is the meaning of true reality being detached from both the organs and the objects. Ānanda did not understand this and again gave rise to erroneous attachments. This section consists of three parts.
First, he raises the previous refutation: "Internally there is nothing seen" means that if [the self] were inside, it would not be the case that there is nothing seen.

"Externally they do not know one another" means that if [the self] were outside, they should not know one another. Next, he clarifies that [the self] cannot be established as either internal or external;
the three directions then calculate it to be in between. That he does not immediately settle upon this reflects his state of hesitation. Question: Above, Ānanda said—
"Furthermore, it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. Why then do you now again calculate it as being in between? Answer:
"The 'in between' mentioned above was defined as the hidden root (*mūla*) serving as the center; this differs from the present case.

Now, having been subjected to repeated refutations, one is compelled to cite the statement that [the self] is neither internal nor external as an analogy. Since it is certainly not in the internal or external, yet..."
It abides in the middle. This "middle" actually possesses roots and objects as its two extremes, which reflect and manifest the characteristic of the middle;
it is thus different from the "middle" mentioned previously. II. The Buddha’s Refutation of the Two: A. Refuting by means of the body and location; B. Determining through analysis.
The Buddha said: "You say that within the 'middle' one must certainly not be deluded, and that it is not without a location. Now, as you investigate this 'middle,' where does it reside?
Does it reside in space, or does it reside in the body?"
"One who is certainly not deluded within" means that if one were deluded, one would not know where it is; if one is not deluded, it is not that there is no location.

"Delusion" refers to confusion. "Location" refers to the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*). "Body" refers to the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*). 2. Refuting [the notion of the mind] by logical analysis. 2-1. Refuting [the idea that the mind] resides in the body.
If it were located within the body, then being at the periphery would not be "within," and being in the center would be identical to being "inside.

All visible parts of the body are at the periphery and not in the center; "being in the center would be identical to being inside" refers to the prior assumption that the mind is located within. 2. Refuting its location.

If it exists in a location, is it something that can be indicated, or is it something that cannot be indicated? That which is unindicated is the same as non-existence; that which is indicated lacks fixity.
Why is this so? For example, when a person uses a marker to designate the center, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north.
Since the substance of the marker is thus shifting, the mind should likewise be in a state of confusion.
An indicator (*saṃketa*) is like setting up a staff to mark a location. Since the great earth is so vast and expansive, what could serve as its center?

Therefore, in the absence of an indicator, it would be equivalent to having no center at all. Regarding indicators: first, [the text] refutes the existence of indicators; second, it provides an explanation.

If a person stands to the east of an indicator, they take that indicator to be the west; if a person stands to the south of an indicator, they take that indicator to be the north. Thus, the four directions of an indicator...
Since the directions are already conflated, taking the mind as being "in the middle" also allows it to be said to be "on the edge"; thus, there is confusion.
○ Second, refuting [the position] by means of the sense organs and their objects, in two parts: (1) the rebuttal.
Ānanda said: "What I have spoken does not fall into either of these two categories. As the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
When the eye possesses discrimination and the object of form is present, consciousness arises within them; this is what constitutes the mind being present."
The eye is simply the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Visible form (*rūpa*) is the object (*viṣaya*) of the eye.

If there is an eye but no visible form, consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not arise; if there is visible form but no eye, consciousness likewise does not arise. When these two factors combine, they serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness, and thus visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is produced.
As for the statement that "the eye possesses discrimination," it means that the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is able to induce the arising of visual consciousness.
Because there is subsequent conceptualization (*anusmaranavikalpa*) at the time when visual consciousness arises, it is said that "the eye possesses conceptualization.
This refers to the fact that [the eye] is "possessing conceptualization" because it can give rise to conceptualization. However, visible form (*rūpa*) is ultimately devoid of cognition.

Since the arising of visual consciousness occurs within this state of being both with and without cognition, it incurs the objection of confusion below. Furthermore, in all four preceding positions, [the cause] exists prior [to the effect].

Regarding "mind-consciousness" (*citta-vijñāna*): both the *Pañcavastuka* and the *Ṣaḍvastuka* treatises discuss the arising of the mind. Since they discuss the locus from the perspective of its arising, it is said that "consciousness arises therein," which implies that the mind is present there. ○ Second, the refutation.
The Buddha said: "If your mind were located between the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not encompass both?

If it encompassed both, the entities of the objects and the nature of the mind would be intermingled; since the object is not the knowing nature, they would stand as two opposing entities—how could this be called the 'Middle'?
If it does not encompass both, then being neither knowing nor non-knowing, it would lack any essential nature; what characteristic could there be for the 'Middle'?"
In this passage, there is first an establishment [of the position] and then a refutation. Within the refutation, there is first a refutation of that which combines both [aspects].

However, in the preceding establishment, it was stated that "the substance of this mind" refers to mental cognition (*citta-jñāna*) as its substance; whereas in the refutation, it is stated that "the substance of objects is confused," referring instead to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) as the substance.
Here, "objects" (*wu*) refers to sensory fields (*viṣaya*). This is because Ānanda maintains that the eye possesses discrimination; therefore, for the time being, we proceed from this perspective.

Grasp [the opponent's position] and refute it. Words that are appropriate to the occasion need not be held as fixed dogmas. One should know that the difficulty of this statement lies in the confusion of entities:
namely, that a single consciousness simultaneously encompasses both the sense faculty and the object. The object is the "entity" (vastu) and the faculty is the "substance" (ātman);
these two would thus become confused within a single consciousness. The phrase "The entity is not the substance-cognition" below refutes the impossibility of such a synthesis.
That external objects lack sentience while the sense organs possess sentience constitutes a state of opposition; they are established in relation to one another as opposing phenomena.
There is no further possibility of reconciling them into a single principle. How, then, could this be the "Middle"? This refutes the view that [the self] encompasses both.

To say it is "not sentient" below [the head] refutes the view that it does not encompass [both]. If it does not encompass the sense organs, it is not sentient; if it does not encompass the sense objects, it is not [sentient].

[He] did not know. Generally speaking, that which is called "the Middle" must possess a nature that transcends both [extremes]. Now, if this mental consciousness were to be separated from the sense organs and their objects, it would have no further essential nature.
Where, then, would the Middle be? ○ Third, the conclusion and refutation.
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for [the self] to exist in the interval;
whether it possesses both [aspects] or lacks both, since both meanings fail to be established, it is clear that the theory of its existence in the interval cannot be maintained.
7. Refuting the Non-attached One (Aśaikṣa): Part 1—Establishing the Theory.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma.
He constantly spoke of how the nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location whatsoever and is entirely unattached."
It is called "mind. Now, do I not have that which is called "non-attachment" as my mind?
The six preceding calculations, having all had a locus, were thoroughly pursued and refuted. Ānanda, having no other recourse, calculated non-attachment.
The citation of the Buddha turning the wheel of Dharma together with his four great disciples refers to the meaning of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-naya). However...

Because there is both a general and a specific meaning, it is called "the nature of the mind" (*cittatā*). This means that within the process of awakening, cognition, and discrimination, this nature of the mind exists.
It does not reside in the internal or external, as explained in the preceding text; "in between" should be understood as referring to the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
Since it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between, it is entirely free from attachment—this is the Buddha’s word. Yet Ānanda still [clings] to non-attachment to the internal.

Because one further forms attachments to the external, the internal, and the intermediate, these must be demolished. Lektan said: "Since it is neither internal, external, nor intermediate, one knows that the mind has nothing to which it attaches.
Yet he did not realize that the Buddha’s intent was to demolish the delusion—which has no substance—in order to cause one to recognize the original reality.
As it is said: "When sought throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found; because the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent."
The non-existence of the deluded mind is itself bodhi; birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal.
Failing to understand this meaning, one erroneously cites the Buddha’s words to falsely establish "non-attachment. II. The Buddha refutes this.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Regarding your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location whatsoever—consider that all things in the world, including empty space, water, land, and all flying creatures, as well as all material phenomena, are called 'everything. If you do not cling to them, does this [nature] exist or does it not exist?"
If it were non-existent, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could there be non-attachment? That which is non-attached cannot be called non-existent.
If it lacks characteristics, it is non-existent; if it is not non-existent, it possesses characteristics. If characteristics exist, then it is present; how then can there be non-attachment?
Ānanda’s false calculation arises from the non-attachment to all things; therefore, the Buddha takes up this single phrase to refute it.
Within this, he first examines the essence of non-attachment, and subsequently, with the words "If there are characteristics," etc., he concludes by rebuking what is not true non-attachment.
"Regarding all existing phenomena—whether in space, water, or on land—Ānanda reckons these as truly existent. You say that you do not cling to these phenomena;
do you mean that there is a truly existent 'non-clinging mind' that merely does not become obstructed by objective forms?
Or do you mean that even this non-clinging mind does not exist? This sentence poses two questions simultaneously. Below [the text] provides the direct answer."

Yan said: "If there were simultaneously no mind that does not cling, then the mind would be like a tortoise’s hair—having a name but no substance—and it would not even be necessary to speak of 'non-clinging.
Ānanda said that one who does not cling must necessarily possess a mind that does not cling;
this is precisely having a mind, not being without a mind. Below the section on "formlessness," he again uses the distinction between form and formlessness to further explain the preceding sentence.

Because the characteristics of existence and non-existence have not yet been discussed above, they are now definitively established. Once existence has been established, the refutation follows immediately.
One should understand that Ānanda actually harbored the conceited notion within his mind that there is a mind, yet he forcefully claimed it was non-attached; therefore, he was refuted by the Buddha.

Thus, that which is refuted is a counterfeit Asaṅga and not the true Asaṅga. The subsequent passage stating, "This is impossible," likewise refers only to the impossibility of Ānanda’s own conceptualization.
If one were to refute the statement regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma as well, it would be like stopping for a throat-ache and abandoning all food.
Question: An ancient commentary states: "Is it existent or non-existent? You ask whether the mind is unattached, yet that..."
Are phenomenal objects existent, or are they non-existent? Why does the present [interpretation] differ from the ancient commentary? Answer: The ancient explanation states:

"If those phenomenal objects were empty and non-existent, they would be the same as a tortoise’s hair. Consider this: water, land, and space encompass the *niśraya-vipāka* (the objective environment);
the classes of flying beings encompass the *mukhya-vipāka* (the subjective sentient beings). Thus, it is said that if my mind does not cling [to them], they are the same as a tortoise’s hair.
Because the meaning of "rabbit horns" is likely untenable, I now provide this explanation. III. Conclusion of the Refutation:
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for a mind of awakening to perceive anything called "all things" as being without attachment.

The preceding seven rounds of tracing the deluded mind to its limit so that it has no place for attachment may indeed be called the "initial expedient" (*ādikāra-upāya*), which is the gateway for initiating contemplation within *samādhi*.
Within the ten stages of the contemplative method (*daśa-yāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā-dharmāḥ*), the first stage—discerning and indicating the object of contemplation—states:
"Discard the fathom and take up the cubit; discard the cubit and take up the inch; set aside the four aggregates of form and so forth."
One contemplates only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This aggregate of consciousness is precisely the mind (*citta*). This point is identical to the present text.

In that *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* text, because the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) are first eliminated, it is likened to discarding the *zhang* to focus on the *chi*. Within the five aggregates, one further eliminates the four aggregates and takes up only the aggregate of consciousness;
thus, it is likened to discarding the *chi* to focus on the *cun*. The *Fuxing* commentary states: "One directly contemplates the mind."

The meaning is that one should contemplate the King [of Consciousness]. Zhiyi’s *Sijiao yi* states: "To take the contemplating subject as the object of contemplation makes it easy to sever discursive thought.
This is precisely that intent. One must know that within the exposition of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, two levels of the object of contemplation are clarified:

first, taking the sixth consciousness-mind as the object, which refers to the passage on "discerning the object"; second, contemplating the inconceivable realm, which is a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*).
The "three thousand" refers to this. By contemplating the six consciousnesses, the mind, and the will, one reveals the inconceivable realm. Thus, Gushan said:

"By contemplating the deluded mind of a single thought-moment, one reveals the true principle of the three truths. The deluded mind constitutes the first layer; the true mind constitutes the second layer.
Although these two layers are established, if one contemplates them without ceasing, the realm of the aggregates (*skandhas*) is transformed into the [true] reality."
This is the realm of contemplation. This present sutra is likewise so. In the first seven sections, the inquiry exhaustively pursues the deluded mind as its object.
Later texts state: "All dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind; all causes and effects, the worlds, and even the finest motes of dust, take the mind as the substance of their existence.
It further states: "Your body and your mind are both things within the wondrously luminous true mind. Furthermore...
It is said: "If one can turn back the objects [of perception], one is identical to the Tathāgata; from the tip of a single hair, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
Is this not the teaching that the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-trisāhasra*) constitutes the object of contemplation?

Furthermore, in the third fascicle, it says: "The nature-consciousness within the Tathāgatagarbha is luminous knowledge; the true consciousness is the awareness of luminosity. Thus, one contemplates the six consciousnesses to establish the inconceivable object of contemplation.
This is undoubtedly so. Thus, the first three fascicles of the present sutra primarily elucidate the first of the ten vehicles: the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
At the end of these three fascicles, Ānanda and the great assembly speak verses in praise of the Buddha, saying:
"As long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter *nirvāṇa* here. This constitutes the second [vehicle]: the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta.

"Requesting entry into the magnificent hall" is the third skillful method for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Among the ten vehicles of contemplation, the first three are the most essential; therefore, they are briefly correlated here.

The fourth, "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas," pertains to the time of realizing the fruit. The twenty-five perfect penetrations (*pañcaviṃśati-vyūha-samyak-prativedha*) are precisely this pervasive destruction.
As for the fifth, "Discerning Penetration and Obstruction," it is merely a supplementary point to the pervasive destruction. This is the current [topic].

When it passes through the faculty of hearing, it is unobstructed; when it passes through other faculties, it is obstructed. The sixth [practice], the "Aids to Opening" (*pratipakṣa*), can be correlated with the construction of altars and the recitation of mantras.

The seventh, the "Adaptation of the Factors of Enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), is derived solely from the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). One should discern the sequence of these stages.

"Able to endure" and "free from attachment to dharmas" properly belong to the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). This is because only through being able to endure and being able to detach can one attain entry into the stage of perfection.

This concerns the method of cultivation and realization throughout the beginning and end of the ten sublime contemplations (*daśa-yāna-mahā-vipaśyanā*) regarding the mental activity of universal ignorance.

As for the demons of the five destinies and the five aggregates, these are the retributive minds consisting of the five sense-consciousnesses and the fifth consciousness (the manovijñāna). Furthermore—
One should practice and realize this through the ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dharma*).

Only when each and every aspect becomes the inconceivable realm of "one thought-moment containing the three thousand worlds" (*ekacitta-trisahasra-lokadhātu*) will the two layers of the object of contemplation be revealed; contemplating consciousness as such is itself the realization of the True.

Indeed, these two layers of the object of contemplation and the ten modes of contemplation accord with the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Yet some claim that Tiantai masters contemplate exclusively [the first layer].

Regarding the six consciousnesses: it is not necessarily the case that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* employs exclusively the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Tiaoxi says: "Taken together, these seven sections seem to refute the four modes of being (*catur-koṭi*).
If the four modes of being have not been refuted, this cognizing mind is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not ultimate truth (*satya*).

Only after the four modes of being have been refuted is it called conventional truth. Conventional truth is provisional and still persists within appearances; only when these appearances are refuted..."
It is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) and is also termed the "Truth of the Primary Meaning. Thus, the Great Master Zhizhe said:

"The Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refutes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while the Ultimate Truth refutes the provisional (*prajñapti*). When the provisional is refuted, it is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); when intrinsic nature is refuted, it is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

In the present text, the sevenfold interrogation refutes intrinsic nature, whereas the single shout refutes characteristics through the Ultimate Truth. As it says in the *Mohe Zhiguan*: "The beginner contemplates that provisional names are empty."

The preceding "provisional" (jia) is what the sutras call *samādhi*. At that time, the three truths had not yet been revealed; because one was merely observing that all phenomena are unreal, it was called "provisional.
How could it be said that the deluded mind is substantially real, given that the present text employs seven successive refutations?
It simply belongs to the nature of emptiness. As in the passage below, the Tathāgata’s single shout causes the speech and thought of the recipient to be severed.

Only when the deluded mind is entirely empty does one enter the True Truth (*satyadharma*). This manifestation of the True Truth is named *śamatha*, which is the entry from the provisional into emptiness.
For those of sharp faculties, by contemplating the provisional prior to emptiness, they immediately awaken to the Three Truths. Therefore it is said:
"There is a *samādhi* called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices. As for those of dull faculties...

Since the ultimate truth has not yet been revealed here, this belongs merely to the provisional stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, the subsequent text further requests instruction on the path of *śamatha*.

Whether the progression of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) succeeds or fails depends upon this source. Question: When one investigates through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), is this *śamatha* or *vipaśyanā*? Answer: [It is both.]
Speaking generally, this should belong to *zhi* (stopping). In the *Fuxing* commentary, while explaining the essence of *zhizhiguan* (True Stopping), it says:
"According to the text’s interpretation, the explanation is still brief. Fully [explained], one should investigate and examine by means of four propositions;

only after destroying both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*) and being fully endowed with the two kinds of emptiness can it be called 'empty. Based on this text, it should belong to *zhi*. However, when the *Fuxing* explains the Great Vows..."
In the middle [section], one uses the four lines of reasoning to investigate the two kinds of emptiness—of nature and characteristics—as the wisdom that performs contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

It should be understood that, in relation to the principle of the truth as the mind comes to rest, it is called "stopping" (*śamatha*); in relation to the capacity for clear illumination, it is called "contemplation. Second, revealing the truth by means of *śamatha*.

Although previously the delusion was refuted as if merely using conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one had not yet used ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to refute characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This subsequent "shouting" refutation of the deluded mind—how could this not be the refutation of characteristics as being emptiness? Nevertheless, both the Perfect (*yuan*) and Distinct (*bie*) teachings clarify this:

in the Perfect teaching, the three truths are present within a single moment of mind; in the Distinct teaching, there is only the sequential progression of the three truths. Therefore, there are three stages.
The meaning of progress and stagnation must be understood. First, regarding the classification of śamatha:
at that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata.

Having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, although I have now left the household life, I still rely upon his indulgent affection. Consequently, despite my extensive learning, I have not attained the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*).
I was unable to subdue the *Sāvitrī* spell and was turned by it, falling into a house of debauchery; this must have been because I did not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that those of the icchantika class may be led to abandon their Mleccha ways.

Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; together with the great assembly, they waited expectantly with thirsty hearts, longing to hear his instructions.

"Rising from one's seat" means rising from the seat where one was listening to the Dharma and requesting instruction. Within this act, there is reverence through the three types of action (*trikarma*).

Exposing one shoulder and joining the palms constitutes the bodily action (*kāyakarma*); "reverence" constitutes the mental action (*manaskarma*); and addressing the Buddha constitutes the verbal action (*vākkarma*).
In the text, first comes the confession of transgressions (*deśanā*), followed by the request for the Dharma. Within the confession, each preceding phrase gives rise to the subsequent one.
[The text ends with] "sentence. Youxi said: There are six layers of faults in the practitioner's repentance. The fault of being mired in a brothel arises from an inability to subdue the depraved.
The fault of an inability to subdue the depraved arises from the presence of outflows (*āsrava*). The fault of outflows arises from excessive learning.

The fault of excessive learning arises from relying on the Buddha’s affectionate favoritism. The fault of relying on the Buddha’s favoritism arises from being the Buddha’s youngest cousin. These are the six layers.

Among these, what one regrets most deeply is not having attained the untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the fetter (*saṃyojana*) is heavy because of the failure to know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one attains the untainted, one immediately knows the destination of the true limit. Regarding the term *kōrin* (憍憐) used herein: "kō" (憍) means not being distressed by difficult matters;
"rin" (憐) refers to the World-Honored One’s compassion and pity. As for "being turned by that," "that" refers to [the aforementioned].

The *Savira* mantra. The reason for this self-narration is that although I have previously received the Buddha’s compassion, I have never been pursued and interrogated as I am today in these seven rounds;
therefore, I have made this statement. I only pray that you will next request the Dharma.

Alternatively, it is said that the house of the *tathatā* (true limit) is called a "path" because *śamatha* is what enables one to arrive there. However, the previous heading of *samādhi* was derived from...

One gives rise to contemplation based on provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*). What is now called *śamatha* is precisely the entry from the provisional into emptiness. The previous seven inquiries merely refute the four modes of existence;

this is termed the refutation of existence at the level of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The subsequent "Aha! refutes the deluded mind; this is the refutation of characteristics at the level of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because characteristics are empty, one is able to perceive the true mind—is this not the path? Upon perceiving the truth, one attains the fruit of sainthood and is able to eliminate [afflictions].
The *icchantika* holds evil and perverse views. *Icchantika* is translated as "lacking faith," and *mleccha* is translated as "evil views.

According to what is stated in the sutras, one who knows there is the fruit of the Path is able to extinguish the perverse views of sentient beings; yet they do not perceive the True Dharma (the ultimate truth).

How could there be the fruit of the Path? Since the Buddha had already pursued this matter through seven rounds of questioning, Ānanda understood that he must now sweep away appearances to reveal emptiness, and therefore composed [this verse].
This is the request. However, there are two meanings. First, when *samādhi* and *śamatha* are united such that emptiness and existence are non-dual, this is precisely *dhyāna*.
This is called the three contemplations existing within a single mind; it is not necessary to separately mention the name "dhyāna.
Second, when entering from the conventional into emptiness, the emphasis is on emptiness; thus, *śamatha* is properly so named. This is precisely [the case].
This is what Ānanda seeks. “Tilting and thirsting” means tilting one’s heart toward [the teaching] with thirsty longing. “Qiáo” (翹) refers to raising one’s head in expectation;
“zhù” (佇) conveys the sense of standing and waiting. II. Expounding Śamatha. A. Manifesting Auspicious Omens.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face. These lights shone brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns.
The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways, and in this manner, lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions were simultaneously revealed.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all worlds were merged into a single realm.
Within that realm, all the great bodhisattvas residing in their respective lands stood with palms joined, listening attentively.
Now, the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious omens in this sutra are numerous; this [opening] is their foremost. It serves as the general omen, crowning the entire scripture.
As he is about to reveal the perfect and wondrous Threefold Contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), he first provides a demonstration through form. Demonstration through form is sudden (*tadānīm*);

those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom perceive the Way through direct observation. Demonstration through sound is gradual; those of middling and inferior capacities receive instruction through the ear.
Only then do I realize that this present scripture demonstrates both form and sound, and applies both gradual and sudden teachings.

There is no dharma that is not harmonized and no capacity that is not encompassed. It is the gate of the face and mouth; to claim that the face and mouth are the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue is without basis.
Wuxing said: "The manifestation of auspicious signs herein has four meanings: namely, the teaching, the practice, the person, and the principle. From the mouth, various [rays] are emitted.

The six kinds of light symbolize the manifestation of manifold teachings from a single principle; this is precisely what is meant by "the true essence of the teaching in this place is pure and resides in sound and hearing.
The six kinds of earth-tremors symbolize practicing according to the teachings to destroy the delusions of the six sense organs;

this is precisely what is meant by "once one organ returns to its source, all six organs achieve liberation. The ten directions merging into a single realm symbolizes the defilement of the ten realms.
"Purity is identical to the single true mind; it is like the cessation of bubbles where emptiness is fundamentally non-existent—how much more so for the various realms of the three worlds?
All the great Bodhisattvas dwell in their respective lands, signifying that although the gates of practice differ, each realizes the same principle;

this is because the fundamental nature of returning to the source is non-dual, even though the expedient means have many doors. (Text) This is the explanation of Wu-xing, who states that the emission of light symbolizes the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The teaching of this [earthquake] represents the practice of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. That the ten directions merge to form a single realm represents the principle of non-duality.
A Great Bodhisattva is one who dwells in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); thus, both the practice and the principle are complete. Because they dwell in concentration, [the earthquake occurs].
It is not necessary for the Bodhisattva to come from afar; rather, because they have formed a single realm together, even distant sounds are heard without obstruction.

This, moreover, secretly indicates the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). The *Wenju ji* states: "The six kinds of movement are: moving, rising, surging, shaking, roaring, and striking."
To sway unsteadily is called "movement" (*dong*). To rise from below is named "arising" (*qi*). To have a variegated surface of highs and lows is named "leaping" (*yong*).
To emerge and submerge across the six directions is also named "leaping. To have a deep, resonant sound is named "vibration" (*zhen*). To produce a crashing resonance is named "roaring" (*hou*).

To cause sentient beings to awaken is named "striking" (*ji*). Movement, arising, and leaping are the three aspects of form. Vibration, roaring, and striking are the three aspects of sound. This is "trembling movement."

These [terms] "form" and "sound" each represent only one aspect. However, this radiance and this land are the form that represents the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) which shatters all marks (lakṣaṇa).
The single shout in the following passage is the sound that represents the ultimate truth which shatters all marks.
Ultimate truth is inconceivable (acintya) and fundamentally does not belong to form or sound; yet, these very forms and sounds are themselves the inconceivable. 2. The Benefit of Sound.
II.1. Showing the Two Kinds of Roots; further divided into two: I. Indicating.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have various inverted karmic seeds that naturally cluster together like the *akṣa* fruit.
Those who practice cultivation cannot achieve unexcelled Bodhi, and may even instead achieve [other states]."

The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those who have become non-Buddhist practitioners—including the devas, māras, and their retinues—all fail because they do not know the two kinds of fundamental roots and thus practice erroneously.
It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal; even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed.
Ānanda requested instruction on the path of *śamatha*, and the World-Honored One pointed out two kinds of roots as the foundation for subsequently destroying falsehood and revealing the truth.
Regarding "various inversions," sentient beings possess three types of inversion:
inversion of mind, inversion of perception, and inversion of view. An ancient master explained: consciousness possesses mental inversion, while perception and sensation...

There is the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). Some say that the initial false conceptualization is called the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*);

when the mind subsequently forms a perception, it is called the perversion of perception; and when the perception results in external attachment, it is called the perversion of view. From these three perversions, various other perversions arise.
Inversion is delusive confusion; it is precisely the seed of karma. A seed must necessarily produce fruit.

Karma, affliction, and suffering—these three existences share a common root, just as the three seeds on a single branch of the akṣa fruit are always gathered together and never separated. Therefore, they cause sentient beings to transmigrate through the three realms of existence.
The Tathāgata first demonstrated this so that one might see how sentient beings grasp at a deluded mind as their own inherent nature.
This is a perversion. Next, the divergent paths of practice are shown: the fruits of Buddhahood taught in the provisional teachings of the *Āgamas* and *Vaipulya* are not the unsurpassed Bodhi;
and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, though they attain and certify to Nirvāṇa, cannot avoid sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence.
The "external paths" (*tīrthika*) refer to the class of the Six Teachers. The various devas take the ten wholesome actions as their primary principle. *Māra* is translated here as "the Killer";
this refers to those who claim to have attained the unsurpassed path while indulging in the five desires and severing the life-force of wisdom in others.
They are all ignorant of the two kinds of fundamental [causes] and falsely intend to achieve *bodhi*, like boiling sand in an attempt to produce a meal—how could it ever be?
"Is it obtainable? It refers to cooked food. **2. The Proper Clarification.** "What are the two kinds?
Ānanda, the first is the root of birth and death from time immemorial;
this is that攀緣心 (pān yuán xīn—clinging mind) which you and all sentient beings now take as their own nature. The second is the original purity of bodhi and nirvāṇa from time immemorial."

As for the pure essence: it is this fundamental clarity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*) of yours, which is capable of producing all conditions and yet remains ungrasped by those conditions.
Because sentient beings have neglected this original clarity, although they act throughout their entire lives, they remain unaware of it and thus perversely enter the various realms of existence.

Regarding the "mind that grasps at objects" mentioned in the initial fundamental section: this refers to the mind of deliberation and discrimination, which is subsequently refuted in the passage beginning with "Alas!
It is as follows: after seeing a form, one thinks to oneself, "I have seen a form"; after hearing a sound, one thinks to oneself, "I have heard a sound.
This is to use a second moment of thought to retrospectively grasp the events experienced in the first moment; therefore, it is so named.
The攀緣心 (攀緣心; *ālambana-citta*, the mind that grasps at objects). It is because this mind does not cease that sentient beings cycle through birth and death.
Since this mind is a mind that clings to signs (*nimitta*), clinging to signs gives rise to deluded attachment. Due to this deluded attachment, one enters into birth and death.
The matter is clear. [The text] below states to Ānanda: "To give rise to great courage and perform all various difficult practices and dharmic deeds, one must employ this mind.
Even if one slanders the Dharma, it is likewise due to this mind.
If this were not the mind, I would be without a mind, identical to earth or wood. Is this not grasping at this as being the self-nature? Second, the demonstration of Bodhi and Nirvana.
The root of saṃsāra is the virtue of wisdom (bodhi-jñāna), and the root of nirvāṇa is the virtue of cessation (prahāṇa). Sentient beings inherently possess these two virtues;
they do not need to be accomplished through cultivation, for they have been the fundamental reality since beginningless time.

Now, when it points to Ānanda’s present consciousness-essence as "primordial clarity," it means that what is called ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Thus, by observing the present momentary thought of consciousness, one directly manifests it.

This refers to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Some claim that "consciousness-essence" (*vijñāna-sāra*) is the eighth consciousness and "original clarity" (*mūla-prakāśa*) is the ninth consciousness;
however, this is likely not the case. Why? Because the second fascicle states: "Furthermore, you see me; this seeing is the original source of the clarity of seeing.

Although this seeing is not the wondrous, clear, and ultimate mind, it is like a second moon—it is not a reflection of the moon. The subsequent text clarifies that this [seeing] is the "source" (*yuan*).

The second moon is precisely this "original clarity" (*yuanming*); its meaning is likewise so. For the攀緣心 (*pānyuán xīn*, the攀缘心) is the reflection of the moon, and this present "clarity and brightness" (*jīngmíng*) is the second moon—neither of them is the first moon.
The substance of consciousness (*shìtǐ*), being profound and subtle, is called "clarity" (*jīng*).

Because it has not yet been mixed with deliberation and discrimination, it is termed "original clarity. If one gives rise to攀缘 (*pānyuán*) toward this, it entirely becomes the state of birth-and-death.

It is the root of death. If one does not give rise to攀緣 (pān-luán-yán—clinging/conditioning) toward this, then afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves wisdom, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is designated as the name for the two-fold *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis). As for what is said regarding "that which can produce all conditions":
after seeing forms and hearing sounds, a person will inevitably say to themselves, "I have seen forms and heard sounds. It is not that clinging arises from this [seeing and hearing].
Yes. Regarding the phrase "left behind by conditions," there are two meanings. First, it reveals that if the act of grasping at objects (*ālambana*) arises, one immediately loses the true essence.
Second, it reveals that the true essence is fundamentally not an object of grasping; therefore, it is left behind by all conditions.
Because sentient beings commit this error, ignorance is in its entirety wisdom; thus, it is called "original clarity. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Ignorance is clarity."

This refers precisely to the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Having already abandoned this essence, one is consequently buried by the sense organs and their objects, and entangled by speech and thought.
Though originally there is no birth-and-death, one is bound by birth-and-death; this is called "entering the various realms of existence in vain. How truly lamentable! Question:
It was previously stated that [beings] do not know the eternally abiding true mind and instead employ various false thoughts (*vikalpa*). Why is it now...?
Furthermore, does this again bring forth two kinds of fundamental [truths]? Answer: Previously, I wished to demonstrate the principle (*zong*) of *samādhi*;

thus, I first demonstrated the substance (*ti*) of the eternally abiding true mind, so as to establish the basis for the preceding provisional [teachings]. This is because one must first attain the substance before one can establish the principle.
Now, wishing to demonstrate the principle of *śamatha*, I again demonstrate the original purity of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

The pure essence brings about the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional. Previously it was said that "all deluded thoughts are employed"; here it is said that "the攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind of grasping and dependence) is used as the self-nature.

Previously it was called the "ever-abiding true mind" (*chángzhù zhēnxīn*); now it is shown that the fundamental clarity of the consciousness-essence (*shìjīng yuánmíng*) constitutes the substance of wisdom and severance (*zhìduàn*).
This further clarifies what was previously explained, making the indication even more precise. II. Clarifying the Path of Śamatha.
Furthermore, there is another pair of questions concerning the mind and the eyes.
"Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now ask you again.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm, bent his five fingers, and said to Ānanda: 'Do you see this now? Ānanda replied, 'I do.'"
“[Ānanda] spoke of what he saw. The Buddha asked, “What do you see? Ānanda replied, “I see the Tathāgata raise his arm and bend his fingers into a radiant fist that illuminates my mind and eyes.
The Buddha asked, “By means of what do you see? Ānanda replied, “I and the great assembly all see with our eyes.
The Buddha told Ānanda, “Now you answer me: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers into a radiant fist, [by what do you see it?]”
"Shine upon your eyes and mind. Your eyes can see; with what do you take to be the mind that perceives my fist?

Ānanda replied, "The Tathāgata has now questioned where the mind resides, and I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it. That which is capable of such investigation, I shall take to be the mind."
Previously, after demonstrating the eternally abiding true mind, it immediately spoke of "samādhi"; now, after demonstrating the two kinds of roots, it immediately speaks of the "path of śamatha.
In both cases, the essence (*tǐ*) is used to clarify the primary principle (*zōng*). From this point in the sutra text onward, both the provisional and the real are discussed together.
The real refers to the perfect threefold contemplation; the provisional first clarifies the principle of emptiness. It says: "If you wish to know śamatha..."
"Mothalu" points to the clarity of emptiness. Because the practitioner requested the wondrous Threefold Contemplation, [the Buddha] responded with the Perfect [Teaching].
Because it carries the initial expedient means, he responded with the Provisional. Without the provisional, there is no way to enter the real; without the real, there is no way to reach the ultimate.
This is clarified by advancing and retreating through the text, which is quite evident. That one transcends birth and death is the power of the contemplation of emptiness. Now, he asks again:
Below are four questions and answers. Regarding the first point, "bending the five fingers of the hand":
some say that on the tips of the Tathāgata’s five fingers there are the five characteristics of earth, water, fire, wind, and space; these five are all called "wheels" (*cakra*).
Raising his arm and bending his fingers to question the observer demonstrates the basis for the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. He then presents his fist and shows his palm.
Raising a blue lotus and pointing a single finger, he intended for people to directly recommend the Dharma of fundamental luminosity.

While the emptiness-principle of the Tripitaka teachings is a silent stillness of seeing and hearing, now pointing to the substance of seeing as the eternally abiding true mind transcends the Hinayana teachings.
When Ānanda said that his seeing had not yet emerged from ordinary sentiment, the Master next asked, "What do you see?"—this was precisely asking what it is that you see.

"What is the meaning of this? [The questioner asks. Answer: "To illuminate the eyes and the mind. The eye does not know; the mind does not see. Taken together, they mutually illuminate the eyes and the mind.
In the third and fourth questions and answers, the eyes and the mind are treated as two separate sections.

When the World-Honored One asks, "Who sees?", he is specifically asking who it is that is able to see; this is also equivalent to asking who it is that recollects the Buddha. Yet, [the interlocutor] answers, "The eye."
If you say that Ānanda was mistaken because he saw, then seeing must be the mind; how could it be called the eye? His error lay in not being able to separate the sense organ from its object.
These questions, as well as the subsequent shout and the preceding manifestation of auspicious signs, are all the True Reality that transcends words and thought.
How could it be that only the shout at the end is the True Reality? The Buddha did not [immediately...]
[The Master] rebukes him, yet asks again, "What do you take to be the mind? This is intended to expose his profound delusion in order to rebuke him.
To claim that the capacity for deliberation is the mind is to be even more deeply deluded; the root of his ailment lies in his failure to transcend discursive thought. As the preceding text states:
"Because one observes the Tathāgata’s sublime marks with the eyes, a mind of attachment and delight arises. The Buddha pointed this out as being "invaded by thieves. Now...
After pursuing the thief of deluded thought through seven rounds, it finally manifests itself.

Therefore, the Buddha immediately wields the sword that brings about Great Peace, directly delivering a single shout to sever the life-root of discursive thinking. II. Refuting Delusion and Distinguishing Reality.
First, the deluded mind is refuted; next, the true mind is distinguished. That which is refuted is precisely the first: the root of birth and death.
That which is distinguished is precisely the second: the root of bodhi and nirvana. Within the first [section], there are three parts: the first is the "thunderous" refutation.
The Buddha said, "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind.
The dual emptiness of nature and characteristics is the essential path for entering the Truth.

Although the previous refutation of the deluded mind was not located within, without, or in between, it merely refuted the nature of self, other, both, or causelessness. Yet, when one moment of thought is examined..."

Even when examining it with the mind, one is still unable to eliminate it; its characteristics (lakṣaṇa) still persist. Therefore, the Buddha, with the majestic power of a lion’s springing forth, let out a single roar, saying:
"Tsk! This is not your mind. This is what is called "striking a single blow beneath the life-root" (jīvitendriya).
Thus, one should know that discursive thought and speculative reasoning must be urgently severed. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one is free from conceptualization..."
This is called "attaining entry. Furthermore, it says that what is termed the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought.

That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. The single mark of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya.
It further states that if one is free from mental thoughts, then there will be no marks of any objective realms. This is based on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

The text states: "One knows that the faculty of mind must be severed before one can accord with the True Dharma (*satya*). This is what is called the path of the True Dharma that destroys appearances (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, as for designating this single shout as the True Dharma, both the Chan and the Teaching schools have raised doubts and debates. Chan practitioners claim that within a single exclamation of "Ho!
many names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are established; teachers of the Teaching school ask how a verbal dharma could be pointed out as the True. Yet they fail to realize...
Know that this one shout is not mere language, and that ultimate truth is beyond names and forms.

It is just like a person who, when told about medicine, fails to recognize the actual medicine even as it appears before them. This is because the practitioner has already been subjected to many rounds of exhaustive inquiry;
at this point, their wings have fallen and their nest is empty, yet the life-root of the present moment’s conceptualization remains.
[If one merely] cuts [the delusion], yet again bestows meaningful Dharma words, it will further provoke the person's deliberation and discursive thoughts so that they cannot be severed;
this is what is called "increasing confusion all the more.
Therefore, the Buddha directly gave a shout devoid of meaning and difficult to deliberate upon, thereby completely severing the person's deluded攀緣 (pān-yuan) of conceptualization and mental clinging.
There is nothing to which one can resort for deliberation; the delusions of resorting and攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) are severed by the single utterance of "Aha!
This is called the True Truth that shatters appearances. Thus, this single shout is itself the inconceivable realm; it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Although it resembles the sounds of speech, it does not fall into the characteristics of sound or language.
If, from beneath a single shout, deluded sentiments are utterly severed, it is the precious sword of the Vajra King.
If all攀緣 (pān-yuan) [clinging] minds cannot reach it, it is the lion crouching on the ground. What ordinary people regard as a single shout is, for the Tathāgata, his entire being.
The Great Function is such that a single shout does not function merely as a single shout. Regarding this one shout, there are those who grasp it and those who do not;
among those who grasp it, there are differences of depth and shallowness. For instance, when Ānanda said, "I am now as mindless as wood or earth," this was like using a probe to test the water.
Yet, with a single "Huh! he presented the family treasure on a platter—this is precisely [the Great Function].
The substance [of this teaching] is applied suddenly when the occasion arises; this is its function.

One must know that, as previously listed, there are immeasurable Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, devas, humans, and great assemblies who, upon hearing this single exclamation "Tuo," instantly sever their conceptual mind and directly realize non-arising—these are beyond counting.
Furthermore, those in the Eastern Land who stick out their tongues and go deaf are all of superior faculties and sharp intelligence.

Because one drinks from this and deeply accords with the inconceivable realm, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (Paramārtha-satya). Furthermore, how could it be a matter of language, names, or conceptual characteristics?
Ānanda, you have not yet forgotten the marks of sensory objects; you have merely produced a "probing rod and shadow-grass" [a superficial test].
Furthermore, when the Buddha said, "This is not your mind," he was specifically pointing to the delusion within the essence [of the mind] as being "not the mind.

He was not referring to the six consciousnesses or the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as being "not the mind. When delusion is removed and the truth manifests, consciousness itself is wisdom; how could there ever be two?

As stated in the "Great Outline" (Dagang), since the capacity of the audience has been shown to be deluded and their攀緣 (*pānyuan*, object-dependent clinging) remains unsevered, the Buddha now demonstrates in this text the transcendence of conceptual deliberation (*sīliáng*).
Later, in the analysis of the seeing-nature, he demonstrates the transcendence of the sense organs and their objects. This is the sequence for responding to the capacities of the audience.

Furthermore, it is the same with the ear. If one relies on the convergence of light when approaching [an object] and claims that the state where not even a single thought-moment has yet arisen is precisely the characteristic of the sense-faculty (*indriya*), this is a specific instance of giving rise to false conceptualization based on the eye-faculty.
One fails to realize that the seeing-faculty and the hearing-faculty must likewise be stripped away;
how much more so, since when not even a single thought-moment has arisen, how could there possibly be a characteristic of a faculty? 2. The Question of Alarm.
Ānanda was startled and withdrew from his seat. Joining his palms and rising, he addressed the Buddha: "This was not my intention; what should it be called?
He looked about with a hurried and alarmed expression. Seeing that as the Buddha approached him, Ānanda investigated thoroughly and found no trace of anger.

Suddenly hearing the reproach "Pò" (Shame!), as if cold water were being poured over his back, he was struck with a sudden shock. He looked hastily at the Tathāgata, withdrew from his seat, and questioned him.
The *Miaoxuan* says: "A foolish dog chasing a clod of earth merely exhausts itself; the clods will never cease.
It is like a clever lion that, instead of chasing the clod, chases the person who threw it; once the source of the clods is removed, the clods cease.

When Ānanda was rebuked, he suddenly realized that his own mind is not obtained from another—this is like the lion chasing the person and biting them, causing the tongue to loll out and the ears to go deaf. Deep indeed!
There is no time to enter [the Way]. Now, you are still lingering in deluded thoughts and further ask what this state should be named;
how is this any different from chasing after a clod of earth? ○ Third, the Manifestation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is the illusory appearance and conceptualization of external objects that deludes your true nature.
Because from beginningless time until this present life you have mistaken a thief for your own son, you have lost your original constancy and thus undergo the cycle of rebirth."
The first phrase clarifies where the deluded mind originates. "The objects before one" refers to the five sense-objects currently confronting one.
As stated in the second fascicle: "Furthermore, let me and you observe the palaces inhabited by the Four Heavenly Kings;
surveying everywhere across water, land, and air, although there are various forms of darkness and light, they are none other than the discrimination of objects before one."

"Obstructive. This passage merely refers to that which is currently confronted before one as "frontal objects" (*purataḥ-rajas*). However, these frontal objects actually encompass all five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
These frontal objects are already illusory appearances; furthermore, by giving rise to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) upon these appearances, one forms the present deluded mind.
The second phrase clarifies the functional capacity of this deluded mind. Those who are confused claim it causes people not to know [the truth]. This deluded mind is...
The law of arising and ceasing has the power to delude and confuse the true nature—which is neither born nor extinguished—causing people not to know it.

The following passage clarifies how you mistakenly identify with the cycle of suffering; this is precisely what the preceding text referred to as "using the攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn, the攀緣心 or攀緣心, the mind of grasping at conditions) as one's own nature," which is called the root of beginningless birth and death.
