Now, the six consciousnesses are thieves, while the nature is like a father, and the mind is like...
Child, to now take that which is conditioned by objects as one's own mind is to mistake a thief for one's son.
That the Dharma-treasure is depleted and the life of wisdom is lost is entirely due to this; all of it possesses the nature of a thief.

Because one does not know the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, one loses the originally ever-abiding life of wisdom. Is the delusion of the false mind not itself a thief? The very root of saṃsāra truly lies therein.

According to this passage, it is clear that the fundamental root of the preceding cycle of birth and death must be identified as the sixth consciousness, which consists of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
Second, the discernment of the true mind, part one: a question and doubt.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha. Because my heart loved the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life.

Why should my mind be concerned solely with making offerings to the Tathāgata? Even as I travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and spiritual friends, and as I rouse great courage to perform all manner of difficult dharmic deeds, I employ this very same mind throughout. Even so...
That those who slander the Dharma would eternally lose their roots of goodness is also due to this mind.

If what you have now revealed were not the mind, then I would be without a mind, identical to wood or earth. Apart from this awareness, there is nothing else. Why, then, does the Tathāgata say this is not the mind?
I am truly terrified, and among this great assembly, there is none who does not harbor doubt. I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and explain it for us.

This question is most significant as it reveals that [Ānanda] has not yet attained awakening. Generally speaking, human nature requires that one first obtain the true mind before being able to relinquish the deluded mind.
Since Ānanda had not yet attained the true mind and yet suddenly wished to discard the deluded, he was inevitably unable to do so; thus, he raised this question. First, the clarification:
Virtuous conduct arises from the mind. When it is said, "He caused me to go forth," this means that because of my love for the Buddha, the Buddha commanded me to go forth.
Because of my love for a single Buddha, I then desired to serve all Buddhas and spiritual friends;

thus, through the arousal of courageous vigor, I practiced virtuous conduct. This is the merit of the mind. Next, the nature of evil conduct arising from the mind is explained: slandering the Dharma and...
Affection for the Buddha and making offerings to him are opposites; severing the roots of goodness and practicing the roots of goodness are opposites—this is the fault of the mind.

From "If this" onwards, it clarifies that without the mind, one is identical to earth or wood. Ānanda says that if one excludes the deliberating mind, there is no further mind, and thus one would be similar to earth or wood.
To say that apart from this cognitive awareness there is nothing else is the explanation of the aforementioned identity.
Regarding "earth and wood": why are they said to be the same as earth and wood? Because apart from cognition, there is no further mind.
My true intention in being startled and terrified, and then suddenly rising from my seat, was this. Ānanda, this question of yours is like refusing food because one has a sore throat.
Although the Tathāgata has shown that what is inferred is not the mind, nevertheless, the arousal of the mind and the practice of goodness do not necessarily all belong [to that which is inferred].
It is inferred that one must know that within the midst of chaotic conceptualization, there exists an inconceivable essence; this is precisely the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
Contemporary lecturers merely understand that the Buddha refuted the six consciousnesses as being the mind and later revealed that the nature of seeing is the mind;

they do not realize that when the Buddha spoke of the various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*), these are all manifested solely by the mind. Thus, the six consciousnesses have already been clarified.
The original [nature] is the true mind; this is the meaning of the Perfect (yuan). The subsequent clarification that the nature of seeing is the mind belongs to a distinct (bie) meaning.
The intent of the sutra is difficult to fathom; how could one dare to judge it erroneously? II. The Instructional Revelation consists of three successive stages of progress and regression.

Within these three stages, the first stage first briefly indicates the Perfect Mind, followed by a specific manifestation of the nature of seeing. The initial text is divided into two parts, the first of which is a brief indication.
Regarding "Mind-Only," there are two parts: first, the manifestation of Mind-Only.

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
From his lion throne, he stroked Ānanda’s head and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind.
All causes and effects, as well as the atoms of the world, take their substance from the mind."

This first round of exposition advances the clarification of the perfect principle of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). Now, how could the World-Honored One have intended to point to the faculty of sight as the mind?

His true intent was simply to reveal that all phenomena are Mind-Only. Because [the interlocutor] failed to understand due to his difficulties, [the Buddha] subsequently pointed to the nature of seeing as being the mind.
What is shown here is precisely the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Following this, there are three further rounds of advancement.

No. When one advances, the illumination is perfect; when one remains in negation, the illumination is partial. Thereafter, the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha is explained extensively. Regarding the phrase "opening and revealing" at the beginning of the text:
it means that what is taught in the following passages is the opening and revealing of the Perfect Teaching for Ānanda and the great assembly.
As for "the patience of the non-arising of dharmas," it refers to awakening to the principle of Mind-Only, wherein not a single dharma is seen to arise.
To perceive that there is a single dharma which ceases is called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for the "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*), the seat does not have the actual form of a lion; rather, it serves as a symbolic representation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the lion among men.

Therefore, the place where the Buddha sits is called the lion throne, and what the Buddha speaks is called the lion's roar (*siṃhanāda*). That which the Tathāgata constantly proclaims is precisely the primary tenet.

The essential point is this: since it was previously established that that which is subject to investigation and exhaustion is not the mind, the "mind" mentioned here must necessarily be the True Mind.
This is confirmed by the subsequent passage, which states: "All are objects within the wondrously luminous True Mind"; therefore, it must be the True Mind.
Since the arising of all phenomena has no separate substance other than being a manifestation of the mind, they are not non-eternal. As they are all eternal—
Abiding is precisely the various dharmas inherently possessed by one's own mind; therefore, the dharmas that are produced are fully capable of producing the mind.
This passage correctly elucidates the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna-satya*): all dharmas that arise are the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), for they exist only within the mind.
That which manifests is like a reflection in a mirror—unreal and empty (*śūnya*). These three truths reside within a single mind, and there is nothing therein that is not eternally abiding.
This is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). It directly responds to the request for the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
Regarding this, the ancients have said that the true mind is perfumed and transformed by delusion, giving rise to all conventional phenomena—the sense organs, the body, and the physical world.
They held that the true mind is empty while conventional phenomena are not empty; that these two are non-dual, thereby constituting the Middle Way. If this is so, then the true mind is...

The wondrous is so; conventional phenomena are not wondrous. Since the conventional is not wondrous, one should preserve only the Real. Among the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), this would mean preserving only a single contemplation.
Now, it is said that regarding what the ancients explained concerning the two modes of creation (*dvividha-nirmāṇa*), they only grasped the meaning of phenomenal creation (*vastu-nirmāṇa*).

Yet, phenomenal creation is entirely dependent upon the inherent presence of principle (*tattva-sampad*). Because it is inherently present, it is able to create; this is termed "creation by principle" (*tattva-nirmāṇa*). Only in this way...
This accords with the principle of the *Avataṃsaka* regarding the mind-creation (*cittakṛta*). Upon examining the present text, does it not clearly possess these two meanings?
As it says: "The arising of all phenomena is creation through events (*shijiao*); that which is manifested solely by the mind is creation through principle (*lijiao*).

Creation through events is precisely creation through principle; delusion is entirely identical to truth. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are manifestations of the true mind. Creation through principle is precisely creation through events.
Thus, within a single thought-moment when an event arises, the causes and effects of the ten realms are likewise fully present. Therefore, Jingxi said:

"How could the term 'mind-only' refer to the True Mind alone? Question: The commentary on the current passage of the sutra states that "the meaning is already complete by saying 'True Mind-only. Why is this so?
Why, then, do you say it is "only the deluded mind"? Answer: The second fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"The physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind; they are nothing but the true mind. Furthermore, the eighth fascicle states:

"When the mind recollects delicacies, water flows from the mouth; when the mind gives rise to amorous desire, the entire body becomes moist and radiant. Based on these passages, [it is clear that the external world is the manifestation of the mind].
How could there not be the meaning of "merely the deluded mind"? Since they appear together in the same scripture, their meaning cannot be omitted.
It is like a person with abundant wealth and treasures who, upon meeting an unworthy son, has them squandered; can this not still be considered the property of the elder?

Therefore, if the deluded faculties are not established, the meaning of the true faculties will likewise remain incomplete. The essential point of practice lies in realizing that the deluded is itself [the true].
"True. Therefore, it was previously stated that there is only the true mind. Gushan said: "All causes and effects refer to the primary retributions (*pratyātmabhāva*) of the ten realms;
the atoms of the world refer to the environmental retributions (*bhājanaloka*) of the ten realms. This explains how all phenomena arise."
"Because the mind gives rise to substance" explains the aforementioned point that all is manifested by mind alone.

That is to say, because the primary retribution (the sentient being) is mind-only, it constitutes the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses; because the secondary retribution (the environment) is mind-only, it is said that insentient things possess nature.

The primary retribution is the dependent, and the secondary retribution is the basis. Since both the dependent and the basis reside within the one mind, how could the one mind be divided into subject and object?
This passage arises because Ānanda doubted that the mind has no substance; thus, the text specifically highlights this to establish the fundamental tenet. The wording is extremely concise.
It is only upon reaching the second section, which clarifies the principle of perfection, that the text states:

"The various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of cognition, are manifested solely by the mind," and so forth—this is where the present meaning is fully elucidated. 2. Citing Objects.
Moreover, Ānanda, if all that exists in every world— including even the grasses, leaves, and strands of thread— when their origins are examined,
all possess a substantial nature; and even empty space has its name and appearance, how much more so the pure and wondrously pure?
It clarifies that while the nature of the mind manifests as all minds, it is itself without substance.
All that exists pervades the myriad things; even down to grass and leaves, which possess roots and seeds, or threads and knots, which arise from silk and hemp, all possess their own essential nature.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of the four names for emptiness, namely: empty space, which is non-obstructive...
There is that which is immovable and unobstructed. As for its appearance (*mào*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaks of the single color of emptiness (*śūnyatā-eka-varṇa*).
The treatise asks: "Is not this color indeed an appearance? Your letter states: "The azure sky is its primary color, and it is also an appearance.
Thus, although emptiness has no substance, it possesses names and appearances; it is likewise a category of substance. Using this as an analogy, the true mind is ultimately existent.
The essence: because the three truths are formless, they are called "pure. "Subtle" means neither three nor one;

"purity" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), "clarity" is the provisional (*upāya*), and the nature of the mind is the middle (*madhyama*). Regarding "the nature of all minds," this refers to the fundamental nature of the minds of the ten realms.
As the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "All phenomena of the ten realms take the three truths as their unchanging nature."
This is precisely that meaning. How could such a pure mind lack a substance? The above was an exposition based on the Perfect Teaching (yuanfa) in order to resolve Ānanda’s doubts.
II. Clarifying that delusion has no substance. This section has two parts: first, the refutation of delusion; second, the conclusion regarding its faults. The first part further has two sections:
first, the direct refutation; second, from "At that moment, Ānanda... onwards, the silent acceptance [of the teaching]. The first [section] has two parts: first, the direct refutation; second...
Furthermore, [the following] clarifies that [consciousness] lacks intrinsic nature.

If you maintain that the nature apprehended by the conceptualization of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) must necessarily be the mind, then this mind ought to exist as a distinct,
complete essence apart from all objects— namely, the spheres of form, odor, taste, and touch— and apart from all activities, just as you [conceive it] now.

To listen to my Dharma is to have discrimination based on sound. Even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of discrimination regarding the dust of dharmas.

The first phrase restates the [false] calculation. Because it is stubbornly clung to and not relinquished, it is called "clinging and avarice. When the initial mind is directed toward an object, it is termed "awakening" (*jue*);

when the subtle mind discriminates, it is termed "contemplation" (*guan*, referring here to the aforementioned mind of investigation). This mind reaches its limit within the totality of nature, thereby revealing by contrast that it has no essence apart from sensory objects.
Regarding form, odor, taste, and touch, the four objects are mentioned first; the object of sound will be addressed in the subsequent text.
To clarify this: the five sense-faculties each take one object as their condition, whereas the mental faculty takes all objects collectively; hence it is called "the activity regarding all objects.
"Activity" (*karma*) refers to the functional operation that occurs when external objects draw the mind toward them.

According to the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Abhidharma) teachings, the mental faculty cannot independently take external objects as its conditions; rather, it either takes them simultaneously with the five consciousnesses or arises in succession to them.
Discrimination arises entirely because of objects (*viṣaya*). If it were to exist based on something else, it would be composed for the most part of various objects;
how could there be a complete nature apart from objects? Therefore, the Buddha conversely stated that if there were a nature apart from objects, that would be the mind itself.
"As you [say] below" correctly clarifies that there is no nature apart from objects. Sound is the object of the ear; at the time of hearing sound—

There is a simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises, taking the same sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*) as its object as the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); this is the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
If a subsequent thought takes a preceding sound-object as its object, it is called a "solitary-image" (*pratibimba*) object; this is the conceptualization of deliberation (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*).

Since even the hearing of the sound is not truly existent, how could the reflected image (*pratibimba*) be real? As for the phrase "even when [the sound] has ceased," it means that there is not only [conceptualization] by the mental factors (*caitta*).

All conditions are entirely false and illusory. Even when the six consciousnesses have all ceased, they still take mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) as their conditions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The eye is called seeing; the ear is called hearing;

the nose, tongue, and body are called sensing; and the mind is called knowing. Now, the claim that these [consciousnesses] have ceased seems to refer to the state of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Yet, ancient masters considered them to be "solitary" (independent) consciousnesses occurring during the state of distraction (*vikṣipta*), because even within meditative concentration, one takes real entities (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) as objects.
Not only is the analogy of a shadow appropriate; that explanation is also correct. However, according to the subsequent passage, which states:

"Though one may achieve the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) before one's eyes, if one does not attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), one cannot become an Arhat," I suspect this refers to the gradual cessation of the six consciousnesses within the successive attainments, until, in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) no longer function.
The Buddha designated this attainment as "internally maintaining a state of profound stillness."

Because the coarse characteristics of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are absent, it is called "profound and secluded. Although perception and conception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) have been extinguished, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) still remains;
that which it confronts is precisely the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*). To have extinction and to have guarding—how could this not be discrimination?

That which can perceive is discrimination, and that which is perceived is the reflected image. This is merely a reflection of the simultaneous cessation of the five sense objects; it is a phenomenon, not the ultimate principle. For...
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is also inference (*anumāna*); therefore, it is called a "discriminative reflection.
How much more so for those who have not yet attained this concentration—how could their speculative investigations and pursuits not be mere reflections? II. Commanding Them to Examine Thoroughly.

I am not commanding you to hold that this is not the mind. Rather, you must examine the mind with subtle discernment: if the nature of discrimination exists apart from the sensory objects, then it is truly your own mind.
If the nature of discrimination has no substance apart from the objects, then it is merely a reflection of the discrimination of those objects.
Since the objects are not permanent, when they change and perish, this "mind" would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Then your Dharma-body would be identical to annihilation; who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
"Command" (*chì*) means an admonition. Master Jing said: "This, too, is the mind. However, when one realizes the fundamental mind, this [discriminating] mind is illusory.
Yet, the preceding text states that all dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind. How can discrimination, on the contrary, reside in "solely"?

Apart from the mind, however, if one truly awakens to the fact that the luminous clarity of consciousness and the luminous clarity of awareness are the true consciousness, then this mind is itself the consciousness of the nature (*prakṛti-vijñāna*).
Ānanda has not yet awakened; he must not mistake the delusory for the real.

He must first examine for himself how the preceding passage first used reductio ad absurdum to reveal that the delusory mind has no substance, and then how it correctly explained that it lacks an inherent nature apart from sense objects. Now, as before, [the Buddha] exhorts him.

This is an interpretation based on the Buddha’s words. If one were to depart from the preceding [explanation] and employ *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*), since it has already been stated that "discrimination" relies upon external objects and is therefore not the true mind, this sentence serves as a *reductio*.
The Buddha spoke these words with the intention of revealing that it is only when detached from objects and existing independently that something is the true mind.
From "If one divides... onwards is the formal explanation. That which is confronted by the five sense organs is called...

Taking the preceding sensory objects as its condition, the mental consciousness takes as its object the shadows of those objects that have already passed away; this is called "discriminating shadow-objects.

While the previous discrimination based on sound still belonged to *anusmaraṇa-vikalpa* (recollection-based discrimination), here, in the definitive judgment, the mind that investigates and probes belongs entirely to *abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa* (conceptual construction).
This is what the ancients referred to as "solitary [mental consciousness] in the state of dispersion. It clarifies that these sensory objects are not real, but are attachments to the false.

This results in a fallacy. Although the mind relies upon sense objects, those objects are not permanent. Once arising and abiding have ceased, there is only change and extinction; change is precisely alteration.
At this time, just as a shadow vanishes when the form is gone, how could the mind possibly exist? The true mind is the Dharma-body.
If one were to take impermanence to be the true mind, then in principle the Dharma-body would be identical to annihilation. The Dharma-body...

Since even the illumination of the wisdom that realizes extinction cannot arise, who could cultivate the path of "mind-only" and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
The Buddha’s intention lies in advancing toward the clarification of the perfect principle; therefore, he concludes his discourse by mentioning this. II. Silent Comprehension.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in self-reflection.

Having heard the teaching on the Perfect Mind above, they were bewildered and did not understand; yet, when the false mind was refuted as being without substance, they themselves realized their error.
Lestan said: "Because what they clung to has dissolved, it is called 'losing oneself. (2) Conclusion of the Faults.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "All practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive concentrations before their eyes fail to achieve the exhaustion of outflows and become Arhats because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality."
Therefore, although you have now attained much learning (*bahuśruta*), you have not realized the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*).

"Learners" (*śaikṣa*) refers here to those who have attained the three preceding fruits. Since it was previously stated that one must extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, this is matched by the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
Having already accomplished the three fruits through the nine successive attainments, one occupies the stage of "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*); one cultivates these attainments.
One must first cultivate the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).

The first liberation is situated in the first dhyāna; the second liberation is situated in the second dhyāna; the third, the pure liberation (*śubhavimokṣa*), is situated in the third and fourth dhyānas.
Next, one proceeds through the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). The eighth is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); these are collectively termed the eight liberations.
This is the meditation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Although one has previously attained the eight dhyānas, there were intervals between entering them.
Now, wishing to bring them to full maturity, one enters them again in succession from the first dhyāna up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), without any distracted mind in between.

Because this causes that which was not sequential to become sequential, it is called "sequential" (*anupūrva*). This is the meditation of refinement (*pariśodhana*). The *Śīlaskandha-śāstra* states: "The attainment of cessation."
This refers to the extinction of the six complete categories and the total exhaustion of the seven defiled categories.

Since the meaning of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in the fourth fruit has already been realized through the perfection of the contemplation of emptiness, one no longer clings to the deluded thoughts of birth and death. In the final moment of mind of the third fruit, deluded thoughts are not yet exhausted, and one has not yet become an Arhat;
Ānanda was also among those still in training (*śaikṣa*), which is why [the Buddha] here concludes by rebuking him. Now, regarding the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*):
One cultivates both the internal and the external. An inner disciple within the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has already severed the deluded views of present arising and ceasing.

From the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) onward, they differ from those liberated by nature (*prakṛti-vimukta*), who directly enter the contemplation of the skeleton by taking emptiness as their object;

therefore, they must again cultivate the meditative observation of *dhyāna*. Only after severing the eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*vicikitsā-kleśa*) through the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) does one finally [attain it].
One who has exhausted the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) becomes an Arhat liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

If an outsider merely knows to practice the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*), feeling aversion for the lower realms and aspiring toward the higher, and employs the vision of the unreal to extinguish the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), then although they may achieve the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*), they have not yet severed the afflictions of cultivation.

Therefore, even though they achieve the higher meditative absorptions, because the outflows are not exhausted, the fruit is not realized; this is as in the case of one who has transcended humans by severing [the lower fetters].

This refers to the regression from one's stage due to the severance of [delusions] through seeing and thinking (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The two instances of the word "although" (*sui*) are extremely critical;
they precisely reveal that although one has attained the fruit of an Arhat and realized the state of a sage, there remains a deficiency such that one fails to achieve perfection.

This is because the delusions of false views have not been eliminated. My interpretation is exactly as stated in Changshui’s commentary: "The cultivation practiced by ordinary beings follows the dhyāna..."

The principle that the maturation of karmic fruits does not transcend the triple world is now consistent [with this teaching]. The first section above, based on the Perfect [Teaching], has refuted delusion and briefly demonstrated the Perfect Mind.
II. Specifically Revealing the Nature of Vision. The preceding text refuted the deluded mind to reveal the True Mind.
As the Sūtra says: "All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind; the causes and effects of the world take the mind as the substance of their formation. These words...
Although it is brief, its meaning is extremely perfect. Those who are ignorant do not realize that this perfect meaning seems merely to refute the false without yet revealing the true;

therefore, Ānanda, having reached this point, again repents his errors and makes a piteous plea. The Buddha, having no choice, distinguishes the nature of seeing, which in its principle is distinct [from what was previously taught].
This is the negation of the Perfect Teaching. Commentators of past and present have claimed that the preceding section refuted the false.

The discussion on the mind is concluded. From this point forward, we shall clarify the manifestation of the nature. Who would say otherwise? However, the distinction between advancing toward the Perfect and retreating to the Separate has not been clearly elucidated.
If one takes the Separate as being the Perfect, it will inevitably lead to conflating the Perfect with the Separate.

Now, by allowing the Perfect and the Separate to follow divergent paths, their principles remain distinct and do not overlap. Even in the *Avataṃsaka* Sudden Teaching, the Separate is still encompassed while the Perfect is clarified; how much more so [in this case]?
Ānanda requested instruction on the initial expedient means; temporarily employing the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) does not violate the intent of the sutra.

However, that within the progression of "advancing" and "not advancing," one suddenly employs the Separate and then suddenly the Perfect, is precisely the meaning established in the Great Treatise regarding the Perfect teaching's reception of the Separate and the Common.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the repeated earnest entreaty.
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of grief; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha to resolve my mind on leaving the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, constantly thinking to myself that there was no need for me to practice."
I thought that the Tathāgata had bestowed this samādhi upon me, not realizing that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable.
Having lost my original mind, although my body has left the household life, my mind has not entered the Way. It is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees;

only today do I realize that though one may have heard much, if one does not practice, it is equal to not having heard at all. It is like a person speaking of food who can never be satiated by such talk alone.
"World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us who are destitute and exposed, will give rise to his wondrously luminous mind and open our eyes to the Way."
The meaning of this request is the same as that of the previous one, though their specific implications differ.

The former was a request for the path of entering the true [nature] through *śamatha* following the provisional contemplation of *samādhi*. The present request is for the demonstration of the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal;
this is the principle realized by *śamatha*. Thus, the meaning is the same. However, although the former involved a request for *śamatha*, the Buddha demonstrated...
The principle that "all phenomena are mind-only" pertains to the three perfect contemplations (*yuan san guan*).

Since Ānanda, having heard this, still did not know the essential nature of the true mind, he now seeks to have the eye of the Path of Seeing opened for him; thus, his intention differs [from the previous one].

Regarding the phrase "starting from ourselves," although those who have left the household life and received the precepts may follow the Buddha, meditative concentration and wisdom must necessarily be cultivated by oneself; how could one hope to rely on the Tathāgata’s grace?
"I am. Below the phrase "losing the self," there are two successive metaphors and teachings. First is the metaphor of losing the mind:
losing one's original mind is like abandoning one's father; leaving home in vain is like a destitute son; and not entering the Path is like fleeing away.
Next is the metaphor of much learning: much learning is like describing food; if one does not practice it, one will ultimately never be satiated. As for the two obstacles:

This refers to the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Various masters of the past and present, relying on the *Bhūmivastu* (or *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), state:

"The untainted wisdom of the person-selflessness (*pudgala-nairātmya*) of the two vehicles is the wisdom that purifies the afflictive hindrance; the wisdom of the dharma-selflessness (*dharma-nairātmya*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is the wisdom that purifies the cognitive hindrance.
Furthermore, it is said: "Because one abandons craving, one attains liberation of mind, which is the purification of the afflictive hindrance; because one abandons [ignorance],..."
Because of this clarity, one attains wisdom-liberation and the purification of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If the two hindrances are assigned to the two types of delusion, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consist of the delusions of views and thought, while the cognitive hindrances consist of the delusions of "dust-like" ignorance (*rajomoha*) and fundamental nescience (*avidyā*). As stated in the *Xuánqiān*:
"The two hindrances are the afflictive hindrance and the cognitive hindrance," as fully cited in the *Zhìguān* according to the explanation of Dharmatrāta. Now, the Master relies upon...

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) opens up [the afflictions] into three delusions. Therefore, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) encompasses both phenomena and principle.

That which obstructs knowledge of phenomena is the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like) delusion; that which obstructs knowledge of principle is the ignorance (*avidyā*) delusion. To explain this according to the common understanding:
the coarse delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) can cause the mind to be vexed and distressed; for those of the Two Vehicles, these constitute the obstacle to the wisdom of selflessness.

Because it acts as an obstruction, it is called the "afflictive hindrance" (*kleśāvaraṇa*). As for "the knowable" (*jñeya*): this refers to the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
since ignorance, when not yet severed, can obstruct this wisdom, it is called the "hindrance regarding the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding "the tranquil and eternal nature of mind": "tranquil" means quiescent; "eternal" means permanently abiding; "mind" refers to the capacity to respond to conditions; and "nature" is the... (incomplete).
The essence of transformation is precisely that which is realized through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Now, while the term "mind-nature" fundamentally refers to the Middle Way, its current association with emptiness is because *śamatha* is the basis of emptiness and is not separated from the Middle.

How could this be the same as the contemplation of emptiness in the Lesser Vehicle? As for being "exposed and destitute," it is like a poor son who, having turned his back on his father, flees along a long road.
"Eating in the wind and lodging in the dew": according to the established principle, not recognizing one's original mind and lacking the practice of wisdom is called "poverty" (qiong).
Constantly dwelling within birth and death is called "dew. To give rise to the wondrous mind and open the eye of the Way is fundamentally not two separate matters.
As the subsequent text states, "Seeing this nature is the mind, not the eye," it is evident that the manifestation of seeing is the manifestation of the mind. This is primordial clarity.
The essence of this is inconceivable and is named the "wondrously luminous mind. The "eye of the Way" is the eye that perceives the Way.
○ Second, the formal revelation, which has two parts: first, manifesting auspicious omens and granting permission to speak; second, manifesting the omens. First, manifesting the omens.
Immediately, the Tathāgata emitted a jewel-light from the *svastika* on his chest. This light was brilliant and radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors;

it simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, universally bathing the crowns of all the Tathāgatas in all the jewel-adorned lands of the ten directions, before returning to Ānanda and the great assembly.
The previous light issued from the mouth, bearing a scripture upon its crown; now the light issues from the chest, which surely signifies that it is manifested from the heart.
The "hundreds of thousands of colors" signify that the three categories and seven elements expounded therein constitute the myriad practices.

That it universally pervades the ten directions and灌 (pours) upon the Tathāgata’s crown signifies that this Dharma-gate is the Great Buddha-Crown. It manifests the true nature throughout all Buddha-worlds.

That there is nothing to which it does not pervade is its "Great Meaning. Because those present at the assembly shall obtain this benefit, [the light] returns specifically to the ears of Ānanda and the others.
The *svastika* (卍). In Sanskrit, it is called *asidviga*; here it is translated as "Possessing Joy" (*yǒulè*) or "Auspicious Ocean-Cloud" (*jíxiáng hǎiyún*).
It is the mark of the ten thousand auspicious virtues; one who possesses this mark will certainly receive peace and happiness. For this reason, it is auspicious...
This is because auspiciousness is the convergence of myriad virtues. The "Chapter on the Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Marks" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata has a mark of a great man upon his chest, shaped like the svastika (卍) and named 'Auspicious Ocean Cloud' (*Śrī-samudra-megha*).
It is adorned with mani-jewel flowers and emits all manner of precious lights. 2. Granting Permission to Speak.

The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying: "I now establish for you the great Dharma banner, so that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may attain the wondrous, subtle, and secret mind of pure and luminous nature, and obtain the eye of clarity."

The intention of the Tathāgata lies in clarifying the perfect and sudden [teaching], and therefore it is called the "Great Dharma Banner. A banner symbolizes the subduing of the heterodox and the establishing of the orthodox;
"to erect" means to set up vertically. Next, he clarifies that the nature of seeing is the mind. He points to this mind as the wondrous, subtle, secret, intrinsically pure, and luminous mind.
He points to this seeing as the pure eyes and ears. The phrase "also causes" indicates that he is simultaneously clarifying the teaching.
"Subtle" (*miao*) refers to the meaning of forgetting all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

As the subsequent text states, "the subtle and secret contemplation-illumination of *śamatha*," by analogy with "subtle" and "secret" here, these also belong to what is seen by the wisdom-eye of *śamatha*, and thus are called "subtle and secret.
That which is illuminated by *śamatha* is the inherently pure and luminous mind, not something produced through cultivation. Yet it is called the "pure eye"; this means that one sees.

When one is detached from the sense organs and their objects, one is immediately pure. Since the preceding passage requested the manifestation of the wondrously luminous mind, this passage now states that one has "attained the wondrous, subtle, and secret, purely bright and luminous mind.
The preceding passage spoke of the "eye of the Way," while this passage speaks of the "pure eye.

Although the preceding manifestations of auspicious signs and the granting of permission to teach were situated within the section clarifying the nature of vision through specific characteristics, their meaning extends to both the Perfect (Dharmalakṣaṇa) and Separate (Vibhajyavāda) teachings. How could there not be such an intention in the text?
[This concludes] the Interlude. II. Correctly Discerning the Nature of Seeing. The ancients said: "First destroy the deluded mind; next, destroy deluded seeing.

This is because while the previous destruction of the deluded mind allowed one to temporarily leave behind the conceptual marks of discrimination regarding conditioned objects, it did not yet enable one to know that the nature of the mind is eternally abiding.
Now, by destroying deluded seeing, [the text] cites the example of the blind man gazing into darkness and so forth to manifest that the nature of seeing is unchanging.
It is extinguished. Even up to the point where he raises his hand and emits light, it is revealed that the nature is without movement.
One should know that the Tathāgata has shown Ānanda the path of *śamatha* from the shallow to the deep. As stated therein: "Ānanda holds his eyes on his face while his mind is within.

Therefore, speaking in accordance with the capacity of the disciple, it is appropriate first to destroy the deluded mind and subsequently to discern the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*). It appears as such.

There are two interpretations. If one considers it from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s intent, it does not exceed the previous sequence of first refuting the deluded mind and subsequently revealing the true mind;
how could there be two? Nevertheless, the general meaning of the text converges upon perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). As for treating this as a distinct section:
whereas the previous revelation of the mind stated that "all phenomena are mind-only," the present analysis of vision states that "the head itself moves and wavers, yet the seeing has no location."

"Movement: the hands open and close of their own accord, yet the vision neither expands nor contracts. It is clear, then, that movement is contrasted with non-movement, and expansion and contraction with non-expansion and non-contraction.
Furthermore, it is said: 'Though your face may be wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled.
That which is wrinkled is subject to extinction; that which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death. Thus, change is contrasted with non-change."

The contrast between transformation and birth-extinction versus non-birth and non-extinction is thus made even clearer. Therefore, this is the first instance of regressing from the provisional to clarify the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
Indeed, were it not for the Distinct Teaching, there would be no means to discern the nature of vision. Once the nature of vision is realized, all phenomena are seen as eternal;

is this not the case that the Distinct Teaching serves as the gateway to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)? Jiaoguang was unaware that the division of teachings into provisional and real occurs at this point.

He established a tenfold topical outline for "Revealing the Vision" (*xiànjiàn*), which he termed the "Ten Kings with Flat Heads" (*píngtóu shíwáng*). Because it lacked a comprehensive structural framework, it was not adopted.
Furthermore, while ancient masters spoke of "shattering false vision to reveal true vision," Jiaoguang alone claimed that this is "revealing the vision" rather than "shattering the vision.
He further asserted that one should discard the consciousness-mind (*shìxīn*) and instead take the nature of the sense-faculties (*gēnxìng*) as the causal mind.
Now, to claim that "manifest seeing" (*xianjian*) is merely a partial definition of the thesis, and to take the faculty of the eye as sufficient for realizing the gate of awakening, is an error.

In the current passage, taking the blind man’s gazing into darkness as proof that the nature of seeing is without deficiency—wherein the blind man’s visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is already impaired yet the nature of seeing remains intact—it is evident that this has already transcended the realm of both faculties and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*). Yet Jiaoguang, on the contrary, claims that this is merely "taking [the faculty]."

Is it possible for the nature [of seeing] to reside within the sense organs? Moreover, although the nature of sentient beings' seeing and hearing is said to be within the six organs, it has never been even slightly tainted by the objects of the organs (*indriya* and *viṣaya*).
Because those of dull faculties could not understand, the Buddha was compelled to take the blind man as an example;
thus, at the outset, he established the distinction between seeing and its separation from the organs and objects, as when he said, "The external objects are themselves dark."
Seeing what is deficient causes one to leave behind sensory dust. Seeing the nature is a function of the mind, not the eyes; it is thus detached from the sense organs.

If one remains attached to the six sense organs, it is just as Vimalakīrti rebuked: "If you seek seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, then this is seeking seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing, not seeking the Dharma.
Only when one is liberated from the sense organs and their objects does one take the unborn and undying mind as the foundation.
Only after cultivating the causes does one subsequently achieve the perfect realization of the stage of fruition; this essential point must be discerned.
Furthermore, it is the constant rule of the Dharma-gates to first negate and then establish. As the ancients said: "To shatter the false and reveal the true—these words are indeed not erroneous."
As clarified in the sutras, the eye cannot see; it is the mind that sees. Is this not to refute false seeing and reveal true seeing?
Master Jiaoguang, unaware of this meaning, instead wishes to grasp at the sense organs (*indriya*). He further claims that "the false is brought along to reveal the true.
But what is this "false" that can be "brought along"? Is this not the heterodox eternalism of the old physician’s milk medicine? It is merely...

If one were to dismantle or reveal [the meaning], it would appear contradictory; now, by saying "discerning the nature of seeing," both are encompassed. The section is divided into three parts: first, showing that the nature of seeing is the mind;
second, clarifying that the nature of seeing is unchanging; third, clarifying that the nature of seeing is eternally abiding. Within the first of these, there are three sub-sections:
first, questioning to determine whether the fist is seen; herein, the question is posed first.
Ānanda, you previously answered me that you saw the light of my fist. From what cause does this light of the fist exist?
How is it formed into a fist? By means of what do you see it?
The first sentence is general; the following three sentences are specific. Within the general section, the single character "see" (jiàn) is the primary meaning of the text.
Previously, Ānanda said, "I saw the World-Honored One raise his arm and bend his fingers into a radiant fist that illuminated my heart and eyes.
Therefore, the current text says, "You previously answered me that you saw the radiant fist. The following three [sentences] are specific questions; the first asks about the radiance.
The reason for bringing up the ears here is not the primary intent of the text. Next, the question regarding the fist is intended to use the principle of the fist as an analogy for the eye-faculty.
Third, the question "Who sees? asks about this seeing that is distinct from the faculties, yet Ānanda necessarily assumes it to be the faculty;
therefore, he asks this again. [End of Section One. Two: The Answer.
Ānanda said: "Because the Buddha’s entire body is made of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing like a mountain of jewels and born of purity, it possesses radiance;
this I have truly observed with my own eyes. Because he drew back his five fingers and clenched them to show people, there is the appearance of a fist."
In the Sanskrit language, Jambudvīpa is translated here as "Superior" (Yansheng), meaning "blazing and flourishing.
The Buddha’s entire body is golden in color, its radiance shining like a mountain of jewels; this is the proximate cause of this light.

Being born of purity and not arising from desire is the remote cause of this light. Next, he answers [the question] that he truly perceives it with his own eyes; this is at the beginning of the fascicle.
It is said that because one observes the Tathāgata’s sublime marks with the eyes, identifying the eye as "seeing" constitutes Ānanda’s fundamental affliction.

The preceding text further states, "I and the great assembly all see with our eyes"; the present statement that "the eyes observe" likewise indicates that the internal faculties have not yet been liberated.
II. Again, by analogy with the seeing of the fist, there are three parts; first, the question.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I now tell you these true words: those who possess wisdom must rely on parables to attain awakening.
Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand, there would be no fist; if there were no eye, there would be no seeing.
If you take your faculty of sight as an analogy for the principle of my fist, is the meaning not the same?"
"I tell you this in truth": hereafter, the Buddha states that seeing the nature is the mind; as these words are most true, he first demonstrates them.
For those who require analogies to attain awakening, the subsequent reference to the guest-dust and the host-space, as well as the present example of the fist for the seeing, are all analogies.
"Suppose," and so forth, provides the analogy; "if there were no," and so forth, is the dharma [the subject]; "no hand" [is the point].
A fist cannot be formed [without fingers]; without eyes, one cannot form seeing. This is a case where the dharma (the principle) and the metaphor do not correspond.
Because the Buddha saw that Ānanda still recognized the eye as being able to see, he questioned him in this manner. Among the three previous questions, he cited only two matters as examples.
Regarding the "principle of the fist": "principle" refers to the physical nature of things. 2. The Second Answer.
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One. Since there is no self-eye, self-seeing cannot be established;
for the faculty of my eye is analogous to the Tathāgata’s fist, as their underlying principles and characteristics are similar."
To take Ānanda’s argument that the absence of a fist serves as an analogy for the absence of seeing is a great error. Seeing is the fundamental essence of the eye;
seeing does not perish along with the eye. A fist is merely the extremity of the hand; a fist must necessarily perish along with the hand. How can the fundamental and the derivative be equated?
Nevertheless, Ānanda’s words were most humble and compliant; his mention of the "absence of a fist" was not intended to be abrupt.
“World-Honored One, therefore, by personally abiding in the state of being eyeless, you have illustrated it as being equivalent to having no fist; this clearly demonstrates their similarity.
3. Refutation. The Buddha told Ānanda: “Your statement that they are similar is not correct. Why is this? It is like a person who has no hands—how could they have a fist?”
It is ultimately extinguished. That the one without eyes does not see is not because there is a total absence of seeing.
Why is this so? You should try asking a blind person on the road, "What do you see? Those blind people will surely answer you, "Now before my eyes I see only darkness;
I perceive nothing else. Judging from this principle, the external object itself is dark; what deficiency could there be in the faculty of seeing?

Regarding the establishment of this principle by means of a blind person: one should know that since the essence of consciousness and the fundamental luminosity have combined with delusion to spontaneously form the eye-faculty, common understanding knows only that the eye is what sees, and does not realize that seeing exists apart from the eye.
If one wishes to point out the nature of seeing as being separate from the faculties, then perhaps only a blind person can manifest this essence; for the eye-faculty of a blind person has already—
When the physical eye is destroyed yet the nature of seeing remains unclouded, the principle that "one may lack eyes but still possess seeing" becomes clear.

Thus, the Buddha specifically relied upon blind men to open the path of the Dharma-eye, thereby shattering the attachment to the eye as the faculty of seeing. Furthermore, the practitioners did not realize that the mind is what truly sees;
the Tathāgata’s intention was to point toward seeing so that it might be traced back to the mind. It was only because those blind men did not rely [on external conditions] for their seeing...

If the eye is [the seer], then the principle that the mind is what sees is also established. Thus, by specifically employing a blind person to manifest the wondrous mind, the attachment to the notion that the eyes reside on the face is also shattered.
Ānanda previously held two attachments; it is only now that they are first broken.
Within this, first the dissimilarity is indicated. The phrase "For what reason? and following explains the cause of this dissimilarity.
The hand is the basis of the fist; if the basis is lost, the derivative is gone. Seeing is the root, yet while the derivative is gone, the root remains.

The passage beginning "Why is this so? and following explains that blindness is not the absence of seeing. The reference to "all blind people" demonstrates the commonality of this principle among them. All blind people...
Seeing darkness. If one discusses what is seen, it is not entirely non-existent; if one discusses that which sees, it is entirely existent.

Yet, through this, the nature of seeing is revealed as being detached from external objects. ○ Third, the convergence of seeing back into the mind. 4.1. A certain person, representing those who are blind, raises an objection.
Ānanda said, "The blind see only darkness before their eyes; how can this constitute seeing?
This objection is based on the common notion that seeing darkness is not the same as seeing. Ānanda’s intention here is that the eye itself is what performs the act of seeing.
(2) Second, comparing the two types of darkness.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The various blind people who have no eyes perceive only darkness; this is compared to a person with sight staying in a dark room.
Is there a difference between these two kinds of darkness, or is there no difference?"
The various blind people follow from the preceding text. Their lack of eyes is contrasted with the presence of eyes below.

Why does the Buddha not immediately clarify that blind people possess vision, but instead merely compares them using two dark characteristics? The previous Buddha stated that the objects before one are naturally dark; what deficiency is there in seeing?
Thus, the fact that blind people possess vision is clear in meaning and need not be further explained. Ānanda, however, stubbornly clings to the eye.
This is because it is the mind that discriminates and grasps at objects which is still bound by the false root. From this point downward, the Buddha clarifies that the eye is not the seer;
thus, the false root is naturally destroyed and true seeing is naturally revealed. To refute the false root as being the seer, one must clarify that the lamp and the eye function identically.
To clarify that the lamp and the eye function identically, one must first clarify that both lack blackness.
It is distinct. When false views are eliminated, true vision is established; that a blind person possesses sight follows naturally from this principle.
This is because it is not the essential point to insist on manifesting it through mental construction. ○ Third, he answers again in accordance with the question.
"So it is, World-Honored One. There is no difference whatsoever between the blackness of this person in the dark and that of the group of blind men.
Ānanda conceived a sense of wonder, thinking he had not expected that the two kinds of blackness—those with eyes and those without—would be identical.

The Buddha stopped him, wishing to clarify that the two kinds of blackness are the same, and therefore he should have said, "So it is. [Section Four: Correctly Refuting the Sense Organs to Reveal Vision.]

Ānanda, if a person who has no eyes sees only the darkness before them, and suddenly regains the light of their eyes and perceives various forms within that same field of objects, this is called "seeing with the eyes.

In that same way, if a person in the dark sees only the darkness before them, and suddenly obtains the light of a lamp and likewise perceives various forms within that same field of objects, it should be called "seeing with the lamp.
If it were seeing with the lamp, then the lamp would possess the capacity for vision; but the lamp itself does not see.
It is called a lamp. Furthermore, what concern does the observation of the lamp have with you? Therefore, you should know that while the lamp can reveal color, it is the eye—not the lamp—that sees.
While the eye can reveal color, it is the nature of the mind—not the eye—that sees.
The text is further divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that since the two types of blackness are no different, the lamp and the eye function identically. "If" (*yā*) means "suppose.
One who lacks eyes beholds nothing at all—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—therefore it is said they see only the blackness before them.

When one possesses the ability to treat the eyes, the light of the eyes is restored. Whereas previously, lacking eyes, one saw only the blackness before them; now, possessing eyes, one sees [the world].
The notion that it is only the eye that can see external objects is what Ānanda holds within his mind. To apply this by analogy:
when a person in the dark sees the blackness before them without a lamp, and later sees external objects with a lamp, the lamp should likewise be called "that which sees.
For the function of seeing is equal in both cases: having eyes yet not seeing the blackness, and having a lamp yet not seeing the blackness.
Previously, Ānanda maintained that the eye itself can see; now, the Master demonstrates that the eye is merely like a lamp in order to shatter the practitioner's attachment.
Second, he refutes that the lamp cannot see. Herein lies the hidden meaning of refuting "eye-seeing": because he wishes to refute "eye-seeing," he refutes "lamp-seeing.
Since the two are identical in being [unable to see] darkness, they are likewise identical in not seeing darkness. If "lamp-seeing" is thus refuted...
The argument regarding seeing with the eyes is also refuted. An ancient master said: "This is a refutation by concession (*anujñāta-bādha*).

If you assert that the lamp can see, then the lamp would be the person; how could it then be called a 'lamp'? Furthermore, since the lamp is already a separate person who can observe on its own, what concern is that of yours?
Third, the refutation of the sense organ (*indriya*) to reveal seeing. Regarding the text within this section, some take the view that the lamp can manifest color.
When one with eyes is in a dark room, the eye can manifest color; this is also possible when a blind person regains their visual faculty.
However, even for a single person’s perception, it truly relies upon two aspects of manifesting color. Therefore, the word "two" follows from the preceding refutation regarding the lamp and seeing.
As for the lamp being able to manifest color: the substance of the lamp is devoid of cognition, and without the lamp, there is no seeing.
When there is a lamp, one sees; this is the meaning of manifest color (*varṇa*). The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), like the substance of the lamp, likewise lacks cognition.

It merely reflects without further analysis, like an image in a mirror. Since the visual faculty is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in their purified state, according to strict analysis, it is no different from the lamp.
That nature of spiritual awareness is the mind (*citta*), not the eye. By this principle, one should discuss "seeing" as seeing.
The nature is perfectly clear. Since it was previously refuted that deluded thoughts are not the mind, the "mind" mentioned here must necessarily be the eternal mind.
If each mind perceives itself, how could it rely upon the sense organs? The text states: "If it is the eye and not the lamp, then seeing is independent of external objects. It further states:

"If it is the mind and not the eye, then seeing is independent of the sense organs. That its meaning is manifest—being independent of both organs and objects—is clear. Question: Regarding the six sense organs...
All [of these] possess cognition. Now, why do you say that the substance of the eye lacks cognition? Answer: The Buddha’s intention is indeed so; it does not stem from mere conjecture.

As has been demonstrated through the comparison of the two types of darkness, the sense organ of the eye is in every respect identical to the lamp. Since the two types of darkness are the same, the two ways of seeing the objects before them are likewise the same.
Just as the "seeing" by the lamp was refuted, the "seeing" by the eye is also refuted; their meaning is identical. This applies even unto...
The same applies to the designation of "manifest color" (varṇa) as being without cognition. If the eye possessed cognition, how could it be the same as a lamp? Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Seeing and awareness are without cognition; they exist due to form and emptiness. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also provides clear evidence, stating:
"This body is without cognition, like earth, wood, tiles, or stones. Because the essence of the eye is without cognition, the seeing that manifests before one—
This is precisely the true vision that is fundamentally detached from the sense organs and their objects. This is what is meant by "shattering false vision to reveal true vision.
From the initial inquiry regarding the mind and the eyes at the beginning of this fascicle until now, the meaning has finally been concluded. II.
Clarifying that the nature of vision is unchanging. A. A silent request.
Although Ānanda had heard these words, he and the great assembly remained silent with their mouths, yet their minds were not yet enlightened.
Still hoping for the Tathāgata’s compassionate voice to provide further instruction, they joined their palms, purified their hearts, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful teaching.
Regarding "his mouth remained silent": previously, Ānanda took what was the mind to be the seeing; the Buddha rejected it, saying it was not the mind.

Then, Ānanda took what was the seeing to be the mind; the Buddha again said it was the mind. [Ānanda] remained silent because he knew that his intoxicated eloquence was of no benefit. Regarding "those who have not yet awakened":
although they have heard that the nature of seeing is the mind, they have not yet been able to suddenly shatter all delusions; their condition is thus like that of those who have not yet awakened.
Furthermore, although the nature of seeing is detached from the sense organs and their objects, this nature perceives external things due to the conditions of the organs and objects.
Thus, because adventitious defilements have not yet been removed, the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness has not been perfected; therefore, one has not yet attained awakening.
To "await the Buddha’s compassionate instruction" is precisely to request the World-Honored One to open one's eye of the Way. II. The Actual Instruction. Now, as for the teaching:
There are four aspects [of the teachings]: first, the Tripitaka; second, the Shared; third, the Distinct; and fourth, the Perfect. These four teachings collectively elucidate two principles:

the Tripitaka and the Shared elucidate the Truth (*satya*), while the Distinct and the Perfect elucidate the Middle (*madhyama*). The distinction between the teachings that elucidate the Truth lies in their methods—whether they analyze emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā*) or realize the essence as empty (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The distinction between the teachings that elucidate the Middle lies in whether they refer to the "limited middle" (*butian zhong*) or the "perfect middle" (*yuanzhong*). This is the basis by which these four teachings are differentiated. Therefore, it is not...

Regarding the term "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*): the conventional refers to phenomena (*dharmas*). By contemplating the conventional, one realizes the Middle Way of Truth. This "Middle Way of Truth" is termed "principle.

These two principles and the single phenomenon together constitute the Three Truths. Now, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* teaches the Real through the provisional, certainly incorporating the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).

The Separate Teaching explicates the sequential method: first emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then the provisional (*upāya*), and finally the Middle. However, the actual practice of the contemplation of emptiness utilizes the methods of the Treasury [Teaching] (*Kṣetra-śāsana*) and the Penetrating [Teaching] (*prativedha-śāsana*).
This is the skillful means (*upāya*). In the present text, because Ānanda has not yet attained awakening, the Buddha takes as his cause the initial awakening at the Deer Park to clarify this for him;

is this not the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching? Since this text incorporates the *Āgama* teaching, there must necessarily be the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) in the preceding and following passages.

Furthermore, the act of leading the *Āgama* into the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) is precisely what constitutes the Shared Teaching. The purpose of this passage’s introduction is to follow upon the previous discussion of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) responding to conditions.

There are external dharmas. Although the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is manifest, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) still remain; these are merely adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*).

The sense organs and objects are the guests, while the nature of seeing is the host; one must remove the guests to preserve the host. As long as the sense organs and objects have not been emptied, they are collectively metaphorized as "dust";

one must remove this dust to preserve the emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Only then does it accord with the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness (*śamatha-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This is what Cunda [realized].
Awakening can assist in explaining the realization of one's nature; this is the intent behind the Buddha’s inquiry. The text is divided into three parts:
first, the examination of the name to verify awakening. First is the question:
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which possessed the webbed fingers like soft cotton-wool and emitted light, and opened his five wheel-like fingers to instruct Ānanda.

And to the great assembly: When I first attained the Way in the Deer Park, I spoke to Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya and the other five bhikṣus, as well as to you fourfold assembly, saying that all sentient beings fail to achieve the state of Bodhi or Arhat solely because they are deluded by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
By what means did you then attain awakening and now achieve these holy fruits?
*Tūla* (兜羅綿) is translated here as "fine fragrance. In meaning, it is rendered as "ice" (*bīng*). Alternatively, it is called *tūsha* (兜沙), which means "frost";
it is named after its color. Or it is called *dūramaya* (妬羅綿); *dūra* is the name of a tree, and since the cotton is produced from that tree, it is so designated.
*Xunwen* (熏聞) states: "The Buddha’s hands are soft and supple; moreover, they are joined by webbing (*jiaman*) that resembles this cotton. (32)
Regarding the marks [of a Great Man], it is said that the five fingers of the hands and feet are joined by webs superior to those of other people; this is precisely that mark.
It appears that from the time he previously clenched his fingers into fists, he has now finally extended his hands.

As for "Deer Park" (Mṛgadāva), it is called a Deer Garden because it was the dwelling place of a herd of deer. Long ago, when Śākyamuni was practicing the bodhisattva path, he lived in this garden as a king of deer.

The account of the Compassionate One saving the herd of deer is found in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*). When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he resided at the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) preaching the Dharma.

It was named after the trees, and is also called the "Peach Grove" (*Nālika*). It was also known as the "Seers' Garden" (*Ṛṣipatana*), as it was the dwelling place of two seers. As for the five bhikṣus:
when the Prince entered the mountains to study the Way, his father the King, out of longing and concern, sent these five men to follow and attend him. The first was Kauṇḍinya; the second...
Aśvajit is the bhikṣu Aśva-jit. Traipusa is also named Mahānāman. Daśabalakāśyapa is the fourth. The fifth is Kulika-putra.

○ Part Three: The Three Clarities and the Vision of the Permanence of Nature. Section Two: The Request. Subsection One: A Joyful and Secret Request.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil and composed.

They reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with the discriminating shadows of conditioned objects. Today they have attained awakening, like a child who has been separated from its mother’s milk.
Suddenly encountering his compassionate mother, he joined his palms and paid homage to the Buddha, wishing to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false,

Previously, when the primary interlocutor requested instruction on the nature of stillness and permanence, the Buddha, having clearly seen that the nature is unmoving, spoke of its stillness.
Now the great assembly wishes to hear the two types of illumination regarding the nature, further exploring the meaning of its permanence. That which is subject to arising and ceasing is impermanent;
that which is not subject to arising and ceasing is permanent. As for those who have heard the instruction, they have heard that the seeing-nature is detached from the sense organs and their objects.

Upon receiving these instructions, his body and mind became serene and composed, which was entirely different from the previous state when he was startled, left his seat, wept repeatedly, and harbored anxiety and fear;
