Commentators of old have maintained that the former demonstration showed Ānanda’s vision was free from movement, while the latter demonstration showed King Bimbisāra’s nature was free from arising and ceasing.
While these appear similar at first glance, their meanings must necessarily differ. Now, within the midst of arising and ceasing, the Tathāgata reveals non-arising.
"Extinction" refers to the transformation of what is changing into what is unchanging. How could this be considered the same as the view that while the body moves, the seeing itself does not move?
I humbly submit that this passage treats "arising and ceasing" and "non-arising and non-ceasing" as two entirely distinct paths; its general purport does not differ from what preceded it.
However, whereas the previous text did not do so, this section provides a detailed clarification of impermanence in order to reveal the permanence of the seeing-nature. This must be emphasized.
Thus it is explained; therefore, it is said that [the text] reveals the true and the false, and so forth. II. The King Prasenajit’s Manifest Inquiry.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kosala rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha:

"In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I saw Kātyāyana and Ajita Keśakambalin both declare that when this body perishes after death, its cessation is called Nirvana. Although I encountered [them],..."
The Buddha still harbors doubts. How can he manifest and bring to realization this state where the mind is neither arising nor ceasing?
All those present in this great assembly who remain with outflows (āsrava) now wish to hear it.
The *Renwang Banruo Jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) states that King Candraprabha fulfilled the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Now, he is shown as one who harbors doubt in order to refute the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Kātyāyana is his clan name; his personal name is Kālakokāṭa, which translates as "Ox-Neck" or "Shear-Cut.
This man taught that all phenomena both exist and do not exist. Vīrāḍikā is the name of his mother; his own name is Sañjayin, which translates as...
The *samyakpradhāna* (right efforts). It is said that sentient beings attain the Way spontaneously when their time has matured, just as a ball of thread, once fully unwound, comes to rest.
Furthermore, it is said that after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, one naturally attains the Way. Both of these non-Buddhist schools adhere to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, this is translated here as "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) and also as "non-extinction" (*anirodha*). They claim that after death there is total annihilation and nothingness.
The nature of seeing and hearing is itself peace and bliss, nirvana. King Bimbisāra also considered this to be otherwise;

however, once one personally realizes the eternally abiding mind, all doubt will be forever severed. "To develop and transcend" means to cast off and disperse [delusions]. "The ground of non-arising and non-ceasing" refers to the eternally abiding mind.
Ānanda and the great assembly both requested [an explanation of] both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing, as evidenced by what follows.
King Bimbisāra displayed [the nature of] arising and ceasing; because he appeared to already understand impermanence, he requested only that which is without arising or ceasing.

(2) The second part, the response, has two sections: (1) the opening instruction, and (2) the clarification that the body undergoes transformation. Regarding the desire to clarify the eternally abiding while first clarifying transformation:
one must first shatter the false before manifesting the true. If the false phenomena are not exhausted, True Suchness will not [be revealed].
[The Buddha] manifested this. Among those various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who does not claim for themselves that they have already realized the true and eternal?

Because they have not yet destroyed delusion, they immediately manifest [it as] the truth, thereby falling into perverse and inverted views. King Bimbisāra’s rank was equivalent to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and he deeply understood the Dharma-gates;
therefore, [the Buddha] first caused him to realize impermanence.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now. I ask you again: does this body of yours remain eternally like a diamond, indestructible, or is it subject to decay and transformation?
"World-Honored One," [the King replied], "this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and perish."
The Buddha said, "Great King, you have never yet experienced extinction; how then do you know of extinction?

"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has not yet been extinguished, I observe that before my eyes every thought-moment shifts and passes away, renewing itself without ceasing, like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and perishing.
As this process of perishing continues without rest, I am certain that this body must eventually come to total extinction."
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. You have now reached an age of advanced decline. How does your countenance compare to that of your youth?
"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "in my former childhood, my skin was smooth and lustrous; as I grew into adulthood, my vital energy was full."
Now that my age has declined and I am pressed by senility, my physical form is withered and emaciated, and my spirit is clouded and dim. My hair is white and my face is wrinkled;
I shall not last much longer. How can I compare myself now to the time when I was in the full vigor of youth?
The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical form should not have suddenly decayed. The King replied, "World-Honored One, through subtle and secret transformation, I truly do not perceive it;
yet the shifting flow of cold and heat has gradually brought me to this state. Why is this?
At the age of twenty, though I was called young, my countenance was already aged compared to when I was ten. At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty."
Now I am sixty-two years old. When I reflect on my state at fifty, I appear as robust as ever. World-Honored One, I observe this subtle shifting;
although such decay occurs, the interval of its transition is limited to ten years.

If I were to contemplate it with minute attention, would the change be merely once in a decade or two? In truth, it is a change that occurs year by year. Not only does it change year by year, but it also changes month by month.

Transformation! How can it be that the months change and the days shift? Reflecting deeply and observing with discernment, one finds that between every instant and every moment, nothing can remain stationary.
Thus, we know that this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

The text consists of four rounds of question and answer. At that time, because King Bimbisāra was advanced in years, the Buddha did not personally proclaim the meaning of impermanence, but instead had the king describe it himself;
thus, the principle of arising and ceasing was fully revealed through his gradual decline.

Of the four rounds, the first two provide a brief explanation, while the latter two provide a detailed exposition. In the first question, the present is contrasted with what follows after death. For now—
Whether one speaks of annihilation after death or refers only to the present, since the King has already spoken of what follows death, he asks again regarding impermanence;
thus, the word "again" is used. The question concerns two extremes: first, permanence; second, impermanence. Within impermanence, there are further two meanings:
change is one meaning, and destruction is another. Yet, King Ajātaśatru has definitively categorized this body [as falling under one of these].

That final cessation is also the natural law of things; it is not a defiled view of nihilism. Because the Buddha knew that King Bimbisāra was capable of contemplating impermanence, he further examined the causes of transformation and extinction.
In his response, he definitively established impermanence, stating at the outset: "Impermanence is transformation and decay.
This means that by observing what is present before one, one knows the ultimate reality. If what is present does not cease, then the future likewise will not.
It does not perish. Since present transformations perish, one can know that future transformations will likewise perish.

This immediate, moment-to-moment transition and cessation is the subtle characteristic of impermanence. Because these are formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), the text speaks of "moment-to-moment.

In the passage, it first states the reason and subsequently states the newness. This ever-newing is a conventional designation for continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*). The text contains both the principle and the analogy.
Combined. It is like fire burning wood; the statement that there is a gradual dissolution and extinction has two meanings: first, gradual dissolution; second, ultimate extinction.
Regarding "extinction" (*yinwang*) in the subsequent analogy, there are likewise two senses: extinction and disappearance.

The third question compares flourishing and decline, arising from the premise that things shift and pass away without abiding, thereby elucidating the meaning of the initial question and answer. Indeed...
Both body and mind are impermanent. Because the impermanence of the physical form is easily perceived by people, he further inquires about his countenance.

"Fifteen" refers to childhood, before the capping ceremony. However, the Buddha asked only about two periods; the King added the stage of full maturity, thus making three periods—namely, youth, middle age, and old age.
"Infant" (*hai*) refers to one who has just formed a physical body; "child" (*ru*) refers to one who requires others for nourishment.

"Moreover, 'mò' (耄) refers to being clouded and forgetful. The *Lǐjì* states: 'At eighty or ninety, one is called mò. Although King Anāthapiṇḍika was sixty-two years old, he is here described as being clouded and forgetful.
'The physical form is withered and haggard' explains 'shuāi' (衰, decay); 'the spirit is dark and dim' explains 'mò' (耄, senility). 'Dài' (逮) means 'to reach' or 'to approach.
To say he will 'reach' death implies that how could he possibly compare to his former vigor? It is likely that 'dài' (逮) should be read as 'dài' (殆), which means 'almost' or 'nearly.'"
The fourth question. From the King’s response, it emerges that [the inquiry] originated from the three times; thus, the meaning of the second question and answer is established.
Because the Buddha wished for King Ajātaśatru to contemplate impermanence in detail, he asked whether [the body] would not decay instantaneously.

In the response, the phrase "I truly do not perceive" means that since the principle of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) does not abide and fundamentally belongs to the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), it is already unperceivable. Later, the Sūtra says: "Nail... (referring to *nakha*).
This refers to the fact that while the vitality of long hair fades and the wrinkles of a guest appear, day and night replace one another without any awakening to this process.

The phrase "gradually approaching" answers the objection that [the body] does not decay instantaneously. In the subsequent analysis and explanation, the coarse signs of impermanence are first described as increasing over ten years;
within this passage, there are three advances and three retreats: the first advance reaches twenty years, followed by a retreat to ten years, and so on. Next...
Advancing to thirty and retreating to twenty; advancing to sixty and retreating to fifty.

Without advancing, one cannot perceive the aging of the years; without retreating, one cannot perceive the gradual decline. Next, describing the subtle signs of impermanence, there is a reduction by a decade:
tracing back from sixty-two to the age of fifty already constitutes one [period].
To record the past, one calculates by reducing the years; a *kṣaṇa* is the most fleeting of times.
From years, months, days, and hours down to the *kṣaṇa*, every thought-moment passes without ceasing—this may be called a true realization of impermanence. Now, as for this impermanence:
This is the root of entering the Way and the initial gateway for contemplating the Dharma.
To discuss impermanence prior to seeing one's nature is precisely as Mañjuśrī said in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra: "That which can be seen cannot be seen again."
In this way, one does not use the second thought to take the first thought as an object, thereby seeing the nature and attaining its reality.
○ Second, demonstrating that the nature is without arising or ceasing; Part One: Examining the True Nature.
The Buddha told the Great King: "When you see that transformations and changes ceaselessly shift and alter, you realize and know their extinction.
At the very moment of that extinction, do you know of anything within your body that does not perish? King Prasenajit joined his palms and said to the Buddha: "I truly do not know."
"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to change. "Awakening to the cessation" means knowing that you have ceased. Within the body, there is that which does not cease. As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"It is like a bhikṣu observing water free of insects who thinks to himself: 'Is that which moves in this [water] an insect or dust?
After looking for a long time without ceasing, he finally realizes it is dust, yet it is not clearly perceived. Thus it is with the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes.
Observing the Tathāgata-nature within one's own body is likewise not clearly understood. That sūtra contains ten similes;
the present sūtra states that what is indestructible within the body is identical in meaning to *nirvāṇa*.

In that sūtra, the movement of a magical charm (*kṣetra*) is used as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*), while the non-movement of dust is used as a metaphor for Buddha-nature. Here, however, birth and death are taken as the lack of clarity. Not...
The principle that arising and ceasing constitute the Buddha-nature is likewise no different.
Because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes do not yet understand it clearly, the King replied that he did not know. II. The Tathāgata’s Revelation.
The Buddha said, "I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished. Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother led me to visit the deity Jīva, and as we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the water of the Ganges.
The Buddha said, "Great King, according to what you have said, at the age of twenty, you were already in decline."
"From ten years of age up to sixty, days, months, years, and seasons shift and change from moment to moment.

When you were three years old and saw this river, and then reached the age of thirteen, what was the water like? The King said: 'It was exactly as it was when I was three; there was no difference at all.'"
"Even up to this year at sixty-two, there has been no change. The Buddha said, 'Now you see for yourself that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled;

your face is certainly more wrinkled than it was in your youth. Thus, as you now look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between the vision of the river when you looked at it as a child and now that you are old?
The King replied, 'No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, 'Great King, [is there any difference in the seeing itself?]"'
"Though your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled. That which wrinkles is subject to change;

that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes extinction. That which is unchanging fundamentally has no arising or ceasing. How, then, could birth and death affect it?"
Yet [the Buddha] still cites those such as Maskarī Gośālīpūtra, who all claim that after this body dies, there is total extinction.
In the text, the Tathāgata first grants their premise and then demonstrates the truth. He asks: "In how many years have you seen the Ganges? This indicates that what is seen is the true nature.
Or perhaps one might suspect that this "seeing" is the seeing within the sense organ; however, one does not realize that the seeing within the sense organ is actually [the true nature].

To be separated from the sense organs and their objects is truly because the deluded mind has not yet been eliminated; thus, the nature of seeing follows conditions and wanders through birth and death.

If one sees the nature of seeing as separate from delusion, it is also separate from all conditions. If one uses the conscious mind to grasp at conditions, then the sense organs and their objects can never be severed.
If the conscious mind does not arise, where would the sense organs and their objects be? To return to the true source, one must relinquish this [deluded] seeing-nature.
There is no other way. Jiaoguang did not grasp this meaning and alone advocated the doctrine of "using the faculty [of sight] rather than consciousness.
He claimed that the nature of seeing resides within the faculty; when it merely reflects objects like a mirror without further analysis, that is the nature of seeing.
Once thoughts arise and analysis occurs, it belongs to consciousness. I, the fool, say: when thoughts do not arise...
The sense organs (*indriya*) are likewise unobtainable; yet Jiaoguang claims that the organs exist herein, asserting it is merely because the consciousness-mind has not yet been forgotten.
The previous instances of the blind man gazing into darkness and the testing of vision by raising a fist both pointed directly to the present seeing.
Is this not precisely what is meant by "ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena" (*avidyā eva dharmatā*)? One should know that within these two kinds of fundamental roots...
The meaning of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* as the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is seen here. The Ganges is also called the *Gaṅgā*;

it is said to have descended from the heavenly realm, as explained in the *Direct Commentary on the Medicine Master [Sūtra]* (*Bhaiṣajyaguru-vyākhyāna*). Though the world undergoes the transformation of the "blue seas and yellow sands," the Ganges remains unchanged.
Taking this as the object-field perceived is sufficient to manifest that the perceiving subject is without transition. In the King’s response:
Regarding the statement, "He immediately knew it was the water of the Ganges River": the King’s nature was alert and discerning;
through this single instance of recognition, he recorded his past vision. By answering with what he knew, he demonstrated that the nature of seeing is identical to the principle of the mind.
Youxi (Yongming Yanshou) stated that there are three layers of meaning in this passage: first, it relies upon the water of the Ganges; second, it advances to the contemplation of the river.
Regarding the "essence of seeing": the third [verse] clarifies the nature of this essence of seeing. As it says, "The nature of this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled.
Although there are three stages, the primary intent lies in the nature itself.

When the Buddha first asked, "When you were three years old and saw this river, how was its water when you reached the age of thirteen? This clarifies that the water is no different, because it is that which is being seen.

It says, "I see with my ears. The meaning of this passage does not directly reveal the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). In the first fascicle, the faculty of the eye was contrasted with the nature of seeing;
now, the nature of seeing is revealed by means of the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddha*). It is here that the term "essence of seeing" truly originates.

Previously, when distinguishing the faculty of the eye, it was stated that "this nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye," because the faculty of the eye lacks sentience and is fundamentally different from the nature of seeing.
Now, because the essence of seeing (*jijing*) is closely proximate to the Truth, it is said that "the nature of this essence of seeing has never once wrinkled.
If one distinguishes the clear essence of seeing, then the nature of seeing can be recognized; the essence of seeing appears to be the capacity for seeing.
Internally it relies upon the eye-faculty, and externally it relies upon objective forms; therefore, one who sees the Ganges is actually seeing the essence of vision (*darśana-tattva*).

However, the external reliance on objective forms is nothing more than a category of insentient things, and the internal reliance on the eye-faculty is likewise a class of manifest colors (*varṇa-rūpa*).
Thus, the essence of vision is not the true seer; that which is luminously capable of seeing is solely the nature of vision (*darśana-svabhāva*) alone. Vision...
The essence merely absorbs the sensory objects and directs them toward the internal faculties; therefore, that which belongs to the eye-faculty does not belong to the ear-faculty.
Once the faculties and their objects are established, they instead become obstacles to true seeing. How could the capacity for seeing be its own achievement?

According to the present text, it appears that the perceived object, the essence of seeing, and the nature of seeing—these three—are all immutable. However, the term "that which does not wrinkle" refers exclusively to the act of seeing itself.
As for "nature" (*xing*): if one were to claim that the essence of seeing does not wrinkle, one would miss the intent of the text.

However, this passage clarifies the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) and reveals that nature has three layers. First, it says the face wrinkles while nature does not wrinkle; are "wrinkling" and "not wrinkling" two separate paths?
Second, that which wrinkles changes while that which does not wrinkle does not change; are "changing" and "unchanging" two separate paths? Third...
That which undergoes transformation perishes, while that which does not transform has no perishing. Is it not the case that "neither perishing nor non-perishing" constitutes two distinct paths?
The underlying intent is perfectly clear; readers merely avoid speaking of it. For were there no distinction, the realization of the nature would not be certain.

Once the nature has been realized, pointing to the dharmas inherent within that nature constitutes entry into the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). The distinction between the Separate (Bie) and the Perfect lies precisely in whether or not these inherent dharmas are present.
They are different. Therefore, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) serves as the gateway to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which is what is called the "initial expedient means" (chūshì fāngbiàn).
*Mārga* in Sanskrit is translated here as "not seeing the Way" (bùjiàn dào). The phrase "and so forth" (*děng*) refers to the two individuals cited by King Nanda;
thus, among the six heretical teachers, three in total adhered to the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). II. Realization and Enlightenment.

Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe with certainty that after death one leaves this life to take birth in another. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and experienced a state of wonder never before attained.

The phrase "to believe with certainty" refers to the refutation of the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Previously, the arising and ceasing of existence were explained to refute the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); now, the vision [of reality] is revealed.

The nature [of this teaching] serves to shatter the view of annihilationism; therefore, the great assembly all rejoice. Otherwise, how could they feel joy merely by abandoning one life to enter another?
This concludes the first section on the regression of the distinct teaching (biejiao). The second section concerns the progression or regression of the perfect (yuan) and distinct teachings.

It is divided into two parts: first, the perfect; second, the distinct. The first part (the perfect) is further divided into two: first, a thorough elucidation of the perfect principle; second, the following [text].

Having previously sent this inquiry, Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One,
if this faculty of seeing and hearing is indeed neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion?"
"May you rouse your compassion to wash away my defilements.

Here, because the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, Ānanda harbored doubts regarding his previous statement that he had "universally announced" [the Dharma] to the great assembly. Previously, the Buddha spoke of "discerning and seeing";
now, by saying "hearing," it can be inferred that the other faculties function in the same manner. Although one knows that [consciousness] is neither arising nor ceasing, yet...
Not knowing that the faculties and their objects are one's own mind, which fundamentally lacks the characteristic of movement, one falls into perversion.
How could one know that non-arising and non-extinction is precisely the absence of perversion? Therefore, Ānanda’s question was incorrect. 2. The Correct Exposition.
Other masters have established ten stages to clarify the vision [of the nature of seeing]. This constitutes the fourth stage. I have observed Ānanda’s question [and its context].
Among these, the single instance of the character "see" (jiàn) merely restates what preceded; yet it also serves as an inquiry into the nature of hearing.

Why is it that within the Tathāgata’s response there is not a single instance of the character "see," while he nonetheless uses it to manifest seeing? This is because this passage constitutes the Buddha’s second turn of advancing the clarification of the perfect principle (*yuanli*).
In the first turn, the advancement of the perfect principle discussed the "mind-only" (*weixin*), while the retreat [from that] clarified...

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) distinguishes the seeing of nature, yet the Buddha’s intention necessarily lies in the Perfect [Teaching]. Therefore, in the second turn, he again reveals "mind-only" to shatter delusions;

this does nothing more than expand upon what was previously taught. Since within the text both matter-and-mind and the environment-and-beings are shown to be but the single mind, how could it merely be a matter of distinguishing the seeing?
To clarify the distinction between delusion and correctness, three similes are provided.
Immediately, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm and, lowering his hand, pointed it downward toward Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "Worldly beings consider this to be inverted;
as for me, I do not know who is upright and who is inverted. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then..."
"What do people of the world consider to be upright? Ānanda replied, "When the Tathāgata raises his arm, with hands as soft as *tūla* cotton, pointing it toward the sky, that is called upright.

The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda, "If this [arm] were inverted, with head and tail exchanged, and all people of the world looked at it with double the intensity, then you would know that your own body and those of all the Tathāgatas are pure."
The Dharma-body is elucidated through analogy: the body of the Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge," while your bodies are termed "inverted in nature.
When I previously inverted my arm to question Ānanda, it was made clear that it was but a single arm that possessed the distinction between being upright or inverted.
It is just as when there is only a single object, yet a distinction is made between an ordinary being and a Buddha.
*Mudrā* is translated here as "seal-hand" (*yinshou*), which is one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Whether [the hand] is inverted or upright, it merely accords with worldly convention;
its meaning is already sufficient, and there is no need for further explanation. Since the first wheel-hand points downward, the world already considers this to be inverted. Next, the Buddha—
Raising the arm is considered correct according to worldly convention. To speak of this as "inverted" means that pointing the arm downward is the inversion.
When the arm is raised, the tail becomes the head; if this same arm were inverted and hung down, the head would become the tail.
Thus it is said that "head and tail are exchanged. One doubling constitutes two turns: one turn is the inversion, and [the other] is the correct [position].
This constitutes one section. Because the Buddha-body within your own body is said to emerge from the arm, the entire body is cited as the subject of discourse.
The Tathāgata’s intention is to clarify that the wondrous nature is all-pervasive; this all-pervasiveness is precisely the Dharma-body, which is what is meant by Vairocana pervading all places.
Because it is free from all delusions and disturbances, it is called "pure. This is elucidated through analogy.
This can be elucidated by comparing the two arms to the case of hanging down the arms.
Just as the arms are not different [in substance] yet one is upright and the other inverted, so too it is with the body: though not different, there is the upright and the inverted.

For the arm of the Tathāgata is fundamentally neither upright nor inverted; it is sentient beings who distinguish between upright and inverted. This is just like the bodies of ordinary beings and Buddhas.
Originally there is neither correctness nor inversion, yet sentient beings are deluded and perceive them as correct and inverted. The passage "In the Tathāgata... serves as an analogy:

that which is called "correct universal knowledge" (samyak-saṃbuddha) in the Tathāgata is the same "correctness" as the "correct" [orientation] of an upraised arm; though the body is not different, it is termed "correct.
That which is called "inversion of nature" in sentient beings is the same "inversion" as an inverted arm; though the body is not different, it is termed "inverted."
In reality, there is no distinction between "correct" and "inverted" regarding the body and arms; these are merely forced designations of "correct" and "inverted.

As for the term "Samyak-saṃbuddha" (Perfectly Complete Knower): knowing the Middle Way is called "perfect" (samya), and penetrating the Dharma-realm is called "complete" (saṃbuddha). This "knowing" should properly belong to the mind.
That which currently belongs to the body is the meaning of the non-duality of body and mind. Second, [Aniruddha] was left bewildered by the question:
"If your body and the Buddha’s body are called 'inverted,' then in what respect is the name itself designated as inverted?"
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes; they were unaware of where their own bodies and minds were inverted.
Since you have said that by comparing your body with the Buddha’s body one can clarify the point, the meaning of "inversion" seems thereby understandable.
Therefore, he returned to question the great assembly: "If you compare your own body with the Buddha’s two bodies and yet name yourself 'perverse,' where exactly do you point as being perverse?
You should know that the body itself is not perverse; rather, perversion arises from delusion.
The great assembly had previously heard of the eternal, but had not yet realized its all-pervasive perfection; thus, they did not know what the locus of perversion was.
It is as follows: regarding the true and the false, the support and the supported—all are the essence of the wondrous mind, fundamentally pervasive and perfect.

What "correct" or "inverted" could there be? Yet, when they arise, one does not know this. "Deng-zhi" (瞪直) means to stare fixedly; it describes the manner of gazing straight ahead. "Meng" (瞢) is pronounced with the initial *mo* or *meng*. It means the eyes are unclear or dim.
○ Third, the correct demonstration of perfect interfusion, which has two parts. First, the correct demonstration that form and mind are not...
Second, in order to refute the loss and distortion of the true nature,
the Buddha, out of compassion and pity for Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered the ocean-tide voice to proclaim universally to all the sons of good gathered there:
"I have often said that the various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of cognition,"
All is manifested by the mind alone. Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence—the wondrous mind.
Why, then, do you all lose this original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, this jewel-like, brilliant, and wondrous nature, and instead recognize delusion within awakening?
This passage shows how the Tathāgata extensively reveals "mind-only" to clarify the perfect fusion of the three contemplations within the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.
As for the term "Ocean Tide Sound," it refers to the entire ocean surging forth so that no one fails to hear it; this may be used as a metaphor for the universal proclamation to the great assembly.
Now, to clarify that the Perfect Teaching differs from the Separate Teaching, the sound is also different from what preceded it. The text is divided into three parts; first, citing the past.
Regarding the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): what was previously termed the "Pure Dharma-body" (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*) is here called the "Mind.

Because the Tathāgata has realized this all-pervading mind, he enables the Dharma-body to extend vertically through time and pervade horizontally across space. Sentient beings have not yet attained the Dharma-body; they possess only the wondrous mind that can be discussed.
As stated in the first section clarifying the Perfect Teaching: "The arising of all phenomena is solely from the mind..."
This now expands upon what was previously stated. "Matter" (*rūpa*) refers to the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and a small portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

"Mind" (*citta*) refers to the mind-organ (*manas*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*). "Various conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to the aforementioned matter and mind. "Mental concomitants" (*caitasika*) are the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

The "all objective conditions" (*ālambana*) extensively enumerate all phenomena of truth and falsehood, the correct and the deviant, as well as their essential natures, characteristics, causes, and effects.

Regarding "manifested only by mind": the mind is like a master painter who can paint all manner of forms and images. If one were to say that the mind "creates" them, it would imply that there are actual objects to be found;
however, here it says they are "manifested by mind," meaning that the substance itself is entirely empty. All dharmas are provisional; "mind-only" is the Middle Way. Manifestation.
This is emptiness. It is evident that the three truths are present within a single mind. In the passage beginning with "Your body," it is shown that the mind contains both form and mind.
The textual meaning specifically distinguishes this from the Separate Teaching (biejiao). "The wondrously luminous true essence, the wondrous mind" directly points to the mind itself.
"Wondrous" means inconceivable; "luminous" means like a mirror manifesting images—illumination while remaining in stillness. Therefore, it is called "wondrously luminous. Although...
All phenomena manifest as truly devoid of external objects or mutual intermingling; therefore, they are called "true essence" (*zhenjing*).

Possessing the aforementioned meanings, they are further termed the "wondrous mind" (*miaoxin*). Both body and mind are manifestations of this wondrous mind and are nothing other than eternally abiding.

If, as other teachers claim, the principle of emptiness is true while conventional phenomena are false, then the true would be wondrous while the conventional would not be wondrous—how could such a view accord with the intent of the sutras? One must...
One knows that although body and mind are produced by ignorance, they actually manifest from the wondrous mind. Within sentient beings, they are entirely ignorance;
since there is not a single phenomenon that is not delusory, there exists the distinction between inversion and correctness. Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"To investigate the seven realms of existence in detail, one finds them all to be the signs of the various conditioned states of deluded sinking. Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the Tathāgata, they are the wondrous mind."
That which is manifested is such that there is no phenomenon that is not true; thus, it is designated as "non-erroneous" and "correct. Furthermore, in the subsequent text, there is the statement:
"The nature possesses the seven greats, one is the immeasurable, and the immeasurable is one. Considering the present passage, does it not clearly possess both meanings?
The former, when distinguishing from the deluded mind, says "discriminating in relation to objects"; when distinguishing from the sense organs and their objects, it says "the head... [and so forth].

It moves by itself. Now that we know this is the wondrous mind, how could it ever be pointed out as being external to the mind? Therefore, we know that what was taught in the preceding passages were all provisional teachings;

they were initially established as distinct [teachings] in order to lead toward the perfect. Since the distinct has been set aside to establish the perfect, the Perfect Teaching takes "mind-only" as its gateway.
Furthermore, one first contemplates the non-duality of form and mind, as stated in the *Non-duality Gate*: "The mind..."

The nature of the mind and its objects. Is it not thus that what is called "mind" undergoes transformation? Third, the section beginning with "How so? rebukes the loss and distortion of the true nature.
"Originally wondrous" means that it is fundamentally wondrous. As the fourth fascicle states: "Because of clarity, one establishes the object;
thus, clarity also has its faults. When clarity and wondrousness unite, only then is there no fault. Now, by saying "originally wondrous," it is stated that it is fundamentally without fault.
Wenling says: "Mind and nature are mutually designated as essence and function. Mind arises from the wondrous as illumination, like the light of a mirror;
nature is the wondrousness inherent in that illumination, like the substance of the mirror. This explanation is also correct.

Jizhong says that "fundamental wondrousness" specifically refers to the Middle Truth (*madhyamā-satya*). "Perfect wondrousness" is so called because it is perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*); furthermore, it proceeds from quiescence.
Yet there is illumination. That which is called "the mind" (citta) refers to the unchanging following conditions; this is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

As for "precious clarity," "precious" refers to the clarity that possesses all virtues; it further withdraws illumination to return to stillness. This is what is called "nature" (prakṛti), which refers to the unchanging following conditions.

This is the True Truth (*satya*). Regarding this True and the Conventional, if one examines the textual structure, each possesses the three truths; the Middle Way (*madhyamā*) likewise possesses the three. Combining them yields three, while separating them yields nine.
This is the fundamental nature of the mind possessed by all sentient beings, yet they do not realize that the non-duality of form and mind is entirely the wondrous mind.
They have lost much. What Arhat Ānanda previously perceived regarding the immovability of the nature of seeing was his awakening.
The state of not knowing that form and mind are non-dual is precisely the point of delusion; thus it is said, "to recognize delusion within enlightenment.
This passage first discusses the primary retribution of body and mind, while the subsequent text will then point to the secondary retribution of mountains and rivers.
Second, it simultaneously demonstrates the non-duality of the primary and secondary retributions in order to refute inverted conduct.

Obscuration and darkness become space. Within this space of dark obscurity, the coagulation of darkness becomes form. Form is intermingled with false conceptualization; the characteristics of these conceptions constitute the body.
As it gathers conditions, it stirs within; as it pursues external objects, it rushes outward. Taking this state of confused agitation as its fundamental nature, once deluded, it is taken as the mind.

You have determined that delusions reside within the physical body. You do not know that everything from the physical body outward—to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all a thing within the wondrously luminous True Mind.

It is like discarding a vast ocean of hundreds of thousands of miles of clarity and instead recognizing only a single bubble, taking that bubble to be the entire tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea. You are truly people who are doubly lost in delusion.
"Just as my hanging down of the hand is without distinction," the Tathāgata calls such a person "one who is to be pitied.

This passage is divided into two sections. The first clarifies the characteristics of perversion through the process of phenomenal creation; this is the beginning of obscured delusion, namely *anādikāla-avidyā* (beginningless ignorance).
Because ignorance is fundamentally present from the outset, it is called "beginningless. Due to this, the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) and the sense organs are formed.
Therefore, it is further said that this marks the beginning of delusion. Space is produced by ignorance; its entire substance is the delusion of ignorance.
It is like the empty space of the world: without the sun, moon, or lamps, there would be no light. Thus, one sees that space itself constitutes the state of dark obscurity.
Following the existence of space, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were subsequently produced. With the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as the cause and ignorance as...

The conditions that bind darkness constitute the color of the four great elements; this is the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment). Once there is the *niśraya-vipāka*, only then does the *mūla-vipāka* (primary retribution) exist.
By mixing the color of the four great elements with the deluded mind of false conceptualization, the marks produced by such false conceptualization become the bodies of sentient beings.
The upper character "color" (*sè*) refers to the color of the four great elements, while the lower character "marks" (*xiàng*) refers to the marks of sentient beings. [End of] "Zhòng."

The physical existence (*upapatti-bhava*) possesses both upright and distorted, refined and coarse characteristics. Because it is fundamentally formed by the accumulation of darkness (*andhakāra*), the five viscera are not seen as they are obstructed by the skin and membranes.

Following the formation of the body, one discusses the mind and consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*). The shadows of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) accumulate within, vibrating and shifting without ceasing.
The functions of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) each take external objects as their conditions, racing toward them without end. Thus, because there is no... [text ends].
The capacity for stillness and movement is one; yet, through the confusion of movement, it is taken as the nature of the mind. Youxi said: "In the beginning, there was no beginning;
ignorance fundamentally takes confusion and movement as its foundational realm. As the later text states: "Awakened clarity becomes empty dullness."
When they depend on one another, they become wavering; thus, both obscurity and movement are fully explained. The present text merely provides a brief summary.

Later, it is taught that the deluded thoughts of sentient beings take this obscurity and movement as the root of their affliction: being obscured, they are dark and dull, losing the luminosity of their original nature.
When there is movement, one becomes distracted and loses the stillness of the original nature. Once the wondrous clarity has been lost, the cycle of birth and death continues;
since this [deluded state] is taken as the mind, one resolutely identifies it as being within the illusory physical form—is this not the ultimate height of delusion?

Next, the text explains the reason for the inversion that constructs clarity based on principle; this is further divided into three parts: first, the teaching (dharma); second, the analogy; third, the refutation. First, the teaching:

The "intermediate physical body" (*śarīra*) is the "principal" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are the "support" (*āśraya*). All these are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind;
thus, the support and the principal are non-dual. As it was said previously: "All causes and effects, worlds, and even the finest motes of dust take their substance from the mind.
The present passage is likewise an expansion of what was previously stated, similar to the "Inconceivable Realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*) in the *Ten Gates of Non-Duality*.
There are two meanings, general and specific. The general resides in a single thought-moment; the specific distinguishes between form and mind. The present text is likewise so:
the wondrously luminous true mind is the general, while form and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants, are the specific.

If one does not consider the specific, one will not know that one’s own mind originally possesses all phenomena, and will instead assume that all phenomena are produced by deluded thoughts. If one does not consider the general, then...

If one does not realize that all phenomena appearing before us are but the single mind, yet perceives form and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, each as distinct and different, how can one accord with the principle of the single characteristic and single flavor?
To know both the whole and the parts, the intent is to subsume the particulars into the whole;
only then can the entirety of the nature of mind be attained. The scriptural text appears to clarify the true endowment while also encompassing the delusory endowment, by means of form...
The mind, its environment, and the correct [receptacle] world are all the wondrous mind. How could they not be fully present? Jingxi said:

"Others all know that everything is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), yet they do not know that the body and the land reside within the single mind. Siming said: "The single mind manifest before us inherently possesses a thousand dharmas;
this is the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*). Next is the analogy: the measure of the mind is as vast as hundreds of thousands of great oceans. Perfect...

Being free from the three delusions is like the clarity of the ocean. When one contemplates the analogy of the mind, one knows that both the support (the environment) and the supported (the body) are fundamentally wondrous.
If the substance of the support and the supported—the physical form and the mind—were not originally this wondrous mind, why would it be compared to the clear, limpid great ocean?

To discard this measure of the mind and instead recognize only the mind within the body is merely to recognize the essence of a floating bubble. To speak of a "floating bubble" implies that it is not [the true nature].
This is the very foundation of clarification. It means that beyond this, there is ultimately no mind. As Ānanda said: "Apart from this awareness, there is nothing else.
This is like taking a floating bubble to be the tide of the entire ocean, or exhausting the full measure of the vast sea.
How could such a thing be possible? The third censure is twice as severe as the previous two; taking delusion and looking toward enlightenment is called the first "fold."
If one is already within awakening, how could there be a "doubling"? Previously, the hanging down of the hand was used as a metaphor for inversion;
yet this person’s inversion is entirely identical to that hanging of the hand. In reality, the hand has neither right-side-up nor upside-down, and the nature has neither delusion nor awakening.
Sentient beings delude themselves into seeing them as two, which is why they are objects of the Tathāgata’s compassion. [Section Two: The Audience Does Not Awaken. This passage continues until...
How is it that [the mind] acts as the master? This should constitute a separate section. What follows is a further question and answer;

it need not be combined with the preceding section to demonstrate that there is no place for vision to return. The intent of the present section is merely to refute the mind that conditions objects; its text concludes here. First, the presentation of doubt.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

"Although I have received from the Buddha such wondrous sounds and awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the fundamentally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I have awakened to the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma through sounds.

(Because I have not yet been able to forget words, there currently exists the sound of preaching; since I have awakened from the place of verbal expression, it is said that I have awakened to the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma. Now, with these..."

My mind relies upon what it beholds with reverence. (Presently, by means of a攀緣心 [pān-yuán-xīn, the攀缘心 "clinging and discriminating mind"], I believe the words of those whom I respect. I have merely obtained this mind, yet I do not dare to consider it my original, fundamental mind-ground.
I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and proclaim the perfect sound, uprooting the source of my doubts so that I may return to the Unsurpassed Way.

In this passage, the first part summarizes the Buddha’s intent; the second presents the root of the doubt. Those who pity and rescue do so by saving them from their inverted views, while those who provide profound instruction do so by teaching through the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna*).
The recipient of the teaching knows that what is shown is not ordinary, yet his conditioned mind has not been liberated; thus, he comes to weep.
In the first instance mentioned above, the Buddha revealed the perfect principle, but the recipient did not understand it, appearing as if he had not heard it at all. Therefore...
It is no longer doubtful that those of the Two Vehicles present at this assembly are like the deaf or the mute, for they do not know the flavor of the milk of the Avataṃsaka.

Now, with this second round, the teaching of "Mind-Only" is clearly revealed; they seem to have attained some understanding, yet it is not yet true awakening. How easy can it be to hear the Perfect [Teaching]?
The word "although" (*sui*) is a term indicating that [the realization] is not yet complete. As for "wondrous sound" (*miaoyin*), it refers solely to the preceding emergence of the ocean-tide voice.
In the following passage, the nature of the mind is indicated above. Although its names are many, the two characters "wondrously luminous" (*miaoming*) have already briefly encompassed them all.

Since both matter and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants, are all contained within the mind, it is called "perfectly complete" (*yuanman*). The simultaneous mention of "perfect" and "constant" indicates the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

The phrase "but I," etc., correctly describes how clinging to objects has not yet been forgotten. "Present" refers to the present; it means that the Buddha’s sound of the Dharma is currently manifest.

That which was previously relied upon is precisely the *ālambana* (the object of cognition), and that there is indeed within my breast a cognizing mind (*ālambaka*) is likewise presently evident and reliable.
Thus, subject and object are clearly distinct; this is merely the appearance of undispersed conceptualization.
Since the Tathāgata is the one whom we look up to with reverence, how could I dare not believe his words? "Yun" means to believe. I have simply attained this mind.
This "mind" refers to the mind that takes objects as its condition. Such a faculty of faith exists when mindfulness arises, and does not exist when mindfulness does not arise.

Since thought has not yet been abandoned and the faculties have not been detached from their objects, how could this be the original ground of the mind? I earnestly hope you will grant me the perfect sound (*paripūrṇa-svara*) to uproot the root of my doubt.
It seems that the one capable of uprooting the root of doubt is what is called the "perfect sound"; the Buddha cannot help but [respond].
He distinguished them by addressing him separately. 2. The Buddha’s Reprimand of the Two [Views] A. Dispelling the Teaching on the Object of Cognition (divided into three parts:

Dharma, Parable, and Application). The Buddha addressed Ānanda: “You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a mind that conditions objects; this Dharma, too, is conditioned, and you have not attained the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).”
It is like a person pointing out the moon with their finger to another. That person, because of the finger, should look at the moon.

If, however, they look at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose the finger itself? Why is this? Because they have taken the finger used as a marker to be the bright moon.
Would they not only lose the finger, but furthermore fail to distinguish between light and darkness? How much more so... [the case of those who mistake the finger for the moon].
For this reason, you take the substance of the finger itself to be the nature of the moon’s brightness, yet you fail to discern the two natures of light and darkness.
You are just like this.
As the preceding passage states: "I have awakened to the Buddha manifesting the sound of the Dharma," yet now you continue to rely on the conditioned mind as the object of your veneration.
Thus we know that Ānanda valued the sound of the Dharma, believing that the ultimate truth resided therein;

yet he did not realize that by clinging to the literal text and becoming deluded regarding the principle, he had lost the intended meaning of the teaching. Therefore, the Buddha established a metaphor to enlighten him.

In the first part concerning the Dharma, it is said that because Ānanda had not yet attained true awakening, when he listened to the Dharma with a mind capable of objective perception (*ālambana*), the Dharma likewise became an object of perception; thus he had not truly attained the perfect and eternal.
Regarding the *dharmatā*: next, within the analogy of the finger pointing at the moon, there are three layers of delusion. First, delusion regarding the substance of the moon;

second, delusion regarding the substance of the finger—the text first indicates this and subsequently explains it; third, delusion regarding light and darkness, which likewise first indicates and then interrogates and explains.

If one considers this according to the analogy, these refer to those who are utterly ignorant; therefore, their faults are fully set forth. Third, as for the correspondence [to the meaning]: the analogy represents the Buddha employing his teaching.
Pointing to his own heart to show it to others, he intended that those present, upon hearing the teaching, should observe their own minds.

If one clings to the verbal teaching as being one's own mind, such a person is not only deluded regarding their own mind, but is also deluded regarding the teaching. Why? Because they take the expressive teaching to be their own mind.
Not only are they deluded regarding the teaching, they also fail to recognize the distinction between that which is conditioned and that which is unconditioned. Why?

Therefore, one takes the very substance of the object-condition to be one's own mind; because there is no object-condition and nothing to be cognized, it is shown to you that [the subject] is likewise so.
(2) Second, the refutation of the mind that acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka-citta*) also consists of both the dharma and the analogy.

If you consider this discriminating mind that perceives the sounds of my Dharma-teachings to be your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess a nature of discrimination even apart from those discriminating sounds.
It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; having rested for a short while, he departs and never remains there permanently.
Yet the attendant at the pavilion has nowhere to go; he is called the "pavilion master. This is also like this:
if it were truly your mind, it would have nowhere to go. How could it then be separated from the body? It is not merely that sound is the discriminating mind.

They discriminate that the self’s appearance is free from all marks of form and possesses a non-discriminative nature; thus, they continue until discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness.
Kauśalya and others mistake this for the "Dark Principle" (Tattva). It is a non-discriminative nature that is detached from the conditions of all phenomena.
Then your mind-nature each has something to which it returns; how can they be the master?

The meaning contained within this passage involves both concession and refutation. One must understand that the words of Ānanda’s presentation of his doubt in the preceding text were extremely rigorous in their discernment.
Now, the first phrase of this current passage restates the preceding text. "Discrimination" refers precisely to the six consciousnesses; that is to say, by means of the Buddha—
The perfectly wondrous sound of the Dharma you have heard was for the sake of your own perfectly wondrous mind.
Having received the Buddha’s wondrous voice, there is a perfectly wondrous reflection within your breast that seems to be this wondrous mind; therefore, he specifically rebukes you, saying:
"If you discriminate this as being your mind, then there should be a nature capable of discrimination that exists apart from the sound being discriminated. This is a concessive argument (*yokushō*).

Furthermore, when this sound is heard, a simultaneous mental consciousness arises, which is called "discrimination by recollection" (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). The subsequent succession of moments is called "discrimination by calculation" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
Since these all arise in dependence upon objects (*viṣaya*), how could they be intrinsic in nature? In the analogy, the meaning encompasses both concession and refutation.
The "guests" represent the six sense objects and the six consciousnesses; the "inn" may be compared to suffering; and the "host of the inn" represents [the ālayavijñāna].
"True mind. "Going" refers to going at a particular time; that which is eternally abiding is said to have no going.
In this context, the word "going" refers to the discriminating mind. If it were your true mind, then there would be nowhere to go.
This accords with the previous analogy of the innkeeper: having no going means being identical to the true mind. This is the concessive argument (*yong*). How can it leave sound and reach [the ear]?

How is it that [the mind] acts as the host? This employs the analogy of the guest and the host together; though [the guest] is few, they take away much, for the intent of the text lies in this taking away.
This section is divided into four parts. First, taking sound as the primary example: apart from sound, there is no nature of discrimination.
Thus, while the mind sometimes departs, since sound is merely a guest, is this [mind] not likewise a guest? Next, sound is used as an illustration.
Regarding form (*rūpa*): previously it was said that what one reveres is a conceptualization of one's own appearance;

since this conceptualization arises in dependence upon form, it lacks intrinsic nature even apart from form. Third, refuting externalist doctrines: as for the "Primal Essence" (*tattva*), according to the *Śata-śāstra*, it says:

First, one falls into the primordial darkness; from this arises consciousness (*buddhi*); from consciousness arises the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). From the ego-sense arise the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*);

from the five sense objects arise the five gross elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*); from the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties (*ekādaśendriya*). The twenty-fifth principle is the Puruṣa, the Lord of Truth (*ātman-tattva*).
The ancients spoke of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Apart from the principle of darkness (*tamas*), nothing exists outside of matter, mind, and space.

Now, upon analysis, none of these are found to exist. It is not mind; it is not matter, meaning it is not the five objects of sense or the five great elements (*mahābhūta*); it is not space, meaning it is not the element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*).
That which is neither of these twenty-four is precisely the principle of darkness. *Kauśika* is a name for a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), namely Makkhali Gosāla.
These are alternative designations, as explained in detail in the Tongzhou Commentary. Essentially, the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening (prakṛti-vijñāna) is constantly manifest before one;
yet the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), taking this as their primary object of perception, regard it as the "Dark Principle" (amūrta-tattva). Is this not a false view?

Those who have traditionally interpreted this all claim that the six discerning consciousnesses (ṣaḍ-vijñāna) do not function, while the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) as its object, conceiving of it as the "Divine Self" (ātman). This is precisely what the non-Buddhists hold.
This is what is grasped. The four types of retribution can be returned. As analyzed above, even if one were entirely devoid of them, one would still become an outsider;

how much more so when one gives rise to discrimination based on sounds and forms? If one is separated from the conditions of the sensory objects of dharmas, then there will be no shadows of sound or form within the breast.
At this time, that which discriminates the shadow of sound is returned to sound; that which discriminates the shadow of form is... [returned to form].
Returning this to the realm of form, it is clear that the former is a guest while the latter is the host of the pavilion.

This was already addressed in the first section following the exposition of the principle of perfect illumination (*myōen-ri*), where the discrimination of conditioned objects (*enjin-funbetsu*) was likewise criticized; the present point is largely identical to that. Second, the explanation of the Separate Teaching (*bekkyō*) is withdrawn.

In the first instance, when advancing to clarify the principle of the Perfect Teaching (Ekyō), it was stated that "it is mind-only. When retreating to clarify the Distinct Teaching (Bekkyō), it pointed to the nature of seeing.

The second instance is likewise. Furthermore, when retreating in the first instance to clarify the nature of seeing, the text first cites the example of a blind man staring into darkness to directly demonstrate that the nature of seeing is detached from both the sense organs and their objects;
yet Ānanda did not understand this, so subsequently, by means of the metaphor of the passing clouds and dust...
This analogy led those present to a semblance of understanding that the nature of seeing is detached from both objects and faculties; yet, this was not true understanding.

How could it be that the conditioned mind remains undetached while the faculties and objects are supposedly detached? Therefore, in the preceding chapter, the World-Honored One repeatedly refuted the conditioned mind;
now, in this second instance, he withdraws [the discussion] to clarify the nature of seeing, once again raising the point of detachment from objects before finally [proceeding].

Once again, he demonstrates the separation from the sense organs. As it is said, "The seeing of seeing is not seeing"—this is the separation from the organs. Since the objects are that upon which the essence of seeing relies, they are explained first.

Within this section on the "eight returns," the purpose is primarily to distinguish how the nature of seeing is detached from objects. This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the nature of seeing has nothing to return to;
second, responding to the reprimand and submitting a request for further instruction.
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."
In the question, the terms "that which has a source" (*you-huan*) and "that which has no source" (*wu-huan*) are used. That which arises from sound and form returns to sound and form;

it does not intersect with the nature of the mind, and thus it is "without a source. The subsequent text says: "Of these eight kinds of seeing, the clarity and luminosity of the seeing-nature—whom would you have return?
Ānanda did not understand this, and therefore he asked about the substance of that which has no source. (2) Next, he demonstrates that which has no source.
In the third and first sections, he briefly indicates his consent to speak.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for the fundamental source of the clarity of your seeing when you look at me—although this seeing is not the wondrous, ultimate clarity of the mind, it is like a second moon rather than a reflection of the moon.
You should listen attentively; I shall now show you the ground where there is nothing to be returned."
Although Ānanda asked about the wondrous mind, the Buddha did not proceed to clarify the principle of perfect luminosity, but instead used the nature of seeing to demonstrate a distinct meaning.
Furthermore, because the Buddha wished to demonstrate that which cannot be returned, he pointed out its non-returnability within the midst of that which can be returned;

thus he said "for now" (*qie*). In the previous chapter on King Bimbisāra, it first spoke of the "essence of seeing"; here, it again speaks of the "essence of seeing," clarifying its fundamental source.

Essentially, the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness, when located in the eye, is called the "fundamental source of the clarity of seeing. Here, "essence" (*jing*) carries the same meaning as "luminosity" (*ming*).
As the ten-fascicle [Avataṃsaka Sūtra] says: "Looking toward the east, there is already a subtle radiance (*jing-se*)," which is the sign that the marks of luminosity have not yet dispersed.

Because conceptualization and discrimination have not yet arisen, it is termed the "source of luminosity" (*ming-yuan*). This substance is a fusion of the real and the false; because it contains the real, it encounters objects.
One is able to see. Because it contains delusion, the perception of marks has not yet been forgotten.

Compared to the true mind, it lacks nothing but the single character "wondrous" (miao), for "wondrous" carries the meaning of the disappearance of marks. It is pointed out based on the present state, hence it says, "And you see me.
To have "you" and "me" still involves deluded seeing; only when both self and other are darkened in stillness is *śamatha* fully realized.
This illumination is called the "wondrous mind. There are three layers of metaphors. Gushan says: the first moon metaphor represents the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind;
the second moon metaphor represents the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing; and the reflection of the moon in water represents the discrimination of objects.
Gushan’s interpretation here is correct. The subsequent passage states: "Now you observe this assembly of sages throughout;
it is merely like [the reflection] in a mirror, with no separate analysis—this is the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*), which is the second moon. It further states:

"Your consciousness sequentially identifies and points out within it, 'This is Mañjuśrī,' and so forth—this is the mind of discursive thought (*ālambana-citta*), which is the reflected image of the moon."

Furthermore, within the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddha*), the phenomenal aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) is subject to reversion, while the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) is not subject to reversion. The six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are all subject to reversion;
this is the distinction between these two types of revertibility. An ancient said: "The second moon arises from pressing upon the eyes; the essence of seeing arises from delusion regarding the Truth.
However, once the eyes are no longer pressed, the second moon vanishes of itself. If one eliminates both subject and object, then [the essence of seeing likewise ceases]."
The true mind can be realized; therefore, within the essence of seeing, the ground that has nothing to return to is pointed out.
The meaning is as follows. II. Correctly Distinguishing the Objects and Seeing. A. Clarifying that objects can be returned. 1. Showing the eight objects. 1. Manifesting the objects.
Since their mutual nature is such that they can be returned, and their nature cannot be returned, first distinguish those that can be returned so that they may not...
"Ānanda, let that which can be returned be revealed.
This great lecture hall is wide open toward the east. When the sun rises in the sky, it is bright and radiant;

at midnight, during the dark fortnight when clouds and mist obscure the light, it is again dark and gloomy. Through the gaps of doors and windows, one sees through to the outside; yet within the walls and buildings..."
In the intervals between them, one again observes obstructions; in places of differentiation, one again perceives conditions. Within the stubborn void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness;
when the appearance of dense clouds arises, it entangles the turbid dust. When the sky clears and the mists subside, one again observes purity.

First, there are four pairs of signs indicating that [the light] can return: first, brightness and darkness; next, penetration and obstruction; next, emptiness and existence; and next, defilement and purity.
Within these, there are both essence (*tǐ*) and appearance (*xiàng*). The solar orb is the essence, and its brilliant radiance is the appearance.
The dark moon is the essence, and its dimness is the appearance. Among these six phrases, all precede the essence with the appearance, except for emptiness and dust, where the order is reversed.

It refers to the substance that follows after characteristics. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "The stubborn void returns to emptiness; the dense *pò* returns to dust. This is merely a case of alternating phrasing to produce literary elegance.
"Discrimination" (*fenbie*) refers to the differentiation of objective phenomena, such as high and low, curved and straight, blue and yellow, long and short, distant and near, and so forth.
"Conditioning" (*yuan*) means existence; it is spoken in contrast to the objective realm of empty space. "*Pò*" refers to the appearance of rising dust; "*fen*" (atmospheric haze) is also similar.
This is the element of air. ○ Second, clarifying the return:
Ānanda, you have all observed these various changing phenomena. I shall now return each to its original cause. What is the original cause?
Ānanda, these various changing phenomena return to the sun. Why is this? Without the sun, there would be no light; it is light.

Because of the sun, there is day; thus, the absence of the sun returns to day. Because of darkness, there is the black moon; thus, the absence of darkness returns to the black moon. Because of openings, there is light through doors and windows; thus, the obstruction of them returns to walls and eaves. Because of conditions, there is discrimination;

thus, the absence of conditions returns to non-discrimination. Because of solidity, there is emptiness; thus, the absence of solidity returns to space. Because of turbidity and dust, there is obscuration; thus, the clearing of them returns to a cloudless sky. Because of clarity and purity, there is fair weather; thus, the absence of these returns to a clear sky.

Regarding the various manifestations of transformation, there are four pairs and eight aspects, each mutually exclusive. For example, light may transform into darkness, and darkness may transform into light;
turbidity may transform into purity. These can never coexist; this is what is meant by "transformation.
As for their original causes—the sun, the dark moon, and so forth—"returning" means that light returns to the sun, which has no relation to the nature of seeing. Thus...
It is likewise when it returns to clarity and stillness. However, this "returning" is different from the former "returning.

You should know that the essence of vision is attached to the eight objects; once these eight characteristics are returned, the essence of vision itself can no longer be apprehended.
The meaning of the sutra is that if one wishes to exhaustively realize the essence of the non-returning state (*anāgāmin*), one must completely eliminate all returnable characteristics.
Since even presently existing objects such as light and darkness are still returnable, how much more so is the discriminating mind? Therefore, it is distinguished in this manner.

external objects possess characteristics, whereas the nature of seeing is without characteristics; is this not perfectly clear? [This is so] because you have not yet heard...

Ānanda, although these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are all alike what is beheld by your own pure essence of vision.

(2) Second, the conclusion regarding the error concerning objects and the self:

Ānanda, I shall now reprimand you for your failure to grasp the essential point. If, when you see, it is you who see and not I, then since this nature of seeing is all-pervasive, who else could it be?
Why do you doubt your own true nature, claiming that your nature is not real and seeking the truth from me?

yet, if your nature of seeing is all-pervasive and illuminates all things, who else could it be but you?

At that time, it was indeed Ānanda and not the Buddha. Because [Ānanda] asked how he could know that this was his own true nature, the Buddha now concludes by saying, "This is you, not me.

because it is seen in every single instance from the palaces of the sun and moon to the seven golden mountains, it is called pervasive. The word "pervasive" implicitly reveals that Ānanda possesses [this nature].

Although the two preceding sections clarify the Separate Teaching (biejiao) by way of concession, they are nonetheless the method for entering the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).

It is so. By clearly seeing that nature is not a thing, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are naturally shattered. Once the sense organs and objects have been shattered, one can then realize that these very organs and objects are one's own mind.
Otherwise, if one fails to shatter the delusion to reveal the truth, would this not be entirely identical to the views of the non-Buddhists?
The third section, concerning the progression and cessation of the Perfect and Separate [Teachings], is divided into two parts: first, clarifying perfect realization; next...

This clarifies the distinct principle. In the previous two sections, advancing to clarify the perfect principle, the treatise discusses "mind-only"; retreating to clarify the distinct teaching, it discusses "seeing nature.

third, it clarifies that perfect realization is free from both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity (*tathatā*). Regarding the first section, it first poses a question:

To contract and sever [the mind] is precisely to possess signs; only by further removing this doubt can one thoroughly penetrate the principle of signlessness.
Thus, the more Ānanda’s doubts deepened, the more profound the Tathāgata’s discourse became.

Yet, upon returning to the Jetavana Monastery, we see only the monastery grounds; entering the hall by the door with a clear mind, our vision reaches only as far as the eaves and corridors. World-Honored One, this...”
"I have seen it thus: its substance was originally pervasive throughout the entire world, yet now that I am inside this room, it fills only the room.

In the question, the distance of his vision is first described. Because the preceding text stated, "The nature of seeing is all-pervasive;
