When the nose comes into contact with these odors, there arises a consciousness that discriminates them.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that the nose and odors serve as conditions to give rise to nose-consciousness—
does this consciousness arise because of the nose and take the nose as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of the odor and take the odor as its constituent element?

The nose and fragrance are two phenomena; the arising of consciousness is one phenomenon. Since that which arises is singular, when one investigates its causes—the nose and the fragrance—[it is found that they are not the cause].
2. Reiterating the opponent’s position and refuting it (in two parts): 2.1 Refuting the claim that the nose constitutes a distinct realm (in two parts): 2.1.1 Establishing the inquiry.
Ānanda, if [the sense of smell] were produced because of the nose, then within your mind, what would you take to be the nose?
Would it be the physical form of the flesh and its two nostrils, or would it be the nature of the act of smelling and its movement?

The physical form is the *pāśubandha-indriya* (the sensory organ as a coarse, material object); the act of smelling is the *paramārtha-indriya* (the sensory organ in its ultimate sense). In the following text, it is argued that because the fleshly nose has no fixed location, it is difficult to establish the presence of this ultimate sense organ.
2. Refuting [the existence of the sense organs] by means of analysis: 2.1 Refutation based on the *pāśubandha-indriya*.

If one takes the physical form and substance of flesh to be the body, then the cognition of the body is contact; thus it is called the "body," not the "nose. What is called contact is simply an object.
Since even the nose lacks a [substantial] name, how can a sense-field (dhātu) be established?
The first phrase restates the [opponent's] position. According to worldly people, they all claim that the fleshy form constitutes the nose and ears.

By breaking down this misconception regarding the fleshy substance, [the text shows that] the fleshy form of the nose is fundamentally attached to the body; therefore, the fleshy substance is the body itself.

If one takes its object (viṣaya), it consists of categories such as cold, heat, pain, and itching—how could these not be the faculty of touch (spraṣṭavya)? Thus, it is identical to touch and so forth.

The first two lines clarify what is apprehended; the current two lines clarify what is not. Because the body supersedes the nose and touch supersedes fragrance—since they cannot belong to both simultaneously—they are both negated.
Since touch is the sensory object (viṣaya) of the body, it is said to be "identical to the object."
If even that which it grasps loses the name of "nose," how much more so its actual substance? 2. Refutation based on the supreme sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*).

If you take the act of smelling as the cognition, then in your mind, what constitutes this cognition? If you hold that the flesh constitutes the cognition, then the cognition of the flesh is fundamentally tactile and not olfactory.
If you hold that emptiness constitutes the cognition, then since emptiness is itself insentient, the flesh ought not to be conscious. If this were the case, then...

"Empty space is yours; your body is not the knower. If today Ānanda were truly non-existent, then since cognition would be produced by fragrance, that cognition would belong solely to the fragrance—what concern would it have with you?
If fragrant and foul odors must arise from your nose, then those two types of flowing air—the fragrant and the foul—would not arise from *eranda* or sandalwood trees.
If those two substances do not come to you, you yourself would have to smell your own nose."

Whether it be fragrance or stench—what is stench cannot be fragrance, and fragrance must not be stench. If you could perceive both fragrance and stench simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I questioned you, there were two Ānandas present; which of them was your true self?
If the nose were a single entity, fragrance and stench would not be two distinct things; that which is stench would become fragrance, and fragrance would in turn become stench.
Since these two natures do not exist, from what could the sensory realm be established?

The first phrase summarizes the point. "Taking the smelling and knowing" refers to the apprehension of the supreme sense-faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*). The second phrase raises an inquiry: by means of the flesh...

The refutation within the main text is divided into four sections. First is the refutation of the claim that the flesh constitutes cognition. Regarding the statement that "the flesh constitutes cognition":

in the preceding text, if one were to grasp the form of the flesh, one would merely be grasping the flesh itself; however, here, while grasping the form of the flesh, one also possesses the nature of olfactory cognition.
According to the common understanding of worldly people, who is there that does not take the fleshy nose to be the faculty of smelling? How could they possibly recognize their error?
Yes. Since you derive cognition from the flesh, you are still taking cognition as residing upon the flesh; therefore, it is said that the original contact is not with the nose.
Next, [the text] refutes the notion that emptiness constitutes cognition. "Emptiness" refers to the space within the nose that hangs downward.

In this case, there is the fallacy that the sense organ itself would be unable to perceive. Thus, the following expands upon this argument: if the empty space of the nose possessed cognition, then all...
If empty space were to possess cognition, it would follow that it must be you; thus it is said, "Empty space is you.
Since the flesh of the nose lacks cognition, it follows that the entire body lacks cognition; thus it is said, "Your body is not cognition. Mount Gu says:
"To say 'space is you' means one does not see its form; to say 'the body is you' means it cannot cognize. When sought in both ways, it is nowhere to be found. This is his explanation.

This is so. Regarding the third refutation, [the text] refutes the notion that fragrance constitutes cognition. Previously, because worldly people all take the fleshly nose to be cognition, it was refuted as "flesh-cognition.
Because one excludes the flesh and considers only emptiness, it was refuted as "emptiness-cognition.

Now, some may reckon that fragrance can give rise to ultimate reality, and thus rely entirely upon this fragrance; therefore, it is refuted as "fragrance-cognition. This is different from the following [refutation], where fragrance is said to produce consciousness.
The intention is that if one takes fragrance to be the cognition itself, then since there is no cognition apart from fragrance, cognition must inherently belong to the fragrance.

Fourth, the refutation of the arising of fragrance and stench within the nose. This arises as a shifting hypothesis based on the third refutation above. The hypothesis states: "It is not that they are unrelated;
rather, fragrance and stench reach the nose and the nose cognizes them. Since they are not perceived elsewhere, fragrance and stench arise within the nose. This...
It seems that [the opponent] intends for both fragrance and stench to arise together with the nose, yet the place of their arising is the nose.
As for what is called "necessarily," this refers to whether it is flesh or empty space; although the nose itself is difficult to determine, it must nonetheless rely upon the nose.

Since it is said that fragrance and stench arise at the nose, even when adopting the cognition of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one ultimately returns to the faculty of the nose (*ghrāṇendriya*) as the locus. Thus, in the subsequent refutation therein—
The argument consists of five points. First, the refutation based on the production of nasal breath from flowing [air]. "Flowing" means moving.
If moving air does not arise from wood but arises from the root, why is it called "flowing air"? Second, the refutation that two substances do not come together.
If both objects were to come [to the nose], one could say that fragrance and stench arise at the nose. But if neither comes, to what would the nose belong regarding fragrance and stench?
If they do not come and there is no fragrance or stench, it is clear that fragrance and stench do not arise at the nose.
Third, the refutation by means of fragrance and stench being mutually exclusive: fragrance and stench can never coexist. Even if one were to grant that it is fragrant, then it is not stinking;
if it is stinking, it must be distinct from fragrance. Even if one were to grant that it is stinking, the same logic applies.

This appears to be stated in reference to the time when [the object] has not yet arrived. Fourth, the refutation by considering the sense organ in relation to its object: this means that if the nose were not biased toward either [fragrance or stench], it would be able to perceive both simultaneously.

If both [smells] were heard by the same [organ], they would be simultaneous; thus, a single person should possess two noses. Furthermore, since a person is defined by their sense organs, there should be two people.
Should the one perceiving the fragrance be considered Ānanda, and the one perceiving the stench be considered Ānanda? Fifth, the argument refutes [the claim] by following the objects from the organ.
Having previously refuted the existence of two noses, we now maintain that a single person possesses only one nose, and both fragrance and stench [are perceived by it].

That which arises from one nose is again used by that same nose to perceive; this is non-duality. Since the foul is already broken down [into its parts], the arising of fragrance is itself the arising of stench.

Because perceiving fragrance is itself perceiving stench, Changshui said: "If there were no fragrance or stench, what would be called 'arising' such that it could be known as the element of consciousness?
Question: This text speaks of "refuting the ultimate" (*paramārtha*). Why is this considered the ultimate?
Question: "Is it so? Answer: "The olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) is that which knows by smelling; this is its ultimate function (*paramārtharūpa*).
People say that because the ultimate faculty is attached to the physical form (*māṃsapiṇḍa*), one perceives fragrance and stench, and thus take the flesh itself to be the knower. To refute this:

if one takes the body’s peripheral sense organ (*vyañjanendriya*) as the knower, then taking the body’s ultimate faculty would merely amount to the flesh’s cognition. That which is known is actually tactile contact (*spraṣṭavya*) and not odor; therefore, it is the ultimate faculty [that knows]."

Since that which is attached cannot be the agent of attachment, how could it be [the sense organ]? Alternatively, some claim that because one relies on space to perceive fragrance, space is therefore the knower;
thus, he further refutes space, thereby refuting all ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*). ○ Second, the refutation of fragrance as a constituent element (*dhātu*).

If consciousness arises because of fragrance and exists because of fragrance, then just as the eye has the capacity for seeing yet cannot perceive the eye itself, so too, because it exists because of fragrance, it should not know the fragrance.
If it knows it, it is not "arisen"; if it does not know it, it is not "consciousness. Since fragrance would not exist through knowing, the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*) would be unestablished.
Since consciousness does not know fragrance, it is not established based on fragrance. As there is no intermediate state, neither "internal" nor "external" can be formed;
thus, that nature of hearing is ultimately false and illusory.

The first phrase restates the proposition. In the subsequent refutation, the author first establishes an analogy based on visual perception. The text contains the formal argument (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).

The phrase "the cause of consciousness" constitutes the formal argument; "as with the eye" below it is the illustration; and "due to fragrance" and so forth is the application. Following this, he proceeds to distinguish [the position] by contrasting what is known and what is not known:
if one says it can be known, then it is not produced from fragrance; if one says it cannot be known, then it cannot be called [consciousness].

Consciousness. [If you claim] that fragrance is not perceived because it is not manifest, this results in falling into two kinds of extremes: first, the fault that the fragrance-element (*gandha-dhātu*) would be non-existent;
for if fragrance is not known by consciousness, where then does the fragrance-element reside? Second, the fault that the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) would be non-existent;
if consciousness does not know fragrance, then there is no consciousness, so why do you say that consciousness arises from fragrance? This concludes the refutation.
...and so forth. ○ Third, the realization that delusion is itself reality:
Therefore, one should know that the nose, fragrance, and the olfactory consciousness-element produced by them as conditions—these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the nose, fragrance, and the olfactory element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

When both the intermediate and the internal and external are refuted, then all three locations are entirely non-existent. Furthermore, the previous section refuted the nose faculty and olfactory objects from the perspective of both the conventional and the ultimate;
that they cannot produce consciousness refutes the olfactory element (*gandhadhātu*). Thus, all three locations are entirely non-existent.

The mutual causality of these three bases constitutes the meaning of the *pratyaya* (conditions) for the Śrāvakas. If they were not mutually causal, it would be the naturalistic calculation (*svabhāva-vāda*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

When both of these meanings are refuted, the Tathāgatagarbha is revealed. 4. The Sphere of the Tongue, Taste, and Consciousness: This is the point where Pūrṇa attained perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-avabodha*).
The text is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the realization; second, the raising of the inquiry; [and third, the detailed exposition].
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue and thus have the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of the flavors and thus have the flavors as its constituent element?
2. Refuting the [opponent's] assertions by means of analysis (caturvidha-pratyāmarśa-bhañjana): First, refuting [the view that taste] arises from the tongue.
Ānanda, if [taste] were produced because of the tongue, then all the sugar cane, *umbara* plums, *hribera*, rock salt, *śigru*, ginger, and cinnamon in the world would have no flavor at all.
You yourself should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, what would come [to taste it]?

Tasting with the tongue: the tongue does not taste itself; what, then, is it that perceives? Since the nature of the tongue is not bitter and flavor does not arise [independently], how can a "constituent" (dhātu) be established?

In refuting this, one first refutes it by means of the five flavors. Question: This passage distinguishes the consciousness arising from the tongue; why does it first refute [the notion of] "arising from"?
"Does the tongue produce flavor? He replied: "Consciousness arises from the tongue, not from flavor. Without flavor, by what means could consciousness arise?
Therefore, it must first be said that flavor arises from the tongue, and only thereafter can it be said that consciousness arises from the tongue.
To say that there is no flavor at all means that flavor does not arise from external objects but arises solely from the tongue. This was stated by way of citing the absence of the five flavors.
Question regarding the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*): When no tastes arrive, what taste does the tongue itself possess?
Furthermore, as for the nature of the tongue being bitter, this merely cites one taste as an illustration. Who comes to taste the tongue?

This means that once the faculty capable of tasting has already become the object of tasting, there is no other entity that comes to taste the tongue. "The tongue does not taste itself" refers to the tongue-faculty.
Furthermore, one cannot taste it oneself. In these two lines, the self and the other are contrasted; since neither can taste it, who then perceives its bitterness?
Next, the non-bitterness [of the tongue] is refuted: it is said that taste must arise from the tongue, yet the tongue itself has no taste.
Taste itself does not arise. Since taste does not arise, consciousness does not arise. 2. Refuting [the view] that consciousness arises because of taste:
If consciousness were to arise because of taste, then consciousness itself would become the taste. Being identical to the tongue-organ, it should not be able to taste for itself;

how then could it cognize whether something is a taste or not a taste? Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance. Since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise possess multiple entities.

If the substance of consciousness were a single entity, it would necessarily arise as a single flavor. When salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, their various changing characteristics would all become one flavor and there would be no differentiation.
Since there would be no differentiation, it could not be called "consciousness. How, then, could it further be called the "element of tongue-consciousness of taste"?
The first phrase restates the position. In the subsequent refutation, there are three parts. First, the refutation by citing an analogy regarding the absence of cognition:

consciousness arises from flavor, and thus consciousness itself possesses flavor; it is like a father surnamed Zhang whose son is also surnamed Zhang. As stated above, if the nature of the tongue were bitter, the tongue would not taste itself;
how then could it know whether something is bitter or sweet? Second, from "Furthermore, all... onwards, the refutation proceeds by showing that the mind follows the object.
Refutation: Just as the five flavors previously mentioned each arise from a single substance, consciousness, having arisen from flavor, should likewise consist of multiple entities.

Thus, this consciousness arising from flavor-consciousness would itself become manifold. If the essence of these three consciousnesses were one, then by refuting [the position] that the object follows the mind, the manifold nature is already refuted;
one should then reckon with a single consciousness. Yet, this single entity must necessarily arise from flavor.
In this way, many flavors enter into a single substance and thus become one flavor. When consciousness arises, there must be no discrimination.

That is to say, even if they occur at different times—such as first salty and later bitter, which is called "different times"—if there were still no discrimination, how could it constitute consciousness?
Furthermore, what is meant by the "consciousness-element produced by the tongue and flavors"? Wuxing said: "Salty, bland, sweet, and pungent are, for the most part..."
To list the four flavors: in detail, there are six, adding bitter and sour. "Harmonized" (*saṃyukta*) refers to the formation of a composite from various flavors.

"Co-nascent" (*sahaja*) refers to that which is innate and not subject to change. "Transformed" (*vipariṇata*) refers to that which has been altered through burning or boiling from its original state.
○ Third, the production of space by destruction.
It should not be that space gives rise to your mind-consciousness.
The previous [section] clarified that neither the tongue nor flavors can give rise to it; thus, it must be produced by space.
Yet, space itself cannot produce consciousness. ○ Fourth, the refutation of production through combination.
The tongue and flavor meet; yet within this very meeting, there is fundamentally no self-nature—how, then, could an element arise?
To refute their conjunction: if they were to arise through conjunction, then the consciousness produced would be entirely the tongue and the flavor;
how could it possess self-nature? Since there is no self-nature, there is consequently no element of consciousness. Jiaoguang said: "Lack of nature" means that both [tongue and flavor] are absent.
This means that each opens up its own nature. Furthermore, it asks: "How does the element (dhātu) arise?

This refers to the fact that once the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) have already merged as one, they no longer possess a self-nature; how then could there be an intervening gap to accommodate the arising of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*)?
However, the expression "lacking self-nature" is commonly used by teachers of the Dharma, yet such an interpretation has truly not been seen before. This is because... [the elements] intersect.
Guangping said: "One does not ordinarily use the four natures (*catur-koṭi*) to analyze and examine the mind; therefore, it appears so obscure and indistinct. Gushan said:
"First, because the tongue [is the cause], it refutes self-arising. Second, because flavors [are the cause], it refutes other-arising.
Third, because it cannot be space, it refutes causeless arising. Fourth, because it is the conjunction of tongue and flavor, it refutes co-arising. The various [arguments] before and after...
The same applies to all [senses] herein, yet this one is most clearly illustrated. Third, realizing that delusion is itself reality:
Therefore, one should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness-element arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

○ The fifth is the element of body-tactile-consciousness; this is Upāli’s gateway to perfect penetration. The text is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the realization and the raising of the inquiry.
"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand as the body and touch serving as conditions to produce body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the body?"
That which is produced has the body as its realm; that which is produced by contact has contact as its realm.
○ Second, restating the thesis and refuting it through reasoning: 1. Refutation based on the body as the realm.

Ānanda, if [consciousness] were produced because of the body, there would necessarily be no conditions of "conjunction" and "separation" for the two types of mental application—vitarka and vicāra—so what would the body cognize?
"Necessarily being without conjunction and separation" means that one would certainly not apprehend the two kinds of contact, namely conjunction and separation.

Initial application of the mind toward an object is called *vitarka* (applied thought); subtle mental discrimination is called *vicāra* (sustained thought). These two contacts, conjunction and separation, are the conditions that give rise to *vitarka* and *vicāra*. (2)
It is refuted by taking contact as the defining characteristic.
If [cognition] were produced because of contact, then necessarily there would be no "your body"; who then could possess the knowledge of union and separation that is not the body?
"Necessarily there would be no 'your body'" means that one would certainly not apprehend the body-faculty; since contact alone would be without cognition, it is asked, "Who possesses it?"
"It is not that the body knows contact and separation. (3) Refuting the location of the body’s contact and separation:
"Ānanda, it is not that objects touch the faculty of cognition; rather, the body cognizes contact. To know the body is itself contact, and to know contact is itself the body.

Thus, what is contact is not the body, and what is the body is not contact. The two characteristics of body and contact originally have no fixed location. When they meet the body, they become the body itself."
As for its essential nature: apart from the body, it is like the characteristics of empty space. Since neither the internal nor the external can be established, how could a "middle" be posited?
If the middle cannot be posited, then the nature of both internal and external is empty; in that case, from whom would your consciousness arise to establish the sense-spheres (*dhātu*)?
The first two phrases correctly clarify the nature of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*). This is because the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) differs from other objects.

For instance, while objects such as color and fragrance may be designated as "objects" (*viṣaya*) even when they are not seen or heard, touch must necessarily depend upon cognition before it is established;

therefore, a mere physical thing is not called "touch. Furthermore, there is no cognition that exists independently; it is entirely dependent upon the body's cognition before it can be named "touch. Thus, [the first two phrases] establish this point.
It is known that this refers to contact (*sparśa*). This section refutes the notion that the body and contact arise together. First, it establishes [the position], and then it refutes it.
Within the establishment, it says that "knowing the body is itself knowing contact": for example, when one knows cold or heat in the body, this is knowing the body;

yet this cold or heat is precisely contact. It further says that "knowing contact is itself knowing the body": when one knows the experience of the contact of cold or heat, this is knowing contact; yet...

This cold and warmth actually exist within the body. This is refuted immediately below by the term "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*). Since they are called "contact," the internal characteristic is not established; therefore, they are not the body.
Since they are called the "body," the external characteristic is not established; therefore, they are not contact. For this reason, it is said below that "internal and external are not established.

One must understand that once the characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*) are distinguished, the internal and external are always distinct. If these characteristics were mixed, [the distinction would collapse].
Both are negated. As for the statement that there is no locus for body and touch: if it is not the body, then the locus of the body is not established;

if it is not touch, then the locus of touch is not established. This pair of refutations regarding conjunction and separation follows the previous discussion on how bodily cognition of touch occurs only through conjunction.
Now, the phenomena of touch are eightfold: pain/itching, heaviness/lightness, cold/warmth, and roughness/smoothness. Pain and itching are wind.
Characteristics: heaviness and lightness are the characteristics of earth; cold and warmth are the characteristics of fire; roughness and smoothness are the characteristics of water.
All that comes into contact with the body constitutes the nature of one's own body. Therefore, as for the two locations of "body" and "contact," neither is established.

If one speaks in terms of separation, there are likewise no two locations. Why? Although form, sound, and so forth are originally external objects even when separated from the sense organs, they [still do not exist apart from the body].
Only the object of touch cannot exist apart from the body; if it were so, it would be identical to empty space—how then could it be called "bodily contact"?
Thus, the principle that neither of these two positions can be established is clear. The above constitutes the dual refutation of separation and conjunction. Below follows the summary refutation:
As shown above, whether separated or conjoined, both the internal and external are unestablished. Since the internal and external are unestablished, there is nothing manifested in between.
Therefore it is said: "How is the middle established? The middle position is precisely consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Since the middle is not established, then the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another, and both the internal and external are empty. Regarding the phrase "then you all," Changshui says:
"If the three locations are all empty, from where does consciousness arise? ○ Third, realizing that delusion is itself reality.
Therefore, one should know that when body-contact as a condition gives rise to the body-consciousness element, these three locations are entirely non-existent;
thus, the body, contact, and the body-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
One must know that although the eighteen *dhātus* primarily refute consciousness, they also incidentally refute the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

As above, first the "mere body" was refuted, next "mere contact" was refuted, and third, "conjunction and separation" were refuted; in each case, the organs and objects were refuted first, followed by consciousness.

Therefore, the conclusion states that these three locations are entirely non-existent. Furthermore, all the passages in the Buddha’s teachings concerning the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are for the purpose of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Practitioners must rely on these teachings to contemplate their own minds; otherwise, this present life will surely pass in vain.
If one merely expounds the literal text, it is just as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says: "What benefit does a black viper possess by harboring a jewel? It is of no use to a long snake."

○ The sixth is the consciousness element of mind and mental objects (*manas-dharmavijñānadhātu*). This is the sphere of perfect penetration of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana. The text is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the realization; second, the raising of the inquiry; and third, the detailed exposition.
"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises—does this consciousness arise because of the mind?"
That which arises from the mind takes the mind as its realm; that which arises from dharmas takes dharmas as its realm.
If one says that whatever arises from causes and conditions is impermanent, this already pertains to the path of analytical emptiness (vibhajya-śūnyatā) elucidated by the Śrāvakas.
Analytical emptiness is precisely impermanence. Yet, they have not yet clarified that impermanence is itself emptiness, let alone that it is itself the provisional (parikalpita).
Therefore, the present inquiry is raised to demonstrate that the three truths are contained within a single moment of mind, thereby enabling those who are ready to enter the Tathāgatagarbha.

II. Refuting the Adherence by Restating It has two parts: A. Refuting the claim that the mind constitutes the realm; B. Refuting it by examining the existence or non-existence of phenomena. 1. Refuting it by examining the existence or non-existence of phenomena.
Ānanda, if consciousness arises dependent upon the mind, then within your mind there must be something thought of that brings forth your mental faculty.
If those preceding dharmas were absent, the mind would have nothing from which to arise. Devoid of conditions and lacking form, for what purpose would consciousness be used?
"Regarding 'there must be something thought of,' this means that within your mind there must be a mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) upon which you reflect;

only then can the function of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) manifest. If there were no mental objects present as its objective support (*ālambana*), the mind would likewise have no basis from which to arise.
As stated previously in the section on the auditory consciousness element: 'If the two characteristics of movement and stillness do not appear before one...'"
The sense organs do not constitute cognition. Now, we shall apply this same principle to refute [the view that they] exist apart from conditions and so forth. Changshui says:

"If even the form and appearance of the sense organs do not exist, how much less can the consciousness produced by them exercise its function? 2. Refutation based on the identity and difference of consciousness.
Furthermore, is this consciousness of yours identical to or different from the nature of the faculty of thought (*manas*) and its capacity for discernment?

If it were identical to the mind, how could that which is produced by the mind exist? If it were different from the mind, being not the same as it, there would be nothing to be cognized. If there were nothing to be cognized, how could the mind arise?
If there is that which cognizes, how does it cognize the mind? Only the two natures of identity and difference fail to be established; how, then, can a realm be posited?

This passage also refutes the "mind-born" (manomaya). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "That which accumulates and arises is called 'citta' (mind); that which deliberates is called 'manas' (intellect); that which discerns is called 'vijñāna' (consciousness).
In the present text, "consciousness" and "mind" correspond to the first [definition], while "deliberation" corresponds to the second, namely the faculty of intellect (*manas-indriya*).
Furthermore, the nature of "discerning" (*vijñapti*) is the same as that of the third [consciousness], namely the consciousness produced by the mental faculty (*manas*).
Changshui says: "The 'consciousness-mind' (*vijñāna-citta*) is the eighth; 'deliberation' (*manana*) is the seventh; and 'discerning' (*vijñapti*) is the sixth.

Since both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses share the sixth faculty—the mind—as their basis, they are both termed "mind," and thus these two are asked about together. This interpretation is largely identical to the present one.

I agree with the refutation of the identity and difference [between consciousness and the mind]. If consciousness were identical to the mind, then since the mind is already clear and lucid, consciousness would likewise be clear and lucid;
thus, consciousness could also be designated as "mind," and only then would the meaning of being a single entity be established.

How, then, could one claim that the sense organ is the producer and consciousness is the produced? Therefore, if they are identical, the relationship of producer and produced cannot be established. If consciousness were different from the mind, [its] category...
If they were different, that which is produced would have nothing to cognize; thus, difference also cannot establish the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If there were no [basis], it would further clarify that both identity and difference are inexpressible. It is not only that difference does not establish the mental consciousness; since the mind is already manifest, [the point is clear].
How could that which is produced be so dull and ignorant as to be different? This is necessarily impossible. Not only does identity fail to establish the relationship of subject and object;
since consciousness is identical to the mind in its clarity, how could there be a difference between consciousness and the mind?
Therefore, identity is necessarily impossible. For this reason, it is said below: "Only identity and difference—these two natures are not established. As it says:
If this is so, how can the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu) be established? Master Haiyin said:

"Based on the premise that there must be something intended by the aforementioned [inquiry], one should examine it by synthesizing these three meanings. 'The conscious mind' refers to the faculty of mind (manas-indriya).
'All deliberation' refers to the objective spheres (viṣaya). 'The nature of discernment' refers to the essence of consciousness (vijñāna-svabhāva). Because these exist..."
The characteristics of what is contemplated only then constitute the cognition of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). For this reason, these three factors are combined and analyzed together;
this explanation is likewise correct. (2) Refuting the view that phenomena (*dharma*) constitute the sense-field.
If phenomena arise from causes, then all worldly phenomena do not transcend the five sensory objects.
Observe these phenomena of form, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles; their characteristics are distinct and correspond to the five sense organs, rather than being subsumed by the mind.
Your consciousness definitely arises based upon dharmas. Now, observe closely: what is the nature of each dharma?

If you set aside form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all these characteristics—you ultimately find nothing at all. When they arise, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together;
when they cease, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together. Since their cause does not exist, how can there be a consciousness produced by that cause?
What kind of form does it take? Since its characteristics do not exist, how can a realm arise?

First, this is refuted by means of the five external sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The initial character "dharma" refers to mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). In the phrase "all dharmas" and below, all refer to the five sense objects as "dharmas.
Regarding "not subsumed under the mind," this means that the aforementioned various objects cannot be apprehended by the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). If...
In that case, what would the object of the dharma-realm (dharmāyatana) be? Following "Your consciousness," the text below proceeds to refute [the position] specifically regarding the dharma-realm.
When it says "certainly relying on the dharma," the calculation is that because one does not take the five sensory objects as conditions, one therefore relies decisively on the dharma-realm.

Thus, it causes one to carefully observe: what characteristics or marks does the phenomenon of the dharma-realm possess? The passage beginning with "If separated from" below specifically points to the five [sensory objects].
The arising and ceasing of sensory objects (dharmas) constitutes the dharma-dusts. This means that when one thinks of the five preceding sensory objects, they are said to arise;
when one does not think of them, they cease. As stated previously: "When one perceives an object, there is recollection; when recollection is lost, it is called forgetting.

The commentary states: "To recollect them is for them to arise; to forget them is for them to cease. Such arising and ceasing are nothing more than the shadows of the five sensory objects. To transcend this—
It transcends the external. These various marks are the marks of the shadows of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Although these two phrases appear redundant, if one sets aside the literal wording, they collectively enumerate the six sense-objects while emphasizing their arising and ceasing.

The subsequent phrase, "these various marks," specifically refers to the shadows of the five sense-objects within the mental faculty (*manas*), because within the process of arising and ceasing, there is that which precedes.
The characteristics of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as they fall away are manifold; therefore, they are mentioned again.
As for "arising," this clarifies below that the dharma-object (*dharma-āyatana*) has no reality. To think of the preceding five objects is called "arising"—is there any separate dharma that arises?
Not to think of them is "ceasing"—is there any separate dharma that ceases? Indeed, all dharmas are like shadows; such is the nature of all dharmas.
All are empty. Now, since the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is fundamentally a mere reflection, what substantial reality could it have?

The following clarifies that the consciousness which arises based upon it is likewise non-existent. Since the dharma-object—the cause—is absent, what form could the resulting consciousness possibly take?
Thus, the element of consciousness cannot be established. 3. Realizing that delusion is itself the True.

Therefore, you should know this: when the mind and mental objects serve as conditions for the arising of the consciousness-element, yet these three locations are entirely non-existent, then the mind, mental objects, and the mind-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The text, from the five aggregates onward, consistently states that they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, a phenomenon that is not produced by causes and conditions does not exist. If a phenomenon were to exist apart from causes and conditions, it would be of a spontaneous nature;

however, since the nature of phenomena necessarily follows various conditions, it is not spontaneous. This is not non-existence. That which is neither existence nor non-existence is the meaning of the Middle Way. Furthermore, there is...
Regarding the meaning: departing from existence, one enters emptiness; departing from emptiness, one may likewise enter the provisional.

Entering the provisional is a concealed and indirect entry into the true, which is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). Therefore, from the five aggregates onward, both the Perfect and the Distinct teachings are fully present.
Although both the Perfect and Distinct Teachings are present, the primary intent lies in the Perfect;

therefore, this text is titled "All Samādhis" and begins by designating the "Wondrous True Suchness Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Third, regarding the Middle Way as the definitive meaning, it responds to the practice of dhyāna to clarify the Perfect principle.
This section extensively elucidates the nature-inclusion of the seven elements. One who contemplates this nature-inclusion...

It is the same as "mere emptiness" (but-kong), yet it differs from "mere middle" (but-zhong). One who contemplates mere emptiness observes that phenomena do not arise from self, other, both, or neither;

their nature and characteristics are both empty, such that false dharmas do not exist and even the "true" is unobtainable. Now, regarding the principle of inherent nature (xingju), one takes all things from afar and one's own person from near;
since every dharma is perfectly interfused and every particle is omnipresent, it is not the same as [the view of] emptiness.
They are the same. Regarding those who contemplate "mere center" (*but-chung*): they contemplate the eternally abiding true mind as being free from both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity;
it cannot be known by wisdom nor can it be discussed in words. However, because it does not yet possess all phenomena, it is called "mere center.

Now, the principle of the inherent nature possesses both the negation and the illumination in their entirety. Because it is empty despite its possession, and possessed despite its emptiness, it is different from "mere center."
Wenling says: "The great nature was originally neither water nor fire, nor was it space or consciousness;
it is entirely the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma alone. If the seven elements are thus, then all dharmas are likewise.

All that we rely upon—the primary and secondary bodies—was originally neither the sense organs and physical body nor the vessel-world; they are all merely manifestations according to karma. The true nature is perfectly interfused from the very beginning."
"Without arising or ceasing. Youxi said: "Although this statement by Wénlǐng is based on the scriptural texts, those who read it later must understand the meaning of the prior refutation;
otherwise, it would be nearly identical to the teachings of the partial schools.

This is because the nature of the seven elements is not like that of worldly water and fire, which possess the characteristic of mutually overcoming and extinguishing one another; rather, there is the principle of the inherent presence of these natures."
Statements such as "the nature of clouds is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form" are all explicit teachings on the principle of inherent presence (*xingju*).
Thus, we know that the Tiantai school’s profound discourse on inherent presence is identical in its uniformity to the Buddha’s own sincere words.
As it says in the *Jijie*: "The twenty-fascicle *Fuxing* states that the teaching of this single school is forever distinct from other doctrines; it encompasses and subsumes [all things]..."

All causes and effects of the ordinary and the sagely throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time arise precisely from the possession [of the nature]. This "possession" is provisional;

the provisional is emptiness within the middle. Although the rational nature is possessed, if one does not contemplate it, then merely speaking of "contemplating the mind" would not accord with principle.
Furthermore, the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes on the Profound Meaning) explains that contemplating the nature of the mind is called "supreme concentration," stating: "If by..."
Contemplating the nature of the mind as that realm, one finds that both the realm and suchness are empty, yet they eternally possess all dharmas.
They are neither empty nor possessing, yet they are both empty and possessing; they are both negation and illumination, yet neither negation nor illumination.
This is also simply the single thought-moment of the nature of the mind. Is such a samādhi not supreme? Judging from the two passages by Jingxi, regarding "possessing" (ju) and...

The two meanings of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are one in essence; thus, Youxi’s profound elucidation of the inherent nature (*xingju*) truly captures the Buddha’s intent, and Wengleng’s interpretation is likewise not in error.
With this, I respond to those who inquire about *dhyāna*: the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is translated in the Qin language as “quiet contemplation” (*jinglü*).

“Quiet” (*jing*) is emptiness; “contemplation” (*lü*) is the provisional (*prajñapti*). The non-duality of emptiness and the provisional is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Therefore, I now clarify the Middle.
The definitive meaning of the Way answers the question of what delusions exist within *dhyāna*. Question:
Since the "endowment" (*ju*) is provisional, why is it used as the basis for discussing the "Middle" (*zhong*)? Answer: This endowment is a provisional phenomenon within the Middle Way.

Because the Middle Way inherently possesses the three truths, this provisionality of the inherent endowment is precisely the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); only then is it the Middle Way. The present text is likewise not [an exception].
This merely clarifies that nature is inherently endowed [with all qualities]. As the sutra says, "The nature of form is true emptiness," and it further states, "Pure and fundamentally so.
Now, if something is pure, not a single dharma can be apprehended; is this not the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)?
Therefore, the definitive teaching of the Middle Way is the path of the threefold contemplation in perfect fusion. The text is divided into two parts: first, the inquiry and request.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often said that all things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions.

All the various transformations in the world are manifested due to the conjunction of the four great elements. Why, then, does the Tathāgata now reject both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity?
I do not yet understand the meaning of this; I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings.”
The Way is the definitive meaning, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Youxi said: "That which the Tathāgata constantly speaks of as 'concordant causes and conditions' is precisely what was expounded in the previously cited *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) constantly speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions; this is not within their sphere of experience."
Regarding "harmony through causes and conditions": it means that arising occurs through the harmony of two factors—a proximate cause and a remote condition.

Regarding "various transformations": in the case of sentient beings, this refers to birth and death, and death and rebirth; in the case of insentient things, it refers to changing the raw into the cooked, transforming the existent into the non-existent, and so forth.
None of these transcend the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. The phenomena of the world have nothing else; they are solely these.
This concludes [the previous section]. In the past, the correct discourse on spontaneity was refuted by means of causes and conditions.
Generally, when the correct refutes the heterodox, the heterodox departs and the correct remains. Today, both are cast aside; it is unclear to which meaning this principle belongs.

That is to say, the simultaneous rejection of both belongs to the meaning of the Middle Way’s dual negation (*ubhayaprativedha*). Those who hear this have not yet reached an understanding of the Perfect [Teaching].
The meaning of "not knowing" is that one does not know because of following conditions while remaining unchanging; therefore, it is said that the referent of this principle is unknown.

As will be clearly elucidated in the section on the Seven Great Elements below, once one understands this [principle of] remaining unchanging while following conditions, the meaning will have its proper locus.

Furthermore, "remaining unchanging while following conditions" is the simultaneous illumination of both aspects. "Non-causal spontaneity" (non-cause-and-condition-nature) is the simultaneous negation of both aspects. Negation and illumination are non-dual.

When both essence and function are fully present, it is called the Middle Way, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Conceptual proliferation refers precisely to the spontaneity of causes and conditions.
Regarding the term "definitive meaning": although the Middle Way was already mentioned in the preceding text, its meaning had not yet been clearly elucidated;

thus, in contrast to that previous text, it is now termed "definitive. If contrasted with the preceding five aggregates and three categories, it is characterized by the simultaneous negation and illumination.

The title "Definitive Meaning" (*nītārtha*) is established as follows: when contrasted with the various passages from the first fascicle onward, this [text] does not employ emptiness or the provisional, but purely elucidates the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

Within this Middle Way, the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*) are inherently contained; thus, it is termed "definitive meaning. Indeed, this sutra elucidates both the Perfect (*yuan*) and the Distinct (*bie*) teachings;
while it is sequential in its overall structure, it is non-sequential regarding specific points. From the beginning of the first fascicle, there are five such instances.

Regarding the meaning of the perfection, distinction, progression, and cessation: initially, one enters from the provisional into the empty by taking the observation of the provisional as the means for entering the empty.
Therefore, the text first designates *samādhi* and, at the very beginning of the passage, establishes the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), stating:
"There is a *samādhi* named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices. Thus, we know that the provisional [reality] precedes the empty.

To penetrate this is precisely the single mind and three contemplations (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). For those following the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), who do not penetrate the Perfect Doctrine (*yuanzong*), the "investigation of the mind in seven locations" may at best be a provisional teaching for the preceding stage;
this is what is meant by "perfect fusion does not obstruct distinct differentiation.

This is the first point regarding the meaning of the progress or stagnation of the Perfect and Separate Teachings. Next, in the text concerning the actual entry into emptiness and the revelation of the path of *śamatha*, it says:
Regarding the three stages of progression and non-progression: if one progresses, it clarifies the Perfect [Teaching]; if not, it clarifies the Separate [Teaching], as previously explained.
Next, it clarifies that all samādhis emerge from emptiness into the provisional. At the beginning of the text, the "wondrous true thusness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha" is designated;

this also clarifies the single mind and the three contemplations. Furthermore, at the end of each section on the five aggregates and the three categories, it is stated that they are fundamentally not causes.
Conditions do not possess an inherent nature; that which lacks both cessation and illumination is also partial. Thus, the preceding text concludes with five rounds of progression and negation.
Now, regarding the seven great texts: in the sequential teaching (*biejiao*), one has already entered the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
subsequently, through the threefold contemplation, one converges into the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Even in the Perfect Teaching, although there is no distinction between beginning and end—
There is no difference. However, the realization that the mind alone is the essence fully embodies the meaning of the preceding text, which becomes even more expansive later on;

it is for this reason that it is uniquely designated as "definitive" (*nītārtha*). If the lecturer values brevity and concision, there is no error in simply taking the simultaneous presence of negation and illumination as the definitive meaning.
Youxī said: "In this sutra, the teachings suited to the capacity of the audience always proceed from causes and conditions."

However, regarding the questioner, there are two interpretations. First, it is because this sutra is intended for ordinary beings at the stage of "vast ground" (*pṛthagjana*) who can accomplish the Great Matter in this very life through the Perfect and Sudden teaching;
thus, while the question posed is extremely shallow, that which is shown is extremely profound.

Second, it is because the meanings of terms such as "causality" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) inherently encompass the profound, all the more so since there exists a true causality and spontaneity.
This involves drawing near to the profound mystery through the mutual resonance of hammer and anvil. Now, regarding the intent of the questioner:

he asks whether the seven great elements (mahābhūtas), which are initiated by the four great elements, are identical to or different from the aggregates (skandhas), bases of consciousness (āyatanas), and realms (dhātus). Some maintain that the seven great elements are identical to the eighteen realms (*dhātus*):

the five great elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space are subsumed within the six objects (*viṣayas*), while the element of seeing (*darśana-mahābhūta*) is subsumed within the six sense organs (*indriyas*).

Looking at the main text below, it says: "As with the faculty of sight, seeing pervades the Dharma-realm; so too hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of touch—this wondrous virtue is lucid and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Is this not the inclusion of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*)? The element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) is included within the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

Thus, one knows that the seven elements (*sapta-mahābhūta*) are identical to the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), realms (*dhātu*), and the seven elements are merely...

It is merely a difference of opening and closing. Furthermore, since each of the twenty-five perfect penetrations has its own specific correspondence, one must understand that although the seven elements and the [six] sense-fields are the same in nature, they differ in their specific manifestations—just as within the four great elements there are distinctions in the presence or absence of the four subtle particles.
For instance, wind possesses only the particle of touch; fire possesses the particles of color and touch; water possesses the particles of color, touch, and taste; and earth possesses...

Because the sense objects—form, odor, flavor, and touch—as well as the faculties that possess them, cannot be entirely identical, their respective modes of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) also differ.
Although emptiness belongs to the category of form, this sutra constantly contrasts form with emptiness; thus, emptiness is not identical to form.

"The greatness of seeing" and "the greatness of consciousness" refer to the general, while the six faculties and six consciousnesses refer to the specific. Because the general and the specific differ, their modes of perfect penetration also differ. Therefore, it is established.
This is the twenty-fifth section. II. The Exposition, Part One: Admonition.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Previously, you felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolved to diligently seek unexcelled Bodhi. Therefore, at this time, I shall reveal the First Noble Truth for your sake."
Why do you further entangle yourself with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and deluded imaginings?
Although you are learned, you are like a man who knows about medicine but cannot distinguish it when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
"Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal this for you, so that those who practice the Mahāyāna in the future may also penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s sacred instruction.
Question: Where does Ānanda express weariness with the small and seek the great? Answer:

It is at the very beginning of the sutra, where he earnestly requests that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions explain how they attained Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth; this is weariness with the small and seeking the great.
That all phenomena are unarisen and that only the *tathāgatagarbha* is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—if phenomena arise through causes and conditions, they are merely...
Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): the subsequent text states, "I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions;
it does not grasp the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunctions. Now, Ānanda clings to the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

is this not precisely the coarse characteristic of worldly conjunction? It is the most superficial level within conventional truth; in discourse it becomes mere play, and in perception it becomes delusion. Thus, one is ensnared by doubt.
This describes the characteristic of delusion. It criticizes Ānanda for clinging to worldly causes and conditions while remaining ignorant of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Since the Buddhas know the secret treasury [of the Dharma] without exception, it is said that they "prescribe medicine.

Now, hearing the Buddha-dharma, one realizes that all is the *tathāgatagarbha*, the true medicine appearing before one. To cite past expedient means while doubting the present reality is a failure to distinguish between them.
This rebuke of Ānanda points out that although he possesses extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), he is still ignorant of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). "Listen attentively now," it says below;

the true reality is the principle of the three truths (*trisatya*). The subsequent passage clarifies that the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*) are precisely this true reality, serving as the essence (*tattva*) of the Mahāyāna.
To penetrate this is to establish the fundamental tenet (*siddhānta*) of that essence. Next, the audience waits expectantly to hear, as the text describes. [Section] Two.
Second, the formal explanation, which consists of two parts: first, citing the doubt to show it generally; second, citing the doubt specifically.
"Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world."
II. General Demonstration.
Ānanda, if the essence of those great elements were not a state of combination, they could not intermingle with one another;

it would be like empty space, which does not combine with material forms. If they were indeed combined, they would be identical to transformations, wherein beginning and end mutually constitute one another, and birth and cessation follow in succession.
The continuity of birth and death, death and birth, revolving like a whirling firebrand without rest.
In the general demonstration, the term "great nature" (*mahābhūta*) is mentioned first because Ānanda himself cited the words regarding the combination of the four great elements.

Now, in the Buddha’s response, the distinction is made between the great nature and its characteristics as being neither combined nor uncombined; this is intended to clarify that the nature is inherently complete and follows conditions.
Because this is the principle of immutability, it takes "nature" (*xing*) and "characteristics" (*xiang*) as its thematic starting point.

The manifestation of the Great Nature is precisely what is referred to below as the nature of water and the nature of fire. Youxi said: "From beginning to end, this sutra elucidates a single principle—the doctrine that [all things] are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.
As in the passage: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. This serves as...
Exquisite conventionality. Being pure and fundamental by nature, this constitutes "exquisite emptiness" (miàokōng). Pervading the entire dharma-realm, this constitutes "exquisite middle" (miàozhōng).

The perfect fusion of the three truths collectively belongs to the "perfect middle. Because the entirety of the inherent principle manifests as phenomenal creation, there exist the characteristics of the seven elements of the mundane world.
The Tathāgata, wishing to provide an exposition, first demonstrates through both non-harmony and harmony. That is to say, if...
That which is of the nature of "greatness" (mahattva) and is not a composite cannot be mixed or harmonized with the characteristics of greatness. To illustrate this, it is said:
it is like space, which does not harmonize with various forms. Thus, the Buddha-nature cannot transform or create phenomena;

the nature abides outside of characteristics, and characteristics are not identical to the nature. This principle that there is no identity between [the nature and] characteristics applies not only to insentient things, but also to sentient beings.
Furthermore, there would be no time for returning to the truth. Now, the text below clarifies that both sentient and insentient beings possess Buddha-nature;

is this not because nature and characteristics are combined to form them? If nature and characteristics were truly combined, then since characteristics have arising and ceasing, nature would likewise follow suit;
thus it is said they are "identical to transformation. This refers to the characteristics of beginning and end.

Regarding the establishment of the continuity of arising and ceasing: both the beginning and the end are characterized by arising and ceasing. Arising constitutes the beginning; ceasing constitutes the end.

The first phrase clarifies the formation of characteristics; the second phrase clarifies continuity. "Continuity" means that as soon as there is arising, there is ceasing, and as soon as there is ceasing, there is arising.
"Birth and death, death and birth" is spoken in terms of sequential order; "birth and birth, death and death" is discussed in terms of intermittent intervals.
To illustrate this, an analogy is provided: it is like a whirling firebrand that never ceases. The wheel of the whirling firebrand has no substantial reality;

this serves as a metaphor for how illusory appearances form a continuous succession. Thus, while True Suchness follows conditions and becomes defiled, sentient beings have no year in which their delusions cease.
Now, we clearly see people being born and dying; how could there be a cessation of results?
Indeed. Since neither non-conjunction nor conjunction is possible, what else could this be but the definitive meaning of the Middle Way that negates both extremes and illuminates both simultaneously?
This constitutes the general demonstration of the purport of the seven elements. II. The Detailed Exposition of the Seven Elements through Each One.
1. The Earth Element is divided into four parts: (i) Demonstrating that the nature of earth is not solid.

Ānanda, just as water becomes ice and ice returns to water, so too do you wish to clarify that the earth element is both neither-dual nor dual-illuminating: its nature is true emptiness within form, and its nature is true form within emptiness;

it is pure and original, pervading the entire dharma-realm. First, I shall demonstrate that its nature is fundamentally all-encompassing and harmonious, originally devoid of any rigid attachment. Following...
When karma manifests, it does not hinder the formation of the great earth of ignorance, which is solid, obstructive, and impermanent.
Furthermore, when the nature returns to its source, it reverts to the pure, flowing, and perfectly interfused *dharmatā*.
At that time, the *dharmatā* and ignorance together pervasively create all manner of evils, which is termed "defilement," like water turning into ice. Today, this ignorance...
When this [ice] and the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are universally fused within all phenomena, it is termed "purity," just as ice melts back into water.

Is this not the interpenetration of the nature of earth, which from the beginning lacks any nature of solid rigidity? Therefore, it can manifest according to karma, yet it can also be primordially pure.
As will be demonstrated below through logical refutation, this is precisely the function of ice melting back into water.
Now, this simply demonstrates that the nature [of reality] is fundamentally perfect and harmonious. Master Tianxi said: "Ice is earth. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Water becomes earth due to the causal condition of cold. This refers to the "Contemplation of Ice and Earth" found in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
According to the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-pūjā-sūtra*, one should say: "The nature of earth has no master. Now, it says "ice returns."

When it becomes water, it is categorized as having the nature of earth; its lack of solidity is what makes it subtle. Generally, in all six great elements, one must first demonstrate the nature of that element.
Thus, the masters such as those of Wuxing who split the two lines concerning the nature of earth to serve as a general demonstration are incorrect. II.
Second, citing how form and emptiness mutually constitute one another.
Observe the nature of earth: that which is coarse is the great earth, and that which is subtle is the minute particle.
When reduced to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest atom), analyze that ultimate limit of form into seven parts; further analysis of the *paramāṇu* reveals it to be the very nature of emptiness.
Ānanda, if this *paramāṇu* can be analyzed into empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form.
The passage has two meanings. First, it clarifies that by analyzing form (*rūpa*), one realizes emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Xiachuan says:

"When you observe the nature of earth," this refers to the differentiated nature of analyzed phenomena (*dharmas*) and not to the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*). One must not conflate these when explaining the meaning according to the text.

For instance, within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there are two kinds of dharma-nature (*dharmatā*): first, the nature of phenomenal dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*), because of their specific differentiation; second, the nature of substantial dharmas (*dravyadharmanairātmya*).
Because their nature is real: "coarse" refers to the coarseness of that which is large; "subtle" refers to the subtlety of that which is minute.
In the sūtras, there are three names for atoms (*rajas*): first, *paramāṇu*; second, *aṇu*, which is the ultimate limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*); and third, *sanniveśa-rajas*.
When an *aṇu* is divided into seven parts, it becomes a *paramāṇu* (or *sanniveśa-rajas*); thus, one *aṇu* consists of seven *paramāṇus*.

If one further analyzes the *paramāṇu* (the subtle atom), it immediately enters into emptiness.孤山 (Gushan) says: "The *paramāṇu-rajas* (subtle atom-dust) is so named because this dust is extremely fine, bordering upon empty space.
Seven *paramāṇu-rajas* make one *tūla-piṅga-rajas* (gold-transmitting dust); seven *tūla-piṅga-rajas* make one *udaka-rajas* (water-transmitting dust);
seven *udaka-rajas* make one *śaśa-roma-rajas* (hare-hair-tip dust); and seven *śaśa-roma-rajas* [make one *vṛṣabha-roma-rajas* (ox-hair-tip dust)]."
Seven wool-hair-tip particles constitute one cow-hair-tip particle. Seven cow-hair-tip particles constitute one mote floating in a sunbeam.
According to this statement by Gusuan, the "limit of the subtle matter" mentioned in the Sūtra refers to the *suvarṇa-rajas* (gold-dust).
To further analyze the *paramāṇu* (neighboring-void) as being ultimately the nature of emptiness is [the perspective of] the Small [Vehicle].

Within this [system], analyzing emptiness is considered a clumsy method (*duḥkhā pratipad*). If one relies on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, taking impermanence as correct analysis and analyzing down to atoms as erroneous analysis, the *Śamathavipaśyanā-śāstra* (or *Tattvārthā*) quotes the *Vyākhyāyukti* as follows:
"If there is matter consisting of ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), then it has parts in the ten directions;
if there is no matter consisting of ultimate atoms, then it has no parts in the ten directions. If one analyzes matter down to its ultimate atoms and does not reach the end..."

[If one analyzes down to] the ultimate atoms, one falls into the view of permanence and the view of existence; if one analyzes the atoms until they are exhausted, one falls into the view of annihilation and the view of non-existence.

This refers to the analysis of form (*rūpa*) by these non-Buddhists (and so forth). The treatise further clarifies the contemplation of analyzing form according to the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), stating:
"Whether form is coarse or subtle, when observed as a whole, it is impermanent and without self. Why is this? Because coarse and subtle forms, etc., [arise] from nothingness..."
"Clarification arises. Because ignorance is unreal, both the coarse and the subtle are provisional. Being provisional, they are impermanent and devoid of intrinsic nature;
thus one enters emptiness. The above constitutes the text on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

However, since the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) also contains the expression "analyzing particles," we know that within the Buddha-dharma this [method] is still employed as an auxiliary to the Path. Now, in this sutra, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra says:
Contemplate the minute particles of the body and those that compose the world; thus, the minute particles are equal and without distinction. The *Vajra* states:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who grind the trichiliocosm into minute particles..."
As stated in the sutra, these are all signs of the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

However, while the sutra describes the analysis of the body and the elements down to the formation of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the sign that the contemplation of emptiness has already been accomplished, the present text further analyzes even the *anu* (subtler particles) into emptiness, such that neither the [subtle] dust nor the atom can be apprehended.
Next, it clarifies how form arises from emptiness. Regarding this, Youxi said: "If these *anu*..."
"To analyze [form] until it becomes empty space" refers to the analysis of form into emptiness by breaking it down from the small.
"One should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form" follows this same principle to show how emptiness is combined to form matter.

Just as one has clarified emptiness by analyzing matter—breaking the large into the small so that what exists naturally passes into non-existence—one should likewise apply the analogy of emptiness to matter: by accumulating the small, one should achieve the large.

If it is logically necessary that form is constituted by combining with emptiness, such that their cycle has no beginning, then while all phenomena arise from within emptiness, they do not take emptiness as their cause of birth.
According to what is stated in the present text, however, emptiness is taken as the cause of birth;
this was established by the Buddha as a provisional teaching in accordance with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to serve as a foundation for the subsequent discourse.

The method of refutation is identical in principle to the following passages concerning the production of fire from a sun-mirror and tinder, or the receiving of moonlight as water by a *fangzhu* crystal.
Therefore, what follows is the analysis of form (*rūpa*) into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the unification of emptiness with form.
○ Third, the refutation of the delusion of combination.
Regarding your current question that the various manifested forms of the world arise through combination:
consider for a moment how this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom) exists—through what space does it combine? A *paramāṇu* cannot be formed by the aggregation of other *paramāṇus*.

Furthermore, regarding the atom (*paramāṇu*) that is analyzed into emptiness: by how many material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is empty space (*ākāśa*) synthesized? If it were synthesized by material forms, then what is synthesized would be material form and not emptiness.
If it were synthesized by emptiness, then what is synthesized would be emptiness and not material form. Since material form can still be further analyzed, how could emptiness be synthesized with it?

In this passage, the critique is presented first, followed by the presentation of the correct principle starting from the words "If form... and so on. In the initial section, beginning with "You now...", Ānanda’s question is restated;
then, starting with "You should...", the critique is developed. This critique refutes three points: first, the refutation of conjunction;

second, the refutation of form being conjoined with emptiness; and third, the refutation of emptiness being conjoined with form. However, the refutation of conjunction is itself subsumed within the refutation of form being conjoined with emptiness.
It is merely that the combination of form and emptiness is manifested together. First, "you should observe" [the following], which refutes the combination of emptiness into form.
As previously analyzed, one breaks down matter down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom) and stops there. Since these atoms have size, empty space must likewise have dimensions;
yet you do not know how much empty space is used to combine into a single *paramāṇu*. This sentence thus investigates [this point].
This is refuted. For the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the beginning of form; if this were not a conjunction, then everything would be non-composite.
Yet, prior to the atom, there is no further substance; it must necessarily conjoin with space to form the atom. But how can space be conjoined?
One should not anticipate a counter-argument here, which might claim: "Space cannot be conjoined, but it is the substance that is conjoined."

[If one argues that] particles are formed [by aggregation], since there is no particle whatsoever prior to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom), it would necessarily have to combine with a *paramāṇu* to form a *paramāṇu*.
However, while *paramāṇus* may only combine to form a *sūkṣmarajaḥ* (a subtle mote), how could they further combine to form another *paramāṇu*?
Therefore, it is said that "it should not be so," and so forth. Since particles are difficult to combine, they must certainly combine with space; yet, as for space, it cannot be combined.

Ah! This is the refutation of the origin of atoms by means of their own-nature (*svabhāva*) and other-nature (*parabhāva*). The "neighboring atom" (*piṇḍa-paramāṇu*) is the own-nature; "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is the other-nature.

Furthermore, the following section refutes the aggregation of matter to establish it as empty. One analyzes how many material forms must combine to constitute the great emptiness of the ten directions;
this sentence likewise investigates and refutes [that notion]. Some may say that this is merely an analysis...
While this synthesis appears to contradict the Buddha’s intention, his true purpose was precisely to refute contradiction.

If the ten realms are inherently complete, then—just as a gentleman is not restricted to a single vessel—one is capable of both good and evil, and according to the conditions of the ten realms, one can transform and create the ten realms.
If a gentleman performs his deeds solely to manifest his own capability, what fault could there be? Thus, the dharmas of the nine realms need not be overturned or destroyed to be the Buddha-realm.

Here, we have traced the origin of shadows and echoes precisely to demonstrate the existence of forms and sounds. In the preceding section, the refutation of arising from self and other also occurs in three places.

The absence of coming demonstrates that there is no conjunction. Next, by means of the moon-gem (*candrakānta*), two distinct objects are shown to be distant from one another to demonstrate their lack of conjunction;
this refutes co-arising (*sahotpatti*). Third, the phrase "it should not be" refutes causeless arising.

Regarding why only the four natures (*catasraḥ svabhāvāḥ*) are refuted and not the four characteristics (*catvāraḥ lakṣaṇāni*), the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Existence is merely self; non-existence is merely other; and so on, up to the double negation."
It is simply that there is no cause. The scriptural text is abbreviated. According to Jingxi’s explanation here, the refutation of nature can encompass the four characteristics.
