However, the refutation of characteristics within this context does not merely manifest emptiness; thus it says: "From what direction does the water flow here?
Although the cause of its arrival is refuted, provisional dharmas are still established. To exhaust the origin of these provisional dharmas is precisely the Middle Way.
This is the essence of nature. Therefore, the text continues below: "The water of nature is true emptiness," and so forth. Fourth, it clarifies the truth that is neither harmonious nor disharmonious:
"You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the water of nature is true emptiness and the emptiness of nature is true water—pure and fundamentally so."

It pervades the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know. If one person grasps the pearl in one place, water flows forth in that place;

if it is grasped throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire Dharma-realm. Since its arising fills the whole world, how could there be any fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
That the world has ignorance and delusion as its causes and conditions, or that it possesses an inherent nature—all such views are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and lack any real meaning.
"Nature-water is true emptiness" means that wherever there is water, it is immediately emptiness. "Nature-emptiness is true water" means that even where there is no water, it is all water.

Based on the previous statement regarding being submerged and drowned, one might think that emptiness does not produce water; however, in the present discussion, the dharmas of nature-water are fused and identical.
If they are already identical to nature-fire, how much more so for emptiness? "Mind" refers to the mind of delusion and enlightenment; "karma" refers to defilement.
The karma of purification. ○ Youxi said: Regarding the element of water, all five phases are likewise complete.

That metal can produce water is indeed the common discourse on principle and qi. The Sūtra says: "Therefore, when forests and thickets encounter pressure, they become water"—this shows that wood possesses the nature of water.
It also says: "Precious clarity produces moisture; as the fire-light steams upward, there is thus a water-wheel contained within."
In the worlds of the ten directions, this fire possesses the nature of water. Furthermore, it is said that rivers and streams constantly flow from the lakes and ponds of those continents;

thus, this land possesses the nature of water. Now, specifically taking the case of one who, during the bright fortnight by day, holds a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hand to receive the water of the moon, this also demonstrates the excellence of the conditions upon which it relies and the vastness of the locus where it depends. For water is the Great [Element].
The moon is the mother of the Yin, yet the moon itself has no self; it takes that which is the locus of its radiance as its substance.
Relying upon space yet not dwelling in space, how could there be any limit to the pervasiveness of the waters?
This is used to manifest that the water of nature is true emptiness, and the emptiness of nature is true water.

Is it not the case that the conditions upon which it relies are superior, and the locus in which it depends is vast? It is precisely for this reason that the intent behind distinguishing [the two] in relation to space lies here.

The ancients took the phrase "manifesting in accordance with karma" as belonging entirely to the preceding section, while Jiaoguang connected it to the following "the world is ignorant," failing to understand that it follows [the preceding].
The mind merely manifests the True Suchness (tathatā) responding to conditions. If there were no karma of the ten realms—whether defiled or pure—there would be no power to evoke a response.

One must understand that the arising of boundless defiled functions by sentient beings of the nine realms, as well as the arising of boundless wondrous functions by the Buddha, both obtain this way of resonance and response.
Or, one may harbor doubts regarding the nature and function of one's own self.
Why must one provide an interpretation based on "stimulus and response" (*ganying*)? However, the ten-fascicle [version] states:

"The profound channels through which a *pudgala* recompenses karma, and the remote resonance of stimulus and response, are also examples of this. Furthermore, Jiaoguang says: "These four characters possess two kinds of lack of autonomy.
First, if the various pure and wondrous forms of the mundane and supramundane do not follow those various..."
Even if one desires for pure karma to manifest, it cannot be obtained.

Second, as for the various impure forms of suffering and defilement in the three miserable realms and the four evil destinies, if one does not restrain those various defiled karmas, even if one desires for them not to manifest, they cannot be obtained.
(And so forth. I do not know how this discussion can possibly explain only the matters of the second section. Regarding this—

This direct and sudden principle of ultimate truth not only lacks any point of contact [with worldly views], but it even causes the purport of the Sudden and Perfect teaching to become increasingly obscured.
For the Śūraṃgama-samādhi King is such that all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid;
it values principle and does not value emotion. What constitutes emotion? It is the worldly delusion that regards causes and conditions as being naturally so.
What is meant by "principle"? It is this: remaining unchanged while following conditions, and following conditions while remaining unchanged.

Precisely because it remains unchanged while following conditions, one is able to follow conditions all day long without ever changing. Within the process of following conditions, there exists the distinction between being autonomous and non-autonomous;
yet within the state of remaining unchanged, although one may follow emotions all day long without autonomy, one has never ceased to remain unchanged.
Because it is sovereign, the *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* states: "This principle is manifest and eternally abiding in the world.

Although those in the five uninterrupted hells all possess the mark of liberation, and although they are blinded by ignorance and deluded, this principle persists. This is because he has profoundly attained this [principle].
Therefore, this section of the scripture deeply clarifies the eternally abiding true mind and the perfectly sudden ultimate truth, intending to cause every person to realize it.
All conditions that follow along with defilement or purity, when directly confronted, are themselves the unchanging nature.

There is nothing that is not originally pure and pervading the entire Dharma-realm; thus, one achieves the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. This is a state where there is cultivation and realization, yet no cultivation or realization.
To raise the mind is already an error, and to deliberate is already a deviation; this is the essential path of contemplating the mind. (4)
The element of wind is divided into four parts; first, a brief demonstration that it has no substantial entity.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance, for its motion and stillness are not constant.
Within the four subtle elements, wind possesses only the single quality of touch. As for its lack of substance: when it is not moving, one does not know where it is located.

Once it has been brushed away, it can no longer be found at all. Furthermore, if one reckons any one of the four positions regarding self and other as being the reality and the rest as false speech, that [position] possesses substantiality.
If one examines the four natures and fails to find them, yet perceives that "wind is non-existent" as being the reality, that too possesses substantiality.
This applies even up to the perception that "wind is neither existent nor non-existent."
It also possesses substantiality. If one observes the wind through the fourfold negation (*catuskoṭi*) and finds that the wind cannot be apprehended, it is then without substantiality.
Because it is without substantiality, there is no obstruction, and one thus attains entry into the limit of reality (*tattvakoṭi*). Wēnlíng says: "When the robe is brushed away, there is movement;
when the robe hangs down, there is stillness—this is what is meant by movement and stillness being non-constant. (2) Second, citing an example.
When you regularly adjust your robes before entering the great assembly, if a corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and touches a person nearby, a gentle breeze will brush against that person’s face.

*Saṃghāṭī* is translated here as "the miscellaneous or many-piece robe" (*zásuì yī*), because it is made from many small, cut fragments joined together in strips; it is also translated as "the tattered robe" (*huài*).
The term "colored robe" (*rāga-cīvara*) contains many meanings. It is called the "dust-free garment" because it severs the six sense objects;

the "emaciating garment" because it cuts through afflictions (*kleśa*); the "lotus garment" because it is free from defiled attachment; and the "intermediate-colored garment" because its colors are in accordance with the Dharma.
(From *Zhendi zaji*). It is also a general designation for the three robes (*tricīvara*). Youxi said: "This is the Buddha’s intention..."

The seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are explained in detail here, whereas the Confucian classics speak only of the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). As for the element of space (*ākāśa*), they regard it as Heaven.
If one were to contrast the four elements with the five elements: the two elements of water and fire are identical in both name and substance.

Regarding the two elements of earth and metal, the Confucians divide one into two, while the Buddhists combine them into the single element of earth; this is because earth is capable of producing metal.
Before gold has been formed, gold is the solid nature of earth; once gold is complete, gold becomes the structural core of earth.
Therefore, when there is one element of earth, it should correspond to two phases. The phase of wood is that of heaven. Wind takes movement as its nature;
wood belongs to the east and the trigram Zhèn (Thunder), which is the foremost of all movements. If one discusses the nature of wind, it is also among the five elements.

All these are present. For example, when the golden wind roars in fury, the waves of water surge and churn, the flickering light of a flame protrudes its tongue, and the sighing breath of the Great Mass (Mahābhūta) becomes wind—all these are instances of this. Thus, wind is called "Great.

Now, the specific instruction that you should always adjust your robes and so forth is intended to verify that the nature of wind has no fixed substance and that its movement and stillness are not constant. Within this context...
The literary momentum differs from what preceded. Previously, the *yīngsuì* (negative lens) was used to seek water and the *yángsuì* (positive lens) to seek fire;
this demonstrated that "existence arises from non-existence," which sufficiently reveals the inherent nature (*xingju*), yet the matter was somewhat difficult.

Now, the arising of a slight breeze on a garment also demonstrates that "existence arises from non-existence," which sufficiently reveals the inherent nature, and the matter is even more easily accomplished. This is because, among the four subtle elements (*sīmí*), wind alone...
First, contact with water and fire requires slightly more auxiliary conditions; this is the distinction between the difficult and the easy.
That which is easy is all the more sufficient to manifest the inherent nature. III. Investigation and Refutation, Part One: Investigation.
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, arise from empty space, or is it produced within that person’s face?
[The second refutation:
Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, then you would be wearing the wind; consequently, as the robe flutters and billows, it should be separated [from your body].

"Your substance: I am now preaching the Dharma within this assembly with my robes draped down. Look at my robes; where is the wind? There should be no place for the wind to be hidden within the robes.
If it were produced from space, why would there be no breeze when your robes are motionless?

The nature of space is eternally abiding, so the wind should be constantly produced. If there were no wind, space itself would perish. If wind could be seen to perish, then space could be seen to perish as well."
What are its characteristics? If there were arising and ceasing, it could not be called empty space. If it is called empty space, how can wind emerge from it?
If the wind arises spontaneously from the face that is being brushed by it, then it should brush you as well. Since you yourself are straightening your robe, why does it brush you upside down?
Examine this closely: the straightening of the robe belongs to you; the face belongs to that other person. Empty space is quiescent and does not participate [in these actions].
It flows. From which direction does this wind come to stir here? Since wind and space are distinct in nature, they are neither blended nor joined;
yet it is not the case that the nature of wind arises spontaneously from nowhere.

The textual analysis is divided into three parts. First, the refutation of two among the three positions. This begins with the formal citation and refutation. First, the initial phrase of the refutation regarding the production of the robe is cited:
"You then... is the challenge; "That robe... and below is the refutation. As for the statement, "In my assembly, the robe is hanging down":

since your robe is being blown by the wind, my robe is also being blown by the wind. If you claim that because you are adjusting your robe, [the Buddha] exists, then because I am hanging my robe, [the Buddha] does not exist. Thus...
It is clear that the robe does not [arise] from the wind. It should be understood that the opponent’s shifting argument is refuted by the phrase "it should not be so.

Next, regarding the refutation of the claim that emptiness gives rise to wind, it says: "As for your robe, etc. First, this is analyzed by contrasting it with the robe: if emptiness were to produce wind, why would it require your movement of the robe for it to exist?
Next, it clarifies that emptiness has no wind: if you insist that emptiness can produce wind, then the essence of emptiness must be constant.
In that case, the wind should never cease. Since it is space itself that can produce wind, when there is a time without wind, is it not the case that space itself has also perished?
As for the refutation of the destruction of wind: even granting your position that space has already perished, when an object is stationary, the cessation of wind can be observed;
yet if space were to perish, what characteristic or appearance would remain? If there were [any such thing], it would have to arise...

The section beginning with "Extinction" further refutes this by concession. Alternatively, [the opponent] may claim that the arising of wind constitutes the arising of space, and the extinction of wind constitutes the extinction of space.
The refutation states: "Since there is arising and extinction, how can it be established as space? For space is one of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The section beginning with "Named 'Space'" concludes the refutation. This is because worldly people commonly reckon that space is capable of producing [phenomena].
Because of the wind, the knots are manifested. Changshui said: "The nature of wind is movement, while empty space is tranquil.
How could that which is tranquil give rise to movement? Regarding the third point, "arising from breaking the face," the phrase "from you" follows from the preceding text:
the wind returns to brush against you, which is precisely brushing against you in reverse. How could it be that you yourself adjust your robes and then, in turn, brush against yourself?
To state it fully: "Since you adjusted your robes, why does [the wind] arise from the other person's face and instead brush against you?

Next, in the section on "Exhorting Thorough Observation," it says: "The adjustment of the robes is yours; the face belongs to that other person. This clearly shows that the wind does not arise from the face.
This sentence may also suffice to complete the preceding refutation of the notion that [the wind] arises from the face. Space is quiescent and does not participate in the flow [of phenomena].
This clarifies that wind does not arise from space; therefore, it asks, "From which direction does the wind come to stir here?

This collectively summarizes the two preceding meanings to show that the source of the wind's arrival is ultimately unattainable. Second, the refutation of combination (sāmagrī) is the refutation of co-arising (sahotpāda).
Since the natures of the characteristics (lakṣaṇas), the wind, and inert space are necessarily distinct, this was already refuted in the preceding text. [If one claims] that space can produce...

Wind is that which breaks through solitary emptiness; because it can arise from the conjunction of wind and emptiness before they have been broken apart, it is further broken [by the preceding analysis].
Among the three locations, the term "emptiness" alone is used because common sentiment generally holds that there is wind within emptiness.
Furthermore, the phrase "nature is distinct" also follows from the fact that empty space is quiescent and does not participate in movement; this is what is meant by "nature."
This is merely the nature within these characteristics. One should not proceed to refute the absence of causes below. ○ Fourth, revealing the truth:

You utterly fail to understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
it responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the capacity of their knowledge. Ānanda, if even a single person like you makes the slightest movement—
When one wears clothes, a subtle breeze arises; it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm and fills the lands of the world.

Pervading the entire universe, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. Those in the world who lack knowledge deludedly take this to be caused by conditions or to be of a spontaneous nature;
all such views are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind. They are nothing but words and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
In the first section on the realization of the perfect fusion of nature, the first part clarifies the essence of unchanging substance.

In the sutra, earth, water, fire, and wind are all contrasted with space; as the current passage states: "It is named empty space; how could wind emerge from it? The same applies to the preceding three great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Although this clarifies that the four great elements with characteristics are eternally separated from space, the underlying intent is to reveal [the reality] within the nature.

The four great elements and emptiness are mutually identical. Thus, it was previously said that "the nature of wind and emptiness are distinct," yet later it was said that "the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind"—this refers to the inherent nature. To say "pure and fundamentally so" means that true wind is unmoving.
True fire does not burn; true water does not drown; true earth does not obstruct.
How could such wind wait for one to adjust their robes before emerging from this nature-body? Wind is identical to space; where is it not pervasive?

Not only are wind and space mutually identical, but one may also say that the nature-wind is the true earth and the true earth is the nature-wind; the same applies to water and fire. Therefore, it is said:

It pervades the entire dharma-realm; this is the measure of its nature (*prakṛti*). Next, the function of following conditions (*pratyaya*) is clarified. First, it responds to the mind according to its measure; next, an actual instance is cited as verification. Question:
Previously, it was explained that clothing does not produce wind; why is it now said that when one moves slightly while wearing clothes, a subtle breeze emerges? Answer:

The previous passage refuted the doctrine of phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); the present passage clarifies the manifestation of phenomena through causes and conditions. This is the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-samvidita*).
Since wind ultimately does not arise from causes and conditions, it was previously stated that it cannot be produced by any of the three locations.
Nevertheless, although wind is fundamentally inherent, it only manifests when dependent upon conditions. This is like a jar or basin in a dark room containing the seven treasures within a well;
these are revealed only by means of a lamp, yet the lamp cannot produce the seven treasures. The nature of wind is likewise: through the condition of slight movement, there is slight [wind].

The wind arises. When there is the condition for the end of a kalpa, the fierce Vairambha winds manifest from the mind. Since all things are manifested by depending on conditions, how could they be produced by depending on conditions?
In the teachings, it is constantly clarified that phenomena such as jars and garments arise from causes and conditions and are therefore all impermanent;
only the principle of Buddha-nature, because it is manifested through causes and conditions, is eternally abiding. Now...
The Sūtra clarifies that the four great elements and the five aggregates are all the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous essence of True Suchness, which is the primordially existing Buddha-nature;
therefore, they are all manifested by conditions rather than produced by conditions. Furthermore, because the deluded minds of sentient beings do not cease, the blowing of the wind is unending:
it rises "puffing and swelling" from the North Sea and enters "puffing and swelling" into the South Sea—all of these are [the manifestation of the Tathāgatagarbha].
The minds of sentient beings differ: while sentient beings perceive movement, the sages perceive its immobility;
this is due to the difference in the scope of their knowledge. When the mind differs, the karma one follows also differs; wind is merely the retribution experienced as a result.
○ Regarding the five voids and the four great elements, the first briefly demonstrates their formlessness.
Ānanda, emptiness is formless and is manifested through form.
Emptiness has four names: first, empty space; second, non-existence; third, immovability; and fourth, non-obstruction.
Now, to speak briefly, "formlessness" encompasses these four meanings. Youxi said: "Cause" (yin) means "to depend upon. Among the myriad things of the world, their [mutual]...
It awaits the formation of form; because color reveals emptiness, this constitutes the fundamental source of that which depends on conditions. Wēnlíng says:
"To dig into the earth and find emptiness is what is meant by 'revealing through color. 2. Citing an example.

For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, various kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, as well as pāraśavas and caṇḍālas, have newly established a residence and dug a well in search of water.
When they have excavated the earth to a depth of one foot, there is one foot of empty space within;
likewise, even when they have excavated the earth to a depth of ten feet, they still find [ten feet of] empty space in between.
In a space of one *zhang*, the depth of the void corresponds to how much [the object] emerges from it.
Wēn-líng says: "In the Western Heavens (*Indo-Tibet*), the high and low are divided into four castes, similar to the four classes of this land (*China*).
The *Kṣatriya* is the royal caste; the *Brāhmaṇa* is the pure-vowed caste, also called the 'pure-practitioner' (*jìngxíng*), because they preserve the Way and abide in rectitude and purity."
The Brāhmaṇas are those of pure conduct; the Vaiśyas are merchants; the Śūdras are farmers—these are called the four castes (*catur-varṇa*).
The Pahlavas are those of sharp faculties; the Caṇḍālas are executioners. These, moreover, are clans distinguished by wisdom and folly. Gu Shan says:
"Pahlava" is translated here as "swift," which also refers to sharp faculties. Ci'en says: "The Brāhmaṇas, in general..."
The eighteen clans—this is one among them. *Caṇḍāla* translates here as "rigid insignia. Because their evil karma adorns them, they specifically bear insignia;
that is to say, shaking bells and holding bamboo poles. Youxi said: "When one foot of earth is excavated, there is one foot of empty space revealed.
This clarifies two meanings: previously, when the earth was great, it was clarified in contrast to space; now, when space is great, [it is clarified in contrast to earth].
This is distinguished by reference to form (*rūpa*). By analogy with the other three great elements, it should be understood that each lacks one of the remaining conditions. 3.
Investigation and Refutation 1.
The Investigation Is this emptiness produced from the earth as its cause, existing because of the act of digging, or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
[The Master] refutes the second [position]:
"Ānanda, if this space were produced spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth had been excavated?

Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration? If it arose because of the earth, then at the moment the earth was excavated, one should have seen space entering; yet when the earth..."

If space first emerges and there is no entering [of earth], how can space emerge because of the earth? If there is neither emerging nor entering, then space and earth would fundamentally have no different causes.
If they are not different, they are identical; if they are identical, then when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?

If it emerges because of digging, then the digging should produce space rather than producing earth. If it does not emerge because of digging, yet the digging itself produces the earth, how can this be?
"You see the void. Examine this again with the utmost precision and scrutiny: the chisel follows the hand as it moves in various directions, and the earth shifts according to the ground.
From what source, then, does this void emerge? The chisel and the void, being respectively solid and empty, cannot function for one another;
they are neither blended nor joined. It is therefore impossible that the void could arise from nowhere on its own."

The text is divided into three parts. First, the refutation of the three locations. This further consists of two sections: first, the formal citation and refutation; second, the exhortation to examine carefully.
Regarding the three locations, the refutation of the "causeless" (unconditioned) comes first. Since empty space (*ākāśa*) is the most quintessential example of the causeless, it is refuted first.
For instance, when one digs for earth and seeks water, and empty space suddenly appears, can one not doubt its lack of a cause? [End of] Refutation.
"Midway" (*zhōng*) means "far-reaching. This refers to the vast expanse of the great earth, which has never been traversed. Next, [the author] refutes the theory that space is produced from soil.
Changshui says: "If the cause reaches space, one first cites and refutes this: if soil produces space, then when soil emerges from a well, one should see empty space emerging with it;
and when the soil enters the well, one should see [space] entering with it. If you claim that space is congealed beneath the soil, then if the soil emerges first, one should not see empty space."
It leaps out from the earth and returns into the well; how can you say that space arises from the earth? If there were no downward movement, there would be no entering or exiting.
If one does not see space emerging from the earth and entering the well, then there would be no reason for space and earth to be distinct from one another.
To say there is no cause for their distinction means that just as space emerges from the earth due to digging, it likewise emerges due to digging.
The reason for this [objection] is the same. Therefore, the refutation states: "If it is so, then when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?

This is precisely a refutation of the claim that there is no difference [between them]. However, since the earth emerges while space does not, it would conversely seem as though space emerges because of the earth.
Thus, this refutation is used to negate the notion of emergence and non-emergence. This interpretation by Tianru (Tianru Weize) is largely consistent with the text. As he says:
If empty space were to emerge from the earth, one should see empty space emerging from the earth and entering the well;
this is a subtle interpretation. Jiaoguang’s rejection of this and his establishment of the analogy of "opening a pond to draw water" is rather lax;

it captures the sense of space entering, but fails to capture the sense of space emerging from the earth. When reaching the section on "Turning to Refute," if there is neither entering nor emerging...
The phrase must be explained as follows: "If one does not see emptiness coming out of the earth or entering the well. Jiaoguang’s explanation states: "This still inherits the previous objection;
it asserts that the earth itself comes and goes while emptiness has no coming or going," and thus he uses the fact that emptiness has no coming or going to raise the objection.
This, however, does not accord with the intent of the sutra. Third, the refutation of the production [of space] by digging: if one claims that empty space is caused by...

If it emerges because of the digging, then the intention of the digging is reversed to being the emergence of emptiness rather than the emergence of earth. It is not due to the lower [level] reversing and destroying [the former].
If it were not due to the digging that it emerged, then the digging would simply have produced earth; since emptiness is not earth, for what reason would one perceive there to be emptiness?
He exhorts [the reader] to examine this carefully within the middle [truth]. Wuxing says: "One should assign the Three Truths to the preceding [sections]."
The claim that "earth has no cause because it is moved by digging" is correct. Earth is moved from within the ground as it is transported out by digging;
the digging proceeds from the human hand, thus the digging has a cause. Since earth is moved by the ground, the earth has a cause.
Only emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has no cause. To say it has no cause is intended to clarify that emptiness is inherent within its own nature.
[The text continues: "Next, [the author] refutes the notion of a composite whole. The meaning is this: 'solid' refers to that which is solidified earth, taking solidity as its function;

'void' refers to that which is empty and penetrating, taking emptiness as its function. Since these two are fundamentally distinct phenomena (*dharmas*), how could solidity be used to constitute the function of the void, or emptiness be used to constitute the function of the solid?
Tongzhou says: 'Because the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these two are mutually contradictory, they do not [interact]...'"
This refers to the principle that "they do not act as causes for one another. It is not appropriate to refute the absence of a source below;

since the absence of a cause was already refuted previously, to refute it again here is because what was previously called "no-cause" can still be described as a "cause," whereas now, since it is neither a cause nor a no-cause, it is said to be "without source.
4. Revealing the Threefold Unity: First, equalize the four great elements as before.

If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind presently before you are likewise called the five great elements;
their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, all being the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.
Regarding this passage, there have been differing interpretations by ancient masters. Letan (Leshan Tanhua) directly took "great" (*mahā*) to mean the Tathāgata-garbha.

Xichuan (Xuedou Chongxian) said: "The reason why 'space' (*ākāśa*) is subsequently added to the four great elements and collectively termed the 'five great elements' is that while various sutras usually discuss only the four, this instance differs from them;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. The same principle applies below in the section on the faculties and consciousnesses."

The general designation "Great" (Mahā) is established provisionally based on its functional manifestation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the Buddha taught that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) exist nowhere they are not present, they are called 'Great'.
If one speaks of the pervasive nature of the Great, one must point to a specific phenomenon;

thus, when the phenomenal is subsumed within the principle and the derivative is returned to the source, it cannot be named, yet it is named—this is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Alternatively, some directly take the nature of the *garbha* [as the basis].
How mistaken is the interpretation of "Great Name" (Mahānāman)! Regarding the statement in the middle [of the text], "the nature of space is perfectly pervasive":
if one were to say that there is space in some places and no space in others, it would not be pervasive. Space is not like that; therefore, it is said to be pervasive.
This is exactly as explained in the ten successive arguments of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As the subsequent passage states: "It is boundless..."
"Movement agitates space, as well as the earth, water, fire, and wind. According to this passage, the element of space alone is called "immovable.

Regarding the phrase "the nature is truly perfect and harmonious": the nature of emptiness is itself the true four great elements; because the four great elements within the nature are identical to true emptiness, they are said to be "perfectly harmonious.
This means that by means of emptiness, the four are equalized and unified, returning to the hidden nature. It says:
Regarding that which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing: although the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) cease, the Sūtra states that "the nature is emptiness, yet it is true form.

Thus, when emptiness is present, earth, water, fire, and wind are also present; therefore, the four great elements do not cease. Although the four great elements arise, the Sūtra states that "the nature of form is true emptiness.
Thus, when the four great elements are present, emptiness is also present; therefore, the four great elements do not arise. Emptiness is without...
Arising and ceasing can be understood by analogy with this: because emptiness exists when the four great elements exist, emptiness has no arising;

because the four great elements exist when emptiness exists, emptiness has no ceasing. However, what is now called "no arising and no ceasing" refers simply to the absence of arising and ceasing within the context of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
2. Reprimanding Delusion to Induce Awakening.
Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should contemplate whether empty space is emerging, entering, or neither emerging nor entering.
That your mind is deluded and confused—this is because the obscuration of darkness constitutes emptiness; your mental confusion is likewise so. Empty space is what emerges.
This is for the purpose of entering [the realization] as previously explained, such as breaking through the earth to enter a well.

Furthermore, having previously refuted the notions of "entering" and "exiting," as well as the idea that one emerges without being excavated and so forth, it follows that there is neither entering nor exiting. Space is perfectly detached from all conceptual reckonings; its fundamental nature is the true reality (*dharmatā*).

The same applies to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Youxi said: "From the perspective of the characteristics of the five great elements, one is void while four are substantial, and thus they do not correspond to one another.
From the perspective of their nature, however, they are all equally the *tathāgatagarbha*. 3. Non-alteration while following conditions.
"You do not at all know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds according to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is as if one well produces one space:
the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so. Perfectly filling the ten directions, how could it have a fixed location? It follows karma."
I have realized that the ignorance and delusions of the world, whether caused by conditions or arising spontaneously, are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind;
they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real substance.
Youxi said: "Phenomena (xiàng) are the derivative; nature (xìng) is the fundamental. Because the perfect fusion of phenomena fundamentally arises from the inherent presence of nature, it is said:

'You do not know at all' (and so forth). The distinction made here differs from that previously [stated]. Previously, because one wished to equalize the four [elements] with emptiness, they were distinguished by being contrasted individually with emptiness.
Here, because one wishes to equalize the sense faculties and consciousnesses with emptiness, they are distinguished by being contrasted with awareness."
The nature of convergence and storage proceeds in a sequential order. Wēn-líng was not clear about this, and thus explained it in terms of essence and function.
Jiāo-guāng was not clear about this, and instead claimed that [the text] alters its phrasing compared to the preceding section while further inverting its meaning.
Huán’s error lies in his oversimplification; Jiàn’s error lies in his forced interpretation. Jízhōng says:
The analysis provided here is slightly more detailed than the preceding section.

First, it takes up the four great elements from the previous discussion and further correlates them with space (*ākāśa*), stating that their nature is truly perfect and harmonious (*pariniṣpanna*). Were it not for this, it would not correspond with the preceding text.

Now, within the demonstration of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), space is again correlated with awakening (*bodhi*); since space is a phenomenon of obscurity and dullness, it is contrasted with awakening.
To clarify their perfect interfusion: since emptiness is identical to awakening, it cannot be extinguished. Although it cannot be eliminated, it is nothing other than the single essence of awakening.
When it follows conditions and becomes obscured as emptiness, it accords with the minds of sentient beings;
when it is the precious awakening of true emptiness, it accords with the minds of sages. Furthermore, you have been pitting form against emptiness and robbing one of the other within the Tathāgata...
Because it returns to the *tathāgatagarbha*, within this state the wind moves and the space becomes clear.

Since I have united my wondrous clarity—neither arising nor ceasing—with the *tathāgatagarbha*, my body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions; it is merely due to the difference in the scope of what is known.

To take up a matter within emptiness and give rise to a single well is to accord with the Way of grasping emptiness. The emptiness of the ten directions is like the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Awakening to the Way by relying on this is what the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja says: "Space is non-dual; the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same.
By illuminating this sameness, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Sixth: Seeing the Great Four as One.
To briefly demonstrate its lack of cognition:
Ānanda, the seeing-consciousness is without cognition; it exists because of form and space.
"Seeing-consciousness" is a brief designation for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. This cognition within the sense-faculty arises from being separated from its objects.
It has no substance. Therefore, the beginning states that "seeing and cognition are without knowledge. The *Yìhǎi* says: "The faculties have no self-nature; they exist because of objects.
Seeing and cognition are the faculties, which manifest due to form and space. The subsequent text says: "Knowledge is produced by means of the dust [of objects].

Now, I say that all four propositions regarding existence and non-existence involve having knowledge. By now observing that there is no knowledge, one shatters these four views. It says: "The faculties merely..."
Because a mirror lacks the capacity for separate analysis, it is said to be "without cognition. This explanation is also acceptable. Second, citing an example:
as you are now in the Jeta Grove, which is bright in the morning and dark at night; even if it were the middle of the night, the white moon would shine with light.
In the dark fortnight, it is dark; thus, light and darkness are analyzed by means of seeing.
As for what is meant by "analyzed by means of seeing": previously, it was shown that cognition arises from objects; now, it is demonstrated that the appearance exists because of the sense organ.
III. The Investigation and Refutation of the Two [Positions]. A. The Investigation.
Furthermore, does this vision coexist with light and darkness and the great void, sharing the same essence as them? Or is it not of one essence?
Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different?
Xueli said: "This question consists of four propositions: first, identity; second, difference; third, both identical and different; and fourth, neither identical nor different.
However, in the scriptural text, two instances of identity and two instances of difference each constitute a single proposition.

Herein, one first establishes the three characteristics to correspond to the metaphors of the three preceding persons, and subsequently establishes the four propositions of identity and difference as the objects to be refuted."
Regarding the passage below, the reason why the origin of the views is not immediately refuted, but rather the notion of "identity" and so forth is refuted first, is as follows:
since it was previously explained that knowledge arises from objects and that characteristics exist because of the sense organs, the organ and the object appear to be of one essence.

If they were not of one essence, one would then calculate them to be of different essences; this extends even to calculating them as being both or neither. Therefore, these are refuted first. Up to...
In urging a thorough investigation, one first refutes the origin of views and refutes their combination, thereby concluding that they are inherent in nature.

The second section, the refutation of [the self], is divided into three parts: first, the refutation of the four propositions; second, the refutation of combination; and third, the refutation of causelessness.

Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the formal citation and refutation; second, the exhortation to investigate thoroughly. Within the first of these, there are four sections; the first is the refutation of the single essence.
Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally one with light, darkness, and space, then light and darkness—these two entities—would mutually negate each other.
When it is dark, there would be no light; when it is light, there would be no darkness. If seeing were identical to darkness, then light would vanish;
if it were necessarily identical to light, then seeing would perish when it is dark. If it perished, how could one see light or see darkness? If [it were identical to] light...
How can it be established that the seeing is singular and devoid of arising or ceasing?
The first phrase restates the position; "then it follows that" (則明) and below begins the refutation. Within the refutation, one first clarifies how the two objects (dusts) cancel each other out.
Although the seeing is of one essence with light, darkness, and empty space, since the two essences of light and darkness are mutually exclusive, we speak only of light and darkness because—
Emptiness does not reside within contradiction. If one proceeds to the subsequent formal refutation: when light appears, the substance of darkness has already perished;
consequently, the perception that perceives darkness also perishes. Therefore, at the time of light, not only is there no darkness, but there is also no perception of darkness.
The following line should be understood accordingly. If they were one, this would entail the sense of annihilation. But if there is annihilation, how could [perception] exist?
The character "extinguish" (mie) generally summarizes the preceding point: when darkness should be extinguished, then light is lost to sight.

If light is lost to sight, how can one see light? When darkness should be extinguished, how can one see darkness? The following section concludes by refuting this. 2. Refuting the notion of distinct entities.

If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you separate it from light, darkness, and empty space to analyze the source of seeing, what form or appearance would it take?
Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from empty space, this source of seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established?
The first phrase merely restates light and darkness. "If you are apart from" [the following] refers to the refutation based on three matters.

Furthermore, there are three points of intent. First, it clarifies that the characteristic of seeing is difficult to distinguish: when one is correctly perceiving light, darkness, or empty space, if one seeks the essence of seeing separately from these three matters, it cannot be found.
"The source of seeing" refers to the pure, luminous source of seeing. Second, it clarifies that apart from objects, there is no [seeing].

Regarding its substance: previously, when clarifying the three characteristics of correct seeing, it was shown that they cannot be analyzed apart. Now, it is clarified that if one were to separate them from these three characteristics, this seeing would necessarily not exist.
This is because seeing, light, darkness, and empty space are in constant union; people simply do not perceive their union.
Therefore, the Buddha clarified that if one were to separate it from these three characteristics, seeing would fundamentally have no substance. Third, the three are all...
It is distinct from the view of non-existence. Ignorance depends upon darkness; ignorance and darkness depend upon emptiness.
When these three things are all absent, this view cannot be established. (3) The third refutation: the view that it is both.
Light and darkness are mutually exclusive; how could they be the same? Apart from these three [elements], nothing exists; how could they be different?
Previously, you only calculated one side, raising but a single difficulty. Now, by calculating both sameness and difference, you raise two difficulties.
If you do not mention emptiness within "sameness," it is because form subsumes emptiness. ○ Fourth, the refutation of "neither-nor."
The divisions of space and the divisions of vision are fundamentally without boundaries; how could they not be identical? Seeing darkness and seeing light—their nature does not undergo change;

how could they not be different? That they are not identical refers to space; that they are not different refers to light and darkness. This is merely a matter of alternating patterns appearing in the text. They are boundless.

Because its boundaries appear to be identical, it cannot be said that they are not identical; because its nature is unchanging, it appears to differ from light and darkness, so it cannot be said that they are not different.

Question: Since none of the four propositions regarding identity and difference can be established, are these merely delusive appearances lacking any certainty, or are they the inconceivable Middle Way? Answer: All four propositions of identity and difference are... [as before].
Deluded views. Since deluded views do not establish deluded marks, which are fundamentally empty, the inconceivability of the Middle Way can likewise be understood therein.
Why is this? If even delusion has no fixed existence, how could the Middle Way have any place for dwelling or attachment?
Non-dwelling is precisely inconceivability. 2. Exhortation to Careful Contemplation.
Examine this further with extreme subtlety, scrutinizing it with meticulous care and profound clarity: light comes from the sun; darkness follows the dark moon;
pervasion belongs to empty space; and obstruction returns to the great earth. From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise?

Regarding the four instances of the character "shen" (審) in the preceding four lines, Xi-chuan’s *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Within the 'Great Root' (*kendai*), there are four instances of the character 'shen.
The first line provides a general heading; the subsequent three instances of 'shen' examine how brightness, darkness, and space cannot give rise to the Great Root.
Within the preceding 'Space-Great,' the term 'shendì' (審諦) is likewise a general heading; what follows—'the boring proceeds from the hand of man'—is the specific examination (*dì*)."

This is a careful examination. "The earth shifts according to the ground" refers to thorough observation (*prativedha*). At the bottom, where it says "within the Great Mean there are only two details," these two "details" correspond to the two meanings of "seeing" (*darśana*) and "appearance" (*nimitta*).
Xiachuan’s interpretation pairs this with what precedes; the "Supplementary Notes" pair it either with what precedes or with what follows, but the numerical correspondence is still inconsistent.
However, observing the flow of the text, the first sentence is actually a general heading, while the following two sentences mean:
"Fine" (*sūkṣma*) means not only fine but also extremely subtle; "thorough" (*parīkṣā*) means not only thorough but also meticulously detailed.
Furthermore, in terms of the object, it is "thoroughly discerned" (*parīkṣita*); in terms of the observation, it is "thorough observation" (*parīkṣā*).

Having provided this explanation, one then correlates these four instances of the character "thorough" (*parī-*) with the preceding four propositions of identity and difference, or alternatively, with the four propositions of light and darkness, or penetration and obstruction.
Thus, it is untainted (*anāsrava*). Previously, the four propositions—identity, difference, and so forth—were refuted to demonstrate the origin of the arising of views.
Now, the statement "clarifying that [vision] proceeds from the sun" means that while light and darkness, as well as openness and obstruction, all have causes, vision itself has no cause.
Regarding the term "seeing-essence" (*jiàn-jīng*), it refers to the six sense-faculties as the essence of seeing. ○ Second, the refutation of conjunction:
seeing and cognition are empty and insentient; they are neither conjoined nor combined.
The mention of "empty" alone subsumes form. Previously, in the refutation of distinct entities, it was shown that the appearance of clarity and the characteristic of seeing seemed to be conjoined.
Furthermore, in the refutation of the "neither-nor" position, it is said: "Since the divisions of emptiness and the divisions of vision originally have no boundaries, how could they not be identical?
Upon thorough investigation, the nature of seeing and awareness is vast and distinct from the nature of empty and inert matter; they cannot be said to be in union.

The previous refutation of them not being a single entity was like a refutation of their union; however, since that only refuted their being a single entity and did not refute their union, they are now refuted once more. ○
Third, it refutes the absence of cause.
One should not see that the essence of seeing arises from nowhere on its own.
For the essence of seeing is of the same substance as the Truth; it has existed eternally since beginningless time, so why must one seek its point of origin? Nevertheless...
Since beginningless ignorance has already been distinguished as arising from the delusion of the True [Nature], it cannot be said that it emerges without a cause.
Having clarified above that the essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*) appears to have no cause from which it arises, he now once again refutes the notion of causelessness.
○ Fourth, revealing the threefold unity of the True [Nature] such that all equally constitute the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).
If one perceives that the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that the boundless,
unmoving void, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally termed the six great elements whose natures are truly and perfectly interfused.
All are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.

Gushan said: Previously, in the extensive refutation regarding the six sense organs, the visual faculty was analyzed in detail while the others were treated briefly. Now, by way of analogy, their nature is revealed as being universally pervasive.
"Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty; "perceiving" refers to the nose, tongue, and body faculties;

and "knowing" refers to the mind-faculty. The reason "perceiving" is not explicitly mentioned [in the verse] is for the sake of brevity. Because their nature is perfectly round and all-pervasive, they do not see color and emptiness in a biased manner. Fundamentally...
Though it wavers, it ultimately remains far removed from arising and ceasing; yet, as this is still discussed in terms of phenomenal events, it is not necessarily the ultimate truth.

As previously stated in the refutation of "oneness": "If light and darkness are distinct perceptions yet lack arising and ceasing, even though the sutras say there is no arising and ceasing and no transition or change, can this be called the Truth?
Therefore, it is like the unmoving void compared to the wavering earth.

Water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "six great elements" (*ṣaḍdhātu*). Only when one reaches the realization that the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is fundamentally without arising or ceasing can it truly be called "real.
Youxi said: "In this context, first the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are equated with space (*ākāśa*), and subsequently the sense-faculties are equated with the remaining five great elements.
This is intended to reveal that the two [sets of] great elements are more expansive and superior than the former; as for space..."
The faculty of the immovable and signless is superior; the faculty of the cognitive is superior in that it possesses awakening yet lacks cessation.

However, these distinctions of superiority and inferiority do not transcend the conceptual differentiation of characteristics (*nimitta*). Just as the abbreviated expressions of the *pitaka* contain no difference in meaning, we now unify them by stating that the nature is truly perfect and harmonious, such that all are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.
Thus, the profound patriarchs equated the faculties with the great emptiness.
As for the "Great" (the faculty of sight): as the Sūtra says, "Its nature is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving. Therefore, the faculties and the Great [Element] are equally empty.
○ Second, censuring delusion to bring about awakening.
Ānanda, your nature is submerged and you do not awaken to the fact that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

You should observe this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they arising or ceasing? Are they identical or different? Are they neither arising nor ceasing? Are they neither identical nor different?
Those who are mired in delusion stagnate in the principle of non-action and quiescent extinction.

Because it is said that within ultimate truth there is no seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, one should contemplate the very seeing, hearing, and so forth that manifest before one. To be able to perceive that which lies beyond objects is to be subject to arising and ceasing;
to stand in opposition to external objects is to be concerned with identity and difference. Wénlǐng says: "Arising and ceasing, identity and difference—all are due to..."
Delusive objects are neither produced nor differentiated, yet they do not depart from deluded conceptualization. To be free from these various delusions is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
3. Unchanging while following conditions:

You have never known that within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, the essence of awareness and the purity of seeing. It is fundamentally pure and original.
It pervades the entire Dharma-realm, corresponding to the minds of sentient beings and the scope of what they know.

Just as with the faculty of sight, where seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of touch—all these wondrous virtues are brilliantly pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Perfectly filling the ten voids, how could they have a fixed location?
They manifest according to karma; those in the world who lack knowledge mistakenly take them to be caused by conditions or to possess a nature of spontaneity.
All of these are merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind; they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
First, it clarifies that the awakened nature is perfectly interfused. Within the section on "The Unchanging," it first clarifies the principle of the inherent completeness of the nature.

The seeing of the original nature is precisely the luminosity of the essence of awakening. Because the essence of awakening is not intermingled with deluded phenomena, it is called "pure" (*vimala*). As for the essence of awakening—
"Essence" (*jing*) refers to the seeing that is clear and distinct. Here, the function is distinguished from the substance: "nature-seeing" and "clear seeing" are the function;
"awakened clarity" and "awakened essence" are the substance. The same applies to the subsequent [four] great elements.

This principle of the Middle Way as inherent nature differs from that of the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings. In those teachings, the true reality is neither seeing nor hearing, nor is it the substance of awakening. Now, this is...
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), this differs from the partial truth (*pian zhen*). In the Separate Teaching (*bie jiao*), it is held that the very act of seeing and hearing is itself Buddha-nature;

however, the nature of seeing and the nature of hearing are considered to be utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects. Now, by pointing out that the various faculties of seeing and hearing are themselves the essence of awakening, the Separate Teaching is refuted.
This is the doctrine of the inherent presence of nature (*xing ju*). As for "pure," it means that within the nature, the six faculties are fundamentally devoid of [substantial] faculties.
It is pure by virtue of its marks. Fundamentally, this essence of nature is not something produced by causes and conditions. Regarding its "pervading the entire dharma-realm":

although within the essence of nature according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao) seeing and hearing are both present, if one holds that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature while insentient things lack it, then it would not be all-pervasive.
In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the very substance of form and fragrance is itself seeing and hearing; therefore, it is only...
Form is solely mind, capable of pervading the entire Dharma-realm; this is its essential nature and magnitude. The preceding section clarifying the unchanging essence is now complete.
Next, the section on following conditions is clarified: according to the pure minds of sentient beings, it becomes the six sense organs of the Buddha-realm;
according to the defiled minds of sentient beings, it becomes the six sense organs of the nine realms. As the Sutra says: "In the world, who possesses true divine vision? There is.
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, perceives all buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics, the scope of his knowledge is the most vast.
The nine realms become progressively narrower as one proceeds. This passage fully encompasses the six sense faculties; since the faculty of sight is easy to understand, it is first used for analysis.
By analogy with sight, the same applies to the other five, without exception. When it says that "sight pervades the dharma-realm," it refers to the vision of sentient beings present before us.
The faculties gaze upon their respective objects, which pervade the entire dharma-realm. Wēnlíng says: "The tongue-faculty is called 'contact' because it perceives only when in contact with flavor;
the body-faculty perceives touch; and the mind-faculty perceives through cognition. The functional application of these six faculties is entirely wondrous virtue (*miao-de*).
To say they are 'luminously clear' means they are transparent and penetrating; they are all identical to the seeing-faculty and pervade the entire dharma-realm."
Regarding the "realms" (*dhātu*) and the "following of activities": because the activities of the ten realms differ, the seeing and hearing of the ten realms are each distinct.
The phrase "the world below" criticizes deluded sentiments for lacking a fundamental aim; one must know that the Great Nature (*mahā-bhāva*) is universally beyond names and words.

As soon as it belongs to the realm of conceptual thought, it is no longer the true meaning. This is the Dharma-gate entered by Mahāsthāmaprāpta, for he is said to "completely gather the six sense-faculties."
Therefore. ○ Section Seven: The Greatness of Consciousness. This "greatness" is the point of Maitreya’s awakening. It is divided into four parts. First, a brief demonstration that it has no source:
"Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of sense organs and their objects."
The substance of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is intimately close to the Truth; therefore, it is said that "the source of the organs and objects is the same.

The nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is illusory and thus lacks a source. If one were to take the organs and objects as the source, since the organs and objects themselves are already false, they would have no source.
Consciousness arises from the sense faculties and their objects. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The two terms 'eye' and 'form' give rise to the single term 'consciousness. Question:
Previously, you explained that the nature of fire and so forth are devoid of a self by means of the fourfold negation (catuṣkoṭi).

Can this same explanation now be applied to the term "sourceless" (*anidana*)? Answer: The four propositions of existence and non-existence are all conceptual constructions of the discriminating mind. Now we know that the nature of consciousness is empty.
Deluded views arise from consciousness and are entirely untrustworthy; they are, in fact, the very root-source that transcends the four propositions.
○ Second, citing an example:
"Now you should observe the assembly of sages in this gathering, surveying them with your eyes; as your gaze ranges over them, it is merely like [seeing reflections] within a mirror."
There is no separate analysis. You must identify them one by one within this assembly: "This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa;
this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti; this is Śāriputra."
The initial mention of the "root" (*indriya*) serves to distinguish it [from consciousness]. The term "universally observing" differs from the subsequent "pointing out" mentioned in sequence.
Zhenji said: "The root merely illuminates the object, like a mirror; consciousness possesses discrimination, and thus it is able to point out. Jiaoguang said:
"When the myriad phenomena are reflected against one another and not a single thought arises, this is precisely the characteristic of the root. Youzu said: "The holy assembly amidst the dust..."

It is also the pervasive observation of the faculties. The "seeing-essence" (*darśana-viśuddhi*) revealed in the second fascicle and the "consciousness-essence" (*vijñāna-viśuddhi*) pointed out in the first fascicle are precisely this substance.
Because Master Jiaoguang considers this to be true and eternal, he uses the phrase "having a determinate function.

He fails to realize that although the eyes' sequential observation is like a mirror—lacking distinct analytical discernment—it still belongs to the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). [This is] intended to provide proof.
Awakening must necessarily involve seeing the seeing. However, employing the eyes to scan objects is not yet the state where not a single thought arises. Why?

Where there are sense organs (*indriya*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*), there must inevitably be deluded thoughts. Just as within the eight consciousnesses there is the mental factor (*caitta*) of attention (*manasikāra*), how could the six sense organs be free from attention?
This [state of scanning] is merely fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*); one must not give rise to it here.

To claim that the object of perception (*ālambana*) is itself the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), or to point directly to it as ignorance (*avidyā*), or to point directly to it as the nature of phenomena—these errors are all equal.
Only if this very nature of awakening is realized can one be said to have attained the essential meaning. What follows in your text clarifies the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the preceding sense organs are like mirrors, they are able to give rise to consciousness. Thus, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), along with the five types of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the sixth consciousness, are all termed "consciousness.
When the eye and form directly apprehend the characteristics of form, there is a "natural discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).

This does not involve verbal designations (*nāma-pada*) nor does it involve "conceptual discrimination" (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*); furthermore, it belongs to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Regarding this, the root of grasping and clinging does not arise.

Dust (*rajas*) being empty in itself is precisely the *dharmatā*. From that, the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) gives rise to a third moment of thought, which conceptually grasps names such as "so-and-so" and so forth;
this is the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of recollective estimation (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).

However, while the five sensory consciousnesses and the fivefold mental consciousness all take the objective realm (*svalakṣaṇaviṣaya*) as their object, when the sixth consciousness operates apart from the five sensory consciousnesses, it takes its own unique, projected images (*svavikalpamātraviṣaya*) as its object. It is also thus.
This is now subsumed under the great element of consciousness. III. Investigation and Refutation (1) The Investigation:

Does this consciousness that cognizes arise from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), or does it arise from the appearance-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), or does it arise from empty space, or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?

The *Yihai* states: "The non-arising of the four locations manifests non-arising. To say 'without cause' means that since the three locations cannot produce [anything], one might reckon that it exists without a cause.
II. Refuting the Divisions, Part One: Refuting the Four Locations, Section One:
Direct Citation and Refutation.

Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing—just as there are the four factors of darkness, light, and form—then these four would necessarily not exist, and you would fundamentally lack seeing.
If the nature of seeing itself does not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If the nature of your consciousness were produced within the objects and not from seeing, then you would neither see light nor see darkness; since light and darkness would not impinge upon it, they would not exist.
Form is empty. If those marks do not exist, from what would consciousness arise?
One who conducts such an investigation clarifies that the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has no source.

In the previous explanation, it was stated that because the sense organs and their objects are illusory, consciousness has no source; now, by investigating how the organs and objects cannot produce consciousness, it is said to have no source. This is the first section.
Destruction arises from seeing. If consciousness arises from seeing, it necessarily does not arise from signs.
Just as when there are no signs, seeing itself cannot be obtained; at such a time, since even the faculty-nature does not exist, how could consciousness possibly arise?
This seeks to take the "seeing" (*darśana*) as the source, yet it cannot be established. Next, the refutation proceeds by way of the "characteristic" (*nimitta*).
If consciousness were definitively produced from the characteristic, it would not be produced from the seeing; however, without seeing, there is no characteristic.
At such a time, since even the characteristic itself cannot be established, how could consciousness exist? This seeks to take the characteristic as the source, yet it cannot be established.
It is so. If one were born within emptiness, it would be neither characteristic nor vision. Without vision, there is no discernment; by itself, one could not know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

Without characteristics, conditions are extinguished, and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place to be established. Abiding in these two absences, emptiness is then identical to non-existence.
There is that which is not the same as the object; even if you were to give rise to your consciousness, what would you distinguish?

Third, the refutation of its arising from space: first, the refutation of the space that could produce it. Regarding "neither-nor" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*), this means taking neither characteristics (*nimitta*) nor seeing (*darśana*) to be space.
It is called "not characteristics" because it does not arise from objects (*viṣaya*); it is called "not seeing" because it does not arise from the sense organs (*indriya*).

It is said that this is not seeing. Because emptiness has no form and is manifested through color, once the colors of light and darkness as well as the characteristics of space are unobtainable, this emptiness becomes yet another layer deeper. Since it is not seeing, one cannot discern external objects;
therefore, the four kinds of external sensory realms are not known. This is because there is absolutely no opportunity for consciousness to arise. External realms are the "objects" (ālambana).

Regarding conditions: if there are no characteristics (*nimitta*), then the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are extinguished; yet if there are no characteristics, there is likewise no seeing. There is certainly no way for consciousness (*vijñāna*) to arise.
All that has been discussed above clarifies that seeing and characteristics exist as a causal relationship between them.

Hereafter, the text properly refutes the notion that consciousness arises from emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meaning) states: "Because it is neither characteristic nor seeing, it is called 'the negation of both'"; this directly refers to emptiness.
"Being empty is the same as non-existence" means that if the arising of consciousness were empty, it would be identical to a tortoise’s hair.

Alternatively, even if consciousness were existent, it would still not be the same as the sense organs and their objects. As for the phrase "even if it gives rise to your consciousness," it is because [consciousness] is the same as the sense organs and objects that it is able to differentiate external objects;
since it is not the same as the sense organs and objects, even if it gives rise to your consciousness, how could it possibly differentiate external objects?
"O Dust! If [consciousness] were to emerge suddenly without any cause, why would you not perceive the bright moon at midday?
To perceive the moon at midday would mean it arises without a cause; yet since such a perception does not exist, how can you claim there is no cause?"
Second, the exhortation to examine thoroughly:
"Examine further with meticulous detail; examine with subtle scrutiny. You see that [the visual consciousness] relies upon your pupils to project toward external objects.
It can be characterized as existing when it is established, and as non-existent when it is not so established. Thus, from what source does this consciousness arise as its condition?"
The Supplement states: "You must further examine the general heading in detail; you must minutely scrutinize the specific enumeration.

Indeed, the explanation of the general and the specific is most thorough, and the detailed characteristics and detailed manifestations are also contained therein. 'Seeing' relies upon the sense organs."

Regarding the mutual entrustment of subject and object: that which emerges can be characterized; that which does not emerge is non-existent. Thus, both the sense faculties and their objects—whether empty or existent—possess causes from whence they arise;
yet consciousness itself has no point of origin. 2. Refuting the Conjunction [of Causes].
When consciousness moves, vision becomes clear; they are neither blended nor conjoined. This is likewise true for hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognition.
When there is movement, it is consciousness that is able to discern; when there is clarity, it refers to the sense organ merely reflecting its object.

Ānanda previously raised an objection based on the concept of "blending," so I have now reaffirmed my position to refute that blending. If consciousness were produced from the sense organ, then the principle of blending would apply; however, since—

If it does not arise from the sense organ, how could it possibly constitute a combination? Xunwen says: "The consciousness is active while the seeing is still; this is neither a combination nor a union.
This refers to the lack of combination because the activity of the organ and consciousness is contrary to the stillness [of the object].

If one considers it in relation to another object, it likewise refutes the notion of self-arising. Furthermore, regarding the element of wind, it says: "Wind and space are separated by their natures; they are neither combined nor united. Since...
The discussion on objects (*ālambana*) is for the purpose of refuting production from another. If it says regarding the element of fire: "The sun and its object are distant;

they are neither conjoined nor combined," this is precisely the refutation of the nature of conjunction when comparing self and other. Because these are stated according to the context, they do not follow a single uniform path.
The subsequent examples, such as "hearing and listening," refute the remaining consciousnesses. "Hearing and listening" distinguishes between the ear and the nose.
The nose is so named because it smells and perceives. Third, the refutation of arising from nothing:
consciousness cannot arise spontaneously from nothingness as its condition.
"Condition" refers to the causal basis for the arising of consciousness. Since the refutation of causelessness has already been established previously, causelessness is likewise [refuted here].
Since there is no source from which it arises, its non-arising is further established. IV. Revealing the True Three-in-One and Unifying the Seven Elements:

If this consciousness-mind originally has no source, one should know that its capacity for discernment—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfect, tranquil, and its nature does not arise from any external locus.
Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly interfused and perfectly harmonious.
All are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
To say they are "fundamentally without a source" means precisely that because they have nowhere from which they come, they are inherently present within the nature.

The discernment of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing does not refer to the six consciousnesses; it points to the aforementioned sense organs as the great elements. This nature does not arise from an external source, nor...

This demonstrates that the faculties and natures are inherently complete; once one realizes that consciousness and the faculties are equal, one then sees that the sentient and the insentient are likewise equal.

Because all things are inherently complete in their nature, they are subject to neither birth nor extinction. Wēnlíng says: "Since this is true of the earth and so forth, it applies to the world, its beings, and every single object.
Not only are the earth and such called 'great,' but even grass, weeds, dust, and a hair may all be called 'great. Question: The five...
The consciousness [in question] is the eighth consciousness; its seeing-part fundamentally belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and can be traced back to the Tathāgatagarbha.

The five sensory consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness are the "clinging mind. Now, since this sutra denounces them as the root of birth-and-death, how can they also be the Tathāgatagarbha? Answer:
The clinging minds of the nine realms are none other than what is inherently possessed by principle (*li-jù*). As the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary) says:
This is precisely the meaning of the statement that it is only through the inherent presence of principle (*li*) that phenomenal function (*yòng*) can arise. This攀緣心 (攀緣心;

*pānyuán xīn*, the mind that grasps at objects) entering into the essence of principle is entirely the Buddha-dharma, and is called the Tathāgatagarbha. Question: Within the Tathāgatagarbha, what use is there for this攀緣心? Answer:
