Therefore, it is not grasped. If this is so, why does the Tathāgata figuratively simulate it by saying that one perceives other objects and so forth?

The Buddha’s intention is to clarify that within the dream there are both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), yet his primary intent lies in demonstrating that the nature of hearing is not extinguished.
Question: Since the hearing in a dream is this very nature, how can it be said to correspond with external objects? Could the nature itself possess such correspondence?
"Is it external objects? He replied: "All sentient beings harbor this doubt. One must know that if one does not recollect external objects, then the appearance of objects ceases;
this is the essential path to forgetting objects. ○ Second, the conclusion: the dissolution of form is not extinction.
Even though your physical form may dissolve and your life-force (prāṇa) may pass away, how could this nature be extinguished by you?

Since you already understand that one is not deluded within a dream, you should know that the body dies but does not perish. For the true nature is fundamentally detached from the sense organs and their objects;
how could it perish along with illusory shadows? As for what is called "the light of life," the preceding text states: "Adhering to the false, it emits light."
This is precisely the light of life. "To be" means to be affected. True nature is eternally thus; it is not extinguished by being affected by the relinquishment of retribution.
Previously, Ānanda had raised a general doubt that the six sense organs have no substance when separated from their objects.

The Tathāgata therefore specifically revealed the nature of hearing as permanent, truly wishing to stimulate the faculty for the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ. Part Two: Showing that the Nature of Hearing is Permanent is concluded. Part Three.
The section on the summary and comprehensive demonstration is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies that because of delusion regarding permanence, there is impermanence.
Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have followed after forms and sounds, flowing and turning with every thought.

They have never awakened to the pure, wondrous, and permanent nature of their own essence. Instead of following what is permanent, they pursue various states of arising and ceasing; consequently, birth after birth, they flow and turn through defilement.
This clarifies that the transmigration of sentient beings through birth and death arises entirely from their failure to recognize the eternally abiding nature.

The term "beginningless" refers to the delusions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*). "Following" means to conform; when the sense organs and their objects encounter one another, one follows sounds and pursues forms, thereby giving rise to consciousness.
This is to transmigrate with every thought-moment, never realizing that the nature of seeing and hearing is fundamentally and eternally abiding.
It is pure and signless; yet, being deluded by impermanence, one lacks the wisdom that perceives the Path.

Because one does not realize the permanence of the nature [of reality], one does not rely upon the permanent to initiate cultivation. To flow and circulate with every thought is to pursue all that arises and ceases.
Because of this, one sinks forever into birth and death; what is not pure and wondrous is defiled. What is not eternal is subject to transmigration.
What was previously called "transmigration" referred to transmigration within mental conceptions; what is now called "transmigration" refers to transmigration within birth and death.
This arises from the accumulation [of suffering] which gives rise to suffering. 2. Explaining that abandoning the impermanent is itself the eternal.

If you abandon arising and ceasing and maintain the true permanence, the light of permanence will manifest before you. At that moment, the faculties, their objects, and the consciousness-mind will all dissolve away.
Conceptualization and appearances act as dust; cognitive attachment acts as grime. When both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.
Why would one not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

The former involves the arising of accumulation that invites suffering; the latter involves cultivating the path to realize cessation. It is the abandonment of birth and death to maintain the true permanence.
Changshui said: "To roam within wondrous constancy and quiescence where thought is severed; to illuminate within true awakening and clarity where conditions have perished—this is it.

If one examines the meaning of the text, discarding the faculties, objects, and consciousness constitutes discarding the arising and ceasing; maintaining the nature of seeing and hearing constitutes maintaining the true and constant.
As for "constant light," it refers to the inner luminosity emitting radiance as previously described. When the faculties are completely uprooted, the objects...

Consciousness is also eliminated. The above constitutes the Path of Cultivation; now, the cessation [of suffering] is realized. Regarding the passage beginning with "The characteristics of perception" (*saṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*), it explains the meaning of the dissolution of the sense objects, the faculties, and consciousness.
Now, as for the sense objects (*viṣaya*): they exist when remembered and vanish when not remembered; these are the characteristics produced by perception (*saṃjñā*).
If the mental state of consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises, love and hatred follow it; therefore, they are called "defilements" (*mala*) and should both be distanced from. And...
The root lies solely in transformation. When the eye-faculty transforms, it becomes the eye that sees the Dharma; once one enters the six purities, the other faculties may be understood accordingly.
When dust and defilements are removed, clarity and brightness arise. The term "far removed" means to relinquish birth and cessation and to maintain the true permanence.
The clarity of the Dharma-eye is the explanation of the manifestation of the eternal light before one. As for the phrase "how," it correctly explains the dissolution [of delusions].
As the preceding text stated, "Just as boiling water melts ice, one should contemplate the transformation into supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The previous passage cited the essentials merely to clarify the extraction from the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Now, it further clarifies that one should eliminate consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"Supreme enlightenment" here should be understood as referring to the fruition of Buddhahood, both in its partial (*prādeśika*) and complete (*paripūrṇa*) aspects. The first principle previously clarified the cessation of suffering (*nirodha*), while the second principle clarified the origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*). Now...
The two gates are used in conjunction. *Śūraṅgama-sūtra:

*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
*Contemplating the Mind: Resolving Doubts*, Scroll Five, Part Two:
Clarifying that the Unraveling of the Knots is Non-dual, following the second point. The previous second point stated:
"Ānanda, if you cultivate Bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know the illusory nature of the roots and objects."
Abiding in inversion, you do not even know where you are; how then can you subdue [the afflictions] and attain the rank of Tathāgata? Observe this:
when one in the world unties a knot, if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it?

It seems you must necessarily sever the afflictions before realizing the rank of Buddhahood, and untie those knots before it is called liberation. Is this not merely following principles to sever the nine grades of affliction in a sequential and distinct manner?
Regarding the gate of practice: I now clarify that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source, and bondage and liberation are non-dual.

To establish views based on knowledge and vision is the very root of ignorance; when there is no establishing of views through knowledge and vision, this is *nirvāṇa*. Thus, these six faculties are the true reality within delusion, the fundamental basis of non-abiding. As the Sūtra says:
"That which causes you to wander in birth and death—the root of your fetters—is none other than your six faculties."
It is not some other thing. This delusion is precisely the circulation through the three realms of existence.
That which enables you to swiftly realize the wondrous, eternal bliss is also nothing other than your six sense faculties; this awakening is the supreme function within the state of fruition.
It is like a single flowered cloth: when it is knotted, it becomes six; these are produced by the false conjunction of causes and conditions. When untied, they cease to exist.

First, this separation caused by conditions is called "extinction" (nirodha), yet it is utterly unable to know that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness (tathatā) of the Tathāgatagarbha.
There is no duality between the tying and untying of a single flower-scarf;

is this not the decisive penetration from the provisional and distinct into the perfect and harmonious? Is this not the great essential for initiating practice? Furthermore, as previously stated regarding the path of Bodhi:
Nirvana is cessation; afflictions are accumulation; birth and death are suffering. By means of the Path, one remedies accumulation, brings about cessation, and transcends birth and death.
These are the Four Truths of the three previous teachings. Now it is said that bondage and liberation are non-dual, and the knots and their untying are one and the same.

This demonstrates that the unconditioned Four Noble Truths are none other than the true reality (dharmatā) within the single perfect circle. The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery), Volume 4, Part 1, states:
"The wisdom of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths is formed by the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening, thus constituting four. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"A precious jewel is within one's body, yet one cries out in grief and weeps, claiming it has been lost; one sees only the body and the wound, but does not see the jewel."
The jewel and the mirror—possessing only sorrow and no longer having joy—this is the cessation of the path of delusion and the arising of the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

One should know that by establishing cognition upon what is perceived, one becomes subject to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If one understands that the very substance of the ulcer is itself the precious jewel, then one rejoices and does not weep;
by extinguishing ignorance (*avidyā*), one immediately attains the blazing lamp of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This is the understanding.
To realize that causes and conditions are themselves the cessation of the path is to know that seeing is non-seeing, thereby returning to the wondrous permanence of peace and bliss.
Is this not the case that the Four Noble Truths are, in essence, a single ultimate reality? As the Great Sutra says: "There is no suffering and no truth, yet there is reality;
there is no accumulation and no truth, yet there is reality; there is no cessation and no truth, yet there is reality; there is no path and no truth, yet there is reality. This reality is—
The Middle Way, empty space, and Buddha-nature are none other than the six sense faculties; they are not separate entities.

In this sutra, the dual negation of emptiness and existence, as well as the instruction that "if one wishes to untie the knots, it must be at the very center of the knot," both reveal the Middle Reality as the non-dual foundation for untying the knots.

Only in this way can it be called "arising from nature through cultivation" (*xingqi xiu*), thereby accomplishing the wondrous practice of non-action (*wuzuo miaoxing*). Therefore, this is the section [heading].

This is called the section on the Meaning of Mutual Integration. It consists of two parts: first, the primary clarification that the untying of knots is non-dual; second, the simultaneous manifestation that when the six are untied, the one perishes.
Within the first part, there are two sections;

the first is the request born of doubt. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the secondary gate of meaning, as I now observe the world, I do not understand..."
“World-Honored One, if a person does not know the root from which their fetters arise, I believe that such a person will ultimately be unable to untie them.

World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: since beginningless time, we have been born and extinguished together with various forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained these roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left the home life,’ we remain as distant from the goal as a day.”
"Māra! I only pray that you, with great compassion, take pity on those drowning in suffering. Today, what constitutes the binding of body and mind?
From what does liberation arise? Furthermore, may all sentient beings facing future hardships be enabled to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself fully before the great assembly, shedding tears and raising his palms in sincere devotion, awaiting the unsurpassed opening [of the Dharma] from the Buddha Tathāgata.
[The Buddha] showed [this]. In the second section on the definitive meaning of the preceding [text], it says: "Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots;
if they do not see what was knotted, how can they know how to untie it? The Buddha’s intention was that the sense organs (*indriya*) are themselves the knots, yet Ānanda, regarding...
Because one seeks the original source of the knotting beyond the sense organs, this question arises.

It is as if one were to ask, "How did this knot originally come to be? The subsequent text asks, "What is this knot? and later states, "To establish cognition within seeing and knowing is the very root of ignorance;
this is the original source of what is knotted. Youxi (Youxi Daoshi) comments: "Yuan" (original) means the fundamental; it refers to the initial moment of knotting.
To give rise to the root-source: if one understands the origin from which the fetters arise through the realization that "knowledge is established upon seeing," then seeing will be without seeing;
this is precisely Nirvana, and it truly constitutes the method for untangling the knots. Regarding the initial statement in the analogy, "The Śrāvakas who are still in training are also like this":
those who have not yet attained the four fruits of the path are called "those in training. As for the phrase "beginningless ignorance": [End of excerpt]
Changshui said: "From the very beginning of deluding the truth, it follows sentient beings through birth and death without ever departing from them.
Therefore, the previous passage states that 'through combination they falsely arise; through combination they falsely die,' and this passage states that 'they perish together and arise together.
The meaning of these is identical. Xunwen says: "There are two meanings here. First, regarding Ānanda’s provisional realization of the first fruit [of the path], even his innate [afflictions]..."

When [the practitioner] abides, they arise and cease together with the ignorance within the realm (*dhātu*). Second, regarding Ānanda’s specific delusions (*paryavasthāna*) which have not yet been eliminated, he arises and ceases together with the ignorance outside the realm.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a tertian malaria patient:

the abandonment of the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) is like the "resting day," while the failure to break the innate delusions (*sahaja-kleśa*) is like the "onset day. Furthermore, the prior falling away of the common delusions is like the resting day.
Day. Although the secondary delusions still remain, just as when the sun rises, the roots of goodness from extensive learning can lead one out of the three realms; thus, it is called "leaving home.
Yet, because ignorance remains entirely intact, there is only the presence of fetters without knowing how to resolve them.
"I only pray that your great compassion," [he said,] requesting instruction. Ānanda’s intention was that beginningless ignorance must surely be the root of the fetters; however, today’s body...
Having already severed the eighty-eight afflictions (*āsrava*), he did not know which among them was the knot of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*). His words "How?
were a question regarding the origin of the knots. Furthermore, he did not know from where to apply effort in the method for untying the knots. Thus, he asked once about the knots.

Second, the explanation of the question: Since it is not yet known whether bondage and liberation reside solely within the six sense organs, the Buddhas below provide a dual demonstration that both bondage and liberation are found only within these six organs.
Second, the opening instruction, which has two parts: first, the manifestation of auspicious omens.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training,
and also to serve as a cause for transcending the world and as eyes for the future for all sentient beings, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand of Jambūnada purple-gold light.
Immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust...
Those dwelling in their respective worlds each had jewel-lights emerge from the crowns of their heads;
these lights simultaneously came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and descended upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.

As for the Buddha’s compassionate act of alone stroking Ānanda’s head to address the capacities of both present and future beings: he uses the immediate recipient as a means to signify that all sentient beings shall likewise realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

According to the verse below, which states that "a single snap of the fingers transcends the stage of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*), even those at the stage of no-more-learning are included among those to be benefited.

However, because those still in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet escaped the cycle of birth and death (*bhavāgra/pariccheda*), the Buddha specifically takes pity on them. The preceding characters refer to [the aforementioned].
"Various people. The character "various" (zhū) below refers to those in the three fruits and four stages of realization (*pratipannaka*).

If future sentient beings hear this Dharma-door of untangling the knots, they will not only be able to transcend the *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) realm, but will also transcend the *pariṇāmi-vedanīya* (transformative) realm;
therefore, it is called "producing the cause for supramundane [attainment]. Thus, the words spoken by the Buddhas serve as eyes for the future. Immediately below, the present reality is revealed.
Auspicious sign. Regarding the light from the crowns of all Buddhas pouring over the crown of Śākyamuni:

this demonstrates the proclamation of the unsurpassed *uṣṇīṣa*-dharma—the principle that non-characteristic is not non-characteristic, and that non-characteristic is characteristic. Within the sutra, the emission of light occurs here in four instances;
the first three are all in the first fascicle: first, the *uṣṇīṣa*-light speaks the mantra; second, following the seven signs, it is emitted from the face-entrance (*mukhadvāra*).
The light immediately reveals two kinds of roots. Third, after the precious light surged forth from the *svastika* on his chest, he then revealed the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

In the previous three instances, it was Śākyamuni who emitted the light; now, all the Buddhas emit light to consecrate Śākyamuni’s crown, signifying that the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust have collectively realized the Dharma of the Crown (*uṣṇīṣa-dharma*).
Furthermore, this manifests that the Buddhas are about to expound the unconditioned (*anabhisamskāra*) within the Perfect [Teaching].
Regarding the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, he first manifested supernatural powers. The sixfold shaking of the earth symbolizes the destruction of the delusions of the six sense faculties.

II. The Main Exposition has two parts: 1. The Universal Proclamation by All Buddhas; 2. Śākyamuni’s Detailed Explanation. First, regarding the universal proclamation where all Buddhas speak with one voice to Ānanda:
this is because, at the beginning of the first fascicle, Ānanda had originally requested that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions explain how they attained [Buddhahood].
This is because it constitutes the initial expedient means for the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna of bodhi.
Although the meaning of the six sense organs presented here encompasses the three contemplations, the emphasis lies on the Perfect Middle.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly together heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice to Ānanda:

"Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know the root of the fetters that causes you to revolve in birth and death—the innate ignorance—it is none other than your own six sense faculties. Furthermore, if you wish to know unsurpassed bodhi,"
"I shall cause you to swiftly realize the blissful liberation of wondrous, eternal quiescence. Furthermore, these six faculties of yours are nothing other than this very thing.
Ānanda asked: "What constitutes the knots of my present body and mind? From what can they be untied? Thus, all Buddhas point back to the six faculties.
As stated in the following text, "The cause of both the binding and the unbinding is the same; there are no two paths for the holy and the ordinary."

Now, first, this is explained according to the perfect and true reality (*satya*). Next, it will be analyzed according to the text. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*);

birth and death are the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); bodhi is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); and nirvāṇa is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). When these four truths are present within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), they constitute the single true reality.
This is the purport of the non-fabricated four truths (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-satya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*). The *Miaoxuan* states: "Because of delusion regarding principle..."

Therefore, awakening (*bodhi*) is the name for afflictions as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), and nirvāṇa is the name for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Because one is able to understand [this], afflictions are themselves awakening as the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), and birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

One should know that the principle is solely a single reality; it is in accordance with sentient beings that one speaks of the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of cause and effect, which is called suffering and its origination.
Yet its essence is itself the cessation of the Way; therefore it is said that those who transcend the world know this to be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus, this passage fully encompasses the meanings of the one truth, the two truths, and the four truths. This principle is pure, perfect, and eternally transcends partial teachings.
Because all Buddhas realize this Dharma-gate and attain perfect enlightenment, they speak of it in common. Next, we shall analyze the text according to its specific passages. It says:
Regarding innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*): not knowing the three truths is called ignorance. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"All phenomena are non-existent; yet they exist in such a way. That they are thus non-existent—this fact not being known is called ignorance.
This precisely accords with its true meaning. This is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Because of this ignorance, sentient beings revolve through two kinds of realms.
Regarding "birth and death": as for the phrase "the root of bondage," this is the direct answer concerning the source of what is bound.
Because sentient beings give rise to thoughts toward objects, pursuing sounds and chasing after forms, they enter the cycle of saṃsāra; this is solely due to your six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

Since bondage arises because of the faculties, liberation likewise depends upon the faculties. Bodhi is the fruit of cultivation, standing in contrast to the aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*). Nirvāṇa is the fruit of fruits.

In contrast to the aforementioned cycle of birth and death, Nirvāṇa possesses four virtues: the virtue of bliss (*sukha*), which is peace and happiness; the virtue of permanence (*nitya*), which is wondrous eternity;

the virtue of purity (*śubha*), which is tranquility; and the virtue of self (*ātman*), which is liberation. The phrase "swiftly realized" corresponds in meaning to the passage below concerning "transcending the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in the snap of a finger.
As for the interpretation, it cites the subsequent text: because one establishes knowledge through knowing and seeing, one revolves in saṃsāra. Knowing and seeing...
Non-seeing is the realization of wondrous permanence. It allows the two paths of birth-and-death and nirvana to be distinguished, their features clearly manifest.
Now, the intent of the Buddhas is precisely to clarify that the Path and Cessation are identical to Suffering and Origination, and Suffering and Origination are identical to the Path and Cessation.

Their very substance is such that there is no need for reversal or negation; this is the meaning of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Because delusion and awakening differ, the Four Noble Truths are established.
The four realities are not four; that is to say, all sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi and cannot be further attained, and they are great nirvāṇa itself and cannot be further extinguished.
However, Jiaoguang says: "It is certain that the faculties (roots) are used, and it is certain that consciousness is not used.
He truly cites the present text as proof. Yet, the dharma-gates of the Perfect Teaching fundamentally possess no discrimination. If one...
A distinction must be made based on their different meanings. Those who sink into birth and death possess the six sense organs of ordinary beings;
those who realize wondrous permanence possess the six sense organs of mutual function. Furthermore, these must be distinguished. ○ Second, Śākyamuni provides an explanation, which has two parts:
first, the inquiry.
Although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear. He prostrated himself and said to the Buddha:
"How can it be that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both identical to these six faculties and nothing else?"

What has been explained above constitutes the true reality within the Perfect [Teaching]: namely, that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, and afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*).

Ānanda was unable to remain free from doubt regarding this; previously, he had suspected that the knots were not the fundamental source, yet now he hears that the knots are themselves the source of the knots.
