Having thus demonstrated that [the afflictions] were exhausted, he concludes by summarizing them. ○ Second, concurrently revealing that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished: 1. The request arising from doubt regarding the one;
2. The narration of events by the sūtra compiler.
At this time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, [received] the *geya* and *gāthā*.
The mixture was refined and pure; its wondrous principles were clear and penetrating, opening and illuminating the mind and eyes. [Ānanda] marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
"Master Youxi remarked that when the scribe records events, the expressive words (the *nirukti*) come first, followed by that which is expressed (the *vācya*). Next, Ānanda..."

In terms of their referents, that which is expressed (*vācya*) comes first and that which expresses (*vācaka*) follows. The initial passage states that "unsurpassed compassionate instruction" refers simultaneously to both the prose (*gadya*) and the verse (*śloka*).
*Ge-yeh* (Geya) means "corresponding verse" or "repeated verse," which is precisely a verse that reiterates the preceding prose.
The term *gāthā* refers to "recited verses" (*fèngsòng*), also abbreviated as *jì* (verse). These are not based on prose but are instead recited and chanted for their beauty.
Because the two types of verse are combined and clarified, they are described as "intermingled yet refined. This refers to the expressive words (*nengquán*).

Mount Gu said that the first four verses are "repeated verses" (*chóngsòng*), while the latter five verses are "independent verses" (*gūqǐ*). I, however, maintain that within the first four verses, the word "false" (*wàng*)...
This demonstrates that the various "True Ones" (*tathāgata*) and so forth are also independent verses (*udāna*).

Furthermore, among the five subsequent verses, the five lines beginning with "The mind grasps its own mind" are likewise reiterations (*geya*). If this is the case, then the blending of the refined and the brilliant makes the meaning clear.

Although the two types of verses are intermingled, the words that express the principle are refined and not confused. "Brilliant" (*yìng*) carries the sense of illuminating. Next, it says "wondrous" (*miào*).

"Clarifying and penetrating" (*qīngchè*) refers to the principle that is elucidated. As explained above, one contemplates the eight consciousnesses through the three contemplations. That the principle transcends thought and deliberation is called "sublime" (*miào*);
that it is undefiled is called "pure" (*qīng*); and that it reaches the very bottom is called "penetrating" (*chè*). Since the principle is thus luminous and visible, [it is so termed].
Thus, it causes the human mind to open and the eyes and ears to become clear. II. Ānanda’s Petition:
“I have now heard the Buddha’s words on the unobstructed great compassion, the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of reality, which are true and authentic.

Yet my mind has not yet fully grasped the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six are resolved and the one is extinguished. I pray only that you will bestow your great kindness once more upon this assembly and those of the future.”
Bestowing the sound of the Dharma to wash away deep-seated defilements;
responding to the requests of those present with unimpeded great compassion speaks of its universal salvation.

Within true nature, the Middle Way transcends all dualities, and as both existence and non-existence are discarded, it is the pure, wondrous, and eternal essence. To speak of "Dharma-phrases" (dharmapada) further refers to that which can express [this truth].
Regarding the prose and verse sections: having already heard the principles of the three contemplations within the *Dharmapada*, you are fortunate to have gained clear insight.
What remains unawakened is the sequence for "the six dissolving and the one perishing" (*liu-jie yi-wang*) and "unfurling the knots" (*shu-jie lun-ci*).
Ouyi Youxue said: "Although the text consists of two phrases, the meaning comprises six points: first, the six dissolve; second, the one perishes; third, they are unfurled; fourth, they are knotted."
[This is] also [the case]. "Categorical order" (lunlei) is the fifth; "sequential order" (cidi) is the sixth. Categorical order takes its meaning from the formation of knots;

sequential order encompasses the meaning of untying the knots. Please grant me your response to this request. II. The Instruction in Two Parts: A. Clarifying the Sequential Order of Knot Formation. B.
Clarifying that the Six Are Untied and One Is Extinct. In Part A, there are three sections: 1. Using the six knots as a general metaphor for the six [senses].
At that moment,
the Tathāgata adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* on the lion throne, gathered his *saṃghāṭī*, and took hold of a seven-jeweled desk.
Reaching out his hand over the desk, he took the flowered cloth offered by the deva Kāpila and, before the great assembly, knotted it into a single loop.
The Buddha tied it up and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called a knot.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata took the folded flower-cloth and tied another knot, asking Ānanda again, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again replied to the Buddha, "This too is called a knot. In this manner, he successively tied up the folded flower-cloth.
The cloth was thus formed into six knots. As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot that had just been formed in his hand and asked Ānanda, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly likewise responded to the Buddha in succession, saying, "This is called a knot."
*Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* refers to the inner robe. In this region, it is called a skirt (*qún*). *Saṃghāṭī* refers to the great outer robe (*dàyī*). *Kāpila* means "time" (*shífēn*);
alternatively, it is said to be the Yāma Heaven, or the Kapāla Heaven.

These were the sons of the Four Heavenly Kings who offered a flower-woven cloth to the Tathāgata. *Gǔxiǎng* states that "folded" (*dié*) is a name for a type of fabric; the character may also be written as *tié*.
The commentary therein states: "These six knots in the cloth must surely symbolize the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

The ancients regarded this as too simple and merely annotated it according to the literal text, which led to the emergence of the divergent theory by Jiaoguang, who claimed that the six knots do not symbolize the six sense organs.

He failed to realize that from the fourth fascicle onward, the analogy of the sense organs to the knots has been clearly established through both the dharma and its metaphor. Furthermore, the preceding text states: 'The knots...'"

Regarding the sequence of the causes for liberation: when the six are liberated, even the one perishes. Since the faculties must choose a perfect penetration (*pariṣuddha-vyūha*), if one does not point to the root faculty, what could serve as an analogy?
This is not difficult to see; why then do you remain stubbornly deluded? In the text, the Buddha takes a flower-scarf and ties it into knots, asking, "What are these called?
His intent lies in the names themselves; only by means of names can the sequence of the six knots be determined.
"Knot" is the general name. Once formed, they may also be called the first knot, the second knot, and so on.
A name must have a corresponding reality; however, in this text, there are six realities and six names, which is considered most essential.

Yet, reality is the basis of the name. "Reality" (shí) refers to the actual tying. Regarding the "sequence" (lúncì): "sequence" (lún) means category or type; the six knots are similar in kind, and their order follows this sequence.
This refers to their sequence; the preceding and succeeding are not confused. Since there are six faculties (*indriya*), the knots likewise become six.
Thus, it is appropriate to use the six knots as a metaphor for the six faculties. Next, the six faculties collectively are metaphorically termed "knots."
The Buddha told Ānanda, "When I first tied this cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally but a single strip;
why do you and the others call the second and third folds 'knots' as well?

Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, although this precious folded flower-cloth was woven into a handkerchief from what was originally a single entity, according to my contemplation, the Tathāgata has obtained [a knot] with each single tie."
"A knot is so called because when a hundred twists are completed, it is named 'a hundred knots. How much more so for this cloth, which has only six knots;
they never reach seven, nor do they stop at five. Why, then, does the Tathāgata allow that only the first is called a knot, while the second and third are not?"
The next section of questions and answers clarifies that although the cloth has but a single knot, it does not hinder its manifestation as six;

likewise, although the fundamental luminous consciousness is one, it does not hinder its manifestation as the six sense faculties. This is the meaning of this subsequent section. First, the Tathāgata poses a counter-question.

"I [shall now]... introduces the preceding point. "This [is like]... introduces the counter-question. The "single strand" serves as a metaphor for establishing the one luminous consciousness. The Buddha’s intention seems to be to...
A headcloth has but one knot; since the headcloth is singular, the knot likewise ought not to be twofold. How can both "two" and "three" be called knots?
You and the great assembly may point to Ānanda and simply ask about "two" and "three," and what follows will become clear.
The Buddha asks this because such a doubt might arise regarding the Dharma—for instance, doubting how that which is a single, pure brilliance could be divided into parts.
The six sense organs can be understood by comparing them to this cloth. Next, in Ānanda’s response, he first grasps the meaning of "one refined spirit," hence the term "single substance.
"Jiji" (緝績) carries the meaning of weaving; it merely clarifies the origin of the cloth.

As I contemplate this, it is clear that while the knots may be many, they do not exceed them. First, he speaks generally of "a hundred knots"; next, with the words "how much more," he specifically points to the six knots.
By stating that they neither reach seven nor stop at five, the metaphor for the six sense faculties becomes evident.
This Ānanda answered the Tathāgata with correct reasoning. ○ Third, the analogy of the six sense organs having a single substance but different functions:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Regarding this precious flowered cloth, you know that this cloth originally consists of only one strand.
When I tied it into six knots, they were called 'six knots. Examine this carefully: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet it appears different because of the knots. What do you think?"
"The first knot tied is called the first. In this way, up to the sixth knot being formed—now I wish to take the name of the sixth knot and make it the first.
Is this possible, World-Honored One? No, World-Honored One. As long as the six knots exist, the name of this sixth one can never become the first.
Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence over many lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their names?"
The Buddha said, "It is so. Although the six knots are different, they all trace back to their original cause, which was fashioned from a single piece of cloth;

yet, if you attempt to confuse them, they can never be made into one. Thus it is with your six sense faculties: from that which is ultimately identical, you have produced that which is ultimately distinct."

The third question concerns whether the substance of the cloth and its name are one or can be confused. Ānanda’s answer is that although the cloth is one, the names for the knots are difficult to exchange;
this is the meaning of the third question. In the question, the phrase "you know" and what follows restates the preceding point.
This refers to the second turn [of the dialogue], not the first. It means that you know how a single essence of clarity and brightness is divided into the six sense organs.
Since you have carefully examined and reversedly questioned the names of the six [objects], you ask: "The substance of the cloth is the same, yet it differs due to the knots.
You must no longer explain this by saying that a single essence of clarity and brightness is divided into the six sense organs; rather, the Buddha used the cloth...
This is merely an example used to conclude [the previous section] while intending to exchange the names of the preceding and following [parts].

That is to say, although the meaning of the six knots has been established by you as having a sequence of before and after, I still intend to establish the principle of their mutual interchangeability. In the passage below, "at the intention" (*yì xià*), the author precisely clarifies this desire to exchange the names.
Previously, they were collectively termed "knots. Here, we further specify their names in sequence from one to six.
Since each is named according to its initial binding—first being called "one," and so on up to six—their designations appear to have a specific basis and cannot be interchanged.

Yet, since the substance of the cloth is ultimately the same, could the sixth knot not also be called the first? This is analogous to the six sense faculties, which are fundamentally one brilliant clarity. Thus...
"Can the faculty of seeing be disregarded and easily replaced by hearing? Can the faculty of tasting be disregarded and easily replaced by smelling?
Then Ānanda again answered correctly: "The sequence of the six knots cannot be disordered; it can clearly demonstrate that the six faculties are ultimately distinct."

The six knots are a precise metaphor for the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). If the six knots exist, they are substantially distinct; that there are six names rather than one is what constitutes their difference.
To say they are "substantially distinct" means they are substantially distinct because the times of their formation differ.

This metaphor illustrates that the substance of the ordinary being’s faculties is partitioned and distinct, such that there is ultimately no occurrence of the eyes hearing, the ears seeing, the tongue smelling, the nose tasting, or the six faculties exchanging their functions.

Furthermore, as for the passage beginning with "Even if I," it means that if one does not follow the actual facts but merely indulges in forceful rhetoric to seize the logic, desiring to use sophistry to confuse names—how could such a thing possibly succeed?
Regarding this point, Jiaoguang has a divergent interpretation, stating that the six knots are vertical.
The six sense organs are horizontal. Using the vertical as a metaphor for the horizontal makes the analogy inconsistent.

[The author] establishes his own position, stating that the sequence of their binding is not horizontal, unlike the eyes, ears, and so forth; this is because the binding of those faculties is fundamentally never such that the eyes come first and the ears later.
According to the explanation of the six stages of binding found in the subsequent section on Perfect Penetration, these are: first, movement; second, stillness; third, hearing; fourth...
Awakening. There are five voids and six cessations; this sequence corresponds to the six knots. As stated in the *Zhongjing*: "The interpretation by Jiaoguang is clearly contrary to the Sūtra.
The Buddha’s original intention was to use the differences among the six knots as a metaphor for the different functions of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

While the sense organs differ in their functions—such as seeing and hearing—the knots differ in their names according to their order. Thus, the differing names are used to illustrate the differing functions."

The Dharma and the analogy are perfectly aligned; why discuss their horizontal or vertical order? Moreover, since the six knots are formed in succession, the manifest text provides a basis for reliance.
Yet, what is the proof that the six sense organs necessarily lack such a sequence? As the later sutra says: "Because of movement there is sound;
because of sound there is form; because of form there is fragrance; because of fragrance there is touch; because of touch there is taste; because of taste..."
One knows the Dharma. Because the six types of distracted delusions form karma, the twelve divisions revolve accordingly;
this is the sequence of the world’s arising as stated in the sutras. Since the six sense objects have a fixed order, how could the six sense organs not have one?
Furthermore, it accords with the sequence in which sentient beings enter the womb and develop their faculties, as stated in the *Zhiguan*: [text follows].
By the power of karmic actions, it naturally gives rise to a single thought-moment that invokes its mother.
The mother then perceives the color blue, hears a calling voice, smells a pungent odor, and tastes sourness. Through the power of these thoughts, a subtle vapor arises;

this vapor transforms into water, the water transforms into blood, and the blood transforms into flesh. As the mother’s breath enters and exits, it provides mutual nourishment and moisture, whereby [the embryo] is formed.
It forms the liver organ; moving upward, it becomes the eyes; moving downward, it becomes the thumbs of the hands and feet.

If one contemplates white color, the sound of weeping, a fishy odor, and a pungent taste, it then becomes the lung organ; moving upward, it becomes the nose; moving downward, it becomes the second fingers of the hands and feet.
If one contemplates red color, the sound of speech, a scorched odor, and a bitter taste, it then becomes the heart organ; moving upward, it becomes...
The mouth faces downward; it becomes the third fingers of the hands and feet. If one contemplates yellow color, song, fragrance, and sweet taste, it becomes the spleen organ (*pittaka*).
Facing upward, it becomes the tongue; facing downward, it becomes the fourth fingers of the hands and feet.
If one contemplates black color, chanting, foul odor, and salty taste, it becomes the kidney organ (*vakkaka*). Facing upward, it becomes the ears; facing downward, it becomes the hands.
Regarding the fifth toe, as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there is also a sequential order to the formation of the sense organs within the womb.
How can it be claimed that the six sense organs are fixed simultaneously without any sequence? However, in the present sutra, sound is mentioned first and form second;

thus, the ear is formed first, followed by the eye. Since the various schools of the Sūtra-piṭaka differ on this point, there is no need for reconciliation. The primary intent of the current text is as follows:

This is merely using different names to illustrate different functions. The Buddha’s statement beginning with “It is thus” uses the analogy of the knots to correspond to the dharma and to clarify the correct meaning.
First, within the analogy of the knots, the six knots represent the differences among the six sense faculties. The single piece of cloth represents the one refined spirit.
Regarding the term “following and looking back”: “following” has the meaning of circling around; it refers to returning to and reflecting upon the original cause. He causes them...
The following clarifies that although it is but a single cloth, its names cannot be confused; this corresponds to your subsequent analogy.
Ultimately, they are the same single bright essence, corresponding to the single cloth above. Ultimately, they are distinct as the six faculties, corresponding to the six knots above.
Thus far, both the questions and answers have distinguished the different names of the six knots; the text states that "to cause them to become intermingled and confused can never be accomplished."
This demonstrates that names cannot be confused. Furthermore, it says that "from ultimate identity arises ultimate difference" to show that the functions of the sense organs are distinct.
"Difference in name" means that the first is not the second, and so on up to the fifth being not the sixth.
"Difference in function" means that seeing is not hearing, and tasting is not smelling. Since the phenomena and the metaphors are perfectly consistent, what [discrepancy] could there be?

Is it delusion? ○ Second, clarifying that the six are resolved and the one perishes, which has three parts: first, a metaphor for the simultaneous extinction of the six; second, establishing the metaphor for the one;
third, the actual application. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you must find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish to have them become one, how can this be achieved?"
Ānanda said: "If this knot remains, disputes will arise; within it, there naturally arises the notion that 'this knot is not that,' and 'that knot is not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots did not arise, then there would be no 'this' or 'that.
Since they could not even be called 'one,' how could they be called 'six'?"
The preceding explanation of the sequence of the six knots is now complete. Next, the explanation of the "six being untied and one vanishing" follows.
The Buddha again asked this question so that Ānanda would answer for himself. Regarding "the six knots not forming": this means the six knots do not form a single unity. The Buddha’s intention was:

"In your mind, you must surely find the false partitioning of the six sense organs undesirable and wish to achieve their integration into a single entity. What skillful means can be used to bring this about?"
"Is it one? Ānanda’s response, stating that "if this knot remains, the disputes will arise like sharp blades," establishes a metaphor based on ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*).
His statement that "if it is completely untied," establishes a metaphor based on the sages (*ārya*). This is because, while there are six names, they constitute a single [knot].
When the six are resolved, the one naturally vanishes; how could there then be six characteristics? Master Youzhu said:
"The explanation above proceeds from the root toward the branches. When viewed from the perspective of the branches, the six sense organs cannot but be different.
Thus he said: "Your six sense organs are likewise so; ultimately, within identity, difference arises. This concludes the meaning of their categorization as a class.
This clarifies returning to the root by following the branches: when the six are understood, the one also perishes. Therefore it is said, "If even 'one' cannot be named, how can 'six' be established?
Thus, the text on the convergence of dharmas says, "The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one are likewise so," thereby concluding that the six dissolve and the one disappears.
2. The Section on the Convergence of Dharmas.
The Buddha said: "The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one is likewise so. Because from time immemorial your mind-nature has been deranged and your perceptions have falsely arisen;
because these false perceptions did not cease, your wearying vision gave rise to the dust of the world. It is like having blurred vision, which causes the appearance of floating flowers;
they arise without cause within the serene clarity of the spirit. All the worlds, mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and nirvana—all are precisely this."

Regarding the "wild, laborious, inverted flower-like appearances," in the Buddha’s response, he first aligns the analogy with the principle: if the six sense faculties are understood, even the single luminous intelligence (*ekaprakāśa*) perishes.

One must not follow the interpretation of Jiaoguang, who takes movement and stillness, hearing and cognition, and emptiness and extinction as the six knots. As stated in the previous fascicle: "Entering into one..."

He falsely claims that those six cognitive faculties are simultaneously purified. The preceding verse states: "The cause for the binding and the liberation follows a sequence; when the six are liberated, even the one perishes.
Since all [faculties] take the six as their six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*), how could they produce any other kind of liberation?

From the passage beginning with "Because of you," he intends to clarify that if the faculties are liberated, then the objects (*viṣaya*) are also purified; therefore, he first demonstrates the characteristics of inversion. The nature of the mind is precisely the primordial enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
"Principle. "Mad confusion" refers to beginningless ignorance (*anādikāla-avidyā*). "The false arising of knowledge and vision" refers to the six sense organs acting as knowledge and vision.
As the preceding text states: "Since that which is perceived has been falsely established, your false capacity [to perceive] arises. Now, this knowledge and vision belong to the false capacity.

Regarding "the ceaseless arousal of delusion causing the laboring faculty of vision to give rise to dust," it is as the preceding text says: "In this way, through mutual disturbance and dependence, they are formed."

"Exhausted toil" refers to the long-accumulated arising of dust. Within this passage, there is the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their application (*upanaya*). In the analogy, the pupil of the eye represents the nature of the mind; "toil" represents madness and confusion;
and the "mad flowers" represent the deluded arising of cognitive views, culminating in the exhaustion of seeing the arising of dust.

In the application, the mountains, rivers, and great earth are the *pariṇāma-vipāka* (retributive environment), while birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are the *vipāka-phala* (retributive body). These are formed through the conjunction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Birth and death; having escaped birth and death, one further perceives nirvana. Birth and death constitute the six [realms], which are known and perceived;

nirvana constitutes the one, which is likewise subsumed under knowing and perceiving. All are metaphors for delusory flowers; thus, both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, are all delusory flowers.
The text combines these elements from the coarse to the subtle: the four characters "delusion," "exhaustion," "inversion," and "upside-down" combine with "exhaustion" and "the eyes."
Furthermore, throughout this sutra, what has been clarified from beginning to end is that the environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*) is established first, followed by the body (the *sambhoga-vipāka*).
That the present passage alone speaks of "dust" (*viṣaya*) arising based on the "roots" (*indriya*) is simply in accordance with the principle stated previously: "Cognition arises because of dust;

appearances exist because of the roots. Since the essential point of bondage and liberation is subsumed within the six sense-faculties, it is explained that when the faculties are liberated, the dust [is likewise liberated].
It is also pure. The subsequent passage states, "If the root-knots are removed, the appearances of dust will naturally cease," which corresponds with the present text.
Next, the metaphor for untying the knots through the mind has two parts: first, the actual manifestation that it depends on the mind.
Ānanda said, “This knot is identical to the [original] entanglement; how can it be untied?
The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth in his hand, pulled its left side askew, and asked Ānanda, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One.
He then turned his hand and pulled the right side askew, asking again, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda: “I—”
Now, though you pull with both hands from the left and right, you cannot untie it. By what skillful means (*upāya*) can you resolve this?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, one should untie it at the very center of the knot, and then it will disperse. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot."

Although the preceding passage unified the six [senses] so that the one [bond] was lost, from the words "Because of you" (*yūr*) onwards, it still clarifies the binding (*bandhana*) without yet discussing its liberation (*mokṣa*).

Therefore, the present section clarifies that the liberation of the bonds depends on the mind. Since the wearisome characteristics of the six sense organs arise from the six knots, the question "How is it liberated?
is asked in terms of the phenomena (*dharma*). The Tathāgata again uses a metaphor to clarify this, citing the ancient practice of pulling and tugging from both sides.
The two extremes are illustrated by this metaphor. Regarding the "centered heart" (*jiexin*), ancient masters used it as a metaphor for the Middle Way; these words are indeed most accurate.

Nevertheless, those who cling dogmatically to this expression may fear they lose the true intent of the ancients. One must understand that all dualistic extremes are designated as "left" and "right," while non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is collectively termed the "centered heart.
As stated in the *Yuan-tong zhang* (Chapter on Perfect Penetration), the two extremes of movement and stillness are precisely...
Left and right. When a Bodhisattva realizes non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the two marks of movement and stillness clearly do not arise;

this is "tying the heart" (*jie xin*). Next, when the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) correspond, these are "left and right. When one is detached from both the organs and the objects, this is "tying the heart.
Even worldly and world-transcending phenomena are called "left and right"; to suddenly transcend them is "tying the heart. Tying the heart is a metaphor for the absence of conceptualization.

Regarding the place where knots are tied: just as when one folds cloth and ties it into a knot, its substance is fundamentally empty. If one unties it at the point of emptiness, the knot then disperses.
If one attempts to distinguish them by means of the faculties and their objects, it is like pulling from both the left and the right;

one should know that within the faculties and objects there is a place apart from the faculties and objects. As stated in the first fascicle: "Thus, the nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye. Is this not so?
The nature of seeing within the sense organs and their objects is itself not the sense organs or their objects; this is the essential path for liberation from the sense organs and their objects.

This can be inferred by applying the same logic to movement and stillness, as well as to the mundane and supramundane. Therefore it is said: "If you wish to untie the knots, you must do so at the very heart of the knot."
The binding of the mind has four meanings: first, it is not the binding itself; second, it is not separate from the binding; third, the binding arises from this [mind];

and fourth, liberation arises from this [mind]. Regarding the dharmas, there are likewise four meanings: first, they are not the sense organs or objects; second, they are not separate from the sense organs and objects;

third, the sense organs and objects arise from these [dharmas] as a binding; and fourth, the sense organs and objects are removed through these [dharmas]. Ānanda said, "One should apply this to the binding of the mind for its liberation."
This is the analogy of dispersing [the clouds]. The Buddha said that if one wishes to eliminate the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one should apply the Dharma to the mind of the fetters.

One should know that this refers to the mind itself as the central reality, wherein the perfect contemplation simultaneously negates both extremes. ○ Second, the explanation clarifying the causes and conditions, which has two parts:
first, the resolution of doubts.
"Ānanda, when I speak of the Buddha-dharma arising from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), I do not mean to grasp at the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunctions.

This passage clarifies a doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If the binding of the mind and the unbinding of the knots are themselves causes and conditions, why did the preceding text reject causes and conditions?
Therefore, it is explained: "When I speak of the Buddha-dharma... The Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions exhaustively reaches the subtlest level.
The subtle immediately penetrates the principle that is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous; how could it be the same as the coarse phenomena of worldly conjunction?

If one refers to the preceding passage in the original sutra which states that the conjunction of the four great elements gives rise to the various transformations of the world, this refers to the coarse phenomenon of conjunction.

Speaking exhaustively according to the principle, within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is explained that suffering arises from the accumulation of causes and conditions, and the Path [arises from]... [the cessation of such causes].

The cessation of existence is due to conditions. Is this not the coarse aspect of the convergence [of causes]? Although the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna encompass both the ultimate and conventional truths, when contrasted with the Mahāyāna, they are merely termed conventional truth.
Since the Hīnayāna has not yet exhausted the subtleties of worldly causal conditions, how much less so for supramundane causal conditions?
And how much less so for the fact that causal conditions are themselves non-conditions and spontaneous? ○ Second, the explicit clarification.
The Tathāgata has elucidated the mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes as they emerge according to their respective conditions.
Thus, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is known by its count;

the various forms before us—whether the straightness of pines, the crookedness of thorns, the whiteness of cranes, or the blackness of crows—all have their origins fully understood. Therefore, Ānanda, choose from among the six faculties according to your own mind.
If the root fetters are removed, the marks of dust naturally perish. Once all delusions have been extinguished, what need is there to wait for the unreal to vanish?
This clarifies that when the Buddha teaches that causes and conditions are exhausted, the subtlest level is immediately penetrated and one enters the Truth.

The Buddha’s teaching on worldly causes and conditions already transcends coarse appearances; furthermore, he possesses complete knowledge of supramundane causes and conditions. Therefore, he is supreme.
Mandārava said: "The immeasurable Four Noble Truths are the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Four Noble Truths. 'Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges' refers to the most distant;
'a single drop of rain' refers to the least. Even knowing their number, there would be no failure of illumination."
Why are the pines before our eyes straight? Why are thorns curved? Why is the crane white?

Why is the crow black? Only a Buddha can know this. Thus one knows the worldly dharmas: when the roots of entanglement are severed, the marks of dust naturally perish; this too is due to causes and conditions.
Thus one knows the supramundane dharma. As the previous fascicle said: "If you merely do not follow the twelve links of conditioned existence..."

"Accompanying one another, pull out a single root, detach from its stickiness, and settle within," and so forth. This was because consciousness is triggered by objects (*viṣaya*); therefore, one first detached from the objects.

Now, since the characteristics [of the faculties] exist due to the faculties (*indriya*), one first eliminates the faculties. According to the "Perfect Penetration" of Avalokiteśvara discussed below, one likewise first extinguishes the objects and subsequently purifies the faculties.
The intent of this passage is likely to prevent people from suspecting that the practice lies solely in the six faculties.

Why not speak of the "objects" (dust)? Therefore it is said: "If the faculties are eliminated, the characteristics of the objects will forever perish. When both faculties and objects are dissolved, what need is there to wait for them to become unreal?
How could the real belong to either causes and conditions or spontaneity? Third, the explanation by analogy follows next;
first, twenty-one analogies are established.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding these six knots currently manifest in this *karpāsa* cloth, can they all be untied and removed simultaneously?
No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in successive order; today they must likewise be untied in successive order.
Since the six knots share the same substance but are not tied at the same time, how could they be removed all at once when they are being untied?"
In the Buddha’s question, it appears as though he intends to use the analogy of the cloth to demonstrate that the knots should likewise be removed together;
yet he does not realize that because the six knots share the same substance, they cannot be untied simultaneously. This meaning is implicitly contained therein but has not yet been revealed.
Ānanda is precisely discussing the substance and the knots, asserting that their untying proceeds from the knots themselves and not from the cloth, for the knots were tied in succession.
Therefore, the six knots have distinct names, from the first through the sixth. Regarding today’s untying of the knots, how could they be removed simultaneously?
Your silence accords with the Buddha’s intention. It is precisely because the six knots differ in their timing that the six sense-faculties are used as a metaphor for their differing functions;
it is not necessary that they all possess a fixed sequence. However, since the sequence of the six knots is not uniform—
If they were liberated at different times, how could the distinct functions of the six sense organs be liberated simultaneously?

2. Correlating with the Dharma: The Buddha said, "The liberation of the six sense organs is also like this. When this organ is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimukti*). Once liberation from phenomena has been achieved, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise; this is called a Bodhisattva emerging from the three [realms]."
In this *samādhi*, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Within the text, there are first six sections clarifying the understanding of the faculties (*indriya*). Following these faculties, the sequence of the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) is further clarified.

Although the five faculties have not yet been fully understood, because it is already known that the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is devoid of self, it is said that one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). As stated in the previous fascicle:

Prostrating to return to the primordial truth, one awakens the fundamental luminosity. This luminous nature manifests so that all other five types of clinging may be uprooted and completely liberated;
this is the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness. When both faculties and objects are simultaneously resolved, it is called "Dharma-liberation.

"Both being empty and non-arising" means that both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are non-arising. The former refers to the sixfold liberation, while this refers to the single extinction. Therefore, it reaches—
This text conveys the meaning of "the six being resolved and the one vanishing," both in its square and circular aspects.

*Soyin* states that the untying of the knots of the six sense organs cannot be illustrated by the example of a flowered handkerchief. While untying the handkerchief proceeds sequentially from one to six, the six sense organs follow the sequence of the three voids (*śūnyatā*).
As it says in *Jijzhong*: "Although the 'uprooting' and 'perfect liberation' have no before or after, nevertheless..."
Just as within a single mind there are arising, abiding, change, and cessation, yet despite possessing these four characteristics, it remains but a single thought-moment;
so too should one understand the dissolution of the five faculties. Although they may occur within a single thought-moment with a sense of sequence, is this not indeed perfect liberation?
As for *samādhi*, it is the name for the accomplishment of contemplation through *samāpatti*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All..."

The mind in meditative concentration is all termed *samādhi*. T’ai (Tanyao) says it is the sphere where the mind acts correctly. This mind has been constantly crooked and unstraightened since beginningless time;
upon entering the sphere of correct practice, the mind becomes upright and straight, just as a crawling snake is always curved but becomes straight when entering a tube.

It is also called *samāpatti*. As for "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one does not perceive the arising of a single dharma, nor does one perceive the cessation of a single dharma.

One should accept this principle within the mind. This is the realization attained through abiding in the perfection of the distinct stages (*bhūmi*). Alternatively, one may ask: "Previously it was said that both emptiness and existence are neither;
why do you now say they are both empty? The answer is: when speaking in terms of persons and phenomena (*pudgala* and *dharma*), they are called "empty."
Regarding the True Suchness (tathatā) thus revealed, it is called the "Middle. How much more so when both are empty and non-arising;
then its status as the Middle Way is clear. Does the preceding verse explaining the Middle Way not enter [it] from emptiness and existence?
From the beginning of the fifth fascicle until now, the explanation of the non-duality of the knots has been clarified, thereby completing the first section on the second meaning. II. Manifestation.
Cultivation and Realization. This section begins from the fourth fascicle, where Ānanda asks about entering the Heavenly King’s Flowered Hall, and the Tathāgata specifically expounds upon it.
There are two parts to the correct practice: first, the initial arousal of the awakening mind; second, the demonstration of cultivation and realization.
These are now divided into five sections: (1) Ānanda’s inquiry regarding the perfect faculty; (2) [The Buddha’s] exposition and Ānanda’s statement of his doubts.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction on the perfect penetration of wisdom and enlightenment, were freed from all doubt.
At once, they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding.
Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being non-existent, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration."
The "single mind and threefold contemplation" shown previously is termed the awakening of wisdom (*prajñā*). "The six dissolve and the one perishes" belongs to the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
However, this has not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration; this is the primary meaning of the present inquiry. II. Stating the Intent and Making the Request.
"Bhagavān, we have drifted through the ages, left orphaned and exposed for countless kalpas. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming kin to the Buddha?

We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk and suddenly encounter a compassionate mother. If, through this meeting, the Way is realized, then the secret words we receive will be identical to our original awakening;

they would then be no different from never having heard them before. We pray only that you will extend your great compassion and bestow upon us the secret adornment, so that we may achieve realization."

The Tathāgata gave this final instruction. Having spoken these words, [the disciple] prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, withdrawing to conceal his secret intent while hoping for the Buddha’s hidden transmission.

When the opportunity arose and the Way was realized, he followed the preceding text: that which had been solitary and exposed before, now in this life he has joined the celestial kinship of the Buddha.
Yet, this coincides with the time when the Tathāgata’s Way was perfected. To not immediately declare the fundamental root of perfect penetration is a secret teaching.
Since you have not yet understood where this fundamental root lies, it remains identical to that which you previously realized: a state where there is no place for effort.
Since there is no place upon which to exert effort, this is no different from not having heard the meaning of "the one and the six perishing.
To say that it is not bestowed upon those who are not fit vessels is called "mysterious solemnity" (*biyan*). Although it is explained, its solemnity remains; it must ultimately be granted to me.

The preaching of the sutra occurs between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and is named the "final revelation. Having completed the manifest request, one should simply contemplate it silently within the inner mind.

Because it is for the sake of those with the capacity [for understanding], it is called the "Secret Capacity. The Buddha does not speak of it himself; that it is expounded by the assembly is the "Mysterious Bestowal" (mingshou).
II. The Tathāgata Questions the Holy Multitude.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats free from outflows within the assembly.
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats, having been born within my Dharma and attained the state of no-more-learning, I now ask you:
regarding your initial aspiration for enlightenment, which of the eighteen realms did you realize as the perfect penetration? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi?"
Changshui said: "Born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma" means being born within my Dharma;
the initial awakening that is first aroused is precisely the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and the realm from which it arises is expedient means (*upāya*). Gushan said:
From this point downward, the twenty-five sages contemplate the eighteen realms and the seven elements; these are merely differences in the expansion and contraction [of the categories].
The element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) corresponds to the six consciousnesses; the element of the faculties (*indriya-mahābhūta*) corresponds to the six sense organs;
and the remaining five elements collectively comprise the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), for the substance of the six objects does not transcend earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Thus, by mentioning the eighteen [elements], the seven elements are already subsumed. Therefore, the preceding text states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, regarding the eighteen elements..."
By practicing each one, all shall attain the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi. Furthermore, these eighteen [elements] are merely the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), as each is divided into three:
faculty, object, and consciousness. Thus, by speaking of the six, their meaning is already complete. Therefore, it was said previously:
"I cause you to turn through the cycle of birth and death, yet the blissful, wondrous, and eternal is likewise these six faculties; it is nothing else."
III. The various sages each explain their perfect penetration (yuan-tong), five parts. I. Observing the six sense objects to achieve the Way, six sections. I. Cennapa observes sound.

Regarding the six sense objects, Upānanda’s observation of odors should logically come first; however, we now begin with the sense object of sound. Master Youzu [Zhiyi] states there are three reasons for this:
first, because in the Sahā world, vocal sounds constitute the Buddha-work; second, because it was through sound that the Tathāgata attained enlightenment...
Yet Dignāga realized it first; thus, the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is established as the primary expedient for this region.
This precisely demonstrates that what was practiced in the Universal Gate is indeed appropriate. This section is divided into two parts: first, the narrative of the conditions for his realization.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"While I was in the Deer Park and at the Kukkuṭārāma, I observed the Tathāgata Buddha when he first attained enlightenment. Through the Buddha’s voice, I realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, 'Do you understand? I was the first to declare that I did. The Tathāgata confirmed me and named me Ajñāta."
The verse concerning the five men says: "Aśvajit, Baḍrika, and Kauṇḍinya—these three were paternal kinsmen; Cunda and Daśabala were maternal kinsmen.
When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, these were the ones he delivered first.

When the Prince first entered the mountains to seek the Way, his father the King, filled with longing, sent these five men to follow and serve him. Two of them delighted in the five desires, while three delighted in asceticism.
As he practiced, the two who had been attending him abandoned him and departed; three remained in service.

When the Prince abandoned his asceticism and returned to partaking of ghee, oil, and warm water, those three again abandoned him and left. Having attained the Way, the Prince remembered that the five men had attended him with great hardship at Vārāṇasī.
Having thought this, he went there and preached the Four Noble Truths for them. At that time, the three...
When the Buddha first went for alms, he instructed two people; Kūṭadanta attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, while the other four had not yet attained it.
Next, when the other two went for alms, they in turn instructed three people; these three attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

During the third discourse on the Dharma, eighty thousand devas were freed from dust and defilement, and five people attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*). When the Buddha asked three times whether they understood the Dharma, they replied three times that they did.

He knew. The earth deities proclaimed it, and the air deities transmitted it, until it was heard throughout the Brahma world that he had known it. Kūṭadanta was the very first to behold the signs of the Buddha-way;

he was the first to hear the drum of the Dharma, the first to don the fragrance of the Way, the first to taste the nectar of immortality, the first to enter the stream of the Dharma, and the first to ascend to the True Truth.
Among all humans and all devas in Jambudvīpa, he was the foremost to attain the Way.
Before all the Arhats, there was one surnamed Kauṇḍinya—this translates as "Fire-Vessel.
*Ajñāta* is his name; this translates as "Known" or, alternatively, "Non-Known. "Non-Known" does not mean that he has nothing known; rather, it means he knows "nothing [of the mundane].

If one relies on the Two Truths, this refers to knowing the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). He is named thus because he possesses the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). As the present text says:
When I first said "understanding," I meant the attainment of Arhatship; it did not refer to the time of attaining the first fruit. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the eminent bhikṣus resided at Kukkuṭārāma. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
formerly, there was a forest fire that burned a grove. Within the grove, there was a pheasant that entered the water to soak its feathers in order to extinguish the flames.
The *Zaoyao* states: "This is the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery. 2. Citing evidence to conclude the answer:
"My wondrous sound is subtle and perfect; through sound, I have attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme."
Regarding "wondrous sound, secret and perfect": if referring to the Treasury Teachings (Hīnayāna), the Dharma-nature is indicated as the wondrous sound.

This is because in the Hīnayāna, the original spirit of the Dharma-nature is characterized by cessation; thus, it is the subtle and wondrous sound. The subsequent mentions of "wondrous form" and "wondrous fragrance" can be understood by analogy with this.
"Secret" refers to its being free from sensory dust, and "perfect" refers to its universal penetration. This applies to the Lesser Vehicle teachings. If applied to the Great Vehicle teachings:
Thus, permanence is taken as the wondrous, the three virtues as the esoteric, and the complete possession of all dharmas as the perfect.
There is this meaning in opening up the provisional to reveal the real and entering the Great from the Small. Wuxing said:

"The teaching of opening the provisional to reveal the real is a secret matter of the Buddhas alone, not something that can be displayed by bodhisattvas or arhats. It is like [the authority over] ritual, music, military expeditions, and punishments."
That which issues from the Son of Heaven is not a matter for the feudal lords.

Now, as for what the Buddha has asked—regarding who among those who first resolved their minds and awakened to the eighteen realms possesses the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*)—this is merely intended to have the various sages each describe their own fundamental roots and the path of provisional and ultimate truth.
In the past, through expedient means, they had not yet realized the true reality; thus, the śrāvakas spoke of entering [enlightenment] together with the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), who does not claim to have attained realization and entered perfect penetration?

Although those such as Dignāga are said to have possessed "sublime sounds that were secretly perfect," this refers merely to the subtle and secret perfect awakening to the four noble truths within the context of arising and ceasing;
it must not be conflated with the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Thus, the *Madhyama Āgama* states: "I went to Vārāṇasī and beat the drum of the sublime nectar," and it further says: "As if..."
To speak of the excellence of the beginning, middle, and end of the Dharma—does the name "excellent" therein necessarily equate to the excellence of the *Lotus Sūtra*?

Consider, for instance, what is said later in the text regarding the śrāvakas of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "the supreme and wondrous manifest perfection," and "the manifestation of the supreme nature," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said that Mahābrahmā’s body and mind are wondrously perfect and complete, and his wondrous vision is perfectly clear and tranquil.
Could this "wondrous perfection" be the same as the nature of the wondrous clarity of Perfect Enlightenment?

One should know that the Tathāgata first had the various sages speak in succession until they had finished, and subsequently addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "These twenty-five great Bodhisattvas of the stage beyond learning and the Arhats..."
The Arhats each spoke of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all saying they had cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their respective practices, there was truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. This is the formal text that reveals the provisional to unite with the real.
As the verse by Mañjuśrī says: "The holy nature has nothing it does not penetrate; whether following or reversing [the path], all are expedient means. This indeed expounds upon the Tathāgata.
This is the purport of what follows. II. Upānanda’s Contemplation of Form. 2-1. Narrating the Circumstances of His Awakening.
Upānanda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I too, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, contemplated the signs of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion. I realized the nature of all forms and thereby followed [the path of renunciation]."
The pure white bones and subtle atoms dissolve back into empty space. When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The Tathāgata has sealed me with the name Niṣadha.
For those who contemplate impurity, the contemplation of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*) is practiced prior to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and is not included within the nine notions themselves. Nine...
From the first visualization of bloatedness up to the eighth, the contemplation of white bones, is accomplished. This is divided into two types: 1. Those who destroy the Dharma (dhamma-vināśaka):

Upon entering the ninth visualization of burning, they burn away the skeletal person and swiftly attain the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). 2. Those who do not destroy the Dharma (adhamma-vināśaka):

Abiding in the contemplation of the skeletal visualization, they observe the eight-colored radiant flows and advance in the cultivation of the liberations (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana).

Abiding in dhyāna, he sequentially contemplates, refines, and cultivates [the meditations] until both name and form are liberated, thereby becoming a Great Arhat. Now, this is an Arhat who destroys phenomena;
when the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) are perfected, he attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*).

Furthermore, it is said that one proceeds from impurity through the seven notions, such as bloating and lividity, followed by the notion of white bones and subtle dust returning to empty space. This then proceeds from the first...
The eighth contemplation on the skeleton leads into the ninth contemplation on burning. After being burned, only minute particles remain; these particles, in turn, return to emptiness alone.
With both form and emptiness being non-existent, one further transcends the two extremes. Furthermore, form constitutes the desire realm and the form realm, while emptiness is the formless realm.
Because the analytical contemplation of emptiness is perfected, the Buddha designated it as *niṣadha*. As for the nine contemplations: the first is the bloated corpse.
1. Swelling; 2. Bluish discoloration; 3. Putrefaction; 4. Blood-stained; 5. Pus-filled decay; 6. Disintegration; 7. Devouring;
8. Skeletons; 9. Burning. ○ Second, the citation of evidence and the concluding response.
"Once the dust-like forms have ceased, the wondrous form becomes subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through these physical characteristics.
When the Buddha asked about the most direct path to perfect penetration, according to my realization, the cause of form is supreme."

The section on "Dust-Color" concludes by manifesting perfect penetration. "Dust-color" refers to that which is composed of impurity; "dharma-nature" is wondrous color. Regarding the term "cause of color":
"element" (dhātu) carries the meaning of "cause," for the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness act as causes for one another.
3. Xiangyan’s Contemplation of Fragrance: 3.1 Narrating the Conditions for Awakening to Dependent Origination.
The youth Fragrance-Rigidity (Gandharvaśrī) immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was tranquil as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent: it was not wood, nor was it space."

It is neither smoke nor fire; departing, it has no place of attachment; arriving, it has no point of origin. Thereby my mental constructs were dissolved, and I realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
Thus, the Tathāgata conferred upon me the title "Incense-Veneration" (*Gandhavimala*).
I instruct you to contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) with precision, so that you may perceive the principle within the very facts themselves.

As for the statement "it is not wood," this is as explained in the third fascicle, in the section on the nose and fragrance: if one smells fragrance after being struck by smoke, one might say, "the fragrance arises from the wood.
However, when the fragrance is still and one has not encountered the smoke, it does not arise from the wood. If it were [inherently] produced...

If fragrance were to exist within emptiness, then the nature of emptiness would have to be eternally fragrant. Since one smells other things like smoke and fire yet perceives no fragrance therein, how can it be said that fragrance is produced from smoke and fire?
It does not go to the east, west, south, or north; it does not come from self, other, both, or neither.
Since fragrance has no arising, how can there be discrimination? Therefore, it is said that the mind is dissolved. When discrimination does not exist, subject and object are absent.
Both [the dust and the fragrance] vanished. Because the Dharma-body was adorned by means of exquisite fragrance, I am called the Youth Fragrance-Adorned (Gandharati).
Second, the citation of testimony and the concluding answer:

"The scent of dust suddenly ceased, and the fragrance became subtle and pervasive. Through this 'Adornment of Fragrance,' I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [this is my response]."
As I have realized it, the "Purity of Fragrance" (Gandhahastin) is supreme.

When it was previously called the "Fragrance-Purity Youth" (Gandhahastin-kumāra), he received that title from a Bodhisattva; yet when it is further asked how he attained Arhatship, this is merely a narrative of what he realized in the past.
It is like the case of the Moonlight Youth (Candraprabha-kumāra), who first attained the Lesser Fruit (śrāmaṇyaphala) and later [attained the Great Fruit] in the presence of the Buddha.

One attains the name of "Celibate Youth" (Kumārabhūta) and is merely admitted to the assembly of Bodhisattvas. 4. The King of Medicine Contemplates Flavor. Part One: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening.
The two Dharma-Prince sons, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Throughout beginningless kalpas, I have served as a skilled physician for the world.
Within my mouth, I have tasted the plants, trees, minerals, and metals of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand, all of which I know completely."
Whether tastes be bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, or pungent; whether they be combinations, innate, or transformed;
whether they be cold, hot, poisonous, or non-poisonous—he is able to know them all completely. Serving the Tathāgata, he has realized the nature of taste: it is neither empty nor existent.
"It is neither identical to body and mind, nor is it separate from body and mind. By discerning the causes of flavor, one attains awakening through this.
The Buddha-Tathāgata has bestowed his seal of approval upon the names of us two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. We are now Dharma princes within this assembly."

Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata were originally skilled physicians in the world. It was by means of this path that they served the Tathāgata. As for the statement that [reality] is neither empty nor existent:
it is not empty because the various flavors are vividly present; it is not existent because it is entirely free from the four modes of being (*caturvidha-svabhāva*). As the preceding verse says:
"The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, for they arise through conditions and are thus like illusions; unconditioned phenomena have no arising."

To extinguish what is unreal is like [extinguishing] flowers in the sky. Thus, it was previously not existent and subsequently not empty; now, it was previously not empty and subsequently not existent.
All of this is for the purpose of clarifying the Middle Way. As stated in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the Buddha tells the Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha-Āryavimalatejorāja:
"What, furthermore, is called the meaning of the profoundly deep? Although..."
One knows that sentient beings truly have no self, yet the fruits of karma are not lost in the future.
Although one knows that the five aggregates perish and cease here, the karmic actions of good and evil never fail. Although there are various karmas, no agent is seen.
Although there is a destination, no goer exists. Although there is bondage, no one who is bound exists. Although there is...
That even nirvāṇa has no extinguisher— this is called the profoundly deep and secret meaning. According to this scriptural passage,

Profoundly deep! The karmic actions of sentient beings are neither permanent nor discontinuous, yet they obtain their retributions.
Although they perish moment by moment, nothing is lost; although there is no agent, there is action; although there is no experiencer, there is retribution.

It is explained that the twelve links of dependent origination are neither existent nor empty, which is precisely the Middle Way. Now, the essential meaning of the fact that the nature of flavor is neither empty nor existent is largely the same.

First, an account of the conditions for his awakening to dependent origination.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen fellow bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

They addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. At the time of the monks' bathing ceremony, we entered the bathhouse according to custom.
Suddenly, we realized that the cause of water neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the interval between these two, we attained a state of tranquil non-existence.
Our former habits were not forgotten, and thus we have followed the Buddha into the homeless life until now, attaining the stage of No-more-learning."
That Buddha’s name is Bhadrapāla.
Bhadrapāla means "Worthy Protector" (Xiànshǒu) in this language, or also "Worthy Guardian" (Xiànhù). This is because he protects his own virtuous qualities and also protects sentient beings.
That water which is touched is a phenomenon among the eighteen *dhātus*. A *dhātu* is defined as a cause (*hetu*). It refers to the sensory object (*viṣaya*).
Since defilement is fundamentally not my own substance, the intent of washing does not lie in the dust. If one is separated from external dust, the substance is originally without defilement;

The intermediate state is the common nature (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*). Since each is already without washing, how could there be washing in the common [state]?
Washing away [defilements] leads to tranquility. Seeking that which is washed away, it cannot be found; this is the attainment of non-existence. 2.

II. Contemplating the Five Faculties to Accomplish the Path. 1. Aniruddha Contemplates the Eye. (1) Narrating the Conditions for Awakening.
Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.
The Tathāgata rebuked me as being of the same class as animals. Hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself."
After seven days of sleeplessness, I lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination.
No longer relying on my eyes, I perceive the ten directions as pure and true, as transparently clear as looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand.
The Tathāgata has certified me as an Arhat.

"Delightful Vision" (Nayananda) may refer to the mind that practices samādhi; however, it must be understood as "delightful vision" because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) never fails to be beheld.
"Self-nature illumination" means that its inherent capacity is luminous. Regarding the "Vajra-like Vision": the nature of seeing is indestructible, like a vajra. As for "pure and true":
it is called "pure" because it is unmixed with the sense organs (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya); it is called "true" because this mind is not the eye. Naluo is Āṭavika.
Dha (Pūrṇa). This is translated as "Free from Poverty" and also as "As One Wishes. He was the son of King Śuklodana.
