While the Buddha was teaching the Dharma to the assembly at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, Aniruddha fell asleep there. The Buddha rebuked him with a verse, saying:
"Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; having slept for a thousand years, you have not heard the name of the Buddha.
Thereupon, Aniruddha remained awake until dawn, and his faculty of sight was lost. Because of this, he cultivated dhyāna and attained [the divine eye].
The four great elements are pure forms; with half one’s head, one sees [the world] such that the three thousandfold world-system is viewed as if it were a fruit in the palm of one’s hand.

Now, regarding the statement that through the Vajra-samādhi one contemplates and perceives the ten directions, wherein the essence and truth are transparently clear—differing from what was previously described—it is because this sutra reveals and clarifies [the truth], and thus speaks in terms of the internal secret [teaching].
Previously, when guiding sentient beings according to their capacities, it was taught by way of the manifest smallness [of the body]. (Wuxing)
This means that while the *Āgama* speaks of "cultivating dhyāna" as a general and concise indication, the present text specifically reveals its name as the "Vajra-samādhi.
This does not mean that "vajra" is used solely as a metaphor for the Great Samādhi;

for instance, when Ānanda entered the *vidyut-prabhā-samādhi* to sever his final afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*), it was also called "Vajra-samādhi," which serves as a metaphor for the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the Hīnayāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Nanda lost the half of the head where the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) and the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) of the four great elements were pure;
the Buddha’s divine eye (divyacakṣus), however, has the derived matter of the four great elements throughout his entire head, which is pure. The Master Zhiyi says:

"In the Tripiṭaka, the Buddha’s divine eye is complete across his entire head, seeing through all things without obstruction. Thus, we know that the designations "whole" and "half" refer merely to the comparison between partial and complete [purity], and not to the size [of the faculty].

This is to show their difference. Furthermore, if one relies on the *Āgamas* to observe the trichiliocosm while this sutra perceives the ten directions, it would certainly be incorrect to claim there is a superiority or inferiority between them.
That sutra states that Nanda’s divine eye sees the realms of the ten directions; is this not the same?
Since the analogy of the fruit in the palm is identical, how can the words regarding "refined truth" differ? The following passage clarifies the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudṛśa*).

Master Shang said: "If even the refined and true [nature] manifests before one such that it molds and transforms things without obstruction, how much more so now for an Arhat who has developed the truly non-outflowing state—can it not be said that the refined and true nature is transparently clear?
From the beginning of the first fascicle, it was shown that the blind man’s ability to perceive darkness is the mind and not the eye;
thus, it was already clarified that the seeing-nature does not belong to the faculty of the eye. Now, although Nalanda has lost his sight, he has attained universal vision.

This is precisely the meaning of that passage. In the subsequent "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara," it is taught that one must enter the stream and forget the object of hearing until what is heard is exhausted;

only then does the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty manifest within emptiness. This clearly demonstrates that the nature of hearing is the mind and not the ear, and thus hearing does not belong to the ear-faculty.
Alas, how is it that people of the world still cling to the view that perfect penetration resides in the sense-faculties and not in the mind?
...and so forth. ○ Second, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, [I replied]: "According to what I have realized, turning back the seeing and following the source is the foremost.
"Turning back the seeing and following the source" means to turn back the seeing of the eye-faculty and return it to its original source. —Gushan.
It is said that the thorough penetration of the fundamental luminosity through the exhaustion of all views has been clearly established. 2. Cūḍapanthaka’s Contemplation of the Nose 2-1.
Narrating the Circumstances of His Awakening Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I am deficient in my recitation.”
I possessed a nature of little learning. Having first encountered a Buddha, heard the Dharma, and gone forth into homelessness, I memorized a single verse of the Tathāgata;

for one hundred days, I was unable to retain what came before while grasping what followed, or retain what came after while grasping what preceded it. The Buddha, pitying my folly, instructed me to observe the *anāpāna-smṛti* (in-and-out breathing) during the retreat.
At that time, I contemplated the breath with such subtlety as to exhaustively realize the moments of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Then, his mind suddenly opened up and he attained great unimpededness; eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows, he became an Arhat.
Sitting beneath the Buddha’s seat, he immediately attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding Cūḍapanthaka, previous commentaries have not distinguished him as two separate individuals, likely because of his perfect penetration.
The names are identical, though they omit that his brothers were not only one. *Cūḍapanthaka* is also called *Cūḍa*; this means "born by the side of the great road.
The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states: His mother was the daughter of an elder. Following her husband to another country, she became pregnant after a long time.
As her delivery neared, she longed to return home; while traveling halfway there, she gave birth to her son. Thus it was.
He fathered two sons twice; they were distinguished by their seniority and juniority. The elder was Cūḍapanthaka, and the younger was Svāgata.
Some say he was Pāṇṭhaka, which means "born by the side of a narrow path" (*kṣudrapanthaka*);
because he was born on the road following his elder brother, he is also translated as "Successor of the Path. According to this, it is clear that there were two individuals. (From the *Lotus Sūtra*)
The *Jing* (Sūtra), in the chapter "The Prophecy Bestowed upon the Five Hundred Disciples," further provides one such proof by listing Cunda, Śāgata, and others.
Zizhong states: "Pūrṇa was formerly a great Dharma master who was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras.

He had five hundred disciples, yet he was secretive and stingy regarding the Buddha-dharma, refusing to teach others. Because those later-born disciples were dull-witted, they encountered the Buddha due to their past roots of goodness."
He left the household life. Five hundred bhikṣus were taught the same single verse by their teacher for ninety days, yet they could not master it.
The Buddha, knowing their faculties, instructed them in *ānāpāna-smṛti* (counting the breaths). The *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* states: "Regarding the one sentence [taught] for a hundred days:
the elder saw that his younger brother could not recite it, and so he said to his brother, 'If you cannot recite it, why do you not return to being a layman? *Pán*.
Upon hearing this, he went to the gate of the Jeta Grove and wept. The Buddha asked him, and he related the aforementioned circumstances in full.
The Buddha said, "The attainment of *bodhi* depends upon your elder brother. The Buddha then took him by the hand and led him into a quiet chamber, instructing him to recite:
"Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress; one who practices thus shall transcend the world. He mastered the recitation. The Buddha said, "Now that you are old..."
To recite a single verse is not to be considered extraordinary; one must understand its meaning. This refers to the ten paths of action of body, speech, and mind.
One observes their arising and examines their cessation. Through them one is born in heaven; through them one enters the abyss;
through them one attains the Way. Awakening is natural; by this, the mind opens and one attains arhatship. The two characters "subtle" (wei-xi) extend throughout every moment (kṣaṇa).
Because the breath is subtle, the mind is also subtle; it is able to exhaustively penetrate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Breath possesses four characteristics, namely:
arising (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*). These four characteristics are themselves termed "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*).

Some say that a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) possesses these four characteristics, which would mean it contains four hundred *kṣaṇas*. How could this not also apply to the breath? Within the arising [of the breath], there are various *kṣaṇas*, and so on...
The same applies to their distinct cessation; this is termed the "momentariness of conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra-kṣaṇa*). By contemplating impermanence, one destroys the four inversions.

Because the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world all enter into the principle of emptiness, it is said that one "suddenly attains great unimpededness. Youyixi cites the *Six Gates of Subtle Dhyāna*, stating:
"Regulating the inhalation and exhalation of the breath is the first, counting; the second is following; from 'I at this time' [onward] is the third, stopping; and the fourth is contemplation."
The mind then descends through the five stages of return and attains the sixth stage of purity. Second, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, that which I have realized—reversing the breath and following emptiness—is the foremost.
Changshui says: "Reversing birth and cessation, one rests in accordance with the emptiness of non-arising. This emptiness is precisely the great, unimpeded perfection.
Reversing rest, one enters penetration. 3. The Contemplation of the Tongue by Kauṇḍinya. A. Narrating the Conditions for Awakening to Dependent Origination.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have committed verbal karma;
during past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas. Consequently, in life after life and birth after birth, I suffered from the affliction of rumination like an ox.

The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-door of the single-flavor, pure mind-ground. Having attained this, I have extinguished the discursive mind and entered samādhi, contemplating the cognition of flavors."

Neither a substantial entity nor a material object, one should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally, one is liberated from body and mind; externally, one leaves behind the world.
Far removed from all modes of existence (*bhava*) like a bird escaping its cage, free from defilement and with dust extinguished, the Dharma-eye becomes pure, and one attains Arhatship.
The Tathāgata personally certified me as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Gavāmpati—here translated as "ox-chewer"—is also said to have been called so because in a previous life he saw an old monk who was toothless yet eating, and laughed at him for resembling an ox;
consequently, in every lifetime thereafter, he was reborn with an ox's tongue and constantly chewed like an ox. Wēnlíng [comments]: "By means of mindfulness..."
The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma-gate of the single flavor (*ekarasa*) and the pure mind-ground may not be correctly understood [by you].
It should be as Gushan said: "To realize that flavor is flavorless is called 'single flavor. This is because, in observing flavor, the text below clarifies the method of observation:
if the tongue alone does not know it, it is not the essence; if the object alone does not know it, it is not the object. Since it is neither essence nor object, one knows it is not [either].

They truly exist. To know that they do not truly exist is precisely to know that they are empty; this is entering emptiness from the conventional. Because it is not a substantial entity, one is internally liberated from body and mind;

because it is not a material object, one externally relinquishes the world. By contemplating this, one attains transcendence, and thus remains far removed from the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
Regarding "leaving defilement behind and dissolving the dust": the previous fascicle stated that "perceptual marks are the dust" and that "consciousness..."

"Affliction (*kleśa*) is the defilement (*mala*). Some take "dust" (*rajas*) to refer to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and "defilement" to refer to the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). However, dust is light and easily removed, whereas defilement is oily and difficult to cleanse;

therefore, it is not necessarily the case that these metaphors correspond directly to the delusions of views and thought. One should know that both the removal of defilement and the dissipation of dust occur at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Defilement refers to the delusions of views, while dust refers to the appearances of dust. Since the six [sense-faculties] have already attained cessation at the first fruit, they are termed "dust."
[The text] dissolves. The purity of the Dharma-eye is precisely the stage of Srotāpanna; from this first fruit, one progresses to become an Arhat.
2. Conclusion of the Answer on Perfect Penetration:
The Buddha asked about perfect penetration. According to what I have realized, returning to flavors and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.

One should contemplate that transcending [the senses] constitutes penetration (*abhijñā*). Being free from internal and external [objects] constitutes perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Returning to the flavor results in attaining the single flavor. By turning back the cognition, one enters the state of non-cognition. Since the tongue perceives within the union [of object and organ], it is spoken of together with flavor. 4.

Biliṅga’s Contemplation of the Body 4.1 Narrating the Conditions for Awakening to Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) The tongue is the organ of taste; its nature is to perceive flavor. It is not the case that there is no perception when the tongue is in contact with the object. Therefore, it is said to "perceive" by combining with the flavor. This is why it is explained in conjunction with taste. 4.
Biliṅga’s Contemplation of the Body 4.1 Narrating the Conditions for Awakening to Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)
Pilingavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first resolved to attain enlightenment and followed the Buddha into the Path, I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of how all worldly things are not to be enjoyed. While begging for food in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gate;
unaware, a poisonous thorn pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache with pain. As I reflected upon this..."
I knew that I knew this profound suffering. Although my awareness was aware of the pain, my awareness of the pure mind was free from any sensation of pain or awareness of pain.
I further reflected: "How could there be two simultaneous cognitions within a single body? Before long, as I concentrated my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty.
Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and I became an Arhat. I received the personal seal of approval and attained the realization of one beyond training.
Piliṅgavatsa is translated here as "Residual Habit. For five hundred lifetimes he was a Brahmin, and thus his residual habits were characterized by much pride.
His insulting of the river deity was not his actual intention, but rather his habitual tendency (*vāsanā*).
Having frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the things in all worlds that are not to be enjoyed—referring generally to the eight types of suffering—he contemplated these unpleasant phenomena.
When one encounters an unpleasant object, the arising of pain is precisely suffering. I reflect that this is what was realized by the Blessed One;
first, he established the pair of perceptions. I reflect that there is a knowing which knows this deep pain—this very reflection is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding "even though one perceives," although the perception of the body-faculty perceives the pain of the body-faculty, the mind is fundamentally pure and without [intrinsic nature].
The pain of the body-faculty and the awareness that knows the pain—these I further dispatch as a pair of cognitions.
This "pair of cognitions" refers to the awareness that knows the pain and the awareness of the pure mind. Thus, through the three illuminations, mindfulness is gathered below.
Changshui says: "The non-arising of a single thought of 'attainment' is called 'gathering.

This is identical in meaning to the previous [passage] regarding the leaves arising and ceasing while maintaining the true and eternal; when both body and mind are empty, one will certainly not perceive pain.
The term "outflows" (*āsrava*) does not exceed the three realms of existence. Delusion and karma are the causes of the outflows, and [they result in] birth and death.
It is the fruit of all outflows. Second, the conclusion and answer regarding the perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, that which I have realized—pure awareness leaving the body behind—is the foremost.
"Pure awakening is simply the one true awakening"—this answers the question of Perfection (Yuan). "The body and mind suddenly become empty"—this answers the question of Pervasion (Tong).
○ Fifth, the contemplation of the meaning of emptiness arising, in two parts: first, an account of the conditions for awakening to dependent origination.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “For kalpas as vast as space, my mind has been free from obstruction.
I recall my births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from the moment I was first in my mother’s womb, I knew emptiness and stillness.

Thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and I also enabled sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness. I have received the revelation of the nature [of reality] from the Tathāgata.”

Awakening to the true emptiness whose empty nature is perfectly luminous, he attained the state of an Arhat. He suddenly entered the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like clarity and emptiness, becoming sealed with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one beyond training.
Through liberation in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he became supreme among those who are selfless.

First, the explanation of practice and understanding (*sambhāra-mārga*) is set forth. That the mind attains non-obstruction means entering fully through the mental faculty (*manas*). Non-obstruction is the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Knowing emptiness within the mother’s womb refers to the emptiness of the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*); that the ten directions become empty refers to the emptiness of the secondary environment (*bhājana-loka*).

After emerging from the womb, one also causes others to realize this. Next, the realization and entry (*darśana-mārga*) is clarified: "The nature of awareness is true emptiness" is the meaning of the Middle Way. Emptiness...
The nature of perfect luminosity is not only empty of the afflictions of views and thoughts, but all six sense faculties are likewise empty.

Alternatively, one may merely abide in the thorough realization of the principle of emptiness according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*); because of this emptiness, one attains the fruit of an Arhat.

Because one is subsequently received by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one enters the ocean of jewel-luminous emptiness. Regarding the "ocean of jewel-luminous emptiness," Changshui says: "Because emptiness is the Tathāgata..."

Because it is hidden within, it is complete and pervasive, possessing all phenomena; like a *maṇi* jewel, it gives rise to things according to one's wishes, for its luminosity universally illumines the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Like the great ocean, it is deep and vast, encompassing and containing all.

Because its cause is the Middle Way of True Emptiness, it is identical to the knowledge of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom) and the vision of the Buddha-eye. Or, one might suspect this to be the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Even this emptiness is not yet the essential substance of nature; how, then, can it be called "the true emptiness of the awakened nature"?

It must be the Middle Way’s correct emptiness as proclaimed by the Tathāgata. For those born into emptiness, they first realize emptiness and are subsequently received by the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

I merely accord with the partial teachings and take the seal of being "beyond learning" as my standard. That both the person and phenomena are empty, and that their simultaneous emptiness is non-arising—this is the nature of liberation, which is emptiness.

Sundarananda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Daily I saw the breath entering and exiting my nostrils like smoke; within my body and mind, there was inner clarity, and the world became a perfectly hollow and transparent void, as pure as lapis lazuli.

To go toward the east, south, west, or north is movement; that which is not substantially real is precisely delusion. Yet, since there is nowhere from which one comes, there is no coming;
and since there is nowhere to which one goes, there is no going. This absence of going and coming is the nature of immovability (*acalata*).

From the perspective of delusive appearance, one establishes the two contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and conventional designation (*prajñapti*); from the perspective of immovability, one establishes the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
The three correct contemplations are contained within a single mind. Previously, in the Moonlight Contemplation of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the sequential realization was extremely slow;

now, because this contemplation of the Dharma is skillful, the realization is extremely swift. Regarding the passage "the dust motes of the ten directions," first one establishes the two contemplations of emptiness and the provisional.
Since they come from nowhere and go nowhere, they are identical to inverted views.
It is said that they are "the same" because of false views. To illustrate this with a metaphor: a single vessel represents *samādhi*;

the vessel represents the great trichiliocosm, while the hundred gnats represent sentient beings. Furthermore, the vessel is extremely small, being no more than a mere fraction of an inch, yet within it there is only frantic clamor.
Because the Bodhisattva knows that the source of all movement is solely the power of wind, his vision is thus. II.
Entry into Realization:

Not long after meeting the Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that time, his mind opened and he beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the eastern direction.
Acting as a prince of the Dharma for the Buddhas of the ten directions, his body and mind emit light that penetrates all things without obstruction.
This constitutes the realization of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) within the Middle Way.

It differs from the aforementioned Arhat’s "knowledge or abandonment," which is not the same as a Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena. The eastern direction is the head of all movement, and such is the name of the Buddha-land.

It is unmoving. Is it not the case that within movement there exists that which is unmoving? Regarding "the body and mind emitting light," etc., this precisely states the source from which [this state] derives its name.
Because one thoroughly penetrates the three truths as being within a single mind, the internal and external are transparently illuminated like pure lapis lazuli.
2. Conclusion and Response on Perfect Penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "I attained enlightenment through the Bodhicitta by observing that the power of wind has no basis, thereby entering samādhi.
This transmission of the single wondrous mind with all Buddhas of the ten directions is the foremost."

Regarding the wind that has no support: all things, both the environment and its inhabitants, rely upon the wind to abide; yet the wind itself has nothing upon which it relies, and thus it is not substantially real.
Regarding the "wondrous mind": exclusive movement is not wondrous, and exclusive stillness is also not wondrous.

When movement and non-movement are unified within the single mind through the three contemplations, this is what is called "wondrous. Question: Above, you clarified the three truths. How is it that two are coarse and one is wondrous?

To clarify "immediate identity" (*ji*). The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "The 'sequential immediate' means that only after [the stages] are completed does one now achieve immediacy.
The sub-commentary explains that pointing out that biased emptiness and biased provisionality is itself the Middle Way; this is called "sequential immediacy.

Later, by pointing out that these three are simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle, one establishes the wondrous Three Truths. Therefore, if one wishes to know the principle of the Perfect Teaching, one must first understand that very [sequential immediacy].

The Sequence. ○ Five: The Contemplation of the Emptiness of the Treasury of Space (Ākāśagarbha). Part One: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening to Dependent Origination; Part Three: Identical to What the Buddha Attained.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I and the Tathāgata..."
He came to attain the Boundless Body under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Second, the full manifestation of his spiritual power:
at that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminated the Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.
Furthermore, within the great round mirror manifested from one’s own mind, ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light are emitted, flowing and pouring into the ten directions.
All the various *dhvajarāja* (banner-king) lands, reaching to the limits of empty space, enter into this mirror and penetrate my body.
My body becomes identical to space, without mutual obstruction; it is able to skillfully enter lands as minute as motes of dust, extensively performing Buddha-deeds and attaining great accordance.

Youxi said: "The four great jewels represent the wisdom that contemplates the four great elements. The dust-motes and lands of the ten directions represent the objects of contemplation—the four great elements.
In the fourth fascicle, it was already stated that earth, water, fire, and wind are ultimately merged into empty space.
Here, the hand is used as a metaphor for the wisdom that contemplates emptiness; because emptiness encompasses the four great elements, one grasps the four jewels. The four jewels...
Because it is fundamentally empty, the illumination of the Buddha-fields also becomes empty space.

As the previous fascicle further states, "the true awakening of the emptiness of nature," the Great Perfect Mirror manifests within one's own mind to represent the essence of awakening. Because it illuminates the ten directions, it manifests as the ten rays of light.
By means of light, one gathers all lands and causes them to enter the mirror of the mind. Yet, the extent of what is reflected within that mirror does not stop at the boundaries of the mirror;
it penetrates my own body. Since the substance of the body is fundamentally empty, how could there be any obstruction?
At this time, there is no need to say that all lands are empty; rather, it is simply that the body of space does not obstruct the earth. Thus, the body is able to enter skillfully.
Thus, this great body enters various lands without losing its original form, and the lands do not become cramped; therefore, it is called "skillful entry.
Furthermore, previously the lands entered the body; now the body enters the lands. Because the body is like empty space, it is called "skillful entry.
Generating the good and extinguishing evil is called "Buddha-work. The mutual containment of the small and the large constitutes "conformity. Part Three: Causes.
Through contemplation,

I attained realization of this great spiritual power. By my diligent observation that the four great elements have no basis and arise and perish as deluded thoughts, and that empty space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical,
I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through the illumination of this identity.
The four great elements rely upon space to exist. That which is named "space" has nothing upon which it relies. Having no basis, there is no substantiality;
it is nothing more than the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts. Since the lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty, they are said to be fundamentally identical.

Once one realizes that the four great elements enter into emptiness, one further clarifies that emptiness is itself the nature of emptiness. When even emptiness is forgotten, this is called "non-existence."
Patience toward beings. Second, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied, "By observing that space is boundless, I entered samādhi;
the wondrous power of this clarity and perfection is foremost."
That space is boundless means that one realizes the four great elements enter into emptiness. Entering into *samādhi* means manifesting the nature of enlightened awareness (*jñāna*).
The mutual interpenetration of body and land constitutes "perfection" (*yuan*); the illumination of lands by light constitutes "clarity" (*ming*);

and the mutual intercommunication of the five great elements as the essence of awakening constitutes "pervasion" (*tong*). Furthermore, perfect clarity is itself perfect penetration, as it says later: "The present Bodhisattvas now..."
Each enters perfect clarity. ○ VI. Maitreya’s Contemplation of Consciousness, Part Two: I. Narrating the Conditions for Awakening; III.
Meeting the Buddha and Receiving His Teaching.
Bodhisattva Maitreya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall the past..."
After the passage of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness;

however, my mind was preoccupied with worldly fame, and I took pleasure in frequenting the families of the laity. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the samādhi of consciousness-only and enter into samādhi.

Attachment to worldly fame is a pursuit that runs outward; therefore, by breaking through the external and turning inward, one is led to cultivate the meditative concentration on consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

The *Shoujian* states: "There are two types of meditative concentration on mind-and-consciousness-only. That which is practiced as preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called the 'contemplation of the image-as-consciousness-only.

Upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*) during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one performs the 'contemplation of reality-as-consciousness-only. All phenomena take consciousness as their characteristic. True...
If it were according to its nature, then the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) should refer only to the eight consciousnesses.
Upon attaining the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the mind of consciousness, it refers to the ninth consciousness. II. Refuting Errors Based on the Teachings.
Throughout kalpas past, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges by means of this samādhi. The seeking of worldly fame and reputation has ceased and no longer exists.

Cultivating this contemplation is precisely the remedy: knowing that worldly fame, profit, existence, non-existence, thickness, or thinness are all transformations of my own *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and do not come from another, the frantic pursuit of them suddenly ceases. III. The Three Contemplations are Accomplished.
I attained the Way.
When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then achieved the supreme, wondrous, perfect Samādhi of the cognitive mind.
Furthermore, all the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—are all manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.
"World-Honored One, because I have thoroughly understood that it is solely the mind and consciousness, and that from the nature of consciousness flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas,
I have now received the prediction of future Buddhahood to succeed to the Buddha’s place.

This unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect Samādhi of the Consciousness-Mind is precisely the 'True Awareness of the Awareness-Light' within the third fascicle, 'The Nature of Awareness is Luminous Knowledge.'"

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). Its wondrous awakening is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Now it is said that from the nature of consciousness flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas.

Since the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, internal and external, self and other, and all beings—sages and ordinary people, living beings and Buddhas—are not separated from one another, is this not the supreme, wondrous, and perfect principle?
Regarding the manifestation of lands: Xiachuan says there are two meanings for "manifestation. The first is in terms of principle (*li*).

"Manifestation is itself possession. Second, regarding phenomena, this refers to the manifestations of the three periods of time. It is precisely because of the inherent possession of principle that there can be the manifestation of phenomena.
The first three fascicles correctly clarify this inherent nature; what is meant by "manifestation is itself possession" is this.
What is now stated as "mind-only," up to the words "purity and impurity, existence and non-existence," refers to the manifestations of the three periods of time. However, in both instances...

All [phenomena] are fully present as the two [aspects of manifestation]. Taking "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) as their nature is the gateway of inherent presence; inherent presence is the very foundation of mind-only.

If one does not provide this interpretation, how can one harmonize with the text of the third fascicle? Furthermore, mind-only would lose its fundamental basis. Next, regarding the manifestation of all Buddhas:
all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are entirely the inherent presence within my own mind-nature.
Therefore, it again flows forth from the nature of consciousness. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"If a person wishes to thoroughly know all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the mind as it truly is, for it creates all Tathāgatas. Is this not in perfect accord with the present?
Regarding "creation," there are two meanings, which may be explained based on the two preceding manifestations. 2. Conclusion of the Answer on Perfect Penetration.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are nothing but consciousness; as the conscious mind becomes perfectly luminous, I entered the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Having distanced myself from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is the foremost.
If the words "contemplating with clarity" (*di-guan*) include that which is cultivated within the causal stage, they encompass both the real and the false.

When it reaches the "perfectly luminous consciousness-mind," it refers exclusively to the ninth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It is "round" (*yuan*) because it universally encompasses both the environment and its inhabitants; it is "luminous" (*ming*) because wondrous awakening is profoundly still; it is "penetrating" (*tong*) because it extends to the Buddha of the fruition stage.

As for the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), sentient beings are deluded and fail to realize that all phenomena are fundamentally empty; they falsely [impute existence] upon...

I and all phenomena are grasped as being substantially existent. As for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it refers to all cognitions and dharmas that exist through the correspondence of various conditions;
they possess no intrinsic nature at all and are merely illusory.

As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it refers to the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which is unchanging, immutable, and perfectly accomplished. Furthermore, the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is precisely the self.
Attachment. Attachment to the dependent nature is attachment to dharmas. ○ Seven: Śrī-Maitreya’s Contemplation of the Roots of Greatness. Part One: Narrating the Awakening to Dependent Origination.
Part Two: Encountering the Buddha and Receiving His Teachings. Furthermore, two sections: Part One: The Dharma.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of that kalpa, the last of whom was named Suryaprabhācandraprabhābhibhū."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
There are twelve Buddhas from whom I have received this transmission, their radiance shining forth in succession: first is Immeasurable Light;
second is Boundless Light; third is Unobstructed Light; fourth is Peerless Light; fifth is Great Flame Light; sixth...
The first is named Pure Light; the seventh is named Joyful Light; the eighth is named Wisdom Light; the ninth is named Uninterrupted Light;
the tenth is named Inconceivable Light; the eleventh is named Incomparable Light; and the twelfth is named Surpassing the Light of the Sun and Moon.
Thus it is said that twelve Tathāgatas succeed one another throughout a single kalpa. Those Buddhas instructed us, clarifying the beginning of upholding the Teaching.
The name "establishing practice" is used here. Mindfulness is that which contemplates; the Buddha is that which is contemplated. Samādhi is called "right reception.

By the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, one does not undergo various sensations and thereby attains right reception. However, among all dharmas, the method of mindfulness of the Buddha’s name is the most pervasive.
The four types of samādhi are collectively referred to as "Buddha-recollection" (nien-fo). All other samādhis involve recollecting the Buddha of one's own original nature.
This present samādhi, like that described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, takes another Buddha as its object of focus.

Although the sūtra’s account of past practice does not explicitly state that it was exclusively focused on Amitābha, its underlying intent follows the practitioners of today who single-mindedly direct their attention toward the Western Quarter.
II. Two Similes. The following two layers of parables clarify the reason why one must necessarily practice mindfulness of the Buddha. First, the simile of mutual recollection;
second, the simile of being perfumed by incense. Regarding the first simile: 1. Establishing the metaphor; 2. The metaphor for the loss incurred when sentient beings do not practice mindfulness.

For example, suppose there is one person who is exclusively intent on remembering and another who is exclusively prone to forgetting. Such two people may encounter each other and yet not encounter each other;
they may see each other and yet not see each other.

The one who is exclusively intent on remembering is a metaphor for the Buddhas, who from their initial resolve give rise to the *saṃnāha* (armor of diligence) and, through ultimate great compassion, rush to the aid of those in distress.

There is no time when he does not keep sentient beings in mind. If there were even one person who completely forgot him, it would be like a child turning his back on his father and fleeing, wandering aimlessly through the five realms of existence, craving only coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. As for "if they encounter [him]" and so forth:

at no time and in no place do the Buddhas fail to manifest their form bodies (*rūpakāya*) to bring about liberation; rather, following the omnipresence of the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), they respond with their transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

It is likewise all-pervasive. However, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and lack the conditions for resonance with the Buddha, they do not encounter him even when they do, or they see him and yet do not see him.
○ Second, the analogy for attaining through mindfulness of the Buddha.
The two people remember each other, and their mutual mindfulness is profound. In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging.

The two people remembering each other is a metaphor for how the Buddha, having already brought sentient beings to mind, sentient beings should likewise bring the Buddha to mind. Now, as for the Buddha’s mindfulness...
There is no time or place where sentient beings do not bring this mindfulness to mind;
once this mindfulness has become deep, there is likewise no time or place where sentient beings do not bring the Buddha to mind—this is what is called the "depth of the two kinds of recollection.

In this way, one will constantly see the Buddha in every birth and behold the Tathāgata in every land; therefore, they are likened to form and shadow, which never deviate from one another. (2) The Application to the Dharma, Part One.
This addresses the fault of failing to maintain mindfulness.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If a child has run away, what is the use of the mother’s remembrance?
The previous two cases of mutual remembrance were merely general metaphors; therefore, the analogy of mother and child is again cited to specifically address this point. [The father...]

Because a strict mother is also compassionate, only the mother is mentioned. Regarding the phrase "the son has run away": it refers to a single person who is exclusively forgetful; even if he remembers, what is the use?
It is as if meeting him and yet not meeting him, or seeing him and yet not seeing him. [Section] Two: Combining the Attainment of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
This also has two parts: first, the combined metaphor.
If you, my son, remember your mother as she remembers you, then mother and child will not be separated throughout successive lives.
The method for teaching your son to remember his mother must be exactly as she remembers him: one must not, for even the duration of a finger-snap, think of the five worldly desires;
this is right mindfulness. (2) Second, the formal application.
If sentient beings, with their minds, recollect the Buddha and think of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future; they will not be far from the Buddha.
Without relying on expedient means, they will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
"Recalling the Buddha" means to long for him with the desire to see him. "Mindfulness of the Buddha" refers to recollecting his various meritorious qualities and dharma-gates.
Regarding the phrase "appearing before one," it is like the relationship between a mother and child throughout successive lifetimes, never being far apart. As for "not being distant from the Buddha":

although sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha have not yet attained Buddhahood, they will certainly attain it before long; thus, their distance from the Buddha is not far. This is what is meant by "without depending on... [the expedient means].
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): although the twenty-four gates differ in being either Great or Small, partial or complete, they all rely upon expedient means.

Now, in this practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*), it is sufficient merely to recollect; one need not labor to perform other meditative visualizations. For although mindfulness of the Buddha belongs to the faculty of mind, it does not require discursive calculation.
As a previous sutra states: "It is simply like [an image] in a mirror, without further analysis. Now it says "not... [to emphasize that no such analysis is required].
Regarding "provisional means," it does not involve using the mind to speculate on the underlying intent; rather, its general meaning is the same as that of the ancients. As the ancients said:

"Holding fast to the name is called 'one-pointedness of mind in terms of phenomena' (*shishi-ichinen*); mindfulness without [conceptual] mindfulness is called 'one-pointedness of mind in terms of principle' (*ririshin-ichinen*). Now I say:

if one does not give rise to conjecture and deliberation, then one-pointedness of mind in terms of phenomena is itself one-pointedness of mind in terms of principle. 2. The Analogy of Being Perfumed by Incense.
Just as a person who has been perfumed with incense has a fragrance upon their body, this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

To provide another analogy for why sentient beings must practice mindfulness of the Buddha: it is because they will come to possess a fragrance, just like the person who has been perfumed with incense.

The body was originally not fragrant, yet it acquires fragrance because of its association with incense. Birth was originally not that of a Buddha, yet one becomes a Buddha through mindfulness of the Buddha, thereby possessing the fragrance of Buddhahood.
"Adorned with fragrant light" means that one adorns oneself with the light of the Tathāgata’s virtuous fragrance.
(2) Self-cultivation and transforming others.

"In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, within this world-system, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
Tiaoxi said: "In verifying one's cultivation, the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha must not be understood as being limited solely to its phenomenal aspects."

Maintain mindfulness of the three contemplations. The Buddha possesses the three bodies; the mind must shatter the three delusions before one can enter the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. This constitutes the essence of Buddha-recollection.
As for "Pure Land," it specifically refers to Sukhāvatī, while generally encompassing the *Dharmadhātu-prabhāsvara* (Jigaku) realm. 2. Conclusion and Response on Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. I have no preference; by universally withdrawing the six sense organs and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, one attains samādhi—this is the foremost method.

If the faculty of mind is purified, all the other faculties are withdrawn of their own accord, without the need for deliberate selection. It is like when reciting the Buddha’s name: the eyes do not [wander].
Contemplating form with the eye is mindfulness of the Buddha; even to the point where the body does not crave touch, this is mindfulness of the Buddha through the body.
To contemplate only Amitābha and seek only the Pure Land throughout one’s daily life without interruption is called "the succession of pure mindfulness.
Because this dharma-gate directly accords with the ground of the mind and transcends other gates, it is the foremost.
*Śūraṅgama Sūtra: Commentary on the Meditation on the Mind*, Fascicle Five.
*The Great Buddha-Topknot Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
Commentary on the Meditation on the Mind*, Fascicle Six.
○ Fifth is the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara on the Ear-Faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

If one were to follow the sequence of the Three Categories and Seven Elements, this should come immediately after the Contemplation of the Eye-Faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) within the Dharma of the Auditory Organ (*śrotra-dhātu*).

However, because the meaning of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) is most extensively realized through this very skillful means, it fully reveals the gates of cultivation and realization and broadly sets forth the manifestations of the transformative teachings. Therefore, it is listed as a separate chapter at the very end.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, an account of the conditions for awakening to dependent origination; second, meeting the Buddha and receiving his teachings.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named..."
Avalokiteśvara, I resolved upon Bodhicitta under that Buddha. That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
Avalokiteśvara, this Great Being possesses a primordial treasury of great radiance that silently perceives the capacities of sentient beings. This world...
The thirty-two transformation bodies are the secret of the body, universally manifesting; the voice is the secret of speech through the four types of unimpeded eloquence in preaching the Dharma.

All of these arise because the Great Being has realized the Middle Way as the basis for manifestation; thus, he is able to perform inconceivable transformations through the three wheels, providing inexhaustible edification.
To pronounce this directly as a single phrase precisely indicates the Perfect Middle as the basis for manifestation. If one reads it according to the characters...

Regarding the phrase "Guanshiyin," if read as a single unit, it means that the Great Being universally observes the capacities of beings across the ten dharma realms and responds as soon as they call upon him;
this is as expressed in the saying, "By observing their sounds, one immediately attains liberation. If, however, "Guanshi" is read as a single unit...

If the characters for "sound" and "letter" are taken as a single phrase, it means that the Great Being first observes how the capacities of beings across the ten realms differ in their responses, and accordingly preaches the Dharma.
This is as it is said: "By whatever body one may be saved, by that very body he shall preach the Dharma."
These two belong to the contemplation of compassion and the contemplation of the provisional.

If one simply invokes the two characters "Guanyin," this refers to the Great Being’s initial hearing of the Buddha's voice, which enters the mind and forms contemplation. Contemplation is the wisdom that contemplates; sound is the object contemplated.
When object and wisdom are both merged in stillness, one directly penetrates the ten realms, the five abodes, and the two types of death to realize the truth.
This is the contemplation of the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is as described in the passage: "From the midst of hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object...

until birth and death have ceased and quiescent extinction manifests; suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds. This is explained in detail in the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter).
These three sublime gates of contemplation are that by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time attain Bodhi.
The subtlety of this śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna is such that the Buddhas of antiquity were named Avalokiteśvara, and the Buddhas of the present are likewise named Avalokiteśvara;
thus, the principle of the sages of past and future is one and the same.

Nevertheless, entry into the gate must rely upon hearing with the ears as the very first expedient within cultivation. Yet there are those in the world who cling to these expedients as being the ultimate truth.
Truly, those who exert all their strength to reject the three contemplations are severing the wondrously adorned path of the Buddhas’ and Avalokiteśvara’s Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration.
Furthermore, there is the distinction between the *Lotus Sūtra*’s transforming others and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s self-cultivation;
one must know that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* enables those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions to attain liberation simply by contemplating sounds. Thus...

This is precisely practicing for oneself while transforming others. Furthermore, the character *guān* (contemplation) possesses two meanings: the level tone (*píngshēng*) and the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

As it is said, when "contemplation" is read with the departing tone, it explains its essence as the mind alone capable of conceptualization. When "contemplation" is read with the level tone, it reveals its function as that which simultaneously summons the object it confronts.
The *Zhìguān* states: "To contemplate the darkness with contemplation is to make the dark luminous. Thus, these two—[the essence and the function]—...
All these meanings must be employed. It is also as stated in the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) chapter: "One enters samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
These three types of wisdom have both horizontal and vertical dimensions. Horizontally, they exist at every stage from the level of names and words (*nāma-pada*) upward.
Vertically, "names and words" constitutes hearing; "contemplative practice" constitutes contemplation; and "resemblance [to the fruit]" constitutes cultivation. (Nirvāṇa Sūtra, Vol. 22, p. 10).
Regarding the seventh merit among the merits, the text states: "When a bodhisattva cultivates this subtle and wondrous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he reflects thus:
'What dharmas can serve as the proximate causes for Mahāparinirvāṇa?
The bodhisattva then knows that there are four kinds of dharmas that serve as proximate causes for Mahāparinirvāṇa. The first is to draw near to virtuous friends."
Second, listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; third, contemplate it with focused mindfulness; fourth, practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the three types of wisdom (trividya) in this present text differ from other systems: generally, those who uphold the teachings all hear them through the faculty of the ear.
