First, entering emptiness: initially, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object; once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise.

Thus, as this gradually increases, both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted. When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell therein; when there is nothing to be perceived, the perceiver is empty. When the emptiness of the perceiver is perfectly fulfilled, it reaches ultimate perfection.
Emptiness and that which is emptied are both extinguished.

As previously stated, within their own abiding samādhi, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas perceive that the seeing, the objects of seeing, and all conceptualized appearances are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. This seeing and its objects...
The original essence is the wondrously pure and luminous body of bodhi. According to this scriptural passage, emptiness comes first and the middle follows.
"The seeing and the objects of seeing" refers to emptiness; "this seeing and its objects" refers to the middle. The text regarding the Bodhisattva entering samādhi is likewise.
One should use the two principles of emptiness and the middle to determine this passage, from the beginning at "within hearing" up to...

It is the emptiness of that which is empty and the extinction of that which is empty. From "the arising and ceasing having both ceased" up to "harmonizing with what is above and harmonizing with what is below" is the middle section.
The statement "first, within hearing" is made by relying on the provisional to establish the ultimate emptiness;

it causes one to enter through the provisional dharma of the faculty of hearing, which is the very first expedient means. If both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted, then this faculty of hearing is also empty.
It is not that perfect penetration can be attained by clinging to the ear-faculty alone. Master Wuxing divides this passage into four sections:

the disappearance of external objects, the exhaustion of the internal faculty, the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness, and the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Regarding the middle section, he says:
"When a Bodhisattva practices, they must fundamentally enter through the movement and stillness of hearing. As for the phrase 'entering the stream,' 'entering' means returning. As stated previously:
"You now wish to go against the current of the desire for birth and death, returning to the very root of that current until you reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction.

These words constitute the correct understanding of "entering the stream. For ordinary people, the faculty of hearing flows outward and chases after sounds; this is what it means to move toward the external.

Now, to refrain from giving rise to discrimination is called "entering the stream. This is because, since beginningless time, the reason one has established oneself [in samsara] has been due to the harm caused by such outward movement.
It has been a long time. Now, although you hear sounds, you do not give rise to discrimination; this is the moment when the dust of sound perishes.

Since that which enters [the senses] is already stilled, this is the time when the practice attains its fruition. That the two characteristics of movement and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising is itself "stillness" (*jì*).
At this time, it is not that one is unaware of movement and stillness, but rather that one does not give rise to the appearances of movement and stillness. If one were unaware of movement...

Quietness is not the ear-faculty itself; if one discriminates between the two characteristics of movement and quietness, that belongs to the ear-consciousness. Because consciousness arises, it can produce afflictions and karma.
Now, although one hears movement and quietness, one does not give rise to the characteristics of these external objects (*viṣaya*).

As for the Bodhisattva who fundamentally enters through the faculties (*indriya*) yet first eliminates the objects of movement and quietness: it is because knowledge is triggered by objects; once the objects are detached, the faculty [is no longer bound].

It must be eradicated; therefore, it perishes first. Next, as for the complete exhaustion of the internal faculties (*adhyātma-indriya*): knowledge arises from objects (*viṣaya*), and characteristics exist because of the faculties.

These two phenomena form a pair; the existence of one is impossible without the other. Although the external objects have already perished due to the faculties, [the faculties themselves must now be exhausted].

If the faculties are not extinguished, one will ultimately not attain liberation. This is truly because, when wisdom is lost, there are degrees of intimacy and distance; hence it is said that [defilements] gradually increase.
When discrimination does not arise and the appearances of dust are extinguished, at that time, although the faculties remain lucid, how could there be any further appearances?
This is the state where both hearing and that which is heard have together ceased. This is precisely entering through the faculty of the ear. Once entered...
Thereafter, the characteristics of the faculties completely vanish. One should know that when an ordinary person hears a sound, there are originally no characteristics of faculty or object;

it is only when they give rise to a thought and grasp at them that the faculty and object first come into being. Now, the Bodhisattva has restored them to their original state. Therefore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
Although one sees men and women, there is no characteristic of "men and women"; although one sees the five aggregates, there is no characteristic of the "five aggregates.

Even if the ear-consciousness enters its object, one immediately discriminates and then shatters that discrimination. Were this not so, delusion and karma would arise; how much more so for the ear-faculty itself?
Therefore, by not giving rise to subsequent thoughts regarding this faculty, one immediately shatters the faculty and its objects to enter the nature of hearing. This is the nature of hearing.

It is precisely the mind. Do not say it is of no use. As for those who possess the wisdom of the three contemplations of emptiness, they have all heard the principle that the preceding faculties are exhausted;

yet they do not dwell upon this as the clear elucidation of the appropriateness of empty awareness-illumination. Later, they come to know that non-arising differentiation is fundamentally devoid of awareness-illumination.

For example, when ordinary people have not yet made conceptual distinctions, what awareness or illumination exists? It is because of emptiness, the sense organs, and the sense objects that the provisional designation of "the cognizer" is established.
This is like prescribing medicine according to the illness; once the illness is gone, the medicine also perishes.

If the illness is gone but one clings to the medicine, the medicine itself becomes an illness. Therefore, when the wisdom that cognizes its object reaches this state where both [subject and object] are empty, it is the primordial source.
It returns to itself. Regarding the principle of the four truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*): the essence of the awakening to emptiness is supremely perfect;
even emptiness is emptied, just as in the previous analogy of fire and wood. Once all the fuel has been consumed, it likewise returns to its natural state.

That which is emptied refers to the aforementioned sense organs, objects, and cognition; that which performs the emptying is the principle of the truth itself. This is truly because conceptual discrimination has already ceased.

Is it because one clings to the principle of emptiness that it receives the name "extremely perfect"? It is simply that a single non-conceptual mind spontaneously possesses these fourfold meanings. Why is this?
When facing objects, if one does not cling to the objects, the characteristics of objects vanish.

When present in the sense faculties, if one does not cling to the faculties, the characteristics of the faculties vanish. How could one dwell in the illumination of wisdom and yet cling to that illumination? [This applies likewise] when dwelling in the truths...

Is it not rather that one should accord with principle and instead cling to the truth of the principles? Question: Since principle is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, what further extinction could there be?
Answer: If one speaks of "quiescent extinction," this extinction is still a form of arising. It is merely the destruction of deluded attachment, not the destruction of the principle itself.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "One does not destroy the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages; rather, because those who have not yet attained it cling to it and produce frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*), [the teaching] is therefore [presented]. Thus...
It must be broken down. As Vimalakīrti said: "One should only eliminate the illness, not the dharma.

Observing this, one can see that the Bodhisattva’s initial stage of practice must first involve breaking through the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) before one can enter the gate of emptiness.

How is it, then, that the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Lineage) insists that the *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration) must reside in the ear-faculty? Such insistence on a particular view by the *Zhengzhi lun* (Treatise on Right Wisdom) constitutes mere frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).

The attachment to purity and the grasping at illness have not been eliminated. If one attains the Great Being’s (Mahāsattva) principle of the prior extinction of sense-faculties and their objects, then perfect penetration can be cultivated and there will be a gateway for entering the Way. ○ Second, entering into the Middle Way.
When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one. Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains two kinds of extraordinary excellence:
first, above, one merges with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as all the Tathāgatas;
second, below, one merges with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing [the same nature] as all those beings.
Sharing the same compassion and yearning:
regarding "arising and ceasing," the four successive stages mentioned above involve a process of mutual arising and ceasing; the former gives rise to the latter, and the latter ceases the former.
Even the final cessation, being in opposition to arising, must itself cease. Through this, quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) manifests before one. Quiescence...

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) is the principle of the Middle Way. Changshui’s commentary states: "This gate of contemplation is precisely the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations within a single mind.

First, 'within hearing' refers to the provisional (*parikalpita*). 'The extinction of the external objects and the purification of the internal faculties' refers to the contemplative wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is the principle of the truth of cessation.
'Quiescent cessation manifests before one' up to 'transcending the two extremes' refers to the Middle. Question: If this is so, then...

If there is indeed a sequence of before and after, how can it be called "one mind"? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the passage concerning the three knowledges (*trividya*), states:

"Although [these] are attained within a single mind, there is still a sequential order of beginning, middle, and end, just as a single mind possesses the three characteristics: arising, abiding, and ceasing."

Abiding in the cessation of causes and conditions, Master Huxi said: "The object is the wondrous provisional, and contemplation is emptiness. When both object and contemplation are forgotten, this is the Middle Way.
How could there ever be a sequence between forgetting and illumination? The single mind is fused and absolute, leaving no trace whatsoever.

"Suddenly," and so forth, explains and clarifies quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). First, there is the dual negation; next, the dual illumination. "Worldly" refers to the mundane; "transcending the world" refers to the supramundane.

Truly, transcending the two extremes is none other than the Middle Way. Those who have understood it from the past have failed to realize that emptiness and the phenomenal are interfused, and thus they have lost the true meaning of the Middle Way.

"The ten directions" and below refer to the simultaneous illumination of both [aspects]. Since perfect luminosity is the essence of the Middle, one is able to simultaneously illuminate both and thereby attain these two kinds of excellence.
Although the Bodhisattva’s fundamental nature is profound and his traces are vast, he manifests here as an Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) Bodhisattva.

It can ascend to harmonize with the fundamental mind of wondrous enlightenment—this refers to the fundamentally inherent mind of wondrous enlightenment. Compassion (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness;

among the thirty-two responses below, which are not matters of bestowing happiness? Furthermore, because his station is that of a Bodhisattva, he descends to harmonize with sentient beings through a shared resonance of sorrow and yearning.
"Sorrow" (*karuṇā*) refers to compassion for suffering; "yearning" (*adhimukti*) refers to compassionate aspiration. The Great Sage is without self.
One grieves with prior concern. However, there are two meanings to this "sorrow" (*karuṇā*): when applied to sentient beings, it is the arising of sorrow due to their suffering;

when applied to Bodhisattvas, it is the arousal of sorrow for the purpose of uprooting that suffering. Furthermore, sentient beings look up in reliance upon the Bodhisattva, while Bodhisattvas look upward to appeal to the Dharmakāya;
the significance of these is identical. The fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) that follow are none other than the uprooting of suffering.
This is the matter. ○ Second, revealing the perfect penetration. 3. The thirty-two transformations. 1. General explanation.
"World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of illusory-like hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation.
Because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become [capable of] thirty..."
Second, one should enter all lands.

This first section generally clarifies the thirty-two manifestations, which accord with the "Superior Compassion" mentioned above. Since the path within emptiness must necessarily be manifested through the conventional, it is first described as being "like an illusion.

This refers to the contemplation of the ear-faculty as a conventional illusion. Regarding the phrase "perfuming by hearing and cultivating by hearing": *Note: The provided text fragment contains a structural outline regarding the thirty-two manifestations and the contemplation of the ear-faculty within the context of the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, specifically addressing the relationship between the ultimate (emptiness) and the conventional (illusion).*

Regarding this: previously it was said "hearing, contemplation, and cultivation" (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*); now "contemplation" (*cintā*) is changed to "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Contemplation seems to involve deliberate mental effort, whereas perfuming occurs spontaneously;

because the mind is sovereign in its engagement with objects, it is appropriate to make this change. The ancients said that because it is perfumed by the sound of the teachings, it is called "hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*).

Because one hears and then further cultivates it, it is called "hearing-cultivation" (*śruta-bhāvanā*). However, according to the subsequent section on the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), there is the phrase "perfuming through hearing" (*śruta-vāsanā*) which has been established.
Regarding the phrase "hearing and so forth," how can it be explained exclusively as the auditory teaching? It is because the nature of hearing perfumes the other faculties and other objects;
furthermore, by means of the nature of hearing, it perfumes the ear-consciousness and the object of sound, as well as the faculty of hearing itself.

Since all these become the nature of hearing, it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Cultivating practice based on this hearing is called "hearing-cultivation" (*śrutabhāvanā*). Although the effort proceeds from the provisional [nature of] contemplation...
The true nature manifested therein is like a vajra; this metaphor signifies that while the true nature itself is indestructible, it is capable of shattering ignorance.

The thirty-two manifestations refer to the cloud-like bodies of the dharma-realm appearing without obstruction, universally manifesting the ten dharma-bodies to perfectly respond to the capacities of all sentient beings.
Youxi said: "The two instances of the character 'to hear' (wen) refer to the object of contemplation. To permeate and cultivate..."

These two characters refer to the contemplation that is capable of observing. Regarding the term "perfuming cultivation" (*vāsanā-bhāvanā*): "perfuming" (*vāsana*) means to permeate through habituation; "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means to refine and rectify.
This dharma-gate consists of the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation, and the entirety of cultivation abiding within nature.

When the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation, one uses the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) to perfume initial enlightenment (*ādi-avabodha*). When the entirety of cultivation abides in nature, one uses initial...

Awakening to this and cultivating it is to practice within original awakening (*mūla-awakening*). Cultivating in this manner constitutes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), wherein emotions vanish and conceptual understanding is severed.
Because all fetters and delusions dissolve upon encountering it, it is called the "Vajra Samādhi of Hearing and Cultivating as Illusory.
2. A detailed enumeration of the thirty-two [manifestations]: 1. Manifesting the body of a Buddha.
“World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in their cultivation until their untainted resolute understanding becomes manifest and complete,
I shall manifest the body of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.”

At the outset, the Bodhisattva enters samādhi and advances in the cultivation of the untainted Middle Way. Because their wisdom of meditative concentration differs from that of the śrāvakas, it is called "superior understanding" (adhimukti).
When they are about to bring this to full completion, it is termed "manifest perfection. As for the manifestation of the Buddha-body:

[The Buddha] must manifest the attainment of enlightenment through the eight phases and preach the Dharma during the five periods. Question: Since it is said that "superior understanding manifests its perfection," one will surely realize self-verification;

why then is it necessary to manifest a physical body? Answer: The interaction between the response of the Buddha and the resonance of the practitioner is like the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, intended to cause them to realize [enlightenment] swiftly.
Guishan says: "This refers to the capacities of the Bodhisattvas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings. If they enter the stage of semblance *samādhi* and advance..."
When one cultivates the untainted Middle Way, the true and superior understanding manifests in its perfection.
Even further, when one advances to cultivate the adamantine untainted state, the ultimate superior understanding manifests in its perfection.

Great Beings all manifest the body of a Buddha to preach the sudden Dharma, so that others may attain true and ultimate liberation. As for why these Great Beings are able to manifest the body of a Buddha, it is because...
This is because they harmonize with the Buddhas above, sharing the same power of compassion. Second, manifesting the body of a Pratyekabuddha:

if those in training (*śaikṣa*) attain a tranquil, wondrously bright, and supremely excellent perfect manifestation, I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve liberation.
Those who appear in a world without a Buddha, who observe the transformation of phenomena and personally realize non-arising, are called Pratyekabuddhas.

The term "Rhinoceros-like" (Khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa) is as stated in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra: "The rhinoceros is characterized by solitary conduct. "Subtle" (miao) carries the meaning of the extinction of marks (animitta).
"Wondrous clarity" (*miaoming*) refers to the contemplation of emptiness. Because the principle of true emptiness is luminously self-evident, it is called "wondrous clarity.
To say it is "supreme" means that the most excellent principle of true emptiness surpasses all those in training (*śaikṣa*), as it is about to manifest before one.
○ Third, he manifests the body of a *pratyekabuddha*.
If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and for whom the excellence of that severance— the supreme, sublime, and perfected manifestation— appears,
I manifest before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma to bring about their liberation.

Both pratyekabuddhas and solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddha*) are able to attenuate habitual tendencies; the only distinction lies in whether they have seen a Buddha and received his teachings, or have not seen a Buddha and have not received his teachings.

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two gates: the gate of cyclic flow and the gate of cessation. To sever the twelve links is precisely cessation.
When the conditions are severed, the supreme nature manifests; this supreme nature is emptiness, which is called the most excellent true emptiness.

This principle surpasses that of all those in training (*śaikṣa*). Among the former *pratyekabuddhas*, it is said they possess "superior wondrousness" (*viśeṣa-adbhuta*) but not "superior nature" (*viśeṣa-dharmatā*);

among the latter *śrāvakas*, it is said they possess "superior nature" but not "superior wondrousness. This seems to imply that those who have mastered practice through cultivation are termed "wondrous," while those who have received the teachings are termed "nature.
Since the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are all the Buddha’s teachings and cannot be altered, they are called "nature."

Furthermore, the Pratyekabuddhas of the past also contemplated causes and conditions; for instance, they attained realization by observing conditions such as the falling petals of a flower or the movement of a bracelet.
However, they did not hear of the twelve links of dependent origination in their forward and reverse progression, because these characteristics of the Dharma cannot be taught except by a Buddha.

Moreover, because the faculties of a Pratyekabuddha are sharp, they do not undergo the gradual stages of fruition, and thus there is no distinction between them and those still in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is judged by the passage through three births and sixty kalpas. Fourth, manifesting in the body of a śrāvaka:

if there are those among the learners (*śaikṣa*) who have attained the emptiness of the Four Truths and, through the path of cultivation, enter cessation such that their superior nature is fully perfected, I manifest before them in the body of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.

Xunli said: "The three fruits all belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*). Because one severs the afflictions belonging to the four truths through the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and realizes the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is said that 'one attains the emptiness of the four truths. Subsequently, after the first fruit, one advances to sever the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions;

because one realizes a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*) at each grade, it is said that 'one enters cessation through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*')."
The nature of the most supreme true emptiness is about to be perfected; the Great Being manifests his body to preach the Dharma so that they may quickly realize it.
5. Manifesting the Body of a Brahma King:
If there are sentient beings who desire mental clarity and awakening, who do not transgress the dust of desire, and whose bodies are pure from desire, before them I [manifest].
He manifested in the form of Brahmā and preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
Gu Shan stated that this Brahmā King is the Lord of the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu), named Śikhin; in Chinese, this means "Crest" (Dingji).

Regarding the passage in the text where it says "desire-mind and so forth are exhausted," there are those who interpret this as referring exclusively to sexual desire, but this is not necessarily the case. It refers to the desire for the mind and the desire for the body.

"Desire" refers to the desire for sensual objects; "lustful desire" refers to the desire for sexual passion. "The mind of desire attains clear awakening" means to clearly awaken to the dharmas of the first dhyāna, such as the five factors (*pañcāṅga*), the eight contacts (*aṣṭasparśa*), and the ten merits (*daśaguṇa*).

Furthermore, it is because the Brahmā King can expound the discourse on transcending desire, and because he possesses the methods of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) as well as the faculty of speech that he becomes the lord of a thousand worlds; it is not through mere awakening to clarity [without these].
"Can one be thus? By not transgressing against the defilements of the desire realm, the faculty of the body becomes pure;
liberation is that which causes one to leave behind the dust of desire. ○ Sixth, manifesting the body of Śakra.
If there are sentient beings who desire to become lords of the heavens and exercise authority over the celestial realms,
I manifest before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve their goal.
To joyfully practice the ten wholesome deeds is to aspire to become a celestial lord. Among those heavens, there are horizontally thirty-three heavens, which Śakra governs.
"Expounding the Dharma" refers to expounding the dharma of the ten wholesome deeds. 7. Manifesting in the body of a Paranirmita-vaśavartin Deva.
If there are sentient beings who desire to travel freely throughout the ten directions with mastery over their bodies,
I manifest before them in the form of the god Īśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve this.
Īśvara is the highest heaven of the Desire Realm. In full, it is called Vaśavartin; this translates as "Mastery over Others' Transformations.
It refers to one who achieves their own pleasure by utilizing the creations of others; he is the Māra King.
Alternatively, it is said that there is a separate palace of the Māra King atop the sixth heaven, which is also subsumed under Īśvara. ○ Eighth, manifesting in the body of Maheśvara.
If there are sentient beings who desire to attain mastery over their bodies by flying through the void,
I manifest before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve this.
Gushan said: "The *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* refers to Maheśvara as the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*). This is precisely the Mahesvara of the Peak of Form (*Rūpāgra*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he is the one who has three eyes, eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk."
Ci'en identifies Īśvara as Yāma and Maheśvara as Tuṣita, Sūnirmita, and Paranirmitavaśavartin;
this is not necessarily so. ○ Ninth, manifesting in the body of a Great General of the Heavenly Realm.
If there are sentient beings who desire to govern spirits and deities to protect their lands,
I shall appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.
The above cites the orthodox tradition to clarify the ministers and assistants. In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Saṃjñeya is designated as the Great General.
The *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* states that Aṣṭabhuja-Kārttikeya is a warrior among the gods. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to Umāraga, which is translated here as "Boy" (Kumāra);
he rides a peacock, holds a cock, carries a rattle-drum, and grasps a red banner. Furthermore, there is the god Viṣṇu, which is translated here as...
Vibhūṣaṇa: four-armed, holding a conch and a wheel, riding upon a garuḍa. As these are all great generals of the devas, no one yet knows for certain what he truly is.
What prevents a bodhisattva from manifesting in various forms according to the needs of beings? 10. Manifesting as the body of a Caturmahārāja.
If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants,
I manifest before them in the form of a Four Heavenly King and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve their goal.
Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings: The Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra—translated as "Holder of the Nation"—resides on a terrace of gold and governs the gandharvas and piśācas.
The Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka—translated as "Growth"—resides on a terrace of lapis lazuli and governs the kumbhāṇḍas and pūtanas. The king has ninety-one sons. [The Western...]

In the north dwells the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (translated here as Duōmén, "Much Hearing"), who resides on a terrace of crystal and leads the piśācas, venomous nāgas, and others. Because he restrains these spirits and ghosts so that they do not harm people, he is called a Protector of the World (*lokapāla*). The *Miaoxuan* states: [The text continues: "Vaiśravaṇa is also called 'Much Hearing' because his wisdom is vast and profound;

he hears all things and possesses great renown. He is also called 'King of Wealth' because he bestows wealth upon sentient beings. Furthermore, because he protects the four quarters, he is called a 'World-Protector. Regarding the four heavenly kings, their names are derived from their respective functions:

Dhṛtarāṣṭra is called 'Holding the Realm' because he holds the realm of the asuras; Virūḍhaka is called 'Increasing Growth' because he increases the growth of the world; Virūpākṣa is called 'Broad Eyes' because his eyes are wide and far-reaching; and Vaiśravaṇa is called 'Much Hearing' because his hearing is extensive."

By observing the precept against killing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). By observing the precepts against both killing and stealing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).
○ Eleventh, manifesting as the body of a prince of the Four Great Kings:
if there are sentient beings who desire to be born in the celestial palaces to command spirits and deities, I manifest before them as one of the Four Heavenly Kings.
He manifests as the crown prince of a kingdom and preaches the Dharma for them to bring them to fulfillment.
Crown Prince, it is like a worldly prince who, when entering [the capital], oversees the state, and when departing, leads the military.
(12) He manifests as the body of a human king.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings, I manifest before them in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve their goal.
"King" (*rāja*) means "one who goes toward";
it means that all people turn toward him. Whether they rule over the four continents or are minor local lords, they are all masters of men. [This is like] a hand-mirror.
It is said that the four types of Wheel-Turning Kings—those of gold, silver, copper, and iron—rule over the four, three, two, and one continents respectively.

As for the "scattered grains" (śālī-kalāpa), they are the retribution of the medium and lower grades of the ten wholesome paths of action. Because the many minor kings are like those scattered grains, they are given this name by way of analogy.
Furthermore, it is said that "scattered grains" is like a person holding scattered grains and placing them on a tray, each occupying its own distinct position; the king is the metaphor for this.
It is the same here. When those above transform those below, there are none who do not comply; as it is said: "When one person has cause for celebration, ten million people depend upon it.
Furthermore, the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma increases the vital essence (*ojas*). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "When a king protects the Dharma, he increases three kinds of vital essence:
first, the vital essence of the earth, which means the five grains ripen in abundance; second, the vital essence of sentient beings..."

Vital essence refers to having a dignified and upright physical appearance, free from all illness and suffering. The vital essence of the three wholesome dharmas refers to cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, faith, and so forth.
○ Thirteenth, manifesting in the body of an elder.
If there are sentient beings who cherish their noble lineage and are esteemed by the world,
I manifest before them in the form of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, so that they may achieve fulfillment.

The title of "Elder" (*zhǎngzhě*) appears in both Confucian and Buddhist traditions. In India, one who possesses billions in accumulated wealth was called an *elder* (*śreṣṭhin*), yet such a person is merely wealthy;
moreover, there are those who possess wealth but lack benevolence, and thus they do not fully merit this name.

In the *Mozi*, Master Han states that one who dwells in gravity and sincerity is called an "elder," while one who treats others with frivolity and insincerity is called a "petty person. Thus, [the term]...

This refers to their virtuous reputations. In the *Shiji*, it is recorded that when the Han Gaozu enfeoffed his nephew as the Marquis of Diaogeng, he remarked, "It is only because his mother was not a person of long-standing virtue.
When Wang Ling’s mother confronted the envoy, she said, "The King of Han is a man of great virtue; you should serve him well."
Inferring from this, the rank of a Marquis can be attained through exertion, whereas the reputation of being a "Venerable" (Changzhe) is difficult to obtain by mere chance.
For while a Marquis is accorded his title by the whole world and merely served outwardly, a Venerable is accorded his substance and is truly revered in the heart.
Thus it is said that in the world, one yields to another; this is the meaning of the Confucian name as understood by the Confucians. If...

In the Buddhist scriptures, a "householder" (*gṛhapati*) possesses ten virtues: noble lineage, high status, great wealth, majestic power, profound wisdom, advanced age, pure conduct, complete etiquette, praise from those above, and the devotion of those below.
This is the original text of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. However, one must distinguish between the worldly and the world-transcending householder.
Regarding the worldly householder, as for lineage, they are descendants of the Three Kings or Five Emperors... (left blank).

Regarding his station, he was a high official with a sable fur fan tucked at his right side, serving as a counselor or prime minister—like the "salt and vinegar" or the "Arheng" who balanced the state.

Regarding his wealth, he possessed copper hills and golden valleys, overflowing with abundance and luxury. Regarding his majesty, he was like the severity of frost; though not ostentatiously strict, his presence alone commanded awe.
Regarding his wisdom, his mind was like an armory, extraordinary and transcendent. Regarding his age, he was hoary and imposing, one whom all things bowed down to. Regarding his conduct...
His integrity was as flawless as white jade, and his conduct matched his words. His ritual propriety and decorum served as a model for the world;
thus he was revered by the sovereign above and sought after by the four seas below.

As an eminent figure who has transcended the world, as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, he had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and deeply planted the roots of goodness. (Noble by lineage) He attained the patience of non-arising. (High in rank)
Possessing unimpeded eloquence and having attained all *dhāraṇīs*, he is (Greatly Wealthy). Renowned for fearlessness, he subdues all adversaries and afflictions; he is (Majestic and Fierce).

Skilled in the *prajñāpāramitā* and proficient in skillful means (*upāya*), he clearly understands the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and can further discern whether their faculties are sharp or dull;
he is (Profound in Wisdom). Having long practiced the Buddha-way, his mind is already fully matured; he is (Venerable in Years). Resolute in the Mahāyāna, he [is endowed with] all...
Whatever he does, he is able to deliberate with skill. (Purity of Conduct) Abiding in the majestic deportment of a Buddha, his mind is as vast as the ocean.

(Perfection of Reverence) Praised by all Buddhas. (Supreme Admiration) Honored by his disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the lords of the world. (Ultimate Refuge) ○ Fourteenth: Manifesting in the form of a layman.
If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terminology and dwell in self-purification,
I manifest before them in the body of a layperson and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
The layperson (*jushi*) also emerges from both Confucianism and Buddhism. For now, I shall first analyze these two characters. The *Jingyun of the Six Scripts* states:
"Of the ten characters above, 'one' is the beginning of numbers and 'ten' is the end of numbers. To cite 'ten' is to encompass exhaustively the myriad phenomena of the world;
for example, ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand, and ten thousands make ten thousand. Ten...
Ten myriads make one hundred million. Generally speaking, all the myriad phenomena of the world—those thousands and tens of thousands—are what I must know within my own domain.
As for using "one" beneath "ten," it means that everything should be unified by this single principle. Therefore, the title of "scholar" (shi) is a noble appellation.

Such as the *yanshi* (excellent scholars), *maoshi* (eminent scholars), *xiushi* (outstanding scholars), *wenshi* (literary scholars), *duoshi* (many scholars), *boshi* (learned scholars), *durenshi* (scholars of the capital), and the superior, middle, and inferior scholars;

the *gongshi* (recommended scholars) and *jinshi* (successful candidates). Because the Three Dynasties had no hereditary nobility, the sons of state (*shizi*) all initially entered the rank of *yuanshi* (junior scholar).

Since the ministers and high officials waited upon the kings and emperors, they all took the *shi* (scholar) as their foundation, just as in the sequence of painting where the details follow the outline.

It is naturally so. Thus, it has long occupied the foremost place among the four classes of society. Now, as for the character "ju" (to dwell/reside) used by scholars at the beginning [of this term], "shi" (corpse/occupant) is synonymous with "wu" (house).
That which is contained within the house is the single Truth (zhen) that all sages and ordinary people have shared throughout the ages.

It is as the saying goes: "Dwelling in the broadest dwelling under heaven. This character "ju" does not refer to a large mansion; rather, it points to the ancient sages who penetrated the Way and its Virtue.
"Benevolence and righteousness are both that which I ought to cherish within my own domain. In India, one who maintains the Way and abides in rectitude is called a *gṛhapati* (lay practitioner).
Yet, the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the *Yuzao* (Jade Adornment) section, states: 'The *jushi* wears a brocade sash. Zheng Kangcheng’s commentary explains this as 'a recluse of the Way and the arts.
Is this not precisely what is meant by the 'wide-sleeved robe' and the 'Zhangfu cap,' referring to one endowed with manifold natural talents? If it were according to the Buddhist scriptures..."
The origin [of this term]: In Sanskrit it is *kula-putra*. This refers to the layman Vimalakīrti, who is the "layman" (*gṛhapati*) mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The Supplement states: "He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory, yet he did not seek official office. He lived in great wealth, yet maintained a will of integrity and purity;
thus he was called a 'layman' (*jushi*). This is how the term is understood. Nowadays, when wealthy landowners hear themselves addressed as "layman," they immediately become indignant.

These are merely light and trivial designations used within the Buddhist community; little do they realize that these are actually titles of the utmost reverence and nobility found in Confucian texts.
Regarding the terminology: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describes them as "wind-like elegance and classical principles. ○ Fifteenth, manifesting in the body of a civil official.
If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts,
I manifest before them in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.
A state is a city. A "great" state is called a *bāng* (邦). *Bāng* means "to bestow"; it is here that those who have merit are enfeoffed. A *yì* (邑) is equivalent to a commandery (*xiàn*).

The Three Dukes, the Ministers, the Governors of the States, and the Commandery Magistrates are all titled *zhǎi guān* (宰官), or "governing officials. ○ Sixteenth, he manifests in the body of a Brahmin.
If there are sentient beings who cherish various arts and sciences for their own protection and maintenance,
I manifest before them in the body of a Brahmin and preach the Dharma to enable them to achieve success.
"Brahman" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Pure Conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*). It is one of the four castes in the Western Regions (India).

Because their lineage was naturally secluded in the mountains and fields at the beginning of the kalpa, they were named "Pure Conduct. In the Eastern Land (China), they correspond to the class of the gentry with yellow headbands, the Daoists.
During the Zhou dynasty, Li Bo-yang was born with white hair and was thus named Laozi. He authored the *Dao De Jing* in five thousand words. Zhuang Zhou... [text continues]
The *Nanhua jing* (Scripture of Southern Florescence) consists of various internal and external chapters.

During the Han dynasty, Zhang Liang (Zi-fang) received scriptures from the Yellow Stone Man (*Huangshi*) to practice grain-avoidance (*pi-gu*) in the mountain forests, thereby attaining the Way of Complete Perfection (*quan-zhen*). Later, during the Later Han, Zhang Daoling received the "Cloudy Peak" (*Yunzhong*) teachings from Laozi and became a Celestial Master (*Tianshi*).
He transcribed talismans and records to exorcise and employ ghosts and spirits on behalf of others; he was then known as the "Three Bushels" (*Sandaoli*).

The "Mizhang" (Grain-Expanding) is precisely the *fangshu* (square-script) of Zhengyi. Later, Quanzhen split into two categories: first, internal alchemy (*lian-yang*); second, elixir ingestion (*fu-shi*). Zhengyi split into two categories:
first, talismans and registers (*fu-lu*); second, ritual teachings and liturgies (*jiao-ke*).

Furthermore, there were the distinctions between the Southern School’s cultivation of nature (*xiu-xing*) and the Northern School’s cultivation of life (*xiu-ming*), as well as the Daoists of Maoshan and the Heavenly Masters of Jiangxi; these are all distinct from the Golden Elixir (*jin-dan*) practices they cultivate.
There are over a thousand heterodox schools; their methods are both numerous and their varieties manifold.

Incantations, divination, arts, and methods of cultivation are all among these heterodox techniques and numerology. To deliver such beings, the Great Being likewise manifests within them as teacher and leader.
For instance, Mārīcī was originally a manifestation of great skillful means, yet she maintained pure conduct.
For the Venerable One to manifest as the Mother of the Constellations (Doubu), there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

○ Seventeenth, manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu: if there is a man who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various precepts, I shall manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him so that he may achieve fulfillment.
One should joyfully practice the Three Vehicles to distance oneself from the prison of the household. *Śīla* is called "precept" (*jie*), and *Vinaya* is called "discipline" (*lü*).
By relying on the laws of the Vinaya, one prevents wrongdoing and ceases evil. A *bhikṣu* is here translated as "mendicant" (*qishi*):
above, he begs for the Dharma from the Buddhas to sustain his life of wisdom; below, he begs for food from donors to sustain his physical life. There are two hundred and fifty precepts.
The names and meanings are as in the first fascicle. ○ Eighteenth: Manifesting in the form of a bhikṣuṇī.

If there are women who delight in study, leave the household life, and uphold the various prohibitive precepts, I will manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
She is a *bhikṣuṇī*, a female practitioner. The text states that "female" (*ni*) is a general term for women; thus, she is a female *bhikṣu*. There are five hundred precepts for a *bhikṣuṇī*.

These include the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) and the *anuvartana* (consequent) rules, which restrain physical transgressions. Furthermore, there are eight *pārājika* (defeats) for a *bhikṣuṇī*:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are the same as the four *pārājika* precepts for a *bhikṣu*. Regarding the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and the *anuvartana*: "touching" refers to—
Male physical contact: this consists of eight factors, each possessing eight characteristics. That is to say: a man with a defiled mind takes one’s hand; takes one’s garment; enters a secluded place;
stands together in a secluded place; converses together; walks together; leans their bodies against one another; makes an appointment; and conceals the other’s sinful offenses.
According to each individual's needs, he provides robes and food for the great Saṃgha. ○ Nineteenth, manifesting in the body of an upāsaka:
if there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I manifest before him in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him so that he may achieve success.
*Upāsaka* is translated here as "male lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*). This refers to one who maintains himself by means of the five precepts and is thus capable of drawing near to ordained *bhikṣus*.
The five precepts are: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking intoxicants.
The *Upāsaka-sūtra* states that these five precepts are the great prohibitions of the world; if one violates these five...
In heaven, it violates the five stars; on earth, it violates the five sacred peaks; in the quarters, it violates the five emperors; in the person, it violates the five viscera.

Such worldly transgressions are immeasurable. If considered from the perspective of the supramundane, it destroys the fivefold Dharma-body and all Buddha-dharmas, because the five precepts are the root of the śīla (ethical discipline) of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. One should therefore delight in studying them.
To those who appear as pure men, I preach this Dharma. Twenty: appearing in the form of an upāsikā.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I manifest before her in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her so that she may achieve accomplishment.
Upāsikā means "female lay follower" (upāsikā). She likewise maintains herself by the five precepts and is capable of attending upon bhikṣuṇīs who have left the household life.
○ Twenty-first: manifests in the form of a female ruler and so forth.
If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves to cultivate their families and states, I will appear before them in the form of a female ruler,
a state lady, a titled wife, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.

The "Female Ruler" (*nüzhu*) refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven. According to the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*), the consort of the Son of Heaven established the six palaces, comprising three ladies (*furen*), nine concubines (*pin*), twenty-seven senior wives (*shifu*), and eighty-one female attendants (*nüyu*). As for the "State Lady" (*guofu*), she is the wife of a lord of the state;
when the ruler addresses her, he calls her a "lady" (*furen*). A "Lady by Appointment" (*mingfu*) refers to one who received a fief and an official decree due to the honor conferred upon her husband.
Also, "Da-jia" (Great Lady) refers to those such as Cao Shetou’s wife, who was titled Da-jia. ○ Twenty-second:
Manifesting in the form of a young boy. If there are men whose male organs remain intact, I manifest before them in the body of a young boy and preach the Dharma for them.
To cause them to achieve [this], twenty-three:
manifesting in the form of a young girl.
If there are women who delight in remaining in their bodies and do not seek to commit violence, I shall manifest before them in the form of a young girl.
I preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
Twenty-fourth, manifesting the body of a deva:
if there are devas who wish to leave their celestial rank, I manifest the body of a deva and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
While the various devas are currently enjoying their pleasures, one who is able to feel weary of such pleasure has transcended the ranks of the heavens.
Although they wish to transcend their original class, they have not yet attained a fixed station within the three vehicles.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva temporarily manifests a body of the same kind as them, for this makes it easier to guide and transform them. (25) Manifesting as a dragon body.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave the class of nāgas, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve their goal.
Although the seven [realms] described below possess supernatural powers and merit, they are all collectively termed "evil destinies" because each involves suffering and affliction;
thus, all desire to escape from them. 26. Manifesting as a yakṣa.
If there are yakṣas who wish to deliver their own kind, I manifest before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.
"Yakṣa" is translated here as "light and swift.
There are three places where they dwell: on sea islands, in the air, and in the heavens. To "deliver" also means to liberate.
...Furthermore, twenty-seventh, I manifest the body of a gandharva.
If a gandharva desires liberation from their kind, I appear before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.

Gandharva; this is translated as "Fragrance Aggregate" (xiāngyīn). In the new translations, it is rendered as "Seeking Conduct" (xúnxíng) or "Perfuming Hearing" (xūnwén); it refers to the musical deity of Śakra.
He dwells in the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru. When the devas intend to perform music, he manifests extraordinary signs.
○ Twenty-eighth, he manifests in the body of an asura.
If an asura desires to be liberated from his kind, I manifest before him in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma to bring him to accomplishment.
"Asura" is translated here as "not upright"; because the females are beautiful while the males are ugly, the name is derived from the male.
The new translation calls them "non-gods" (*asura*) because they lack the conduct of gods due to their flattery and deceit.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* names these spirits the "most excellent among the fruits of retribution," ranking them immediately below the various devas yet not being devas themselves.

Tiaoxi says that according to the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), the *garuḍa* (the golden-winged bird) is missing from this list; it is likely included within the "miscellaneous classes" mentioned in the subsequent text. II. 2.
Nineteenth, I manifest in the form of a kinnara.
If a kinnara desires liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
The *kiṃnara* resembles a human but has a horn upon its head; for this reason, it is called the "Doubtful Person.
It is a celestial deity of string and wind instruments, slightly inferior to the *gandharva*. In the new translation, it is rendered as the "Singing Deity" (*gāndharva*).
○ Thirtieth, he manifests in the body of a *mahoraga*.
If a mahoraga desires liberation from its kind, I manifest before it in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for it so that it may achieve accomplishment.

Regarding "mahoraga," Master Shi (Kumārajīva) says it means "earth-dragon" (*dìlóng*); Master Zao (Sengzhao) says it means "great python that crawls on its belly. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:
Furthermore, the temple deities of this world who accept the wine and meat offered by people all enter the bellies of pythons.

Those who destroy the precepts, are deceitful and crooked, harbor much anger, and give meager alms; who greedily crave wine and meat, whose discipline is lax, and who fall among the ghosts and spirits while full of wrath—worms enter their bodies and devour them.
They are also called *mahoragas*. Thirty-first, they manifest in human form.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans and cultivate themselves as humans, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.

The Supplement states: "Devas, nāgas, and others all say they delight in emerging from their own kind, whereas those called 'delighting in humans' and 'cultivating themselves as humans' delight in entering their class, or desire to emerge from it; in all cases, I respond accordingly. (32)
I manifest in the forms of non-human beings and the like.
Should there be non-human beings— whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception— who desire to transcend their own kind,
I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success.
Changshui said: "Those with form and the aggregate of form are like those described as 'resting, auspicious, brilliant, or refined.

Those without form and without the aggregate of form are like those described as 'empty, dispersed, dissolving, or sinking. Those with perception and four aggregates are like those described as 'gods, ghosts, spirits, or numina.
Those without perception and without the four aggregates are like those described as 'the spirit transformed into grass, trees, metal, or stone. All of the above..."
"Not a human being. Xiachuan said: "Excluding the realm of humans, the remaining five are all termed 'non-humans':

those with form in the realm of form; those without form in the formless realm; the two heavens of perception—namely, the heavens of infinite space and infinite consciousness; the heaven of non-perception; the heaven of nothingness;
and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Youxi said: "The thirty-two responsive bodies in this sutra are identical to those in the Universal Gate Chapter of the Lotus Sutra."
The teachings they expound differ. They propagate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by speaking exclusively of the Buddha-dharma;
thus its text says: "By whatever body one may be delivered, he shall preach the Dharma by means of that very body.
This sutra reveals that from the wondrous essence arises the wondrous function, manifesting in every land and teaching every dharma. Because it is universal...

If one speaks in terms of function, the application of the *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) and *Ouhoua* (Upāya) is vast. If one speaks in terms of the great essence, the foundation of the true wisdom of the *Fahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) is great.
One [text] bestows provisional means; the other reveals the reality. Their matters are not identical.
One narrates the cause; the other narrates the fruit. Yet the Way is not divergent. ○ Third, the general conclusion.

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies that enter into lands; they are all accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrousness, achieved by means of the cultivation of hearing and the permeation of hearing through samādhi.
Wenling says: "The manifestation of traces among those of the same class while the mind is severed from attachment and views is called 'wondrous purity.
Arising great spiritual efficacy based on non-acting wisdom is called 'wondrous power. Responding to conditions through non-action and non-conditioning is called 'the accomplishment of sovereignty.'"

In the first month of spring, the sun shines upon the heavens and its reflection descends upon the myriad waters. Yet, in both this [chapter] and the Universal Gate (Pumen), there are no Bodhisattvas nor bodies in the hells.
Some say this is an abbreviation of the holy word; others say that since Guanyin is already a Bodhisattva, why must he further manifest such forms?
[They argue that] the suffering in hell is so heavy that it cannot be saved. Zhiyi, relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [established the full account].
He manifests the body of a Bodhisattva-realm. Furthermore, according to the *Śāstra*, Bodhisattvas also transform the hells;
thus, the unimpeded clouds of bodies fully manifest throughout the ten realms. ○ Twenty-four kinds of fearlessness: 1. General explanation.
World-Honored One, furthermore, by means of the unconditioned, wondrous power of the Vajra Samādhi cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard,
and because I share in the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within my body and mind.
The thirty-two manifestations (*dvātriṃśad-ākāra*) and the fourteen fearlessnesses (*caturdaśa-vaiśāradya*) share both similarities and differences with those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The thirty-two manifestations pertain to the person, while the fourteen fearlessnesses pertain to the Dharma; this is their difference. The thirty-two manifestations are compassion (*maitrī*), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are pity (*karuṇā*);
this is their similarity. The thirty-two manifestations are merit (*puṇya*), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are wisdom (*prajñā*); this is their similarity. The thirty-two...
The thirty-two manifestations should be understood as being identical to the Dharma-body, while the fourteen fearlessnesses are identical to the Wish-fulfilling Gem body;
the thirty-two manifestations are identical to the medicinal tree body, while the fourteen fearlessnesses are identical to the hidden benefit;
the thirty-two manifestations are provisional, while the fourteen fearlessnesses are ultimate.
The same. The thirty-two marks of response are the traces (迹), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are the fundamental (本).

The same. The thirty-two marks of response are the conditions (緣), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are the causes (因). The same. The thirty-two marks of response are the cessation [of afflictions] (斷), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are wisdom (智).
The thirty-two marks of response manifest both simultaneously; the fourteen fearlessnesses manifest the latent resonance with the capacities of sentient beings. Next...
A separate listing of fourteen [powers]: first, attaining fearlessness through sound.
First, because I do not observe the sound by means of an observer, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions who observe its sound to immediately attain liberation.
Since the Bodhisattva’s sounds and traces have already been extinguished, why should he observe himself? Sentient beings observe sound;
because the Bodhisattva adds the wisdom of observation, it is said that he does not observe his own voice, but observes with observation.
Furthermore, the sound and voice observed by sentient beings are precisely the voice of calling upon Avalokiteśvara; sentient beings observe this voice, and the Bodhisattva likewise observes it.
Regarding "sound" (*śabda*): both the capacity [of the practitioner] and the response [of the Bodhisattva] involve observing the sound and proceeding to provide rescue.
Wu-xing remarked that the Sage has no self-interest, but only seeks to benefit all things; therefore, he applies the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara to the capacity of those who observe sounds.

Thus, one is liberated from suffering before one can even turn around. It is precisely because the Bodhisattva observes the voices of sentient beings that he received his name. Jiao-guang was not correct.
It is truly strange that Wu Xing himself provides an interpretation of these characters according to their literal orthography. ○ Second, attaining fearlessness through the faculty of the eye:
second, by reversing the process of seeing and perceiving, one enables all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.

The *Bie xing shu* (Commentary on the Separate Practice) explains that there are three kinds of fire-related perils: first, the fire of karmic retribution, which extends from the hells upward to the First Dhyāna;
second, the fire of evil karma, which pervades the Three Realms; and third, the fire of afflictions, which pervades the Three Vehicles.
Since the fire-related perils are thus established, the following cases should all be understood by analogy. Third, one attains fearlessness through the faculty of hearing.
Third is the revolving of vision and hearing. It causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned by them.

Because the six faculties function interchangeably, hearing is itself vision; hence it is called "vision-hearing. Wénlǐng says: "The four elements of the internal and external realms are constantly interacting and influencing one another.
Seeing and cognition belong to fire; hearing and listening belong to water. Therefore, when the karma of seeing interacts, the vision becomes fierce."
Fire: when the karma of seeing and hearing interact, one perceives waves. Now, knowing that seeing has revolved back [to its source], there is no karma of seeing;
observing that hearing has revolved back, there is no karma of hearing. Therefore, water and fire cannot burn or drown you. (4) Fourth, by extinguishing deluded thoughts, one attains fearlessness.
Fourth, by severing delusive thoughts so that the mind is free from killing, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts such that the ghosts cannot harm them.
When delusive thoughts arise, one calculates and harbors resentment; when delusive thoughts are severed and extinguished, one views enemies and kin with equality. How could there be any killing?

How could this be so? If sentient beings themselves forget the impulse to kill, others cannot harm them. Now, being subjected to such [harm] is identical to forgetting the impulse to kill within oneself.
Fearlessness in both past and present mostly arises from liberation from the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Only this fearlessness arises from the extinction of deluded thoughts. Fifth, fearlessness is attained through the restoration and dissolution of the six sense faculties.
Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing, the six sense organs are restored and become identical to the hearing of sound.
This can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed by weapons that sever them limb from limb to perceive those arms and spears as being like cutting through water or blowing across light;
their nature remains unmoved.
