External objects are like sounds, and the internal faculties hear them alike. When a sword cuts [the body] into segments, it is like the momentary extinction of sounds;
when one slices through water or blows across light, it is like hearing without obstruction. The *Yishu* (Commentary) states:

"As for 'the sword cutting the body into segments,' this clarifies that as the person wielding the weapon strikes once after another, each blow severs the flesh; thus, the immense power [of the blade] is made even more manifest."
Sixth, one attains fearlessness through the permeation of hearing.
Sixth, because the permeation of hearing is refined, brilliant, and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, the nature of all darkness cannot prevail.
This enables sentient beings—yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and so forth—to remain at a distance even when they are near.
Beside it, the eyes cannot see.
Regarding the "perfuming by hearing" and the "clarity of the spirit," as stated in the fourth fascicle: "The inner luminosity radiates light;
thus, the appearances of the ephemeral dust and the vessel-world of transformation shall, like ice melting in hot water, be transformed into supreme awakening upon a single thought."
When delusory phenomena do not arise, there is pure, singular brilliance. This clarity pervades the entire Dharma-realm and dispels all gloom and darkness.
Yakṣas and their like all receive this lingering influence of darkness; therefore, although they are nearby, they are unable to see.

The first four [categories] enter the realm of ghosts themselves, whereas now it is the ghosts who come to afflict humans. The yakṣas are as described before. Rākṣasas are said to be "terrible. Kumbhāṇḍas—
The *cāṇḍāla* are ghosts that cause loathing; the *piśāca* are ghosts that devour vital essence; the *pūtana* are ghosts of feverish disease.
○ Seventh, from the dissolution of sound one attains fearlessness.

"Seventh" refers to the nature of sound being perfectly dissolved, whereby seeing and hearing turn back inward, departing from all defiled delusions. This can enable sentient beings to be released from imprisonment.
It cannot be bound by shackles or fetters.
As sounds dissolve and hearing returns to its source, one thereby becomes detached from all sensory dust and delusions. Sensory burdens bind a person like shackles and fetters;
once dust and delusions have dissolved, the shackles and fetters are entirely severed. Wénlǐng says: "When the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved, there is nothing within."
Bound. If one listens so as to return [to the source], then there is nothing within to entangle them; thus, the shackles and locks fall away of their own accord.
○ Eighth, attaining fearlessness through circular hearing.

"Eighth" means that when sounds cease and hearing becomes circular, it universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths where bandits do not [harm them].
It can plunder.

The preceding text states: "The six [sense objects] act as intermediaries for thieves, who plunder the family treasures themselves. Thus, Changshui says that sound can plunder the mind and harm goodness, acting as a thief.
Because the cessation of sound results in perfect hearing, one attains the power to universally generate compassion; thus, one uses sound to dissolve it.
Therefore, bandits cannot plunder them. Furthermore, the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter) states:

"Should they encounter hostile bandits surrounding them, each brandishing a blade to inflict harm, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart. According to this verse, because the bandits' hearts have become compassionate, they do not plunder.
This means that because sounds are extinguished, there are no bandits of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Because the perfect and complete state is attained through a single hearing...

One gives rise to great compassion of the same essence. When there is no thief within one’s own mind, there is likewise no thief without. Because the power of universal compassion is generated, even when a thief appears, they give rise to a compassionate heart.

Indeed, when sound and hearing are established as two, then object and self become adversaries. Now, when sound is extinguished and hearing is perfected, there is no dependence on either internal or external.
Thus, one is able to generate the power of universal compassion, and no longer has enemies or adversaries. ○ Nine: From Detachment.
The dust attains fearlessness.
Ninth, when the hearing is perfumed and separated from the dust, it cannot be plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.

Because it follows from the eighth [consciousness], it is said that it cannot be stolen away. Since the nature of hearing is permeated by the auditory object (śabda), and even this object is already devoid of form (rūpa), how could it possibly be stolen?
However, based solely on the fact that the material substance of sentient beings' faculty of hearing cannot act as an obstruction, the object immediately becomes empty;
thus, there is also the sense of being "separated from the object. Therefore, when the eye is permeated by hearing, form cannot steal it away. [This applies to] the form of sentient beings.
The faculties are so heavy that they cannot be perfumed by hearing alone. ○ Tenth, one attains fearlessness through the pure sound.
"Tenth" refers to the pure sound where the sense-faculties are free from dust; the faculty and its object are perfectly interfused, being without opposition or counterpart.
This can cause all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to leave behind all hatred.
"Pure sound without dust" means that within the fundamental nature, the inherent sound is entirely devoid of the characteristics of dust.

As it was previously stated that "the sound is extinguished and hearing is perfect," and again that "the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved," one should know that what is now called "pure sound" refers to the fact that sound pervades the Dharma-realm;

this is the original nature of sound itself. "Roots and objects are perfectly interfused" means that both the sense organs and their objects are fundamentally identical in nature, being perfectly interfused and non-dual.

Furthermore, anger arises from the violation of one's desires and is produced in response to external objects. Since the nature of sound is pure, being neither violated nor opposed, there is no anger.
○ Eleven: From the revolving luminosity, one attains fearlessness.
Eleventh is "Dissolving Dust and Revolving Clarity. The body and mind of the dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli, transparently penetrating and unobstructed.
This enables all those with dull natures and karmic hindrances, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of delusion.

Delusion arises from being obscured by false objects and shrouded by ignorance. When the objects are dissolved, there is no longer obscuration; when the light is turned inward, there is no longer concealment.
Thus, the external world and the internal body and mind become integrated, clear, and translucent, departing from the darkness of delusion.

The obstruction of one's nature is precisely this delusion. *Adīnava* (in Chinese, *ā-dian-ka*) means "lacking a virtuous mind. Among the ten internal karmas, this [delusion] brings about destruction and extinction.

In the Dharma-body, it is precisely lust, anger, and ignorance that are most profound; therefore, by citing these three, all others are encompassed. ○ Twelfth, one attains fearlessness through the restoration of hearing.
"Twelfth" refers to the fusion of form and the restoration of hearing. Without moving from the site of enlightenment, one enters into the mundane world without destroying the world. One is able to...
Pervading the ten directions, they make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms of dust, serving as Dharma princes at the side of each Buddha.
They enable those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no sons and desire a male child to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.
Because the nature of hearing is luminous and radiant, and the substance of form is entirely empty, it is said that "the form melts away and returns to hearing.

Since the nature of hearing is fundamentally unmoving yet reaches [all things], one enters the mundane world from within the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because physical obstructions have been eliminated, although one enters the world, the world is not destroyed.
It is not by opening a door that it is considered undestroyed; rather, entering the mundane world while remaining undestroyed is what constitutes non-destruction.
The world arises from the Dharma; furthermore, being a prince of the Dharma who is capable of performing many tasks belongs to the function of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
○ Thirteen: Attaining fearlessness through the perfection of the roots.

Thirteenth: The six sense organs are perfectly penetrating and luminously illuminating without duality, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions. This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha.
It receives and upholds the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without fail.

It can cause those childless beings in the ten directions who desire daughters to give birth to daughters who are upright, possessed of merit and virtue, gentle and compliant, and endowed with a multitude of blessings.
People love and revere women who possess auspicious marks.
When the six sense-faculties are liberated, there is nothing that is not perfect penetration; thus, all six faculties attain perfect penetration.

Because they are perfectly penetrating, their luminous illumination is non-dual. This is the essence of the Dharma-body, and therefore it encompasses the realms of the ten directions. As for this luminous illumination:
It constitutes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). When it encompasses the realms (*dhātu*), it becomes the empty Tathāgata-garbha.

This belongs to realized wisdom (*jñāna*). Realized wisdom pertains to principle (*tattva*). Because principle is capable of containing and nurturing, it gives birth to the female. One should know that this is the sphere of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
therefore, it can accord with and follow the secret dharma-gate. ○ Fourteenth: Attaining fearlessness through the wondrous gate.
Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons, there are currently sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Dharma Princes dwelling in the world.
They cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings;

their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, are each different. From the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I have given rise to the wondrous...
The Ear Gate. Thereafter, my body and mind will become subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
I shall enable sentient beings to hold my name, and the merit of those who hold my name together with that of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Dharma-sons will be exactly equal and no different.
World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names. Because...
I have cultivated and attained true perfect penetration.
"Ten billion suns and moons" refers to one thousand times ten million. Cultivating the Dharma is for one's own practice; establishing a model is for transforming others.
To speak of the skillful wisdom that accords with sentient beings belongs to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). That each is distinct is...

Their provisional and ultimate wisdoms differ. This [refers to the fact that] while [Avalokiteśvara] and the other Bodhisattvas are identical in their ultimate reality (*tattva*), they differ in their provisional manifestations (*upāya*).

Because the provisional applications of the various Bodhisattvas are partial, only Avalokiteśvara is perfect in both essence and function, surpassing all other Bodhisattvas. This passage cites what is compared; from the words "by me" (*yī wǒ*) onwards, it cites that which performs the comparison.
That is, the *Zhong* (Middle) [text] says: "The body and mind are subtle and wondrous, containing and encompassing all," as previously stated regarding the "perfection of the six sense faculties."

The term "pervasive" encompasses the realms of the ten directions. Furthermore, the mention of "body and mind" includes the eighteen *dhātus*, thereby fully subsuming the twenty-four kinds of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Thus, the phrase "pervading the dharma-realm" should include the seven elements (*dharma*).

This will be formally compared below. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "Those of the Perfect [Vehicle] are singular; those of the Partial [Vehicle] are many. This compares the sixty-two [views].

"Yi" (億) refers specifically to bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the *Bie xing shu* (Commentary on the Separate Practice) states: "The nature of one and many cannot be apprehended; there are no two characteristics.

They equally enter the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Since the reality-limit is perfectly equal, there is therefore no difference. The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) says: "Because they have ultimately and definitively realized the Dharma.
Here, "Dharma" refers to the Dharma-nature, True Suchness, and the Dharma-body. Therefore, [the number is] six hundred and twenty billion.

It is no different from [the perspective of] Avalokiteśvara. Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the circulating version of the scripture, Zhizhe’s two commentaries (*Shu*) clarify the meanings of the "two subtleties" (the relative and the absolute) through their mutual manifestation.
In those texts, the "equal" aspect corresponds to the meaning of the relative (dai-dai), while the "actual reality" (jissai) corresponds to the meaning of the absolute (zettai).
Furthermore, the original treatise explains "equality" by means of the dharma-nature; now, this scripture serves as...

Regarding the various sages, the text explains the fundamental roots of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong ben-gen*) and compares their relative merits. Thus, the meanings of the two sutras are not entirely identical.
If one were to unilaterally use this as a precedent for that, it would show not only that Master Zhiyi has not fully understood, but also that Vasubandhu’s insight remains obscure.

Alternatively, when the substance [of phenomena] is seen as conventional and the truth is realized, both are partially included within the Treasury of Emptiness; this is what the Bodhisattvas realize.

Alternatively, when the conventional is transcended to reveal the Middle Way, or when the conventional itself is revealed as the Middle Way, both are entirely included within the Treasury of Emptiness. Now, by means of the nature of the Treasury, these are harmonized so that they are entirely undifferentiated;
this is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* opening the gate of expedient means to reveal the true aspect, thereby definitively resolving the status of the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path, by what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
Each world must have that which is appropriate to it; where, then, lies what is appropriate for this world? It is the cause of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
It is the fruit of the unsurpassed Way. By what means of skillful entry (*upāya-mukha*) can cause and effect be made easily accomplished?
The faculty from which one proceeds is called "skillful means" (*upāya*). As stated in the second section on the "Definitive Meaning" in the first four fascicles:

"If one attains [a path] that follows a non-perfect penetration, it will be accompanied by imperfect faculties for days and kalpas; even up to this point in the text, the perfect penetration has not yet been singled out."
This is the fundamental root. Now, desiring to point out the gateway to the magnificent mansion, Mañjuśrī was commanded to select [the disciples].

Furthermore, the preceding text states that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, practicing within each of the eighteen realms, all attain the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi, with no distinction of superiority or inferiority;
therefore, the Buddha did not select them himself. From those below the Buddha level downward, every selection is invariably restricted by their individual faculties.
Thus, the selection of the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong) is the task of the Bodhisattva as a causal practitioner. Is it not therefore appropriate that Mañjuśrī should respond to this command?
○ Second, receiving the command to select and discern; first, describing the respectful demeanor.

II. The Second Part: The Actual Exposition of the Verses, which has two sections. First, a general clarification of the principle realized. This further has two parts. First, the arising of delusion from the truth:

"The nature of the ocean of enlightenment is limpid and perfect; its limpid perfection makes enlightenment fundamentally wondrous. Fundamental clarity shines forth, giving rise to objects; once objects are established, the nature of illumination perishes."
From delusion, empty space arises; based on space, worlds are established. When thought becomes clarified, it forms the land; when awareness awakens, it becomes sentient beings.
If you wish to select the most perfect means of penetration (*yuan-tong*), first examine the origin and trace back to the end, so as to clarify the great path of delusion and enlightenment.

The "awareness" in "the ocean of awareness" is precisely the "nature-awareness" and "fundamental awareness" mentioned in the fourth fascicle. The character for "ocean" may also be understood metaphorically. It is also...
One may follow the Dharma. The essence of awakening is boundless and is therefore called the "ocean. This is the nature-body (*dharmatā-kāya*).

As for the description of it as "clear and perfect" (*chengyuan*), some might claim it is identical to the "wondrously luminous original awakening" (*benjue miaoming*) or the "originally awakened luminous wondrousness" (*mingmiao*). This is not necessarily so. The character *ming* (luminous) appears freely in the subsequent text;

how could one forcibly pair it with the character *yuan* (perfect)? If one were to take the character *cheng* (clear) to correspond to "wondrous" (*miao*), then [the term] would simply be "original wondrousness" (*yuanyao*).
How can one explain this subtlety? "Clarity" (*ting*) refers to clarity and stillness; "perfection" (*yuan*) refers to being complete and full.

The character for "awakening" (*jue*) constitutes the basis for sentient beings below; the character for "clarity" (*ting*) constitutes the basis for the land below. While the subsequent text is entirely delusion, this section is entirely truth.
Within the nature, the virtue of clarity and stillness inherently contains both the fundamental (the mind) and the dependent (the environment). Thus, the primary and the secondary are not...

The second character is called "yuan" (round/perfect). In the next phrase, the three characters "yuan-cheng-jué" (perfectly clear awakening) still refer to the unity of the *shèngyīn* (the primary, i.e., the Buddha) and the *zhèngyīn* (the secondary, i.e., the environment).

"Yuánmiào" (originally wondrous) means that it is wondrous because it is originally without marks (*xiàng*). Next, it says "yuánmíng zhàoshēng suǒ" (originally bright, its illumination gives rise to the objective realm);

only at this point does the character "míng" (bright) come into use. This is because among the Three Truths, there is one truth capable of giving rise to all phenomena—the conventional truth (*sāṃvṛti-satya*).

This refers to the Truths (*satya*). Within the wondrously luminous nature of awareness (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*), there is a single character capable of giving rise to all dharmas; this character is "Ming" (明).
If one takes the first two phrases as the True Middle Two Truths, it would likewise be acceptable to take the present primordial luminosity as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

It is not that the former lacks the conventional; rather, by combining the conventional with the [Middle] Truth, it becomes the True-Middle. Primordial luminosity is precisely the True-Middle combined with the Truth.

In the midst of this, it becomes the mundane world. "Illumination must have that which is illuminated, and illumination must give rise to an object" means that based on illumination, an object is established.

"The nature of illumination vanishes" refers to how, from the clarity of awareness, obscurity is produced. "Deluded ignorance gives rise to empty space" merely explains that the nature of illuminating awareness has vanished.
Within the darkness of empty obscurity, the darkness coagulates into form, thereby forming the world; first, it is formed.
The insentient realm first comes into being, followed by the sentient beings who inhabit it. Regarding "the clarity of thought":
within deluded thoughts there is a substance of clarity and stillness; this is because the clarity of the ocean of perfect awakening manifests as the clarity of deluded thoughts.

Knowing and perceiving are the primary retribution, yet they are entirely the substance of perfect awakening manifesting as knowing and perceiving. Mañjuśrī cites the text from the fourth fascicle in all cases.
The substance of the Three Truths is established; this is the source from which the seven elements and eighteen realms arise. Second, returning to the truth by reversing delusion:
emptiness arises within great awakening like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; the minute dust-motes of all conditioned worlds are born entirely dependent upon emptiness.
"When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences.
Youxi said: "The preceding passage relied on the fourth fascicle to explain how delusion arises from the True [Suchness]. Now, this one line and a half explains the return from delusion to the True.
This is because when sentient beings have not yet seen the Way, they are not only deluded regarding the fundamental emptiness of the myriad dharmas, but furthermore..."
Furthermore, one claims that the object is large while the self is small; these two delusions arise through mutual dependence.
It is solely because of a failure to realize that all phenomena are fundamentally empty that there is heaven, there is earth, and there is the dependent and the primary.

Once fallen into the realm of existence, one claims that the support is large while the primary is small, or that the body is large while the mind is small—this is what is meant by "one delusion becomes the mind, and one is definitively deluded into regarding it as a physical body."

This is what is within. One who is able to see the Way realizes that the nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; that this limpid and perfect awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous.
From great awakening, empty space arises; depending upon empty space, the great earth is established; and depending upon the great earth, sentient beings are falsely established.
This is what is meant by not knowing that everything from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all...

These are objects within the wondrous, luminous, true mind. It is like discarding a clear ocean hundreds of thousands of miles wide and instead recognizing only the substance of a single bubble, taking that bubble to be the entire tide and exhausting the vastness of the sea. Therefore it is said:

"Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The minute, mundane lands of the conditioned world all arise dependent upon emptiness. Herein, for now, [this] is refuted.

The objects are vast and the self is small. This is as if all phenomena were shattered; this also applies to the following two lines. "When the bubble is extinguished, emptiness itself is originally non-existent, let alone the various realms of the three existences.
As the preceding text states: "Now, if your sense faculties are completely uprooted, their inner clarity will emit light.
Thus, the appearances of these ephemeral dust-like objects and the vessel-world of the physical universe, along with all their transformations, will vanish like ice melting in boiling water."

The ice, by virtue of his thought, transforms into unsurpassed enlightened awareness. As the later text says: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions all vanish;
how much more so the lands existing within that void? The extinction of the bubble is precisely the cultivation of the Way;

the extinction of the bubble is the formal expression of realizing the fruit. These two phrases directly refute the existence of phenomena (*bhāva*); once existence is refuted, the myriad [phenomena]...
The essence of the Dharma is emptiness. When the essence is empty, the calculations of "great" and "small" vanish;
there remains only the nature of the fundamental source, the precious awakened true mind. II. Specifically Revealing the Gate of Entry A. General Summary of the Intent

The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; yet there are many gates to the skillful means. The sagely nature is all-pervasive and unobstructed; whether following the natural order or acting in reverse, both are skillful means.
For those at the initial stage entering samādhi, their progress in speed varies and cannot be compared.
The preceding section has concluded the general exposition on delusion and enlightenment. Below follows the formal selection of the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).

These twenty-five gates are called "many gates" because the Buddha accords with the latent capacities (*kuśala-mūla*) of beings according to their inclinations and joys; thus, the Sage’s nature is such that there is nothing he does not penetrate.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attained perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi by practicing within each and every one of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, this sacred nature is all-pervasive. As stated previously at the beginning of the third fascicle, the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are all taught by the Buddha as this all-pervasive sacred nature.
Regarding the statement that "both following and reversing are expedient means":
the faculty of hearing follows the capacities of those in this land, while the various other faculties reverse those capacities. (2)

A further detailed analysis distinguishes two points: first, to distinguish all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from [the state of liberation]; second, to reveal that Avalokiteśvara is [the one who attained it]. Regarding the first, there are four sections;
the first of these distinguishes the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Within this, the first distinguishes the sense object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*).

The conceptualization of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) binds and forms the sense object; its essence is not clearly penetrating. Since it is not clearly penetrating, how could one attain perfect penetration through it?

Upāliṣada, by contemplating impurity, white bones, subtle particles, the sense organs, form, clarity, and emptiness, the coarse color of the particles has vanished, and a wondrous color has become subtle and pervasive.
Now this text clarifies: form is formed from deluded thoughts into various particles.
Because the substance of these particles is coarse and congealed, its nature of refined clarity and discernment cannot penetrate through. How can one [rely] upon this?
Is it by taking sound as the means of perfect penetration? Second, [the Buddha] excludes the object of sound:
"Sounds are mixed with speech; they consist only of phonemes, phrases, and meanings. Since one does not contain all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?"
When Cunda realized the Four Noble Truths, his wondrous voice was subtle and perfect. Jian states that "sound" (*śabda*) refers to direct sound, while "language" (*vāc*) refers to indirect sound;
therefore, they are called "mixed. Regarding "names, phrases, and so forth": names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases (*pada*) express distinctions (*viśeṣa*);
and syllables (*vyañjana*), which are the characters, serve as the basis for these two. For example, the name "eye" expresses its own intrinsic nature. If one says...
The Buddha-eye and the Heaven-eye are manifest phrases that distinguish [the senses]; "flavor" refers to the literal text.
Regarding the question, "If one is not all, how can one attain perfect penetration?"—it means that if one were not identical with all, it could not be called perfect penetration;
yet it is not fixedly "one" such that it cannot contain all. ○ Third, the exclusion of the sense-object of fragrance.
Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it is fundamentally non-existent. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The youth Incense Reverence entered the path by means of fragrance. He observed that its coming had no source and its going reached no destination:

as the coarse scent suddenly vanished, the subtle fragrance became subtly pervasive and perfect. Now this selection states: the phenomenon of fragrance exists when in contact and is absent when separated.
Since it is not its constant nature, it does not constitute a perfect contemplation. 4. Distinguishing the object of taste:
The nature of taste is not fundamental; it exists only when there is tasting. Since that perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, having once tasted various flavors, realized that the nature of flavor is non-arising; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor is it separate from the body and mind.

Through this awakening to the luminosity of flavor, they ascended to the stage of Bodhisattva. Now it is said that the nature of flavor is fundamentally non-existent, and it is only in dependence upon the sense organ that it is perceived.
Because it lacks both root and flavor, it is not the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). "The time of flavor" refers to the time of tasting. 5.

Distinguishing the sense-field of touch (*spraṣṭavya*): Touch is defined by that which is touched; yet, since there is nothing it does not touch, its nature is indeterminate regarding union and separation. How, then, could it attain perfect penetration?
Bhadrapāla suddenly awakened to the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body;
in the interval between these, he attained a state of tranquil non-existence. Through this, the wondrous touch was proclaimed and clarified, whereby he realized the fruit.

Now, it is said that this touch must depend upon the meeting of the object of touch with the body for the characteristic of touch to become manifest. Because its nature is not fixed or constant, it does not [persist].
Perfect Penetration. ○ Sixth, the elimination of mental objects (*dharmas*).

Mental objects are called "internal objects" because they depend upon [the senses] as their basis; since there must be an object for that which depends on it, and since subject and object do not universally pervade all things, how could one attain perfect penetration?
Kāśyapa enters through the dharma-objects (*dharmadhātu*). That which is not grasped by the five sense organs is termed "internal objects. Master Jing said:
"The dharma-objects are the objective conditions (*ālambana*), and the mind is the subjective condition (*ālambaka*).

However, because the mind does not engage in simultaneous deliberation—for instance, when it takes up wholesome mental factors, it cannot simultaneously take up unwholesome ones—it is therefore said that it does not universally pervade [all objects]. 2. Distinguishing the Five Sense Organs into Five Parts: 1. Distinguishing.
Regarding the faculty of the eye:
although its nature of seeing is clear and penetrating, it is bright before one but not behind; the four quarters are deficient by half.

How, then, can it attain perfect penetration? By rotating the vision and tracing back to the source, Śrotāpanna (Lutuo) realized and attained this. Yet, while the front is entirely bright, the rear is entirely dark.

Those observing from the left and right were two-thirds [of the assembly]; therefore, he selected them. One must know that those selected by Mañjuśrī were all at the stage of beginners (*ādikarmika*).
If one has attained even a small measure of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one will penetrate through the ten directions—how much more so for one of noble nature?

Next, this [auditory faculty] is precisely what corresponds to the organ of hearing. This is because Avalokiteśvara presented his understanding later, yet it was precisely this [faculty] that Mañjuśrī chose.
It remains behind. ○ Second, the nose faculty is examined:
"The inhalation and exhalation of the breath manifest before one, yet they are not a continuous, intersecting flow. Being fragmented and not interpenetrating, how can it attain perfect penetration?"

Changshui said: "Cūḍapanthaka, because he was taught to count the breaths until the subtle [processes] of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing were fully exhausted, and because he reversed the breath to follow emptiness, he thereby attained the Way.
Now it is said that although the nasal breath passes through both inhalation and exhalation, each is restricted to its own course and they do not intersect;
since the parts are thus separated, how can this constitute a complete contemplation? 3. Distinguishing the Tongue Faculty.

The tongue is not a sense-base (*āyatana*) because it lacks an independent cause; it gives rise to cognition only through taste. When taste ceases, cognition has nothing to exist upon—how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?

The tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is that upon which consciousness relies, and is thus called the "tongue-base. To make the phrasing flow better, the text reverses the order and says, "the tongue is not a base," and so forth.
However, when Āṭavika contemplates the cognition of taste as being neither the substance nor the object, he is performing a process of analytical exclusion relative to the object;
thus it is said, "When taste perishes, there is nothing at all. (0) Fourth, the exclusion of the body-faculty.
The body and its objects of touch are each distinct from Perfect Enlightenment; since their boundaries do not merge, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Piṅgala-bhāradvāja had his foot wounded by a poisonous thorn and experienced the sensation of pain. His awareness was pure, such that there was no pain within the awareness, yet the awareness of pain remained.

Through this pure awareness that transcended the body, he attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*). "Distinguishing" means taking the body as the subject that touches and the sensory object as the field of touch.

Regarding what is touched: objects in themselves do not touch; it is because of the body that there is touching. The body alone does not touch; it is because of external objects that there is touching. Therefore, they are said to be the same.
However, while there is awareness when there is contact, there is no such knowledge when separated. "Separately" means being apart.

The initial mind abiding in its objects is *jue* (awakening); the subtle mind making distinctions is *guan* (contemplation). Since these are absent when one is detached from the center, how could there be perfect *jue-guan*?
"Limit" (*yilang*) refers to a boundary. Building upon the previous point that not knowing [the center] constitutes detachment, this inability to achieve profound union is further explained:
moreover, "perfect" (*yuan*) means perfect fusion; to know that the body is itself touch and to know that touch is itself the body—this may be called perfect *jue-guan*.
However, when combined they are circular, but when separated they are not; therefore, it is said that each is not the contemplation of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Furthermore, the boundaries of the body and touch communicate when manifest, but do not communicate when latent; therefore, they do not meet in latency.
○ Fifth, the exclusion of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).

The faculty of cognition is chaotic and confused; though thought may be profound and clear, ultimately there is no vision. Since one cannot escape from conceptualization and recollection, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Śūnyatā-born attained unimpeded mind after vast eons. Thus, even unto the ten directions becoming empty space, the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, and one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of space.
Now, to briefly explain the meaning: the faculty of cognition is always chaotic and confused in its thoughts.

This would cause the nature of profound clarity to ultimately remain unseen. Since perfect penetration is fundamentally free from deliberation and discrimination, how could it be attained if one is not liberated from conceptual thought?
3. Distinguishing the Six Consciousnesses into Six Parts: A. Distinguishing the Eye-Consciousness.

Consciousness and vision are a mixture of the three harmonies; in the original text they are called "non-characteristics. Since their own substance does not exist beforehand, how can they attain perfect penetration?
Śāriputra’s mental vision was pure; by encountering the Buddha, his vision-awakening became bright and perfect. The *Jianzhong* states that "consciousness-vision" refers to the eye-consciousness.
The treatise says that consciousness arises from the union of two, yet here it is said to be the union of three; this is because the subject and object are combined.

This is merely a provisional explanation. Since that which arises from causes and conditions lacks a fixed characteristic, the subsequent phrase states that "its own essence was originally without fixity.
If it were as the lower [level] suggests—that the ear-faculty is perfect, pervasive, and always truly a fixed and determined phenomenon—how could it be without fixity?
2. Distinguishing the Ear-Consciousness:
"The mind-hearing pervades the ten directions and gives rise to the power of great causes. How can one who, at the initial stage of the mind, cannot yet enter [this state] obtain perfect penetration?
Only by hearing with the mind and not listening through the sense organ does this become the realm of the Great Being Samantabhadra. This is achieved through the cultivation of the Dharma."
Born from the great causes of realms and activities, a beginner, even if they cultivate the ear-consciousness, will certainly be unable to hear with the mind and penetrate the ten directions.
If one penetrates the ten directions, it is called perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*); if one does not penetrate the ten directions, it is not perfect penetration.
Viewed from this perspective, it can be seen that what has been selected refers to the expedient means for a beginner’s entry.
Why then should one insist that this is the ultimate reality? 3. Distinguishing the Nose Consciousness:

The mental activity of the nose is fundamentally a provisional means intended only to cause the mind to abide. Once it has achieved such abiding, how can the mind’s dwelling itself be used to attain perfect penetration?
"Skillful means" (quanji) refers to employing these appropriate expedients. Because Sunda's mind was largely distracted, he was taught to contemplate the tip of the nose to collect his mind.
Once the mind had become settled, the breath became the locus where the mind dwells; yet, in its true essence, there is no dwelling.
Where there is dwelling, it is not [the truth]. 4. Distinguishing the Tongue-Consciousness.
Regarding the statement, "By employing sounds and characters in preaching the Dharma, one who was previously accomplished attained awakening":
names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*); how, then, could they constitute perfect penetration? "Sound" refers to vocal sound; "characters" refers to names, phrases, and syllables.

Since Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra has possessed unimpeded eloquence throughout kalpas of antiquity, has he not already achieved accomplishment? Now, by being made to turn the wheel once more, he immediately attained awakening. However, the Dharma is detached from...
Because they consist of written characters, names and phrases are not untainted (*anāsrava*); furthermore, they are not suitable for the initial stage of the path, and are therefore excluded.
5. Excluding the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*):

Upholding and violating the precepts merely constrain the body; that which is not the body cannot be constrained. Since it does not originally pervade all things, how could it attain perfect penetration?

The discernment between upholding and violating the precepts merely constrains the body. Although the observance of the precepts employs the consciousness of the body, that which is actually constrained is the physical body with form.
If it were devoid of form and appearance, how could it be constrained? Since the body is a phenomenon possessing form, it cannot pervade all things;
how, then, can it be universally penetrating? ○ Sixth, the exclusion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Supernatural powers are fundamentally rooted in past causes; how could they have anything to do with the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness depends upon conditions and is not separate from objects, how could one attain perfect penetration through it?

Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers were obtained through the habitual practice of his former lives. Although it is said that by turning back the turbidity of the mind, the light of the heart was manifested, this was not unrelated to the discrimination of dharmas as it appeared.
However, the supernatural powers of the Hīnayāna are all produced through intentional effort; they exist only when there is an object to serve as a condition.
If separated from objects, it does not exist; the discernment of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is what constitutes the mental consciousness. 4. Distinguishing the Seven Great Elements:
First, distinguishing the element of earth.

If one contemplates the nature of earth as solidity and obstruction rather than as pervasive penetration, it is conditioned and not the nature of the sages; how then could one attain perfect penetration?
Regarding the contemplation of the nature of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), this refers to contemplating the nature of earth; the same applies to the subsequent passages.

Since maintaining the earth and leveling it still involve conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and are not the true nature of the sages, the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle) states that "arising, abiding, and ceasing are the three marks of the conditioned.
This likely indicates that the nature of earth is itself conditioned. How could this not be the practice of maintaining the earth? 2. Distinguishing the Water Element (*ab-dhātu*).

If one contemplates through the nature of water, then mental conceptions are not real. Since suchness is beyond both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), how could one attain perfect penetration?
When the youth Candraprabha entered samādhi and became water, that was produced by mental conception; within dhyāna, there are still vitarka and vicāra.
The principle of suchness is beyond both vitarka and vicāra. Third, distinguishing the fire element:

if one contemplates the nature of fire, one will grow weary of existence and fail to leave it behind as unreal. Since this is not the expedient means for a beginner, how could one thereby attain perfect penetration?
The practice of Ucchuṣma’s contemplation of fire is not true liberation; furthermore, how could one expect a beginner to be able to fully cultivate the fire-samādhi?
Therefore, it must be distinguished [from the true path]. ○ Fourth, distinguishing wind and fire.
If one contemplates the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without their opposites. If there is opposition, how can one attain the supreme enlightenment?
By contemplating the nature of wind, Vairocana-prabha perceived the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the East; this is the relative opposition of movement and stillness.
5. Distinguishing from the Great Element of Space:
If one contemplates space through its nature as emptiness, it is found to be dull and insentient, not originally awakened. Since there is no awakening, how could one attain perfect penetration?

Darkness and obscurity constitute space; thus, it is dull and insentient. To be deluded regarding space is ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, it is not originally awakened. 6. Distinguishing from... [text truncated]
The Great Element of Consciousness:

If one observes the nature of consciousness with the faculty of observation, one sees that consciousness is not permanent. To fix the mind upon it is merely a false fabrication; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

Maitreya cultivates the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), yet the consciousness he observes shifts and passes away from moment to moment; therefore, it is not permanent. Furthermore...
To say that having a conscious mind is itself "preserving the mind" is like saying: if one uses consciousness to distinguish the mind from emptiness, is this not preserving the mind?
7. Distinguishing the Sense Organs (Roots).

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now differ in their responses—how can one attain perfect penetration?

Of the six gates mentioned previously, each possesses a method of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Only the practice of Avalokiteśvara’s mindfulness of the Buddha does not rely on such expedient means, and therefore contemplation is not explicitly mentioned.

First, it is generally clarified that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent. Next, it is clarified that mindfulness itself is also a conditioned phenomenon and thus is not apart from arising and ceasing;
arising and ceasing are themselves impermanence. This single gate alone [clarifies] the cause of arising and ceasing.
Thus, they attain the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction. The fruit they realize differs from its cause;

by means of the power of others (*parāśraya*), they enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because the cause does not encompass the fruit, it is not perfect; because the cause does not penetrate the fruit, it is not pervasive. Wuxing said:
"The above twenty-four sages all attained their respective roots of perfect penetration, yet these were not the appropriate ones for this land."
The faculties (*indriya*) are what is being distinguished. One must understand that this distinction of the sages is entirely a distinction of their spiritual capacities (*mārga*).

How could Mañjuśrī possess a mind of pride, or how could the various sages possess a sense of shame? To say, as the ancients did, "How can one not sigh deeply at these [beings] who have their foreheads marked at the Dragon Gate?
is truly base. II. Revealing the Avalokiteśvara Section, divided into six parts: I. Clarifying the Expedient Means.
I now address the World-Honored One: when a Buddha appears in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this direction is purity found within sound and hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through the midst of hearing.

The sentient beings of this land possess particularly keen faculties for hearing; moreover, the Buddha takes sound as the essence of his teaching, which is most pure and perfectly suited to the spiritual capacities of those here.
Therefore, if one wishes to attain samādhi, it must necessarily enter through the faculty of hearing.
Sound is the object that is heard; hearing is the faculty that hears. By citing the object to reveal the faculty, the nature of hearing is directly demonstrated;

thus it is said, "If you wish to grasp [it]," and so forth. From the second section on the "Definitive Meaning" down to this sentence, the fundamental root of perfect penetration is clearly pointed out.
There are no words more earnest or more diligent than these. *Samādhi*.
This is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*). The provisional, which is identical to the meaning of emptiness, encompasses the three contemplations. Second, praising Avalokiteśvara:
"How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Having attained liberation from suffering, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he has entered buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust."

Attaining the power of great mastery, he bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings. With wondrous sounds, Avalokiteśvara, with Brahma-sounds and ocean-tide sounds, he brings peace and security to all in the world;
transcending the world, he attains eternal abiding.
"Free from suffering" means being free from the two types of birth and death: the suffering of *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative).

Entering the stream [of the path] first causes one to lose the objective realm; subsequently, one attains the liberation of emptiness. Suddenly transcending these, one attains the middle liberation. "Excellent" (*liang*) means good.

"Sands of the Ganges eons" clarifies that the time spent benefiting sentient beings since attaining the Way has been long. Entering Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, one extols the thirty-two marks.

"Should" (*yìng*) refers to the attainment of mastery; this praises the four inconceivable powers. "Fearless phrases" (*wúwèi jù*) praise the fourteen fearlessnesses. From "sublime voice" (*miàoyīn*) downward, the names are praised in terms of the three truths.
Both the characters "voice" (*yīn*) and "sound" (*sēng*) are objects of contemplation; because they are contemplated by the three wisdoms, the sounds constitute three spheres of activity.
The simultaneous negation of emptiness and existence is the "sublime voice. Avalokiteśvara’s responding to and rescuing [beings] is the sublime conventional truth. This is the Brahma-sound.
The purity of sound extols emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The ocean tide serves as a general metaphor for the three sounds responding without fail to reliance.

Saving the world and bringing peace means benefiting others throughout the trichiliocosm by responding to sentient beings. Transcending the world and abiding eternally means that one’s own practice dwells solely within emptiness.
Furthermore, the three truths save the world so that all obtain peace; the three truths transcend the world such that they are always eternal. This is because...
To cause sentient beings to first obtain worldly happiness and later attain eternal bliss. III. Manifesting Perfect Penetration: 1.
The Reality of Perfect Penetration.
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has described it: For example, when a person is dwelling in stillness, drums are struck simultaneously from all ten directions.
Hearing from ten directions at once—this is the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*).
The ancients said that "the ten directions" refers to the ten realms. "Beating the drum" signifies the movement of the faculty; "hearing at once" signifies the non-missing of the response.
Master Jiaoguang directly explained this in terms of the nature of hearing manifest before ordinary beings; this has application for ordinary people.
One does not personally encounter the sages. However, this passage uses ordinary people to verify the sages, which is why it says, "as Avalokiteśvara has taught," and further states, "for example.
This means that it is not only Avalokiteśvara who should be present throughout the ten directions; even among ordinary people, one may verify [the teaching] by hearing his voice.
II. The Universal Reality.
The eye does not perceive what is beyond obstructions; the mouth and nose are likewise so. The body knows only through contact; the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and disordered.
Hearing sounds across a wall, one can perceive them both near and far. That which the five sense organs do not uniformly grasp is the penetration of ultimate reality.
The eye does not perceive what is obstructed beyond its range; it cannot see external objects through paper, nor can it see the five viscera through the skin.
The mouth and nose are likewise: if there is any obstruction, they cannot perceive anything at all. Only the ear can hear through walls;

it not only hears what is near but can also hear what is far away. For instance, when the Bronze Mountain collapses in the west, the numinous bell responds in the east—how, then, could there be any limit to what is heard?
Question: "This is the faculty (indriya); why do you say it is the true reality? Answer: "The faculty is composed of the four great elements; how could it hear sound?
Since it is able to hear sound, it is entirely the nature of hearing and must not depend upon the four great elements.
Although this nature is real, it manifests by relying on the faculty; therefore it is said that 'it is real, yet not real,' for fear of delusion. Wuxing says: "This clarifies the Perfect [Teaching]."
The "pervasive" (*tong*) is merely used as a provisional designation to demonstrate that the nature of hearing differs from the five sense organs.

Regarding the phrase "perfectly real" (*yuan zhenshi*) in the middle [section], it means that the reality is perfect; regarding the "pervasively real" (*tong zhenshi*), it means that the reality is pervasive.
○ Third, the "eternally real" (*chang zhenshi*).
The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it may be present or absent. When there is no sound, one calls it "no-hearing," yet this is not a true absence of hearing.
Since sound is non-existent, there is no cessation; since sound is existent, there is no arising. When both arising and ceasing are perfectly transcended, this is the eternal reality.

Even if one is in a dream, it is not because of non-thinking that [the nature] is absent; it is because discernment (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) give rise to discursive thought (*saṃkalpa*) that the body and mind cannot reach it.
To demonstrate this permanence, the text first cites the striking of a bell as a test for constancy: when there is movement, there is sound within hearing;

when there is stillness, there is no sound within hearing. This is exactly as stated previously: sound itself undergoes arising and ceasing within the faculty of hearing. The absence of sound is termed "non-existence."
When the sound is heard as before, once the bell has ceased and there is no sound, Ānanda and the great assembly all say, "We do not hear it.

If, as previously stated, there were truly no hearing and the nature of hearing had already perished, then when the bell is struck again, how could you know of it? Therefore, it is now said that it is not the case that there is truly no hearing-nature.
This first line clarifies the departure from the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); the next line correctly elucidates eternal abiding (*nityatā*).
The text proceeds from the non-extinction [of hearing] to reveal the non-arising [of sound].

This means that not only is the nature of hearing unextinguished when one hears a sound, but even when a sound exists, hearing itself does not arise. Therefore, Ānanda’s previous answer—that sound is what is heard—was a total error.
Now, if sound is unextinguished when it is absent and does not arise when it is present, then not only was his answer regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) mistaken, but his answer...

To claim that it exists would likewise result in error. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Whether this auditory object (śabda-dhātu) is absent or present, how could the nature of hearing itself be subject to your existence or non-existence?
The next two lines follow from the first half-verse to conclude its permanence. Question: The explanation of permanence is not yet finished;
why do you conclude with permanence so abruptly? Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, the preceding line eliminates the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Next, one line clearly elucidates that [the nature] is eternally abiding; therefore, it should be concluded as permanent. Second, the line beginning with "Even if" opens the gateway for people to enter the Path.
The perfect penetration always enters through this. Why? Because during the day, what is heard by the ear is mixed with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
however, when hearing occurs only during dreams, it is divorced from the mental consciousness and is thus the very nature of hearing (*śravaṇatā*). Therefore, it is the gate of awakening.
One must necessarily enter through this. As for what is called "dream-thought" (*svapna-saṃjñā*), it refers to having conceptualization within a dream.

For example, one might wonder at one's own voice, thinking it is the echo of wood or stone. At such a time, there is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the dreaming state, but not the mental consciousness of the waking state.

Therefore, the preceding text asks: "How could one recall stillness or movement, opening or closing, penetration or obstruction? Not recalling stillness or movement means not recalling sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
Not recollecting whether [the door] is opened or closed, or whether it is open or blocked, is "not recollecting the sense organ" (indriya). Thus, the immovability of the sense organ can be known.
Although one does not intentionally think or recollect, the sound of pounding and striking is necessarily heard; this is not because of a lack of non-thinking.

Regarding "vitarka and vicāra," the meaning of vitarka and vicāra appears in the preceding text, as it says: "That person, while dreaming, hears the sound of pounding and striking, yet perceives it as something else."
"Sometimes he beats a drum, sometimes he strikes a bell; this is because the initial mind engaging with objects is called 'awakening' (覺).
Immediately within the dream, he marvels at the bell’s sound as being that of wood or stone; this is the subtle mind’s discrimination, which constitutes 'contemplation' (觀).

These instances of awakening and contemplation within the dream occur beyond the scope of discursive thought during the waking state. Indeed, the five faculties, the body, and the mind are not identical."
This is the nature. Hearing in a dream is precisely the nature; therefore, it was said previously that although the form is asleep, the hearing-nature is not obscured.
If you would perceive this nature, upon hearing these words, you should vigorously extract it for yourself.

Although this passage clarifies the reality of permanence, the perfect, constant, and pervasive [nature] must all enter through this very gate. ○ Fourth, specifically showing delusion and awakening, part one: elucidating...
It is because of following sounds that one becomes deluded.

Now, in this Sahā world, the discourse on sound has been proclaimed and clarified. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; by following sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.

Ānanda, despite your powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts—is this not simply following what you have sunk into? By reversing the flow, you shall attain the state free from delusion.

The selection as commanded above is now complete. I shall now identify those among the assembly who have heard [the teaching], clarifying their delusions and awakenings, merits and faults, to instruct those present so that they may "turn back from hearing" and "hear inwardly," thereby revolving from delusion back to awakening.

This is to respectfully embody the compassionate intent of the Tathāgata in instructing the assembly. Within this text, the merits achieved and the faults committed are first summarized; the discourse on sound proclaims this clearly.
To follow the sound as it flows and transforms is a fault. As stated above, "neither ceasing nor arising" is what is meant by "original hearing.
Yet, if one follows this auditory object which possesses arising and ceasing, one will inevitably encounter the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

Is this not a case where the subsequent section concludes the faults to establish the virtues? To hear by following the sound is the fault of hearing; it constitutes a state of drowning. However, by reversing the flow, one extinguishes delusion.
To immediately attain the true and eternal is the merit of hearing. II. To clarify entering the stream, there are two parts; first, the instruction to listen attentively:
"Ānanda, listen attentively! Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, I shall proclaim the Vajra-King, which is like an illusion and inconceivable."
The Buddha-mother is the true samādhi.
Changshui categorized this passage as "later explaining contemplative practice. Now, let us determine it: the Vajra is emptiness;
being like an illusion is the provisional. Within that emptiness, the illusion is inconceivable; the Buddha-mother is the middle. This is the Śūraṅgama.
The essence of samādhi is the secret treasury of the three virtues of dharmakāya, prajñā, and liberation.
Furthermore, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time emerge from this wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna; therefore, it is named the "Mother of Buddhas.
II. Clarifying the Entry into the Stream: A. Marking the Hearing of Hearing.
Having heard the secret gates of all the subtle-dust Buddhas, you have not first eliminated the outflows; by hoarding what you have heard, you have committed an error.
You intend to maintain what you hear from the Buddha, yet why do you not hear that which hears?
The phrase "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*) urges one to sever the afflictions of thought.

"Buddha-Buddha" means that because the Buddha taught the Three Baskets and the twelve divisions of the canon as all being the Dharma for attaining the Way of the Buddha, it is called "Buddha-Buddha. "Hearing-Hearing" means that when the nature of hearing manifests before one, without engaging in deliberation, one spontaneously hears that hearing itself;
this refers to entering the nature of hearing from the faculty of hearing, which is the "reverse hearing" mentioned below.

This refers to the nature of hearing. ○ Second, explaining "hearing-hearing" has two parts: first, clarifying the perfection of cultivation and realization; second, an analogy. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:

first, clarifying that when the faculties are liberated, the objects are reversed. Within this, there are two further points: first, clarifying that when the faculties are liberated, the objects are reversed.
Hearing is not born spontaneously; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, that which can detach—whom would you name?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
Below, the text correctly clarifies "hearing upon hearing. Jiaoguang says: "The essence of hearing reflects sound, and by rolling back sound, it forms the faculty;
thus there is the name 'ear-faculty' (*śrotra-indriya*). I say this is not so. Because names, phrases, and syllables exist due to sounds, they are called "names" (*nāman*).
"Rolling back hearing" does not mean abandoning movement to seek stillness; rather, it means that at the very moment one hears a sound, no discursive thought arises.
If one discerns that the two characteristics of movement and stillness do not arise at all, then one is liberated from sound.

If this interpretation is adopted, it not only establishes the meaning of liberation from sound, but also causes the principles of the three virtues—perfection, penetration, and constancy—to shine forth clearly.
Since even the directness of sound cannot be found, how could there be the curvature of names?
Once the object-field of sound has perished, the faculty of the ear is accordingly uprooted; thus, all five adhesions are removed and the six faculties become liberated.
○ Second, clarifying that when the faculties are eliminated, the objects are extinguished: 2-1. Entering from the provisional into the empty.

Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust is dissolved and awakening becomes perfectly pure.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through all things, and tranquil illumination encompasses empty space.

The preceding section clarified that liberation from the objects occurs through the separation from them; this verse further clarifies that when the faculties are eliminated, the appearances of the objects are completely extinguished.
First, it clarifies the cause of birth and death: the seeing and hearing of sentient beings are like having cataracts in the eyes.

Because one with cataracts sees flowers [in the sky], the three realms are like flowers in the void. Next, it clarifies the cause for removing these objects: if the cataract-afflicted faculties are removed, the appearances of the objects will naturally vanish.
They perish. Emotion is empty while principle is real, and the awakened mind becomes perfectly pure.

As for the previous statement regarding "leaving the dust and detaching from the faculties," it meant leaving the six objects of one's own portion and detaching from the six sense-faculties of one's own portion. Now it is clarified that after the detachment of the faculties, the empty flowers of the three realms all perish;
thus, the wondrously awakened, luminous mind is complete and pure. When its purity reaches its ultimate limit...

The light of wisdom of the Middle Way penetrates all things without obstruction; even the awakening of tranquil illumination contains empty space, let alone the vessel-worlds contained within that space.

Some say that "hearing and the dust being eliminated" refers to partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), while the later statement regarding "purity reaching its ultimate limit" refers to ultimate realization (*atyanta-prativedha*).
II. Emerging from Emptiness to Manifest the Provisional.
"Returning to observe the world as if it were a dream: while Māraṅga is but a dream, who can detain your form?
"To return" means that after attaining liberation, one subsequently enters the triple world again to deliver sentient beings.
Since the illusions of both self and other have all been dissolved, even Māraṅga cannot detain you. Māraṅga is the dream; one who has attained perfect penetration is the awakening.
How could one who is dreaming possibly restrain or bind one who is awake? (2) The second analogy: one returns to six liberations.
(2-1) The first metaphor further has two parts; the first metaphor illustrates how delusion arises based on the truth.
It is like a skillful worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women; although their faculties are seen to move, they are all pulled by a single mechanism.
This passage—beginning with "As one [cord] moves, the six [limbs] are released"—is a general metaphorical explanation of the Dharma. Within this analogy, there are four intended meanings.
First, the illusionist; second, the men and women; third, the sense faculties; fourth, the single puppet. An ancient said:

"The illusionist is a metaphor for True Suchness (tathatā), which is called 'skillful' because it possesses the quality of following conditions. The illusions created are a metaphor for True Suchness following the conditions of ignorance (avidyā)."
The various men and women should be understood as a metaphor for all sentient beings. The movement of their faculties is a metaphor for the "sixfold conjunction" mentioned below.
"One mechanism" refers to the single, refined spirit (*ekasāra*), which is likened to the string held in the hands of a magician;
if the string moves, the hands and feet of the illusory person move accordingly. "To pull" means to draw or tug. (1) The second metaphor illustrates the return from delusion to truth.
When the workings of the mind cease and one returns to stillness, all illusions become devoid of inherent nature.

If the puppeteer does not move, then the hands and feet of the illusory person likewise do not move. This analogy illustrates that when one locus comes to rest, the six functions all cease to operate.
By the cessation of the six functions, it is shown that all illusions are without inherent nature; such is the essential meaning.
"Most luminous. Master Youzu said: "This metaphor illustrates that the faculties, objects, and mental states of sentient beings are empty and lack reality;
they can arise and they can perish. Just as the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) can give rise to all conditions, so too can all illusions arise."
"When seeing is not seen and hearing is not heard, then all illusions can be extinguished. This is precisely the same meaning as the previous passage which states:
"If the deluded mind comes to rest, that resting is itself Bodhi. 2. Combining the Two: 1. Combining the Arising of Delusion.
The six sense organs are also like this. Originally, they depend on a single brilliant essence that either divides into six or combines as a unity.
If one takes this single brilliant essence and pairs it with the aforementioned illusionist, it does not correspond to a single mechanism;

if one takes the six combined together and pairs them with various men and women, they do not correspond to the various sense organs. Now, I say this is not so. As before, the single mechanism was used as a metaphor for the one.
"Vitality and intelligence. The analogy of the various faculties (*indriya*) to the sixfold harmony is very clear in its meaning.
However, "one vitality and intelligence" refers to the subtle consciousness of *ādāna*, which is a synthesis of the true and the false, serving as the basis for the six faculties;

thus, both the illusionist and the illusory phenomena—this single mechanism—are contained therein. The "sixfold harmony" refers to the six faculties of sentient beings, namely, those of men and women.
It is also contained therein. ○ Second, the convergence and return to the True: "One returns from the six and attains liberation.
When one sense-organ achieves rest and restoration, the functions of the other six are all suspended.
"One place achieves rest and restoration" refers to the aforementioned cessation of activity and return to stillness. "One place" refers to a single faculty (root). Six.
Since all functions fail to achieve union, the various illusions above are established as being without intrinsic nature. Second, distinguishing the stages of partial and complete realization:

when defilements dissolve upon the mere thought [of awakening], one achieves perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity; when remaining defilements are still present, one is at the stage of further study; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.

Gushan says: The two lines beginning with "dust and defilement" refer to ascending to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (the First Abode). The remaining two lines beginning with "remaining dust" refer to the progression from partial realization to fulfillment.
III. Conclusion and Exhortation to Listen and Listen.
"Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back your inverted faculty of hearing; by hearing back toward your own nature, that nature will achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
Perfect penetration is truly like this.
This concludes the explanation of the principle of "hearing hearing. Now, human sentiment inevitably has its biases; if one's mind places greater weight on sound, then...
To neglect that which is called "hearing" is what is meant by "perverted hearing. A "mechanism" (*mēi*) is defined by its capacity for activation.

Since the faculty (*indriya*) can activate hearing, and hearing can likewise activate consciousness, it is termed a "mechanism. To remedy this defect, one speaks of "turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature.
When one discriminates erroneously, one merely hears external sounds; here, one does not hear outwardly, but turns the hearing back to hear [the source itself].

Hearing. At the very moment of hearing, no discrimination arises, and both birth and extinction vanish. The sense organ and its objects are completely liberated; from this hearing, one enters the nature of hearing.
If this nature achieves the Unsurpassed Way, it is as previously stated: "When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through to universal reach;
tranquil illumination encompasses empty space. Returning then to observe the world, it is like a matter within a dream. This concludes the section on "returning."
At that time, there was not a single sound that was not illuminated; this is Avalokiteśvara. Therefore it is said: "The nature has perfected the Unsurpassed Way;
such is the reality of perfect penetration. (5) Explaining the common realization.
This is the single path to *nirvāṇa* for countless Buddhas. All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate;
all Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter through it in perfect penetration; and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very Dharma.
I, too, have realized it from within this; it is not only Avalokiteśvara who has done so.
