From this ignorance, the four abiding delusions (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) arise, whereby within the ultimate non-dependence of the true and the dependent, one establishes the ultimate existence of dependence and the true.
Because the Buddha accords with the emotional views of sentient beings, he speaks of "ultimate existence."
[The text continues with] "the ear. One should know that ignorance (*avidyā*) is also inherently possessed by nature; therefore, it is said that "deluded seeing arises from nature.
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "Dharmatā is precisely ignorance; dharmatā has no place of abiding. Ignorance is precisely dharmatā; ignorance has no place of abiding."
Is it not so? Question: In this context, it is said that the environment and its inhabitants constitute ultimate existence;

yet, how can the subsequent text state that "the nature of delusion has no substance and does not exist as a basis"? Answer: When it is said that the environment and its inhabitants are unobtainable, it merely means they lack substantial reality;

who says they are eternally non-existent? Because they are not eternally non-existent, they are described as "ultimately existent" in accordance with the sentiments of ordinary people. However, because they lack substantial reality...
Because it is the essence, the subsequent text states that there is no essence and no basis. One who skillfully contemplates emptiness contemplates only its unreality;

ultimately, they do not give rise to the view of annihilationism, nor do they speak of a "basis" in the correct sense. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "That which is called 'the three periods of time being unobtainable'..."
To say merely that they do not exist in reality is for someone to claim they are eternally non-existent; this is precisely the meaning [of our position].

The passage beginning with "This existence" (此有) below details the characteristics of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) in order to clarify the meaning of the "root of non-abiding. That which "can have" is the sentient being, and that which "is had" is the world.

According to the subsequent text, the "world" (*dhātu*) is taken to be that which is "had. Regarding the phrase "that which is caused by what is caused," the latter [the cause] refers to the three periods of time.
The capacity to act as a cause becomes that which is caused by a prior condition.

Because it does not abide, that which is called a "capable cause" (hetu) further becomes that which is "caused" (hetumat), and that which is called "caused" further acts as a "capable cause. Therefore, it is said to be neither cause nor that which is caused.
In this way, there is no attachment, nor is there any place of abiding. Within such flux and non-abiding, how could there be any fundamental basis?
Having attained [this state], one dwells in non-abiding; within, there exists beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikāvidyā*), which serves as the root for the birth of sentient beings in the world.
Second, the correct demonstration of the delusions of sentient beings:

being confused regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity gives rise to the false and illusory. This illusory nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it depends. Now, wishing to return to the truth—
Desire, being truly non-real, is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Seeking to restore that which is non-real results in the complete manifestation of non-characteristics.

It is neither arising, nor abiding, nor mind, nor dharmas. Through their reciprocal production, the power of arising manifests and perfumes [the mind] to form karma. Like kinds of karma resonate with one another;
because of this resonance, there is the extinction of some karmic characteristics and the arising of others. It is for this reason that sentient beings exist in a state of inversion.
Although the nature was previously manifested through the investigation of phenomena, at the very moment it was manifested, its perfect luminosity became obscured.
As the preceding verse stated: "The illuminating nature that was established has vanished. Because this gave rise to deluded vision, it is called beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).

Ignorance originally lacks any substantial essence, yet it appears to serve as the basis for all manner of delusions; however, because it is not truly existent, it is said to be "without basis. As the preceding text states:
Based on this "original non-abiding," there is a fear that one might think this original state truly exists; therefore, it is now negated. Furthermore, regarding "returning to the true":

when clarifying the nature of luminous awareness and illumination, one intends to return to the original reality of the nature. However, the very thought of desiring to return to the true is not the true *tathatā* (suchness) itself.
The phrase "not true" up to "not even resembling" explains the preceding statement. Since it is already *tathatā*, [there is no further returning].
Then there would be no need for further [practice]. It must be that one considers oneself not yet truly [awakened], and thus seeks to return to the true source.
If this were so, it would merely result in the appearance of being non-true. "Non-arising" is explained below as clarifying the arising of all phenomena:

that which is considered "arising" subsequently becomes "abiding," and that which is considered "abiding" subsequently becomes "change. Therefore, it is said: "neither arising nor abiding. This is taken as the mind.
Thus, it can produce dharmas; and by taking dharmas as its object, it can further produce the mind. Therefore, the text below states that they "arise sequentially.
Delusion has the most powerful function for producing karma and suffering; this is the power of production.

The force of delusive delusion perfumes and forms karma, and karma can then summon suffering. However, there must necessarily be the mutual attraction of similar karma for the twelve [links] to be fully established.
"Birth by category. The mutual attraction and response resulting from identical karma is called "karma that induces birth. Changshui says: "Because of lustful desire, beings are born together;

because of killing and stealing, they perish together. Youxi says: "The phrase 'identical karma inducing mutual response' here refers only to the two modes of birth—womb-born and egg-born—and does not mention moisture-born or transformation-born beings;
this is because it speaks in terms of those whose power of karmic creation is greatest. ○ Second, the explanation.
The world’s inversions consist of two, one, and the capacity for both the constituted and the constituent, making twelve types in total.
Ānanda, what is meant by the world’s inversions? It is the false arising of segmented existence where there is no real existence;

because of this, the realm is established. It is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in a place of abiding; it is a flux that does not remain still. Because of this, the world is formed. These are the three periods of time.
The four directions harmonize and interpenetrate, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.

The first phrase generally inquires into the inversion of the world; "that which exists" refers to the fact that sentient beings are the "possessor" (the subject) and the world is the "possessed" (the object).
"Segmented" refers to the boundaries of east, west, south, and north having finite dimensions and distinct forms.
Furthermore, sounds, odors, tastes, and so forth exist through mutual causality; taken collectively, the subsequent serves as the cause and the preceding serves as the effect.

Because they do not abide in either the prior or the subsequent, they are said to be "without dwelling. Moreover, because there is no beginningless ignorance, there is nothing upon which they could dwell.

It is by not abiding that the three periods of time are established.孤山 (Gushan) says: "By the periods intersecting with the directions, and the directions intersecting with the periods, both together constitute the twelve [links].
Thus, the causal and resultant retribution of sentient beings, in their harmonious union, also constitutes the twelve. 吳興 (Wuxing) says:

"In the fourth fascicle, the directions and periods intersect, adding the three layers of flux and transformation; this is presented in contrast to the *niśraya-pratyaya* (the objective environment) to reveal [the truth]."
Regarding the primary retribution, the merits of the six sense organs each amount to one thousand two hundred. Within this context, they interpenetrate one another;
based on the primary [retribution], the world’s inversions are explained by establishing the twelve classes of living beings.

Since it was previously stated that these are "merits" and now they are called "inversions," can the ancient masters’ interpretation of the first three sections be considered identical? Tōshū says: "Three..."
The "four directions of the world" refers to the *pariṇāmanavipāka* (retributive environment). It is from this world that the twelve classes of beings arise through inversion;
thus, what Wuxing said is incorrect. Tōngzhōu’s interpretation is the most accurate.

This is because the "twelve" of the three periods and four directions are not the same as the "twelve" of the twelve classes of beings. The scriptural text describes the harmonious integration of the three periods and four directions.
The first set of twelve is formed by the stages of transmigration. Next, it is said that the transformation of sentient beings forms another twelve categories;
this is clearly and explicitly stated. However, the subsequent division into twelve seems to refer to the twelve *āyatanas* (bases), which constitutes yet another set of twelve.
These twelve *āyatanas* all reside within a single body and likewise possess internal components.
Regarding the external divisions: if one takes the three periods of time and the four directions as the world, this manifests the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment).
Subsequently, taking form, sound, taste, and so forth as the world, this encompasses the *samyak-vipāka* (retributive bodies). These two kinds of worlds are non-dual yet dual.

One should know that the subsequent text condenses the twelve factors of the three periods and four directions into merely the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Therefore, it is again contrasted [with the former].

The six types of deluded conceptualization clarify the twelve [bases]. Generally speaking, when the six objects—form, sound, and so forth—are discussed apart from sentient beings, they belong solely to the dependent realm (*āśraya*).
When analyzed in relation to sentient beings, however, they can be understood as encompassing both the dependent and the primary realms.

One must not fail to recognize that the full text of the Sūtra contains both these meanings of separation and integration. Second, the combination of the dependent and primary realms constitutes a single set of twelve.
Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; touch arises from fragrance; taste arises from touch;
and mental objects (*dharma*) are known through taste. Because these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, they form the twelve divisions.
Because of this wheeling motion, the world’s sounds, smells, tastes, and touches undergo twelve transformations and revolve as a single cycle.
This text emerges from that which exists through being, from that which is not caused by causes, and from that which has no dwelling place yet dwells.
Therefore, it is upheld by this. Due to movement, there are sounds and so forth. A teacher of men explains: "It is because of the movement of mindfulness that one hears sound."

To claim that one sees form because of hearing sound is incorrect. At the beginning of the text, the name is established by referring to the "world" (loka-dhātu) to clearly indicate the substance of the insentient;
is it not then erroneous to first discuss seeing and hearing? Only when one knows phenomena through taste does it pertain to the cognition of the mind.

It is only when the six deluded and false conceptions are confronted with the six sense objects that the six sense organs are distinguished. One should rely on the extended explanation to understand this.
It is said: Internally, due to the movement of phenomena, the external wind-circle is stirred, and thus sound manifests. Because of space, there arises agitation;

because of the firm clarity, obstruction is established, and thus form is established. When wind and metal rub against each other, fire-light arises. Where there is light, there is vapor; vapor is fragrance.
From the moisture produced by the brilliance of the jewels, the fire-light steams upward, and from this flows water. Water possesses cold energy.

This constitutes tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*). When the components of tangibility—roughness or smoothness—come into contact with the tongue, there is the arising of taste (*rasa*). When the five objects of sense combine with the mind, this is termed phenomena (*dharma*).
The above are the words of Changshui [Zongze]. Herein, the character "you" (有) has a dot placed above it, indicating that it does not possess actual existence.
The points above the characters are not causes of causes. From sound to form and fragrance, they further point to that which has no dwelling place as the dwelling place of the world.
Since the six objects are thus divided, sentient beings' six sense organs become defiled by them, resulting in chaotic thoughts.

The six sense organs of sentient beings are as false and illusory as a monkey peering through six windows; because it does not remain fixed upon any one of them, they are called the "six disturbances."
Through this, various karmas are performed and the nature of karma is established. The twelve divisions are the twelve *āyatanas*.
These are the retributions experienced, which belong to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). The twelve transformations are precisely the twelve divisions.

Since each instance of taking birth within the cycle of transmigration necessarily involves both internal faculties and external objects, it is called "one revolution. "Revolution" (or "whirling") refers to—
It revolves and then immediately returns.
Next, to specifically clarify the twelve classes of beings, first is the general enumeration:
because they ride upon this wheel of revolving and inverted characteristics, there are worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth.
There is that which has form; that which is formless; that which has perception; that which is without perception; that which is neither with form nor without form;
and that which is neither with perception nor without perception.
In the preceding text, there were two kinds of "twelve": first, the twelve formed by the combination of the three periods of time and the four directions;
second, the twelve formed by the mutual correspondence of the six objects and the six sense faculties.

Now, it says that "riding this wheel and revolving" refers to being closely dependent on the sound of causes such as form and so forth; "invertedly following the world's inversions" refers to the twelvefold divisions.
Since the cycle of transformation and return already comprises twelve stages, the transformation of sentient beings likewise constitutes twelve.
This is merely to accord with their numerical correspondence. The twelve hours of this region and the twelve months are also of this same category. II.
Specifically showing the textual divisions into twelve: first, birth from eggs.

Ānanda, because the world’s false cycle of transmigration is characterized by movement and inversion, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus, there are the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), such as the *kalala* stage, which circulate through the lands;
fish, birds, turtles, and snakes—beings of these kinds fill the world.
The world already possesses twelve aspects; saṃsāra likewise possesses twelve. Perverted speech mostly pertains to sentient beings and mostly resides in the causes.
Regarding the phrase "the world by way of causes," it means that within the world there is false saṃsāra, which is termed "movement" and "perversion.
The term "saṃsāra" encompasses both this life and future lives. Although saṃsāra undergoes...
The three periods of time share the same single type of inversion. An ancient commentary states: "In the egg-born, birth arises solely from thought; this delusion is precisely thought itself.

The essence of thought is buoyant and rising, which is termed the 'inversion of movement. This explanation is most accurate. As for the statement that it is formed through the blending of vital energies:
Beings of similar karma unite, and the egg is formed through the mingling of their vital breaths (*vāyu*). As the *Zhuangzi* says:

"The male cries from the upwind direction and the female cries from the downwind direction, and transformation occurs through the wind. Furthermore, the peacock’s conception upon hearing thunder is also an instance of this.
One imagines the body as light and buoyant, capable of ascending and descending; these eighty-four thousand chaotic thoughts of flying and sinking constitute the perception of the womb-born.

Regarding the manner of birth: fish exclusively obtain the lower [state], while birds exclusively obtain the upper. One should know that at the moment of receiving birth, the characteristics of the upper and lower are already complete;
hence it is called "confused thoughts of flying and sinking. *Kalala* means "congealed slime";
it is the state at the initial stage of entering the womb, when the embryo and the eggshell have not yet differentiated. If the sentient being’s body of perception were separated from its vessel...

When the realms [of existence] arise, one immediately ascends to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). When the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants merge, they become the various classes of sentient beings;

thus it is said that they "flow and circulate" through the lands. Following the egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*), there are fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, filling every category—not limited merely to fish and birds alone.
The egg and the *kalala* reflect the deluded movements above; the fish, birds, turtles, and snakes reflect the flying and sinking above. One.

I have previously provided this interpretation in a partial manner. Furthermore, regarding the statement that all twelve [types of birth] are born of conception (*saṃjñā-ja*), yet it is said that "egg-birth is born of conception alone":
the "twelve confused conceptions" refer to the conceptions at the time of taking birth;
because the conception of egg-birth is a conceptual attachment within the causal stage, it alone receives the designation of "falsehood. 2. Birth from a Womb (*jarāyu-ja*).

Due to the causes of the world’s defiled cycle of rebirth and the inversion of desire, eighty-four thousand transverse and vertical chaotic thoughts are formed through their conjunction and proliferation.
Because of this, there is the existence of the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of fetal development as beings transmigrate through various lands;
humans, animals, dragons, and seers fill these realms.
Within the world, there are places of defilement; for instance, forms such as physical shapes and the characteristics of male and female are all objects of desire.
Sentient beings give rise to the inversion of desire because of these. However, saṃsāra comprises twelve cycles of recurrence.
Wherever there is desire, it is immediately defiled, which is termed "defilement" (saṃkleśa). The character for "desire" (欲) also carries the meaning of defilement. Saṃsāra...
Since "reversion" (huí) is designated as defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it follows that perversion (*viparyāsa*) must have desire (*rāga*) as its essential nature. The womb is affected by emotion;

this emotional attachment is like water, possessing the sense of nourishing and completing growth. Emotion has both biased and correct aspects, termed "horizontal" and "vertical" disordered thoughts (*vikalpa*).
These serve as the cause for entering the womb. *Arbuda*—which here translates as "blister"—is shaped like a pimple; this is the second stage of entry into the womb.
The two positions have already distinguished between the womb-born and the egg-born. The names of their lands differ slightly from those of the worlds;

while the "worlds" encompass both the sense organs and their objects, the "lands" refer exclusively to the insentient. After emerging from the womb, they become humans, animals, dragons, or immortals.
Zizhong said: "When a person harbors the Right Path, they walk with their head held high; when one violates the Right and follows the Deviant, one is born as a horizontal being. Jiqiong said:
"At the very moment of entering the womb, there is only the thought of 'horizontal' or 'vertical. It is only after emerging from the womb that these characteristics first manifest.

The *ālayavijñāna* (遏蒲曇) develops and completes itself based on what precedes it; humans, animals, dragons, and immortals likewise inherit the states of 'horizontal' or 'vertical' from what precedes them. (1)

The preceding refers to birth from a womb. ○ Third, moisture-born birth. Regarding "moisture through union": this is termed "union" in contrast to the "separation" of the subsequent birth by transformation.
Due to the world’s attachment to the cycle of rebirth and its inverted tendencies, beings are formed through the union of warmth, resulting in eighty-four thousand [types].

Through these inverted and chaotic thoughts, there thus arises the moist characteristic of the *kaṭasī* (the corpse in its intermediate state). It transmigrates through various lands, and its species—crawling and wriggling insects—fill every crevice.
Moisture is perceived through conjunction; once conjoined, one becomes attached. Within the world, there are places where attachment can arise, and the multitudes...
Birth arises through these [conditions] and thus forms saṃsāra; therefore, it possesses the six faculties, the six objects, and the twelve factors.
"Trend" (gati) means to incline toward or adhere to. Since saṃsāra is termed "clinging," perversion (viparyāsa) must necessarily take this inclination as its essential nature.
Within perversion, there is a conjunction of two factors: the world and sentient beings. That which is moistened by the vital heat is named "warmth" (uṣman).

Those that "turn over and back" (*fānfù*) are the most numerous among these types; they either turn over or back. Within the state of confused thoughts at the time of rebirth, they already possess this characteristic.
Tiāoxī says: "Turning over and back" refers to the appearance of flying and crouching; this is explained in terms of form, meaning such things as flying, moving, wriggling, and crouching.
Zīzhōng says: "To act contrary to one's heart and turn one's back on trust, turning over and back according to one's own whims, thereby one invokes this type of creature."
"Flipping or overturning" refers to the fact that the destinations of sentient beings differ; they may flip or overturn, being neither a single entity nor fixed in their flipping and overturning.
It seems unnecessary to explain this solely through the lens of violating the mind or betraying trust.

Nevertheless, Zhi’s interpretation also possesses its own validity, as it accounts for the fact that sentient beings frequently betray trust, and thus the retribution for such flipping and overturning is not precluded.
Each obtains one [of these stages] as a recompense for their causal intentions. *Bishi* (蔽尸) is here translated as "soft flesh.
Since those born by moisture (*sāṃsvedaja*) do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages. Moisture-born beings correspond to the preceding stage of "heat" (*uṣman*).

"Containing crawling and wriggling" refers to the preceding stage of "turning over. Generally speaking, while each may be predominant, they must necessarily possess one another. ○ Fourth, the transformation-born (*upapāduka*).
Due to the false inversion of the world’s changing cycle of saṃsāra, the conjunction of contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand types of new and old disordered thoughts.
Because of this, there exist transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands;
these undergo metamorphosis and fly about, their species filling the world.

There are two types of transformation birth (*upapāduka*). There is transformation where something previously non-existent suddenly comes into being, such as the transformation birth of the various devas.
There is transformation where an existing entity undergoes a change of form, such as a caterpillar transforming into a butterfly or a lily bulb transforming into an earthworm.
Commentators of old, such as those from Wēnlíng and Gūshān, have adopted the meaning of the caterpillar transforming into a butterfly. Wúxīng... [text fragment]
This takes up the meaning of how that which is non-existent suddenly comes into being. However, when the Sūtra says "its kinds fill [the world]," how could it be taking only one partial meaning?
As for the initial mention of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*): because transformation is the characteristic of change, it is called "transformation.
Within the world-system, there is the way of transformation; sentient beings ride upon this and possess the twelve bases (*āyatana*), which are termed the "law of saṃsāra."
"Falsehood" (*jia*) means to falsely rely upon a new substance. Wēnlíng says: "To abandon this and rely upon that is called 'falsehood' (*jiǎ*); this explanation is correct.
"Contact" (*chù*) refers to the mutual contact between the new and the old, or as some say, the mutual contact between the sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*).

For example, when first being born in the First Dhyāna, the eight types of tactile sensations must first manifest. Regarding "the chaotic thoughts of the new and the old": if one proceeds from the transformations of the various heavens, then by means of the Desire Realm...

The "old" refers to the first dhyāna, while the "new" refers to the present state. If one considers the transformation of the substance itself, then the old material essence is the "old," and the transformed body is the "new.
This constitutes the basis for taking birth. Next, it says that the *kalala* of the transformation-body should correspond to the aforementioned "transformation.
The *kalala* is the fourth stage within the womb; now, since this is a transformation-birth (*upapāduka*), there are no [stages] prior to it, and thus it constitutes the first.

This is the established position. As for "transforming and shedding to fly": this corresponds to the new and the old; "transforming and shedding" belongs to the old, while "flying" belongs to the new.
This text provides a comprehensive interpretation, listing the ancient exegeses in full. That which Tianru (Tianru Weize) evaluated as most appropriate shall be recorded further below.
Wenling says: Transformation occurs through responding to change by means of detachment; this is precisely detachment (*li*). To leave this and entrust oneself to that is called "false inversion.

To touch upon various categories and undergo transformation is called "the formation of contact through harmony. Because the old is discarded and the new is pursued, it is called "the confusion of thoughts between the new and the old."

Therefore, the process of resonance and response is likewise so. Because one sheds the old, one proceeds toward the new. For example, when a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, its movement shifts from crawling to flying;

when a sparrow becomes a clam, its movement shifts from flying to submerging. Generally, whenever different forms are transmitted to one another, it is a case of transformation and shedding (*parivartana*). *Kalala* refers to hard flesh;
once it has shed [the previous state], it constitutes a physical body and no longer possesses the characteristics of a wriggling embryo (*arbudā*). From this point downward, all...

The term *kalala* is a general designation for all [stages of embryonic development]. If the fifth stage, *praśākhā*, were called "formation of shape," then that name would refer only to its specific appearance and would not be a general designation.
Guishan said: "Transformational appearance does not mean something suddenly comes into being where there was nothing;
it is like a grubs (qichao) shedding its old skin and joyfully assuming a new substance with the intent to fly upward."
Therefore it is said: "transforming and sloughing off to fly. Wuxing remarked: "Transforming and sloughing off to fly does not necessarily refer only to the class of *qichao* (maggots);
rather, it is a metaphorical image for transformation-by-birth (*upapāduka*). As the *Liezi* says: 'Heaven and earth are the discarded husks.'"

The subsequent passage, "If thought is purely [of the heavens], then one flies," employs entirely metaphorical illustrations. This is because the "moult" (zhuan-tui) serves as a metaphor for the ease with which the physical form is shed;
"flying" is a simile for the light, soaring ascent of a new substance. The principle that "what was not suddenly exists" finds its logical coherence here. Tianru says:

"The interpretations of the three masters Huan, Yuan, and Yue—that 'transformation-born' (hua-sheng) accords with the intent of the sutra—are indeed correct. However, if we discuss the various heavens and hells..."

Since ghosts and other such beings all possess manifested forms (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*), the Master Yue’s assertion that they suddenly appear where there was previously nothing also possesses a degree of reason;
it should be fully considered. ○ Five: Those with Form.

Due to the obstruction of inverted views caused by the world’s retention and hindrance within saṃsāra, beings combine and become attached, forming eighty-four thousand types of turbid and radiant deluded thoughts.
Consequently, there are physical forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands;
spirits of auspicious and inauspicious portents fill every category.

Zizhong said: "To cling tenaciously and refuse to let go of the union of sun, moon, water, and fire, such that they obstruct and block one another without penetration, is called 'obstruction' (liu'ai).
Because this clarity and manifestation leads to rebirth, it is termed 'form-characteristic' (sexiang).

That which follows in the *Zhong* [text] states that these four categories below are all those who, despite practicing cultivation, fail to attain the Right Path; they are divided into four types. Now, as for what is said..."
Regarding "obstruction" (liu-ai): when the spirit of sentient beings aggregates in one place, obstruction arises.
Because within the world there are places where things can linger—such as the sun, moon, water, and fire—which sentient beings may honor and serve;
or by swallowing their essence and color, their sincere intent attains resonance—this is the cycle of obstructed saṃsāra. It is an obstacle that leads to perversion.

For instance, when a star falls to the earth, it immediately transforms into stone; is this not an obstruction of its original substance? Thus we know that essence and radiance are fundamentally formed by means of obstruction.
Therefore, through the conjunction of these factors, essence and radiance give rise to disordered thoughts.

As for the physical form and the *kalala* stage, they follow from the aforementioned "staying and obstructing" (*liu-ai*); here, "obstruction" carries the meaning of "staying and obstructing. This refers to the latent fault of essence and radiance.
The superior essence shines brilliantly. Quiescence constitutes auspiciousness; transgression constitutes misfortune. When light manifests its forms, it is called "refined brilliance" (*jingming*).
It belongs to the same category as the celestial star, the celebratory clouds, the auspicious qilin, the majestic phoenix, comets, meteors, shooting stars, rainbows, and the *shangyang* rain-spirit.

The explanations provided by Zizhong and Wenling both possess their own significance; in general, those who cultivate the mind and refine the vital energy (*qi*) are able to evoke their manifestation.
This is the ear. VI. Formlessness:
Due to the world’s dissolution and the cycle of deluded inversions, the combination of darkness forms eighty-four thousand obscure and chaotic conceptions.
Thus, there exist the lands of the formless *kalala* where beings transmigrate; they are dispersed into emptiness, dissolving and sinking away.
These types are pervasive.
This category is the opposite of the "refined radiance" mentioned in the preceding text. Above it was said that they are formed through refined radiance;

now it is said they are formed through darkness and constitute the hidden and obscure—these are diametrically opposed. However, the womb-born arises from emotion (*kleśa*); here, both those with form and those without form are all [produced by] emotion.
Transformation. Although it cannot be called "sentiment" (*qing*) in the sense of its being dispersed and dissolved, the cessation of sentiment is itself a transformation of true sentiment.

Regarding the phrase "arising from causes, etc.": within the world there are methods for dissolution; sentient beings are deluded by these, taking form as something dependent and regarding the body as the root of affliction.
They dissolve and disperse [the self] through the twelve bases (*āyatana*), which is termed "saṃsāra. This cycle—*lun* (wheel)—...
Although there are twelve [types of] inversion, their nature is but a single delusion. Zizhong said:
"Because one is deluded and fails to understand, one suppresses the perception of form and contemplates infinite space; is this not an inversion? Jizhong further stated:
"Since inversion is termed a 'delusion,' inversions are generally spoken of in relation to sentient beings. As for the dark [state], its form is not...
Attachment is called darkness (*andhakāra*). That which exists as subtle matter (*rūpa*) is termed "obscure" (*saṃvṛta*). [Question:

Since it is said that there is no form (*arūpa*), what is meant by *kalala*? [Answer: One should take a portion of subtle matter and apply that name to its class. It cannot be equated with the state of being solid and hard;
it is also a type of *upapāduka* (miraculous birth). Thus, the *Madhyamāgama* says: "When it dissolves, there is no form; it is obscure."

Therefore, it is also called *kalala*. Regarding the phrase "empty, dispersed, dissolved, and submerged," Youxi (Yuanxian) said: "For now, let us discuss those in the desire realm such as the *śūnyatā* deity;
there is no necessity to refer to non-Buddhists of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). His explanation is most excellent."

In the Supplement, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are individually correlated with "emptiness," "dispersion," "dissolution," and "sinking. "Emptiness" refers to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), because one is liberated from the cage of form.
"Dispersion" refers to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), because although concentration arises by taking consciousness as its object, one cannot yet avoid distraction.

"Dissolution" refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), because it dissolves the preceding consciousness. "Sinking" refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), because it reaches the very bottom of emptiness.
This then accords with the meaning of their types filling and obstructing one another; this explanation may also be applied concurrently.

Thus, there is a "lower" section that connects with and receives from the preceding text; it is not necessary to correlate "emptiness," "dispersion," and so forth with the preceding "dissolution," nor to correlate the "formless" with the preceding "concealment.
○ Seven: With Perception.
Due to the world’s causes— the revolving shadows of the formless and inverted— through their conjunction and recollection, eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thought are formed.
Because of this, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of conceptualized forms that circulate through the lands,
where spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences abound in every variety.
The "Wangxiang" (the phantom) is the appearance of unreality; it is grasped by conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and likewise possesses the twelve bases (*āyatana*), being named saṃsāra.
From beginning to end, it takes as its essence the distortions of shadow and echo. Zizhong said:
"Discussing the cause, it may be like the non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who pray to deities and rely upon images, serving them for their entire lives with devoted aspiration."

Spiritual penetration. Because cause and effect recompense one another, one is born into their corresponding class. The discourse on causes in the *Zizhong lun* can explain the eighty-four thousand latent fetters and chaotic thoughts.
Since results are summoned from causes, it can be explained that such things exist as the "kalala" characterized by conceptualization.
However, the "recollection" and "formation" mentioned herein may refer to the chaotic thoughts upon the resultant fruit of a birth-by-class; this is because they are born by class.

The fruit of this is produced by disordered thoughts. Indeed, when ghosts and spirits connect with humans through their hidden presence, whether as a stimulus or a response, it is nothing other than what is focused upon by the mind’s thoughts.
Therefore, ghosts and spirits remember humans more intensely than humans remember ghosts and spirits.
Is it not also appropriate to call them "characteristics of perception" (*saṃjñā-nimitta*)? The term "characteristics of perception" generally refers back to the preceding text;
it need not be restricted solely to those who extend themselves as gods (*deva*) or contract themselves as ghosts (*preta*).

As for those who are refined and possess formlessness yet exist, and those who are numinous and capable of spiritual penetration—when one speaks of their kind filling all space, the *jī*, immortals, shamans, and spirit-mediums are all of this class. Among them today, the most...
There are many such types; the "eighty-four thousand" should correspond to the number of eighty-four thousand afflictions.
Regarding the "eight non-conceptual [realms]":
due to the causes of the world's dullness, cyclic existence, delusion, and inversion, they combine with stubborn rigidity to form eighty-four thousand.
Due to such withered and chaotic thoughts, there exists the realm of the *asaṃjñika-kaḷala*, where spirits are transformed into earth,
wood, metal, and stone, filling the world with their kind.
To abandon skill and cast out acuity, and to treat the six sense organs as external objects, results in the twelve bases (*āyatana*);

therefore, it is called saṃsāra. To claim that the ultimate Way lies therein—is this not delusion? "Stolidity" means a lack of knowledge. "Sentient consciousness" refers to the vital impulse of a person.
When this vital impulse is entirely absent, it is termed "withered desultory thought. Thus, the lower [category] follows upon the upper.

The *Wen* (Text) records that "the flower-tablet gave birth to a spirit" and "the yellow-headed one turned to stone. Those who wish to verify this should consult the notes in the *Tongzhou* (Tong Island).
The *Tiantai Shan Zhi* (Gazetteer of Mount Tiantai) contains an account of a monk who turned to stone, which states: "To the east of Mount Tiantai there is a cave;
entering it for over ten li, there are inhabitants and market stalls where many sell food and drink. During the Qianfu era, a wandering monk entered the cave and..."

He traveled through the marketplace; being extremely hungry, he heard the fragrance of food and bought steamed buns to eat. A fellow monk traveling with him was practicing *qigong* (breath cultivation) and did not eat.
After traveling more than ten *li*, they emerged from the mountain cave door and were already in Mouping County, Qingzhou. The monk who had eaten suddenly transformed into stone.
The two cases above are transformations resulting from mental visualization (*saṃjñā*); from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is how it occurs.
All have practiced cultivation yet failed to attain the True Path, erroneously becoming this class of beings. ○ Nine: Non-material form.
Due to the world’s mutual dependence and the delusive inversion of saṃsāra, these combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand causes based on chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exists the appearance of non-material form that constitutes the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of form, circulating within the lands.
Various creatures such as jellyfish take shrimp as their eyes, and such species abound.

Generally, that which is mutually dependent for support and achieves existence through reliance is termed "falsehood. Within this state of mutual dependence, both sense faculties (*indriya*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*) are present.
As it has been stated above that the eyes are compared to shrimp, so too the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) depend on conditions; how much more so the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*)?

It is the same within the causal state (*hetu*), for being endowed with the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) is called saṃsāra. What is referred to as "defilement" here is not the defilement of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*);
rather, to be attached and inseparable from [the faculties] is what constitutes defiled clinging. Because one is moved by this defilement, it is the cause of dependence and confusion.
Regarding the perception [of the *śiṅśapā* tree]: the water-jelly (*śaṅkhapuṣpī*) takes the froth of water as its body; thus the Commentary states that it does not receive a body from its own kind.

This is a case where that which lacks the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) nevertheless constitutes a characteristic of form. Furthermore, because it uses a shrimp as its eyes, this is a case where that which lacks the characteristic of eyes nonetheless possesses that form.
These instances of mutual dependence and artificial coloring constitute the causes and bases for the phenomena occurring upon the resultant fruit.
It is likewise so within the causal stage; therefore, one relies upon this category to become a *kalala*. Changshui said: "One relies on impurity to form a body and takes external matter as a guide.
This interpretation most closely accords with the case of the *sūkṣma-jantu* (the "water-mother"). Youxi said:

"Among the world’s relations—ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brother—who is there that does not rely on such mutual dependence to constitute their respective categories? One must also seek the correct principle therein."
It is finished. If there is anything that is not upright, it will inevitably fall into this category.

The *shuǐmǔ* (water-mother), commonly called the shrimp-cobra (*xiāshé*) and also known as the *fēi*, is shaped like a sheep’s stomach. The way the *qióngqióng* and the *jùxū* carry the *huì* is also like this.
*Qióngqióng* and *jùxū* are the names of two beasts; their forefeet are so high they cannot eat, yet they are skilled at running. To the north there is a beast...
The creature called the *huì* (the "mole-rat") runs with a crouching gait. When it finds licorice to eat, it must bite off pieces to give to the *qióngqióng* and the *jùxū*.
When these two beasts see a person coming, they will surely carry the *huì* on their backs and flee. It is not that the two beasts love the *huì*, but because it finds licorice to give them;
it is not that the *huì* loves the two beasts, but because it relies on them for its feet. ○ Tenth, there is no formlessness.
Due to the nature of inverted delusion caused by the mutual attraction of world-phenomena within the cycle of saṃsāra, mantras combine to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
Because of this, there exist non-formless appearances and formless kalala-masses that circulate through various lands.
Curses and sorcery arise, their various types filling the world.

"To lead" means to draw forth; by means of incantations and arts, one draws them forth so that spirits may possess [the victim]. That which is fully endowed with the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is called *saṃsāra*.
"Nature" refers to the innate substance received from the natural state. Now, because of mutual attraction, it is provisionally formed through others and is not [inherently existent].
What is this inversion? Within the world there is this saṃsāra; sentient beings possess this inversion, and by means of it, they become beings of similar class.
An ancient commentary states: "It is like frogs and other such creatures that attach their eggs by means of sound."
Indeed, an egg must obtain sound before it can develop; without sound, it perishes. Although this [egg] is joined with mutual attraction and invocation, can it be called a "formless kalala"?
One should know that the power of incantations can cause a spirit to manifest its form; therefore, it is not without the characteristic of form.
However, because it exists due to the incantation and does not exist without the incantation, it is dependent upon [the incantation].
If summoned, it arrives; if not summoned, it does not arrive. This is because it originally lacks a physical substance (*rūpa*).
Within the state of formlessness, there is also that which is called *kalala*; this is merely a designation obtained at the moment of initial conception.

Since the preceding and following passages all speak in this manner, the current transformation mentioned here generally inherits the context of the above and need not be understood as exclusively reflecting it. [Regarding] incantations and curses...

This also refers to summoning. The ghosts of *yān* (suppression) and *dǎo* (prayer/invocation) did not originally exist; they are actually produced through summoning and are thus called "born of suppression" (*yànshēng*).
One should consult the section in the *Fǔxíng* (Sub-commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*) regarding the Brahmin who raised a corpse to command ghosts.

The worldly practice of entering into a refined camphor-wood ghost is also of this same category. The two types mentioned above are transformations resulting from combination. ○ Eleven: Non-existence (*wúyǒu*).

Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): due to the world’s convergence with delusive saṃsāra and its inverted nature, perceptions combine and diversify to form eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and chaotic perceptions.
Because of this, there exist the perceptions of non-existence and existence, as well as the perceptions formed by *kalala* and *arbuda*, which circulate through various realms.
Those such as the *pulu* (a type of insect) and others achieve their distinct forms through the transformation of different substances, filling the world.
Regarding those who conjoin with delusion, Zizhong said: "To abandon one's own root and instead serve as a successor to another's lineage—taking this as the cause—is a most correct statement.
If there is no son yet there is a son, then that son is illusory; if there is no father yet there is a father, then that father [is likewise illusory].
This is immediately false; hence it is said to "conjoin with the false. To take what does not exist and treat it as existing is called "deceit" (*wang*).

"Differently formed" refers to what is stated below as "different substances forming one another. "Reciprocal interplay" means mutual interaction. This chaotic conceptualization may be explained either as the cause for taking birth or as the chaotic conceptualization within the state of fruition.
The phrase "In this way" below generally承接 (links back to) the preceding text, stating that [the self] is not existent.
Regarding the nature of perception: it is that one who lacks the perception of being father and son nonetheless comes to form the perception of being father and son.
The *púlú* and its kind are examples of this. The *púlú* is the *guǒluó* (the mud-dauber wasp). It takes green insects as its "offspring. As the *Fáyán* of Yangzi says:
"When the offspring of the *mínglíng* (the caterpillar) dies and encounters a *guǒluó*, the wasp exclaims over it, 'Be like me! Be like me! After a long time..."
It resembles that. How swift! ○ Twelfth, the Non-Non-Thinking [Hell]:

Due to the world’s cycle of mutual resentment and killing, and because of inverted views, these factors combine to produce the "strange" notion that there are eighty-four thousand beings who eat one's parents.
Thus, there exists the state of the Non-Non-Thinking Mark, where the *kalala* (embryonic stage) flows through the lands.
For instance, creatures such as the earth-owl take clods of earth for their offspring, and the mirror-cracking bird takes the fruit of poisonous trees to raise its young;
once the offspring have matured, both parents are devoured by them, and such species abound everywhere.
Beings of this class take hostility as their cause; because the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are contained within hostility, it is called *saṃsāra*.
When sentient beings give rise to the intent to kill, this is a perversion; through the conjunction of various conditions, they falsely conceive the notion that their parents are food.
This perception is also similar to the confused perceptions that arise regarding the fruits of one's actions. Changshui said:
"When enemies pursue one another in an unceasing cycle, for a father and son—those most closely related—to resort to the ultimate act of killing out of mutual enmity, is this not truly strange?
This statement is correct. The phrase "in this way" below connects to the preceding text; since they have come specifically to settle a grudge, it is not that they lack perception.

The "clod of earth" and the "poisonous tree fruit" are indeed without thought (*asaṃjñin*). Although there have been many ancient interpretations, this explanation accords somewhat better with the *kalala* stage.
Guishan said: regarding the "clod-catcher" (*tǔxiāo*) and the "shattered mirror" (*pòjìng*), the "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu" in the *Shìjì* states:

A. A Question: What are the contributing causes?

Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves independently; they abide by relying upon four kinds of nutriment, namely:

Zhenji said: When the Buddha first left home, he practiced asceticism for six years among the non-Buddhists, subsisting on a daily diet of hemp and wheat.

Ānanda, when one who thus purely maintains the prohibitive precepts has no mind of greedy lust, they do not flow excessively toward the six external sense objects.

"First: 'One whose wisdom is dry' (*khaṇḍa-prajñā*). 'Dry' refers back to the withering away of the craving for desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*).

Second, one has not yet connected with the flow of the Dharma (*dharmasrotas*). As the subsequent text states: "The middle-middle flow is the characteristic of the flow of the Dharma.

First is the abode of faith.
That is, within this very mind, one flows into the center of the center, becoming perfectly wondrous and blossoming; from true, wonderful perfection, one again gives rise to true wonder.

Although one practices Madhyamaka within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), one has not yet realized the sixteen moments (*kṣaṇa*).

Now, in the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is taken as the essence. This single thought-moment is the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*), yet this accumulation of afflictions is itself the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
This single thought-moment is the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra-duḥkha*), yet this suffering of birth and death is itself the Noble Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Although they exist within a single mind, the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), as well as the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), are one.

This is eternally abiding (*nitya*). It is both with deliberation and without deliberation; it is both with exertion and without exertion.

Having already initiated the moment of the first fruit, now, looking from the small toward the perfect, it is simply called "medium-medium"; its meaning can be understood thus.
Furthermore, in the small, one flows into the true and true; in the perfect, one flows into the medium and medium. ○ Second, the mind of two moments.
With true faith and clear understanding, one realizes all-encompassing penetration; the three categories of aggregates, sense-bases, and elements can no longer act as obstructions.
In this way, even throughout countless eons of the past and future, all habitual tendencies from discarding and receiving bodies manifest before one.
These sons of good family are all able to recollect without any loss; this is called the dwelling of the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
"True faith and clear understanding" reiterates the preceding text. Since all ten minds are termed "faith," the second mind establishes the beginning and is thus named "true faith.
All-encompassing perfect penetration is the truth that does not obstruct the conventional; the preceding mind is the limit, yet it is the center.

Now, faith is precisely the middle within the extremes; because the three—the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)—are all illuminated by true faith, they cannot act as obstacles, and one thus proceeds from the ultimate truth into the conventional.
At this stage, one should enter the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). That which is eliminated through the path of cultivation belongs specifically to the habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
When one perfectly illuminates the three periods of time without forgetting anything, one immediately attains dharani. (From the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra)
The passage from the *Thirteen Inconceivable Matters* states: "A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in a single thought-moment, is able to weigh and measure all of birth-and-death;

this is precisely the present intent. Furthermore, while the preceding mind destroyed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) that share the same substance [as the mind], at this stage one should destroy the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) that share the same substance.
Wuxing says: "This refers generally to the two types of death as 'casting off the body,' and is given the collective name [of 'casting off the body']."
That the five abodes constitute habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—how could this not be believed as true? Third is the mind of diligence:

when the wondrous, perfect, pure, and true essence gives rise to transformation through its own quintessential purity, the habitual tendencies from beginningless time merge into a single refined brilliance.
Because one advances toward true purity solely by means of this refined brilliance, it is called the "mind of diligence."
"Wondrous, perfect, and pure" refers to the first stage of faith. "The true essence giving rise to transformation" refers to the second stage of faith;

to enter from the ultimate into the conventional is precisely what is meant by "giving rise to transformation. The passage beginning with "Without beginning" clarifies that the manifestation of the essence is itself ignorance, which is in fact clarity.
The section beginning with "Only" clarifies progress: since ignorance is itself clarity, all delusive defilements become true purity—is this not progress?
○ Fourth, the Mind of Wisdom (*prajñā-citta*).
When the essence of the mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is called the "abiding of the mind in wisdom.
Youxi said: "Previously, delusions were entirely transformed into wisdom; now, there are no delusions, only wisdom. This interpretation is most accurate. The essence of the mind...
This refers to the aforementioned mind of diligence. ○ Fifth, the mind of concentration (*samādhi*):

maintaining the clarity of wisdom so that it is all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound; this state of being profoundly wondrous and eternally凝 (stabilized) is called the abiding of the mind in concentration.

By using present concentration to maintain prior wisdom, the wisdom maintained becomes clear from its former obscurity, and the concentration maintaining it becomes tranquil from its former distraction.
Thus it is said: "Pervasive, tranquil, and profound. Wuxing says: "Pervasive, tranquil, and profound" refers to the function of concentration;
"tranquil, wondrous, and eternally凝 (congealed/stable)" refers to the essence of concentration. Furthermore, the non-duality of concentration and wisdom is called "wondrous."
Sixth is the mind of non-retrogression.
When the light of concentration is emitted and the luminous nature penetrates deeply, advancing solely without retreating is called the "mind of non-retrogression.
As previously stated, "maintaining the clarity of wisdom" implies that concentration already possesses light; from this point on, the emission of light arises from both concentration and wisdom.

This is the essence [of the practice] that brings forth its manifest function. When the essence is clarified through the development of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one is able to penetrate deeply into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and perceive the truth of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) as it truly is.
Thus, one understands the reasons for advancing or retreating; therefore, there is only progress and no retreat. Question:

How does this differ from the "progression" mentioned previously? Answer: In the former case, delusion is transformed into wisdom; thus, because vigor is combined with progression, it is termed the "mind of vigor" (*vīryacitta*). Now, in the present case, it is concentration...

The name "Wisdom Equanimity" (慧均等) is derived from "progression," which distinguishes it from the preceding stage. Furthermore, as previously stated, [the former] appears to be constantly stilled, as if neither progressing nor regressing;
therefore, this present stage is revealed to be non-regressive and superior to the previous mind.
Moreover, while the former combined vigor with progression, the present is the progression of deep penetration. ○ Seventh, the Mind that Protects the Dharma (護法心).

The mind advances with composure, maintaining [the state] without loss. The meeting of the vital energies (*prāṇa*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
The first two phrases reiterate the preceding text. Because it is manifested from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is said that "the mind advances with composure.

What was previously called "non-retrogression" is here termed "maintaining without loss. Because concentration and wisdom are equalized, one is able to see the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is [united] with the Tathāgata.

"The coming breath meets the outgoing breath. Youxi said: "If a Bodhisattva’s mind is set on protecting the Dharma, yet possesses such a mind while there is no Dharma to protect, it cannot be called true protection of the Dharma.
Now, when the incoming and outgoing breaths meet and there is Dharma that can be protected, this constitutes the seventh mind.
The Supplement states: "I fear this refers to the sixth stage being equal to the Arhat, and the seventh stage."
The Way and contemplation enter together into the provisional to transform sentient beings; therefore, they intersect with the "vital energy" (*qi-fen*) of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, to maintain and not lose this is "protection. The vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is the Dharma. Since one does not regress, one will necessarily become a Tathāgata;
thus, there is an intersection of vital energies. ○ Eighth, the mind of dedication.

Maintaining awakened clarity, one is able to use wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and abide therein. It is like two mirrors facing each other with their radiance;
within them, wondrous reflections interpenetrate one another in infinite layers—this is called the mind of dedication.

The first phrase restates the aforementioned mind that protects the Dharma. Since there is a "clarity-awareness" (jue-ming) that is wondrous and indispensable—wherein clarity exists in dependence upon awareness—it is called "clarity-awareness.
To maintain this is "protection. Furthermore, awareness residing in the fruit is the aforementioned Tathāgata;
clarity residing in the cause is the clarity of the aforementioned nature of clarity that has penetrated deeply. Now, because the causal mind accords with the fruit, it is called "wondrous."
Power. When one turns toward the Buddha’s compassionate light, the Buddha faces oneself; when one abides facing the Buddha, oneself faces the Buddha.
If there were not a wondrous resonance with the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), how could one face the Buddha and yet be compared to two mirrors?

As for the term "wondrous reflection," it means that within the cause there is the appearance of the fruit, and within the fruit there is the appearance of the cause; because the cause again manifests the fruit and the fruit again manifests the cause, it is used as a metaphor.

The reflections in two mirrors further manifest reflections within reflections, interpenetrating one another in infinite layers. Wu Xing says: "If we consider the mutual reflection of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, it is likewise;
hence it is called 'layer upon layer'. ○ Ninth: The Mind of Precepts.
The light of the mind secretly returns, attaining the Buddha’s eternal, sublime, and pure constancy. Abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one achieves non-forgetfulness;
this is called the "abiding of the mind in morality.

While in the preceding state of meditative concentration, it was said that the quiescent, wondrous, and eternally constant is what one has personally realized; now, one attains the Buddha’s constancy.
"Concentrated wondrous purity" is that which the Buddha has attained. Furthermore, previously, one used "constant concentration" to dissolve one's own wisdom;

now, by using "constant concentration" to dissolve the light of the Buddha, it is termed "unsurpassed wondrous purity. Because this is a dharma that transcends marks, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Taking this as one's precept is the "precept co-arising with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*). Master Jing said: "The previous mention of 'returning the Buddha’s compassionate light' was shallow."
This speaks of the profound depth of the mind’s luminous, secret return; the previous statement regarding the mutual penetration of wondrous reflections was shallow.

This speaks of the profound attainment of the Buddha’s wondrous purity; as for what is called "secret return," it is like a trigger mechanism connected in solitude, not something coarse or superficial that can be seen.
The passage on "abiding securely" below clarifies that when the practitioner dwells [in this state] without omission, there will be no fault or transgression. Ten.

The "vow-mind" (praṇidhāna-citta) refers to dwelling in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Because one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, going wherever one wishes according to one's vow, it is called the "dwelling of the vow-mind.

The first phrase reiterates what preceded; since the aforementioned text concerns both the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) and those co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), it is now stated as "dwelling."
Mastery over the precepts (*śīla-vaśitā*). As it is said, "Abiding securely in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and attaining non-forgetfulness is mastery.

Seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and benefiting sentient beings—each and every one according to their wishes—is as previously described in the second gradual stage where one attains great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to travel through the worlds of the ten directions;
this precisely accords with the present case. Ultimately, it is by relying upon the precepts that one attains supernormal powers. (Wuxing)

It is said: According to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) of Tiantai, those who have not yet severed ignorance and are born into the Land of Common Dwelling (Tongju) are called "those born by vow" (yuan-sheng).

This precisely accords with the present text. Furthermore, it is taught that those in the ten stages of faith (shixin) emerge into the provisional realm to benefit sentient beings; thus, the current journey through the ten directions also accords with this meaning.
30. The Eleven Stages of Abiding: The First, the Stage of Resolving the Mind (Faxin-zhu).

Ānanda, these sons of good family, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds. The essence of mind radiates brilliance, and the ten functions interpenetrate one another to perfectly accomplish the single mind;
this is called the Abiding in the Arising of the Mind.

In the preceding section on the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), it was stated that "the remaining physical form manifests before one and will no longer continue to be reborn," which clearly indicates that the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have already been destroyed, leaving no conditions to draw forth further birth.
If this is so, then at the very beginning of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), how could one still be destroying the views?
It must undoubtedly be the skillful means (*upāya*) of the True [Path]. Now, the statement "by means of the true skillful means, these ten minds are aroused" is a general summary of what preceded.
These are the ten stages of faith. "The mind-essence radiates brilliance" signifies the breaking of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Whereas previously one broke through the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views) and *bhāva-kleśa* (afflictions of existence) which share the same substance, here one is precisely breaking through the delusion of ignorance.

Because it radiates brilliance, each stage interpenetrates the others, like the jewels in Indra’s net, where each reflects the others in successive layers; thus, within these ten minds, each individual mind possesses all ten minds, becoming perfectly complete.

This constitutes the single-mindedness of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). This is the removal of obstructive and distinct views. Although this substance of the stage does not exist apart from the ten preceding minds, the ten preceding [minds] are the particulars and this stage is the whole;
the particulars serve as the skillful means and the whole serves as the substance of the stage. Together, they constitute the "Stage of Resolving the Mind" (*cittotpāda-bhūmi*).
However, if one simply examines the scriptural text, the distinction between the whole and the particulars is perfectly clear: in the first stage, one attains Buddhahood within the hundred realms.

It takes the mutual possession of the ten minds as its basis. Examining the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), it is sometimes held that the five grades precede the ten stages of faith, while at other times it is judged that the five grades are identical to the ten stages of faith;
for instance, it is said that the first "Grade of Rejoicing" immediately enters the stage of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*).
Dividing one stage into two minds, the five stages constitute the ten stages of faith; these are the stage of the iron wheel of the six sense organs.

Since there are two interpretations regarding the five stages, how could there not be two paths for the ten stages of faith? What is so improper about judging that they enter the preparatory stage (*upāya*) of the true position?
Second, the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*).

The illumination that manifests within the mind is like pure gold appearing inside clear lapis lazuli. Because one treads upon the ground with this previously mentioned wondrous mind, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*kṣitighana-vihāra*).
The first phrase seems to follow from the preceding text; in the analogy, the lapis lazuli represents the mind, and the pure gold represents the illumination that is manifested.
Furthermore, refined gold represents the ground; one traverses it by means of the mind that has already engaged with the ten applications. ○ Third is the Stage of Cultivation (Pratipatti-vihāra).
When both the mind-ground and its cognitive engagement are fully clarified, and one travels through the ten directions without obstruction, it is called the Stage of Cultivation.

The mind and the ground interpenetrate, possessing the meaning of mutual correspondence. Since the ground is originally the clarity that issues forth from within the mind, both the mind and the ground are equally lucid.
"Wandering through the ten directions" means that this mind-ground can reach everywhere throughout the ten directions without being restricted to a single location.
"Attaining freedom from obstruction" means not being hindered by the forms of ignorance.

It is obstructed by its own substance; indeed, there is nowhere that is not the mind-ground. Youxi said: "From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is already called 'cultivation through conditions' (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*), because one has not yet seen the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
From ascending to the stages onward, it is called 'true cultivation' (*bhūta-bhāvanā*), because one has seen the Buddha-nature.
However, although the Buddha-nature is present before the beginner who has resolved their mind (*cittotpāda*), they have not yet applied the effort of true cultivation."

This is the practice. Upon reaching the second stage (*vihāra*), one traverses the wondrous mind with prior realization to establish the ground, whereby partial true awakening (*praveśa-bhūta-avabodha*) illuminates partial true original awakening (*bhūta-avabodha*).
Upon reaching the third stage, both the ground of the mind and the cognitive faculty become thoroughly clear;
thus, initial and original awakenings merge as one, and both initial and original awakenings are forgotten. [The fourth is] the Stage of Noble Birth (*caturtha utpādaviśeṣa-vihāra*).

Their conduct is identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s portion of spiritual influence. Like an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) spontaneously seeking its parents, their subtle faith and communion allow them to enter the lineage of the Tathāgata;
this is called the "Abode of Noble Birth."
Regarding "walking in the same manner as the Buddha": the mountains, rivers, and great earth are all the wondrously luminous true mind; only the Buddha is thus.
Now, since the mind-ground reaches everywhere, when walking one is the same as the Buddha. Since one resembles the resultant Buddha, how could one not receive his "vital influence" (*qi-fen*)?

This is like establishing a metaphor for the middle and lower capacities to clarify the Dharma: the previous Abiding in the Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) is like the first stage of entering the womb.

The consciousness-mind [arises]. Next, the stage of "Purifying the Ground" (Cittaviśuddhi) is like the ground traversed by the intermediate state (antarābhava). The third, the "Abiding in Cultivation" (Pratipattisthiti), is like having a destination when entering a womb.
The "Abiding in Noble Birth" (Janmakulaviśeṣasthiti) is like seeking entry into the womb;

at the time of entering the womb, one seeks out one's own parents, rather than the parents seeking the child. This is because the intermediate state being seeks its parents naturally due to the affinity of karma.
Mutual induction. Now, being certified as equal to the Buddha, they are also naturally induced by one another. This bodhisattva is able to seek out a Tathāgata to serve as his father and mother.
Regarding "dark faith" (*śraddhā*) and so forth: this dwelling in dark faith involves a subtle and secret mutual correspondence, which is precisely the meaning of seeking it for oneself.
○ Fifth, the Dwelling of Fulfillment through Expedient Means (*upāya*).

Having already wandered within the womb of the Way (*mārgagarbha*) and personally inherited the lineage of enlightenment, one is like a fetus that has already attained human form with no physical traits lacking;

this is called the stage of "Perfection of Skillful Means" (*upāyapariniṣpannavihāra*). The first two phrases reiterate the preceding "womb of the Way," while the term "wandering" (*yū*) carries the meaning of roaming through the *dharmadhātu* with the mind. "Personally" (親) [indicates...]
Regarding "serving the Buddha’s lineage" (奉覺胤): this refers to grasping the two wisdoms of the Buddha—expedient means and reality—to coalesce into the holy embryo (*garbha*).

Just as the embryo descends, it clarifies that one now dwells [in this stage]; that the human marks are not deficient is a metaphor for being endowed with the five faculties of the Buddha, namely the five eyes, five ears, five noses, and so forth.
In the seventh dwelling (*vihāra*) following the contemplation, the text generally summarizes the preceding two sections on the fifth and sixth dwellings, stating: "body and mind..."
In this synthesis, it is clear that the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) of the Tathāgata are necessarily taken as the skillful means (*upāya*).

For instance, the eye’s ability to see and the ear’s ability to hear—are these not skillful means? If one were to take the cultivation of immeasurable roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) as the skillful means, that would be the teaching of the provisional vehicle (*neyārtha*).
6. The Abiding of the Rectified Mind (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ saṃsthitacittavihāraḥ*).
The physical appearance is like that of a Buddha, and the mental characteristics are likewise; this is called the "Abode of the Rectified Mind.

When the physical appearance is like that of a Buddha, as described above, the five faculties are fully perfected; the mental characteristics are the same, such that the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is also identical to that of the Tathāgata.

This is what is known as the stage of the true purification of the six faculties. From the moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, this has exclusively discussed the essence of the mind.

For example, at the initial conception in the womb, one merely entrusts oneself with a single thought-moment before any physical form has yet appeared; it is only in the fifth stage that the physical form is clearly manifested.

Now, in this sixth stage, it is further stated that the "mental characteristics" (citta-lakṣaṇa) are likewise called the "Abode of the Right Mind" (*samyak-citta-vihāra*). "Right" (*samyak*) means "sage-like" (*ārya*).

The former [section] clarifies the mind that enters the womb; the present [section] clarifies the mind that dwells within the body. ○ Seventh, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*):
when body and mind are unified and daily increase, it is called the Stage of Non-retrogression.
The integration of body and mind refers back to the fifth and sixth stages. Regarding "increasing day by day":

at this point, the five eyes, five ears, five minds, and so forth, surpass those of the previous stages. This is because the portions of ignorance are progressively destroyed, and the portions of Buddha-nature are progressively revealed.
Since there is increase, there is certainly no retrogression. 8. The Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūmi).
The simultaneous perfection of the ten bodies and their spiritual marks is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*).
The *Xuanqián Huìběn* quotes the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which states regarding the eighth stage: "It is said that all Buddhas manifest their bodies for contemplation;

do not abandon the gate of patience, but exhort the contemplation of the eternally abiding and enter the state of effortless mental activity. This refers to the Bodhisattva manifesting the ten [bodies].
The various bodies: namely, making the bodies of sentient beings one’s own body; the land-body (*kṣetra-kāya*); the retribution-body (*vipāka-kāya*);
the śrāvaka-body; the pratyekabuddha-body; the bodhisattva-body; the buddha-body; the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*); the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*);
and the space-body (*ākāśa-kāya*). Next, making the land-body the head is likewise; even up to making the space-body the head is likewise. *Xunwen* says:
In his discussion, he states that each of the ten bodies possesses ten aspects, thereby forming one hundred bodies. The *Jùjì* (Record of Explanations) says: Question:
In the *Avataṃsaka*, there are ten bodies, whereas here there are only two or three. Since the number of bodies is so small, the encompassing of meanings is not exhaustive;

thus, this sutra’s inclusion of meanings is insufficient. Answer: Meaning has both general and specific aspects. While the general sense may be as you say, the specific sense is not so. That [text] speaks of "bodies" in a general sense.

Therefore, it is said that there are ten bodies of Vairocana. Since this is a specific explanation of the Tathāgata, one should not speak of the "retribution-body Buddha" (karmavipāka-buddha), the "land-body Buddha" (kṣetra-buddha), and so forth.
If one wishes to comprehensively include the ten bodies mentioned in that sutra, they should be opened into four categories:

the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) subsumes the retribution body; wisdom is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya); space belongs to the dharma body (dharmakāya); and all the rest are subsumed under the transformation body. — Guishan.

Furthermore, they are subsumed within the three bodies (*trikāya*): namely, space belongs to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), wisdom to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the remainder to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Question:
Since [the ten bodies] are subsumed within these three or four, why are all ten called *Śākyamuni* (Sāmbhogakāya)? Answer:

Because the body manifested by one dwelling on the stages of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings is precisely the Real Reward-body (*sambhoga-kāya*), while all other bodies are transformations of this very body. Since they receive their name from the original source, they are called *Śākyamuni*.
Furthermore, as for Vairocana, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* translates it as "Pure and Full" (*viśuddha-pūrṇa*). It is called "pure" because all afflictions have been utterly exhausted;
it is called "full" because all virtues are completely perfected. Although the ten bodies differ, their purity and fullness are identical.
Nevertheless, within this identity, one must recognize their distinct characteristics; they must not be confused as three or four without discernment. Why, then, are there ten bodies?
Regarding the explanation of the name "Śākya-kumāra" (釋童真): it is because the ten bodies of Vairocana are translated as "pure and perfect" (*viśuddha-pūrṇa*).
