Since "youthful truth" (*kumāra*) is free from defilement, it corresponds precisely to "purity and perfection. 9. The Stage of the Dharma Prince (*Dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*).
The formation [of the body] and the emergence from the womb are termed the "Abode of the Dharma Prince," as one becomes a true son of the Buddha.
The two characters "formation" (*xing*) and "completion" (*cheng*) refer back to the aforementioned perfection of the ten bodies.

Furthermore, the breaking of a portion of ignorance, whereby the bodily marks become radiant and manifest, is called "emergence from the womb. All the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) heritage of the Tathāgata belongs entirely to the Son.

Therefore, it is said that they are personally the sons of the Buddha. Just as when one is personally a crown prince there are rituals for inquiring after his well-being and providing him with food, so it is for the sons of the Buddha.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of matters of observation, namely:
the skillful means of the Dharma King, the regulations, the palace, the entry into observation, the empowerment, the sustaining power, fearlessness, and tranquility."

He rests. This continues until the Dharma King offers praise; therefore, it is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputrabhūmi*). ○ The Tenth is the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣekabhūmi*).
This signifies becoming a full person. It is like a great king of a nation who delegates all state affairs to his crown prince;
when that son of a Kṣatriya king has reached maturity and is invested with the ceremonial sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*), it is called the Stage of Empowerment.
"Manifestation" (*biao*) refers to outward appearance. Once one has attained such appearance, they have reached the age of "weak-crown" (*ruogan*), signifying full maturity.
The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "When the Crown Prince goes forth, he commands the army; when he enters, he oversees the state—this is the delegation of authority.

According to the Dharma, the eight phases of attaining enlightenment and the five periods of transforming sentient beings are all within his superior capacity. Since the Buddha-work is thus entrusted to him, he adapts to the capacities of beings through both great and small means.
Preaching the Dharma through both sudden and gradual means for the sake of the state. [The Forty Practices: Eleven, the Practice of Joy.

Ānanda, once these good sons have become children of the Buddha, they are fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas and act in accordance with them throughout the ten directions;
this is called the Practice of Joy.
Although there are ten stages of abiding [on the path], the text simply says "becoming a child of the Buddha," which encompasses them all without exception; this concludes the preceding section.
Changshui says there are two reasons for his joy: first, because he is fully endowed with the immeasurable virtues of a Buddha, as stated in the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*:
"I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way"; second, because he has skillfully acquired the four [fearlessnesses].
Regarding "inconceivable and effortless wondrous virtue": since it is called "inconceivable," it refers to the immeasurable virtues of the Buddhas.
Second, sentient beings rejoice because they receive transformation. "The ten directions" means manifesting bodies within the ten realms to benefit sentient beings.

There are two ways of being compliant: first, because the destinies and categories of sentient beings are unequal and their faculties and practices differ, the Bodhisattva complies with them by means of form.

By explaining this illumination, it is shown that it can transform beings in accordance with their capacities; this is the "conformity of the teaching. Second, there is the conformity of sentient beings:

each and every one who receives transformation attains benefit, which is the "conformity of those transformed by the illumination. Since both the capacity (the subject) and the response (the object) are in harmony, joy arises simultaneously in both.
Thus, the *Zhong* [Treatise on the Middle] states that "possessing virtue is the foundation of conformity. The ancients interpreted this through the ten realms.
That which is taught throughout the ten directions is precisely this. To practice for oneself and transform others is the sublime virtue of the Tathāgata.
That it is called "immeasurable" means that he manifests bodies according to the ten realms and teaches the Dharma according to the ten realms;

because every single element—be it the precepts, wholesome deeds, the truths, the conditions, the perfections, the two paths, the threefold Dharma, or the four fruits—is without deficiency, he is able to cause sentient beings to rejoice. 2. The Practice of Benefiting Others.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called the practice of benefiting others (*anugraha-caryā*).
Because of joy, one gives rise to this second practice of benefiting others. Attaining the fourfold benefit is termed "benefit."

Regarding the phrase "skillfully able," this refers to how the four teachings and four gates—each gate with its four *siddhāntas* (universal principles)—all accord with and enter the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Youxi said: "The preceding stage of the Ten Abodes clarifies that the Dharma Prince’s self-awakening is already perfected;

from the Ten Practices onward, it clarifies the guidance and benefiting of all sentient beings. Someone asked: "According to what Tiantai clarified, the three contemplations proceed from the stage of names..."

One comes to cultivate the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional; reaching the stage of the seventh faith, one breaks through the delusions of views and thoughts as the practice for self-benefit.

From the eighth faith onward, one cultivates the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional to break through the delusions of "dust-sand" (countless afflictions) as the practice for benefiting others.

From the tenth faith onward, one cultivates the Middle Way contemplation to break through the delusion of ignorance. Upon ascending to the first dwelling (*bhūmi*), this is termed the practice of benefiting both self and others.

Question: The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* clarifies that the stages of realization reach the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*) before one benefits sentient beings as an "emergent practice" (*niḥsaraṇa-caryā*).
Why is this so? Answer: The statement that the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) break delusions to distinguish between self-awakening and awakening others is merely a provisional explanation.
This refers to the meaning of sequential progression, not the ultimate discourse. Why?

For a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, one cultivates the three contemplations within a single mind, shatters the three delusions within a single mind, and manifests the three enlightenments within a single mind.

How could there be such a sequential order? For instance, when a beginner of the five stages practices sympathetic joy, reading, and reciting—though this is for their own benefit—yet in the middle stage they preach the Dharma, and in the final stage they concurrently practice both types of the six perfections; how could these be sequential?
Is this not the awakening of one who seeks the benefit of others? Nevertheless, within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*), there is no lack of gradual stages.

As it is said: "The principle must be suddenly awakened; with awakening, all is simultaneously eliminated," which reveals the path of perfect cultivation and perfect awakening. "Matters are not suddenly removed;
they are exhausted through gradual stages," which clarifies the meaning of gradual cultivation and gradual destruction. Without the gradual, there is no way to ascend to the sudden. Without...
The sudden cannot integrate the gradual. Only when both are fully realized is the Way of the Perfectly Sudden complete.

Nevertheless, there is the sequence of contemplative practice, namely the five grades; and there is the sequence of semblance, wherein from the seventh stage of faith downward one destroys the delusions of views and thoughts to realize the principle of emptiness, and at the eighth and ninth stages one destroys the delusions of "dust-sand" to realize...

Regarding conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-tattva*): it is the process of destroying the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) through the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) to enter the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), thereby realizing the middle truth (*madhyama-tattva*).

This involves a sequence of partial realization of the ultimate. In the stage of the ten dwellings (*daśa-vihāra*), one destroys ten grades of ignorance to abide in the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

In the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one destroys twenty grades of ignorance to emerge from the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). In the stage of the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), one destroys thirty grades of ignorance.
Furthermore, by cultivating the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*), one ascends to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and realizes the principle of the Middle Way;

this is what is meant. There is indeed a sequence for ultimate realization. Once a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) has realized the True Principle, they further dwell for a thousand kalpas and practice the conduct of ordinary beings in reverse order, thereby shattering and severing all subtle, dust-like, and river-sand-like phenomena that are mere shadows of conditions, such that no dharma-gates remain.

It is not yet exhausted. One must further shatter one grade of fundamental, subtle ignorance to enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, where bodhi is perfected and one returns to non-attainment;
only then is it ultimate. This present stage is the sequential order within the "partial realization" (fenzhen) that occurs amidst the non-sequential.
According to the treatise, a Bodhisattva at the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*) is already able to manifest as a Buddha in a hundred realms to guide and benefit all beings.

Birth. How could it be that benefiting sentient beings occurs only at the stage of the ten practices? Having become a child of the Buddha, one is already fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas;
this summarizes the merits of the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*). To "accord with the ten directions" clearly elucidates the characteristics of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
By means of these very virtues, all sentient beings receive benefit; this is called [the Stage of Joy].
The practice of benefiting others. Third, the practice of being free from resentment:
awakening oneself and awakening others so as to attain freedom from opposition and refusal is called the practice of being free from resentment.
Youxi [Zhanran] identified the practice of joy as awakening oneself and the practice of benefiting others as awakening others; this interpretation is correct.

However, for those who realize [the truth] for themselves, ignorance may not necessarily conflict with their wisdom; for those who awaken others, sentient beings may not necessarily resist their transformation.
This is the constant nature of reality. Now, because there is neither resistance nor conflict, there is no anger or resentment.
○ Fourth, the inexhaustible practices.

The various types of births continue until the end of the future limit; their equality throughout the three periods of time and their penetration into the ten directions is called "inexhaustible practice.
These types consist of the four teachings and four gates, with each gate comprising the four *siddhāntas*. All arise from the *dharmadhātu*;
since the *dharmadhātu* is inexhaustible, that which arises from it is likewise inexhaustible. Because all return to the Buddha-way, they are equal. Furthermore, one penetrates [this truth].
The substance of inherent nature gives rise to all phenomena; because cultivation arises from this nature, it is called "species.
It is like a mani jewel that rains down treasures without end. If it were not for the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation, how could one possibly reach the limits of the future?
Because the three periods of time are but a single essence of nature, they are equal; because the ten directions are but a single essence of nature, they are pervasive.
To deliver sentient beings by means of this is called "Inexhaustible Practice. ○ Fifth, the Practice of Being Free from Delusion and Confusion.
"All are identical" (*sarvam samam*). The various dharma-gates attain the name "transcending delusive confusion" (*mohavikṣepa-vigata-caryā*).

This appears to follow from the preceding text. Since each of the different types mentioned above arises as nothing other than the path of equality, it was stated there as "equality throughout the three periods of time.
Now, following from that, it is said here that "all are identical. (The term *gu* indicates the end of a section.)
Mount Yun said: "Different names and distinct explanations ultimately converge upon a single principle; this is precisely what is meant. Once they converge upon a single principle, there is no error.
When all ignorance is shattered, one is not deluded; when all things converge upon a single Dharma, there is no confusion. 6. The Six Wholesome Manifestations.
Thus, within the identical [nature], a multitude of differences manifests; each distinct characteristic is seen as being equally named "Excellent Manifestation" (*suvyakta*).

The subsequent phrase, "likewise," also follows from the preceding text. Since the Dharma of the ten realms is taught in response to the capacities of the ten realms, how could there not be differences?
Yet, that these differences manifest within the identical [nature] is because principle does not obstruct phenomena. Regarding the next phrase, "each one," and so forth:

This means that each and every [phenomenon] does not lose its identity as one, and they all proceed toward the same destination. *Soyin* says: "The one True Suchness mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices;
yet as these practices are performed, they mutually manifest the one mind. It is like gold being fashioned into vessels—though there are many vessels, each and every one is gold."
This means that within sameness, a multitude of differences manifests; yet within each distinct characteristic, one perceives their respective sameness.

Alternatively, one might assign the preceding six practices to the preceding six perfections, but fearing this would result in a divergent interpretation, it should not be done so. ○ Seventh, the practice of non-attachment.
In this way, even unto the point where the empty space of the ten directions is filled with atoms, and within each single atom the worlds of the ten directions are manifested;
that these manifestations of atoms and manifestations of worlds do not obstruct one another is called the practice of non-attachment.

The following section likewise follows from the preceding text. It states that not only do identity and difference mutually integrate, but when this principle is expanded and applied, the small and the large contain one another, and the one and the many are without obstruction.
Regarding the phrase "the empty space of the ten directions is contained within a single mote of dust," some cite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says:
"Within every single mote of dust of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha), the entire Dharma-realm is manifested. This is not [merely a metaphorical expression].

Regarding mutual obstruction: when the realms enter the sense-fields, the realms do not become small; thus the small does not obstruct the large. When the sense-fields contain the realms, the realms do not become large;
thus the large does not obstruct the small. If there were even a hair’s breadth of attachment, how could the large and the small be mutually accommodated?
Furthermore, although it contains the realms of the ten directions, the characteristic of the sense-field is not lost—this is the manifestation of the sense-field. Although it abides...

To manifest the worlds of the ten directions within a single atom is "manifesting the realms. Here, the great above does not obstruct the small below, nor does the small below obstruct the great above.
○ Eighth, the Practice of Reverence:
All various manifestations that appear before one are called the "first pāramitā," and this is termed the Practice of Reverence.

The phrase "various manifestations" generally summarizes all practices from the preceding section on "joy" onward. Within the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), the ten practices proceed from the ultimate truth into the conventional;
because they involve a gradual entry and a superficial immersion, they are not yet called the first *pāramitā*.

In the present stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), the ten practices for transforming sentient beings are such that the one is none other than the infinite, and the infinite is none other than the one, continuing even unto manifestation.
The phenomena of the dharmadhātu are unimpeded in every respect; all are the manifestations of the *prajñā* of the perfectly interfused three virtues.
If one relies closely on the seventh [stage], as Changshui says, and so forth. ○ Ninth: The Practice of Wholesome Dharmas.
Such perfect interfusion is able to establish the norms for the Buddhas of the ten directions and is called "virtuous dharmic practice.
The eightfold manifestation of enlightenment and the teachings given during the five periods by the Buddhas of the ten directions all employ the power of the aforementioned perfect interfusion.
The eightfold manifestation and the five periods constitute these norms. Although there are no five periods when a Buddha appears in a pure land, nevertheless—
To progress from the sudden to the gradual, and from the gradual to the sudden, is likewise a fixed principle; therefore, it is called a wholesome dharma. ○ Tenth, the practice of reality:
each and every one of these is pure, untainted, the single true, unconditioned nature that is inherently so; therefore, they are called the practice of reality.
The tenth [section] concludes the nine preceding practices. These ten practices are perfectly interfused such that the one does not depart from the ten, and the ten do not depart from the one.
Therefore, the final conclusion states: "Each and every one is... and so forth. In the provisional teachings, the ten practices merely destroy the dust-like afflictions.

Now, because all ignorance has been shattered, it is called "pure and untainted" (*anāsrava*). This means that the three truths and ten realms are subsumed within the state of being free from outflows.

Although one delivers sentient beings, all are of the single Middle Way, whose essence is without arising or ceasing. Although one engages in worldly phenomena and functions, there is nothing that is not intrinsically possessed by nature.
Therefore, it is called "original. The term "real" (*bhūta*) concludes the preceding points, signifying that all these names are truly real.
○ The Eleventh Dedication of the Fifty: The Dedication of Protecting and Delivering All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Concept of Sentient Beings.
Ānanda, when these good men have perfected their supernatural powers and fulfilled the work of attaining Buddhahood, they shall be pure, clean, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions.
They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing the very notion of "delivering" them. Turning their unconditioned minds toward the path of Nirvāṇa is called "Protection."
The Dedication of Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.

When a Bodhisattva fulfills the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), they become a child of the Buddha. Now, with the fulfillment of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), it is said that the work of Buddhahood is accomplished.
Because function arises based on the essence, it is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*). Regarding "pure, clean, refined, and true": pure and clean refers to the severing of [delusions].

The supreme purity is untainted (*anāsrava*). It is the refined and true, the ultimate unity of the One, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since afflictions have been left far behind, practice is perfected.
"When one should deliver sentient beings" clarifies the correct meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).

If one were to eliminate the marks of deliverance merely through the two kinds of emptiness—of nature and of characteristics—how would this differ from the partial emptiness of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*)? "When" means "correctly. It refers to correctly delivering sentient beings.

The characteristic of birth and extinction is existence-emptiness (*yǒu-ér-kōng*). Although this appears similar to the Shared Teaching (*tōngjiào*), the Shared Teaching can penetrate the subtle while that which it penetrates is coarse.
Because it can penetrate the subtle, how does it differ from the Perfect [Teaching]? Because that which it penetrates is coarse, it enters only into partial emptiness (*piānkōng*).
Now, as for the characteristic of "crossing over" and "not crossing over," this is because it can penetrate the subtle and that which it penetrates is likewise subtle. [This is] the turning back.

To turn the mind toward the path of nirvāṇa through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) means to distance oneself from the two extremes of emptiness and the provisional; this is what is called the unconditioned.
One thus returns to the path of nirvāṇa, which transcends both emptiness and existence. As stated previously in the tenth stage:
"Since the one true unconditioned already possesses the unconditioned mind," one now turns this mind back toward the path of Great Nirvāṇa.
This is the dedication of causes toward the fruit. Within the stage of Buddhahood, awakening (*bodhi*) is the fruit and nirvāṇa is the fruit of the fruit.
Now, the mind of dedication directs itself straight toward this fruit of the fruit. II. The Indestructible Dedication.

The dedication called "the indestructible that is far removed from all forms of detachment" means that while the previous elimination of the marks of crossing over destroys that which is destructible, this destruction itself is also detached; thus it is called being far removed from all forms of detachment.
To depart from destruction and thereby realize the indestructible constitutes the second dedication. ○ Third, the Dedication Equal to All Buddhas:
when fundamental awakening is profoundly still and its realization is equal to the awakening of all Buddhas, it is called the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
In the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), it is said that "the mind’s essence radiates brilliance.

In the second, the Stage of Cultivation (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*), it is said that "one treads upon the ground by means of the previously mentioned wondrous mind. In the third stage, it is said that "the mind-ground and its cognitive engagement are both clearly understood.

Now, the third, fourth, and fifth stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) resemble those preceding them; their sequence is likewise the same. However, whereas the previous [stages] were discussed from the perspective of the Bodhisattva...
Although it was previously stated that one's practice is identical to that of the Buddha, it was not yet entirely so.
Now, because the dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā) closely resembles that of the Buddha, it differs from what preceded. Regarding "original enlightenment" (mūla-bodhi):

the aforementioned "indestructible dedication" refers to attaining that which is beyond separation, thereby eliminating all illusions. Thus, building upon this, it says "original enlightenment is profoundly still"; this profound stillness is itself the original.
The essence of awakening is limpid and motionless; even a Buddha merely realizes this original awakening.
Therefore, one’s own awakening is equal to the awakening of a Buddha. ○ Fourth, the dedication of merit to reach all places.
The stage of the "Essence of Purity Illuminating" is called the Stage of the Buddha; this is the dedication reaching all places.
Regarding "reaching all places": in the previous "Stage of Cultivating the Ground," it was said that the mind gives rise to illumination, which is likened to ground made of refined gold.
Now, in this fourth dedication, illumination is likewise taken as the ground. Since one has awakened to the awakening of a Buddha, then—
The ground is like the ground of the Buddha. The ground of the Tathāgata’s true reality (*tathatā*) pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, the second fascicle states:
"From the form-body (*rūpakāya*) outward, including mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.

Based on this, one knows that the ground of the Buddha’s true reality pervades all places, and that the grounds of the bodhisattvas are no different from those of the Buddha. If [it were] as previously...
The stage of "cultivating the ground" (bhūmi-prakāra) does not necessarily entail reaching all places.

Therefore, although the practices of the preceding fourth dwelling were identical to those of a Buddha—meaning that while his conduct was like a Buddha's, his ground was not yet like a Buddha's—now it is indeed like the ground of a Buddha.
5. The Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.
The dedication known as the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit" refers to the mutual interpenetration of the worlds and Tathāgatas, such that they attain freedom from all obstructions.
Regarding this "mutual interpenetration of the worlds and Tathāgatas": both the defiled and the pure, as well as the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*), are entirely non-dual;

even to the extent that world-systems appear upon the tip of a hair and the turning of the Dharma occurs within a single atom, it is therefore called the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. — Tianru (Tianru Weize) supplemented.
The commentary states: According to the interpretation of Wuxing, the world is defilement and the Tathāgata is purity.
○ Sixth, the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.

Within each of the stages of the same Buddha-ground, one respectively generates the causes for purification; by relying on these causes to manifest and take up the path to nirvana, it is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equality.
The sixth dedication also derives from the fourth section of the text.

However, while the first five dedications all take the realized principle as the object to be dedicated toward the cause and the fruit, it is only at this stage that the practiced conduct is clarified.
The ten practices of the preceding section are merits arising from abiding; the merits of the present section arise from being within the same ground as the Buddha. This is because...
The "ground" (*bhūmi*) carries the sense of being able to produce. The term "each and every" (*pratyeka*) has the broadest scope. Being produced from the Buddha-ground is the cause of purity;
since it arises from the Buddha-ground, the cause must be relied upon. To manifest that which comes from this reliance-cause is precisely the meaning of cultivation.
The cause of purity can take up the path to *nirvāṇa*. Gusuan said: [This is] practice.
Arising from principle, it is called "conformity with equality. That which can produce the fruits of the Path is termed "wholesome roots.
(7) Dedication in conformity with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.

Once the true roots have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own fundamental nature. When this nature is perfected and fully realized, one does not lose the designation "sentient being";
this is the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
Previously it was stated that this is "because of conforming to the roots of goodness of equality"; now it is restated as "true roots. These true roots are the cause of purity.
Fearing that one might think these are causes for generating only purity and do not extend to defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa*), it is now said:

"All sentient beings are my own fundamental nature. Thus, it is clear that defilement and purity are non-dual. Tongzhou says: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own fundamental [nature]."
In their nature, there are no sentient beings; yet, because their nature is perfectly accomplished, they do not lose their status as sentient beings, nor are they non-existent.
The two directions of the sixth and seventh stages both clarify that the dharmas of birth all proceed from the fourth dedication. As for "conformity":
This means being able to accord with principle. To attain the non-distinction between self and others through the true roots is what constitutes equal contemplation. 8.
Dedication to the Characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*):
That all phenomena are free from all characteristics; that which is called "the characteristic of true suchness" is the state where both "identity" and "separation" are without attachment.
Dedication.
It was stated previously that not losing sentient beings is precisely all dharmas; yet sentient beings are all by nature free from all marks.
However, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is ultimately neither identical to nor separate from them, remaining unattached to either. —Gushan.
It is said: All phenomena are provisional; being free from all marks is emptiness; and being non-attached to these two is the Middle Way.
Based on this, all three truths are named True Suchness. ○ Ninth: The Dedication of Unbound Liberation.
Truly attaining that which is as-it-is (yathābhūta), unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of liberation without bondage.

"True" refers to the essence of reality (tattva). As for the phrase "truly attaining that which is as-it-is," it should be understood as referring to the fact that the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants, are all identical to true reality;
thus they are termed "that which is known. However, the expression "truly attaining that which is as-it-is" reiterates the preceding text. In this way, the ten...

How could there be any obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants? The previous three truths were discussed in terms of essence (*tǐ*); now, the ten directions are discussed in terms of function (*yòng*).
This refers to the time when function arises, at which point the ten directions are entirely without obstruction. [Section Ten: The Infinite Dedication of the Ten Dharma Realms.
The perfection of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) to the extent of the *dharmadhātu*, wherein [all] measures are extinguished, is called the "Infinite Dedication to the *Dharmadhātu*.

In the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), one realizes principle; in the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), one engages with phenomena. Now, in the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), one turns the causes toward the fruit.

The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "To 'dedicate' means to turn back, exchange, and transform. In the initial stage, one rescues and protects sentient beings while remaining free from the mark of sentient beings."

"Turning back" (*pratyāvartana*) refers to the transformation and transmutation [of the mind]. Having departed from the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*), one attains that which has nothing further to depart from;
this is the second *akṣaya-praṇidhāna-pariṇāmanā*. Are these two not indeed the turning of the cause toward the fruit?

Regarding the third, "equalizing with all Buddhas," it means realizing the indestructible essence, which is precisely original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). This original enlightenment is said to be equal to the awakening of the Buddhas.

One dedicates [the merit] equally to all Buddhas. The essence of original enlightenment is traversed to constitute the fourth stage, which is called the Stage of Reaching All Places, corresponding to the dedication of "reaching all places" as in the names of the Buddha-stages.

The fifth stage is that of the Tathāgatas of the worlds mutually interpenetrating, called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit. "Hui" (回) here means mutual interpenetration (*huixu*).
The three preceding stages mostly concern the mutual interaction between one’s own mind and the Buddha, as well as the sense of turning the cause toward the fruit.
The first five dedications primarily discuss the realization of the essence. Regarding the sixth, the arousal of practice, it states:
"Within each of the stages identical to the Buddha-ground, one individually generates pure causes. The scope implied by the term "individually" is vast. The seventh stage says: "Ten..."

That all sentient beings are my own original nature corresponds to the preceding five directions; this signifies that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in three ways, and that they are mutually interpenetrating.
The eighth [verse] concerns non-attachment to the Three Truths, and the ninth concerns unimpededness throughout the ten directions.
This also discusses the mutual interpenetration (*huixu*) of principle and phenomena. The general purport of the upper nine hexagrams largely clarifies the non-differentiation of the three [natures].
When cause and effect, self and other, and the dependent and the primary are without distinction, the virtues of the original nature are fully perfected.
Since phenomena and principle interpenetrate and fuse into a single entity, all limitations of "this" and "that" are forgotten; thus, there is no need even to speak of one’s own mind or the Buddha.
The stage of the mind and the stage of the Buddha constitute the tenth: the Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm. Six:
The Four Additional Practices. 2-1: General Statement.
Ānanda, these good sons have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds and subsequently accomplished the four kinds of wondrous perfection.
Regarding the stage of application (*prayoga*):
Xie Li states that according to scriptures such as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, the four stages of application are not listed separately.

However, treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* consider the forty minds prior to the [first] bhūmi to be the stage of the external ordinary person’s provisions (*sambhāra*). Following the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*)...

Thus, it is clear that the stages of "clarity" (*āloka*), "warmth" (*uṣmagata*), and so forth constitute the stage of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for those within the mundane level (*pṛthagjana*). Wuxing remarked:

"The four stages of preparatory practice here are exactly as described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. However, the division of the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) into internal and external mundane levels is a doctrine specific to one path of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*).
This is because ascending to the grounds constitutes the sacred stage (*āryabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; since this sacred stage is difficult to enter, these [preparatory stages] are established."
This refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Question: Now, why does this Sūtra of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) employ distinct meanings? Answer:

There are precedents for borrowing the names of the distinct [teachings] to refer to the Perfect; for example, as stated in the *Renwang jing*: "The Three Worthies and Ten Sages dwell in the retribution of fruition.
Master Min claimed that this Sūtra is not necessarily purely Perfect and must incorporate the distinct meanings, but his error is profound indeed. II. A Separate Enumeration of Four.
First is the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).
Taking the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind—whether it has emerged or not yet emerged—is like praising fire that is about to ignite wood;
this is called the stage of Heat.

The first ten dedications all involve dedicating the cause toward the fruit, yet the cause is not identical to the fruit. Now, within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind.
Tianru says: "Although the Buddha’s awakening in the preceding [dedications] is said to be equal [to it], it has not yet been correctly realized.
Since one is now about to proceed toward the holy fruit, one therefore uses the Buddha’s awakening as the causal mind for oneself. This is his explanation.
It is so. Regarding what is called "Buddha-awakening," as the *Saṃpuṭa* (Flower Ornament) Sūtra says: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

The meaning of this is precisely that which is taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus) Sūtra: that the ten realms and their thousand suchnesses are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Question: The preceding sūtra states: "Fundamental awakening is profound and still; when awakening is equal to the awakening of a Buddha, one attains non-separation and thereby eliminates all illusions. How is this explained?
If the Buddha’s awakening is merely the essence of pure reality, why do you now provide this interpretation? Answer:

The preceding passage clarifies that awakening is equal to the stage of a Buddha’s awakening, being like the Buddha-ground itself; the subsequent passage then states that worlds and Tathāgatas mutually interpenetrate.

In the seventh dedication, it says: "Sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature. Is this not precisely the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings?
Furthermore, is this not the fact that the ten realms of existence, both the environment and its inhabitants, reside within a single mind?
The eighth is non-attachment to the three truths; the ninth is unimpededness throughout the ten directions; and the tenth concludes by stating that the inherent virtues are perfectly fulfilled.
All of them deeply clarify the principle that the single mind of the ten realms is itself emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle.

These are all identical to the Buddha’s awakening and the "ten suchnesses" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Although they do not explicitly mention the "three thousand [realms]," the three thousand are contained therein.
However, these still represent the Buddha’s awakening as an object of orientation; now, by taking this awakening as one's own mind, one enters [the Way].
This refers to the stage of the ground (*bhūmi-prayoga*). As for "emerging," it means that although the Buddha’s awakening intends to emerge from the mind, it has not yet emerged;
this is analogous to the heat that precedes the ignition when drilling wood for fire. Fire represents the wisdom of the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*);

the wood represents the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be destroyed; the drilling represents the preparatory application (*prayoga*); and the heat represents the precursor to the noble fire of the first ground. Furthermore, fire may also be used as a metaphor [for the awakening itself].
The Buddha’s awakening to the metaphor of the wood is like his own mind. Second is the Stage of the Summit (mūrdhan).
Furthermore, taking one’s own mind as that which the Buddha treads upon—whether relying on it or not—it is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters empty space;
yet because there remains a slight obstruction below, it is called the Ground of the Summit.

This meaning appears in three places. In the first stage (*bhūmi*), it says: "The essence of mind emits radiance. In the second stage, it says: "One treads upon the previously mentioned wondrous mind to form the ground.
In the third dedication, it says: "Awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddha. In the fourth dedication, it says: "The ground is like the ground of the Buddha.
One should know that the ground is likewise what is to be treaded upon. Within these preparatory practices (*prayoga*), this is the preceding stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

The *Dì* (Ground) says: "One takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind; since awakening is also the Ground, it is now said that one further takes one's own mind to become what the Buddha treads upon.
Now, the Buddha’s awakening is what the Buddha treads upon because it resides within one's own mind;
therefore, one's own mind also becomes what is trodden upon. The old commentary states: "The Buddha is the fruition realized within one's own mind."

As for human wisdom: since one has realized that one’s own awakening is equal to the stage of Buddha-awakening and has been as such as long ago as the Buddha-ground, Buddha-wisdom has long been transparently clear.
If it is "dependent," then Buddha-wisdom returns to depend upon the ground of one's own mind; if it is "not dependent," then the Buddha transcends beyond one's own mind.
Because the characteristics of the mind are about to be exhausted, there is both dependence and non-dependence. This can only be understood by ascending a high mountain.
This is illustrated by analogy: the body entering empty space illustrates "non-reliance"; the presence of subtle obstruction below illustrates "reliance.
This is truly because one's own mind has not yet been exhausted, and thus there remains subtle obstruction. ○ Third, the Stage of Patience (Kṣānti).

When the mind and the Buddha are identical, one skillfully attains the Middle Way. Just as when enduring a person, one neither harbors resentment nor feels pride, it is called the "ground of endurance" (kṣānti-bhūmi).
Although one's own mind and the Buddha have not yet merged into one, their substance is not separated; therefore, they are said to be "identical.
One must know that even upon reaching this stage, one's own mind is not yet fully exhausted. The Middle Way is that which the Buddha has realized. "Skillfully attained" means...

It is said that he has "skillfully attained" this because it surpasses the previous state where one took the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind. The following passage provides an analogy for patience (*kṣānti*).

One who practices patience is like someone whose joy or anger does not manifest outwardly. "Neither harboring nor emitting" means that although it ultimately ought to be emitted, it is not yet emitted.
At such a time, it is as if one wishes to vomit it out, yet it is not harbored; because it is concealed within the mind, it is not emitted. This precisely illustrates "skillfulness."
The characteristics of its attainment: Fourth, the Stage of the World’s First Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
When numerical quantities are extinguished and both delusion and awakening are beyond the reach of conceptual designation within the Middle Way, it is called the Ground of the World’s First Dharma.
This follows from the preceding stage of Patience (*kṣānti*). "Mind" and "Buddha" refer to the two categories of enumeration; "sameness" and "difference" refer to the measure.
Now, as both are extinguished, there is nothing to be designated regarding either the deluded Middle Way or the awakened Middle Way.
Reaching this point, where emotional views are both forgotten, although it is not yet the true realization of the Middle Way, one has already attained the foremost rank among worldly beings.
○ The Seventy Stages: 1. The Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Ānanda, when these sons of good family have attained thorough penetration into great bodhi and their awakening penetrates the entire realm of the Tathāgatas, it is called the Stage of Joy.

Among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the first five stages all belong to the essence of awakening (*bodhi*). The first stage states that "awakening penetrates the Tathāgata," and the subsequent four stages all inherit this meaning.
The latter five stages all discuss *tathatā* (suchness). Because *tathatā* is free from arising and ceasing, it is concluded with *nirvāṇa*.
One should know that the essence of awakening, when free from delusion, is precisely named *tathatā*; there are not two.
Regarding the meaning: furthermore, "Bodhi" is named "Great Nirvāṇa" and "Ocean" because these are the two designations for the Tathāgata’s twofold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The three wisdoms are attained within a single moment of mind and are termed "Great Bodhi. This is what was realized at the Tathāgata’s site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) through quiescence;

now, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is well able to thoroughly comprehend it. As the preceding text states: "Sentient beings within the three realms of existence, as well as those who have emerged..."
The world’s śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom the Buddha’s unsurpassed bodhi; it is only upon reaching the stage after the first *vihāra* that they can attain it.
Yet even then, it is not yet called "wholesome" (*śubha*); only now is it for the first time called wholesome. Guishan says:

"Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata, and wisdom is identical to the Buddha-wisdom. I [the present writer] say: since one has reached the ground of non-doubt, the essence of awakening penetrates the Tathāgata.
Why must one necessarily explain "awakening" (jue) through "wisdom" (zhi)? As previously stated, it is only the wondrously awakened clarity that perfectly illuminates the dharma-realm;
even those who have attained this state at the first stage (prathamā-bhūmi) are still bodhisattvas, and thus it is said they "penetrate" the realm of the Tathāgata.

What is called the "Buddha-realm" refers precisely to the principle that the three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way. Therefore, the Dharma...
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Now, when it is said that one "exhausts the realm of the Buddhas," is this not precisely the principle of being able to fathom the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses within a single thought-moment?

To discuss the realm of the Buddhas while setting this aside would, for the most part, merely be the realm of the Bodhisattvas. As for the name "Joyful" (*Prāmodya*), since it has already reached the ultimate...
Because one naturally gives rise to the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*), it receives this name. ○ Second is the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Because the distinct natures enter into sameness and that very sameness is also extinguished, it is named the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.
Regarding "sameness and difference" as mentioned in the root sūtra: as previously stated, the world is "difference" and empty space is "sameness. [The subsequent consciousness...]
The inscription states: "Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they have already attained their sameness. Why, then, should this principle not be applied here?
Because it was previously stated that 'awakening penetrates the Tathāgata,' it is now clarified that while the worlds differ, they enter into the sameness of empty space."

When both emptiness and extinction are also extinguished, one returns solely to the essence of awakening. As it is said: "If one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish.
Now, that the essence of awakening possesses defilement is due to the fact that the realm of emptiness has not yet been eliminated;
once the realm of emptiness is left behind, one is free from defilement. ○ Third, the Ground of Radiance (Prabhākari-bhūmi).
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity arises;

this is called the Ground of Emitting Light (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*). Because it is pure through the departure from defilement, the text says "purity reaches its ultimate limit" by following the preceding passage. To say "luminosity arises" refers to the luminosity of the essence of awakening (*bodhi*).
Previously, it was stated that "obscuration becomes emptiness, and within the darkness of empty obscuration, the binding of darkness constitutes form. Now, regarding the essence of awakening—

Since one has already departed from the realm of emptiness, how could clarity not arise? Because awakening possesses the virtue of wondrous clarity, if one perceives impurity, then clarity will not arise.
Since it is said that clarity arises, it must be the light of *prajñā*-wisdom.
Is this not what is meant by "while all phenomena do not arise, *prajñā* arises"? 4. The Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The stage where clarity reaches its ultimate limit and awakening is perfected is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).

The phrase "clarity reaching its ultimate limit" refers back to the preceding [stage], the Radiant (Prabhākari), for once the light has reached its peak, awakening is such that nothing remains concealed; hence it is called "perfection of awakening.

While the names of the third and fourth stages are both derived from "clarity" (vidyā), the third stage possesses clarity by virtue of having inherited awakening, whereas the fourth stage is characterized by clarity itself.
Returning to the manifestation of awakening, it is named "Blazing Wisdom" (Jvālā-jñāna) because it receives its name from a metaphor; it signifies the final burning away of ignorance and delusion.
○ Fifth is the Ground of Difficult Victory (Sudurjaya-bhūmi).
It is called the Ground of Difficult Victory because it cannot be reached by any [distinctions of] similarity or difference.

The text above states that "clarity is ultimate and awakening is full. Since the essence of awakening is ultimately free from both identity and difference, it further states that "identity and difference cannot reach it.
Not only does the realm of space vanish, but all conditioned phenomena characterized by identity and difference are likewise extinguished.
The preceding text states: "When sameness and difference are clearly elucidated, one consequently establishes 'neither same nor different.
Based on this, it is known that 'neither same nor different' is itself subsumed under sameness and difference.
If this is so, then the three continuities of the world, sentient beings, and empty space are all utterly transcended. This Bodhisattva is most preeminent; how could anyone surpass him? — *Youxi*.
It is said that although one has previously departed from identity and difference, there still remains the presence of images conditioned by identity and difference.
Upon reaching the stages of Blazing Wisdom and Radiant Wisdom, these images conditioned by identity and difference are entirely extinguished; therefore, nothing can be established by them. 6.
The Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nature of *tathatā*, being pure, luminous, and manifest, is called the "Manifest Stage" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Since the three types of continuity have been abandoned, it is not conditioned; therefore, it is called "unconditioned. Regarding the term "*tathatā*":
when the essence of awakening is free from defilement, it is renamed "*tathatā*. This is why it is said to be "pure by nature, luminous, and manifest. Thus, it is true.
It is as if it were present before one's eyes. ○ Seventh, the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*):
It is called the Ground of Far-Going because it reaches the limit of the reality-limit (*tathatā-paryanta*).
Although the reality-limit was partially revealed in the preceding stages, there may have been parts not yet exhausted; by applying further effort, one exhausts it and transcends far beyond.
The stage named "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṃgamā) encompasses both the preceding and succeeding four positions, all of which derive their designation from *tathatā* (suchness). Wuxing said:
"To reach the limit of *tathatā* is precisely the limit of the limitless. Since the principle is already limitless, how could practice approach it?
8. The Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*).
The single mind of True Suchness is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Previously, even at the limit where True Suchness was fully exhausted, there was still effortful application (*prayoga*); now, with this single mind of True Suchness, there is no further effortful application. Therefore, it is named "Immovable. 9. The Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) 2-1.

The Direct Explanation The single mind of True Suchness is called the Immovable Ground. Previously, even at the limit where True Suchness was fully exhausted, there was still effortful application; now, with this single mind of True Suchness, there is no further effortful application. Therefore, it is named "Immovable. 9. The Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) 2-1. The Direct Explanation
The manifestation of the function of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
While the preceding three stages attain the essence of *tathatā*, this stage manifests its function. Zizhong says:
"In the *Avataṃsaka*, this Bodhisattva is said to possess the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and act as a great Dharma-preacher, expounding immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas]."
The meanings of these phrases are inexhaustible; therefore, it is said that "the function of True Suchness (tathatā) is manifested.

That is to say, True Suchness is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), while its function belongs to liberation (vimukti). Furthermore, taking skillful wisdom as its function also belongs to prajñā. Thus, the three virtues (triguṇa) are fully present.
The ten stages elucidated in this sutra all constitute the realization and entry into the essence of the refined and true. This differs in both terminology and intent from what precedes these stages.

Some attempt to correlate the names of the *pāramitās*, such as *dāna* (generosity), with the various stages; however, such interpretations likely incorporate extraneous doctrines that do not accord with the present sutra.
○ Second, the conclusion and clarification.
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merit to perfection;
thus, this stage is also called the "Stage of Cultivation.

"From this point onward" means proceeding from here. Once they have proceeded, there is no further need for cultivation; therefore, the work of cultivation reaches its culmination at the ninth [stage].
It concludes with the Grounds. Because both compassion and wisdom are perfected in the tenth ground, it is said that "merit and virtue are complete.

Thus, the nine grounds are designated as the stage of cultivation (*xiuxi*). One should know that the tenth ground is the fruit of the Bodhisattva’s practice. Youxi remarked: "The ancients doubted this, asking:
'If there is no longer cultivation, how can there be the severing of obstructions? However, the meanings of cultivation and the severing of obstructions are one and the same."
When one first proceeds, these stages are equal; when proceeding a second time, the nine stages involve both cultivation and the severing of hindrances.
On the tenth stage, there is only the severing of hindrances and no further cultivation. This is because the culmination of the merits of compassion and wisdom lies solely in benefiting others.

Furthermore, the fact that one's benefit to others has not yet reached the level of the Tathāgata is also called the subtle obstruction of ignorance. ○ The tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi):
because the wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of Nirvāṇa, it is named the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.
To desire to bestow upon sentient beings the bliss of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* is called the "Cloud of Compassion" (*maitrī-abhra*).

To provide benefit throughout the entire *dharmadhātu* without exerting effort or practice is likened to a "Wondrous Cloud. "Covering" (*chādayati*) means to conceal. The ocean of *nirvāṇa* is endowed with the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

The cloud has a physical form and provides shelter; here, the physical form is a metaphor for the wheel of body (*kāya-cakra*), and the shelter it provides is a metaphor for the wheel of mind (*manas-cakra*).
The metaphor of clouds having sound represents the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*). The Bodhisattva manifests these three wheels to extensively deliver sentient beings.
Having already realized the Nirvana of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), yet not yet having entered the state of concealment, Nirvana is thus called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*);

this concludes the section on the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). The Three Knowledges and the Three Virtues constitute the "Dharma," while the compassionate canopy is termed "clouds. As stated previously regarding the First Ground:
One attains Great Bodhi. Now, the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) are like clouds covering the ocean of Nirvāṇa; as the stage of the Sage draws to a close, one is about to enter the fruit of fruits.
The designation for the two types of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) is thus complete. ○ Eighth, Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). 2.1 Directly explaining Equal Enlightenment.

The Tathāgata flows against the current; the Bodhisattva likewise proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where awakening and the limit intersect, which is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Since entering the stream, there has been progress but no departure. If one is in the state of a Tathāgata, returning from the ultimate truth to the conventional world and emerging as identical with all phenomena is "flowing against the current.
The Bodhisattva follows the stream of the noble stages and enters them; this single emergence and single entry constitutes awakening.
The point where these two limits intersect and both arrive at this place is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). This refers to the intersection of the two limits:
the place where the Tathāgata first emerges and the ground where the Bodhisattva is just about to enter. It is like one person leaving a door and another person entering a door;
since both are within the same doorway, how could they not be equal? Furthermore, it must be understood that the Tathāgata has already entered [the state of fruition] and returned...
The Bodhisattva also arrives at the place from which [the path] first emerges; this does not mean that he has already reached the ultimate stage.
Second, regarding the "Vajra-like Final Mind":
Ānanda, from the mind of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), this awakening is the initial dryness within the Vajra-like Mind that has just been attained.
The Stage of Wisdom (*prajñā-bhūmi*).
The "Vajra-mind" is precisely the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). In the "Ten Samādhis" chapter following the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it says:
"Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Dharma-realm universally by means of vajra-wisdom. The meaning of that passage correctly pertains to Equal Enlightenment.
Regarding "Awakening" (Jue): Since both [stages] possess the name *vajra-prajñā* (diamond wisdom), it can be understood that they belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
This name is obtained because it is capable of shattering the final ignorance, being likened to a diamond (*vajra*). To examine this Awakening in detail:

its name is identical to that of the preceding "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), yet their meanings differ. The former refers to the initial drying up of desire and love; because its wisdom has dried [the defilements], it is called "Dry Wisdom."
The Grounds (bhūmi). Now, this is the initial stage of ignorance where wisdom is merely parched; thus it is named the "Ground of Parched Wisdom" (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi).

How could it be spoken of as being on the same level [as the higher stages]? To explain this passage by saying that the mind which induces [the path] and ultimate reality are ultimately not distinct seems unlikely to be correct.
Regarding this stage, various masters either include it within Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) or establish it as a separate stage.
Wēnlíng (Wǎn'gōng) maintains that this stage is separately opened following the final mind of Equal Enlightenment; this indeed has its own merit.

For, after realizing the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one must further destroy one grade of ignorance before entering Equal Enlightenment, and after the final mind of Equal Enlightenment, one must again destroy one grade of ignorance before entering [the next stage].

"Wondrous Enlightenment" (*Miaojue*) refers to the initial breaking of ignorance immediately following Equal Enlightenment (*Dengjue*). Because one has not yet entered the stream of the Dharma, it is also called "Dry Wisdom" (*Ganhui*).

Now, this specifically indicates the stage of attaining the Ground of Dry Wisdom. However, it is appropriate to include this within Equal Enlightenment and should not be said to constitute a separate rank.
Wu-xing distinguished this, and Tian-ru evaluated it; their explanations are detailed. Some have claimed that Equal [Enlightenment]...
Awakening to the entrance of the Gate of Profound Mystery, one practices the affairs of ordinary beings in reverse.

Re-traversing the previously mentioned stage of Dry Wisdom means re-traversing the Dry Wisdom prior to the stage of Faith; it does not take the initial drying up of ignorance as its meaning. This shall await further examination. ○ The Ninth Stage:
the Position of Subtle Awakening.
In this manner, through twelve layers of single and double stages, one exhaustively perfects wondrous enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.
This summarizes the aforementioned positions and clarifies wondrous enlightenment. Regarding the "twelve layers of single and double," as stated in the subsequent text:
The sixty stages of the sages consist of five layers of twelve, hence they are called "layer upon layer.
Regarding the terms "single" and "multiple," these simply refer to pairs and singles, or odd and even.
For instance, the first cycle is odd, the second is even, the third is odd, the fourth is even, and by the fifth layer, it is again even. Since the preceding deluded views are each...
It possesses twelve categories of beings. Now, reversing this delusion is also called "twelve.

This is because the single stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) completes the preceding Bodhisattva stages to form the number sixty; thus, it possesses the twelvefold layers of both simple and compound forms.
However, one merely counts the Wondrous Enlightenment and does not name that which is realized by the Wondrous Enlightenment, because the previous question asked: "What is meant by..."
Regarding the forty-four minds of the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), you have asked: "To what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of cultivation?

To what destination does one proceed to be called 'entering the stages' (*bhūmi-praveśa*)? What is meant by the name 'Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva' (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bodhisattva*)? These questions have now been fully answered.

Since your question only reached up to Equal Enlightenment, my answer likewise concludes at Equal Enlightenment. Furthermore, the preceding section ends with the mention of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*).
Regarding the stages [of the path]: what is referred to as "twelve" in the middle [of the text] consists of: first, *qianhui* (dry wisdom); second, *xin* (faith); third, *zhu* (abiding);

fourth, *xing* (practice); fifth, *xiang* (orientation); sixth, *nuan* (warmth); seventh, *ding* (summit); eighth, *ren* (patience); ninth, *shidi-yi* (the highest worldly dharma); tenth, *di* (ground); eleventh, *dengjue* (equal enlightenment);

and twelfth, *miaojue* (wondrous enlightenment). Among these twelve, some are single and some are composite; from *qianhui* through *miaojue*, there is only one stage each, which constitutes the single [categories].

The stages of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) and the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-bhūmi*) are repetitive; they may be applied according to the practitioner's needs, yet it is likely that what was previously explained is more appropriate.
○ Third, the general conclusion of the various stages, which has three parts: first, concluding with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding these various stages, one employs the ten profound parables of the diamond-like contemplation of all things as being like illusions;
within *śamatha*, one uses the *vipaśyanā* of the Tathāgatas to cultivate and realize them through gradual and deepening penetration.
The *vajra* is the subject of contemplation (*ālambaka*), while the ten metaphors are the objects of contemplation (*ālambana*). Changshui states:

"In each and every stage (*bhūmi*), one employs the *vajra-like illusion samādhi* (*vajropama-māyopama-samādhi*) to contemplate all phenomena. Based on this, both the *vajra* and the ten profound metaphors belong to the category of contemplative observation.
The *vajra* metaphor represents the wisdom that is capable of shattering [delusion], while the *māyā* (illusion) metaphor represents that which is to be shattered.
This is the Dharma. *Śamatha* is cessation (*śamatha*), and *vipaśyanā* is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). When contemplation is developed from cessation, there is no error.

Cessation can subdue the fetters (*saṃyojana*), while contemplation can sever delusions (*kleśa*), thereby accomplishing pure cultivation and realization. Regarding the "gradual," it means that one does not skip over the stages.
Regarding the "profound entry," it means ascending directly to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). Question: What are the ten kinds of profound metaphors?

Observation: Is this observation based on analogy, or is it an observation in accordance with the Dharma? Answer: The general purport of the *Sūtra of Contemplation* requires that observation be conducted in accordance with the Dharma.
There are both general and specific ways to cultivate observation in accordance with the Dharma.

Generally, one directly contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions, mirages, the moon reflected in water, or flowers in the sky—appearing to exist but lacking reality, such that nothing can be apprehended. This is the [general] discernment.
The mind naturally ceases. Individually, each has its own specific correspondence.

One should contemplate all karma as an illusion, all phenomena as a mirage, all natures as the moon reflected in water, exquisite forms as flowers in the sky, exquisite sounds as echoes in a valley, the buddha-fields of all Buddhas as a city of the gandharvas, all buddha-activities as a dream, and the Buddha-body [as a reflection].
The reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is like a reflection, and the dharma body (dharmakāya) is like a magical creation. Why is this? Because it is ultimately empty and cannot be grasped or abandoned.
If one employs metaphors to represent the Dharma, there is indeed reason for this; for all conceptual discriminations arise from attachment to signs.
The illness of clinging to signs lies in regarding things as real;

yet when one contemplates an image in a mirror or the moon reflected in water, the mind that regards them as real vanishes of its own accord, and the mind of clinging to signs also ceases. Therefore, while facing the mirror directly, the conceptualization of meaning becomes distant.
Once it has passed, there is no lingering habituation; before it is faced, the mind has no prior engagement. It is thus.

To know that the three periods of time are fundamentally equal, such that even the presence of mental thought is like empty space—this may be spoken to those who have attained the meaning through contemplation of the elephant, but it is difficult to explain to those with distracted, coarse, and floating minds. ○ Second, the conclusion by way of gradual stages.
Ānanda, it is because of these three progressive stages that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five levels of the true path to Bodhi.
Although the stages and positions explained above are profound, when one traces their origin, they all derive from these three kinds of gradual progression. Therefore...

One knows that concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arises from concentration; thus, ethical discipline and concentration are the vanguard and must not be lacking.
When the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, this is the essential gateway for practice. Wuxing said: "The three stages of progress (*vṛddhi*) refer to the gradual sequence.

In the text below each of the first three [sections], it is concluded and demonstrated by stating: "This is called the gradual sequence of progressive cultivation. It further states: "From this, gradually..."

The establishment of the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) is based on the practice of the path as it is set forth; it is incorrect to claim that these three refer to the *vajra-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

As for the fifty-five stages, this refers to the progression from the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), excluding the aforementioned stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
Question: For what reason is the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) abandoned, and why is Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) not taken up? Answer:

Since it is called the "True Path to Bodhi," this reveals that Dry Wisdom is not true and that Perfect Enlightenment is not the path. I now maintain that the interpretation provided by Master Wuxing is most appropriate.

However, the meaning of the phrase "capable of successfully accomplishing" encompasses the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). For anyone seeking Buddhahood, one need not worry about failing to attain Bodhi;

rather, one should only worry about failing to find the path. Therefore, this is specifically mentioned. Furthermore, the request previously made by Ānanda actually stopped at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-saṃbodhi*).
(3) Third, the conclusion regarding the heterodox and the orthodox.
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice erroneously.
Changshui (Zongxing) said: "If a practitioner can cultivate and realize according to this, they will attain cessation through non-cessation, and reach the goal through non-arrival."
This is what is called a true practitioner; therefore, it is termed "right contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).

If one were to say that there are no stages or positions at all, but that one merely adheres to principle, this would be equivalent to a false view that denies cause and effect; thus, it is called a "false view. This is also analyzed in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing).
Having finished explaining the stages, the sūtra immediately states: "If one says that one becomes a Buddha by transcending these [stages], then..."

This is what Māra has taught. Wu Xing says: "Since the fifty-five stages are achieved through the three progressive advancements, we now distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox by speaking in terms of contemplation (*guan*).
One must know that apart from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), all practices cultivated by the Three Vehicles belong to heterodox contemplation.
I, the humble writer, maintain that the aforementioned sixty saintly stages are all matters of contemplating the Dharma. ○

The second section concludes by revealing the title of the sutra. This chapter proceeds from the initial section on the "General Mind of Ignorance" within the exposition of cultivation and realization.

Within the section on correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), there are two major chapters: first, the direct explanation of cultivation and realization; second, the conclusion that reveals the title of the sutra.

The foregoing detailed explanation of the dharma of understanding, practice, and realization throughout the entire course of cultivation is now complete. It is now appropriate to conclude with the title.
It was then circulated. This title, "The Middle," is precisely the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) without addition or omission.

Thus, one knows that this sutra not only has its beginning and end perfectly accord with the path of contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), but its very title and meaning also darkly coincide with our own school.
Śākyamuni in the Eastern Land may now be further believed [in his prophecy]. As explained in detail in the "Explanation of the Title," there are now two parts.
First Question:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?"

Gushan said: "The purpose of initiating this sutra is to save Ānanda; therefore, it first opens up the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), and next reveals the perfect practice (*pariniṣpanna-caryā*).

When the practice is perfected, one enters the stages culminating in the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). To leave a model for future generations, there must be both a beginning and an end.
Thus, Mañjuśrī asks about the name of the sutra and the method of upholding it; 'upholding' refers to its circulation. Next...
Answer: Regarding the title and essence of this sutra, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"This sutra is named 'The Supreme Jewel Seal of the Great Buddha-Crown Sitātapatrā,' the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions."

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Great Master [Zhiyi] used the verses of Mañjuśrī to resolve four latent doubts by means of the four aspects of name, essence, substance, and function (*nāma-vastu-śarīra-prayojana*).

Now, the five titles of this present scripture should likewise correspond to these five layers of profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*). The first title is that which determines the essence of the scripture.
Although "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa*) is the name of a mantra, it is also the name of the scripture; for the Tathāgatagarbha-mind pervades all places.

"Great. Is it not the case that the Buddha is honored and his crown protrudes even further above all beings, such that no characteristic can be apprehended—is this not the essence (*tattva*) of the sūtra?
Indeed, "Great" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Buddha" is Prajñā; and "Crown" is Liberation (*vimukti*).

These three characters may be correlated, respectively, with the three chapters on Essence, Doctrine, and Function. However, while they are distinguished according to their nature (*prakṛti*), they must be unified when applied to cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Now, in contrast to the following text:
The secret cause of the Tathāgata is the primary principle (zōng), while the protective and intimate cause is the function (yòng); these alone are designated as the essence (tǐ).

Thus, the essence encompasses the function and pervades all things in their signless state, corresponding to the Great Buddha-Crown (Buddhoṣṇīṣa). Is it not the case that by uniting the three and separating from the nine, this is precisely so?
Yet, although the name now consists of twenty-one characters, only the first three remain in the current title; the remaining eighteen characters are all hidden.
Thus, it is clear that these eighteen characters do not depart from the meaning of the Great Uṣṇīṣa.

Terms such as *Siddhārtha* and others are esoteric names that also extend to the exoteric; because its nature is fundamentally unstained and it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm, it is named the "Great White Parasol."
In the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, impermanence and non-self serve as the preceding seal, while nirvāṇa and quiescence serve as the subsequent seal;
these seals are the words of the Buddha. Now, however, the three Tathāgatagarbhas serve as the supreme jewel-seal. This seal certifies that all phenomena are entirely true in their very nature.
Furthermore, by means of this, the Tathāgata illuminates the entire Dharma-realm, such that not a single characteristic can be found to which a name may be given.
The Pure Sea-Eye. This is just as the *Myōgen* (Wondrous Profundity) takes what the Buddha perceives as the true essence of the *dharmatā*.

Second, the power and function of the fixed sūtra is also called "Protecting and Delivering One’s Kinsmen and Causes. It delivers Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of the innate nature (*prakṛti-bhikṣuṇī*) in this assembly, enabling them to attain bodhi.
Focus the mind and enter the ocean of universal knowledge.
Throughout kalpas, one has been bound by the signs of affection as a primary cause; now, being able to sever this affection and part from the parents of ignorance is true protection.
To deliver others, two individuals are cited as examples to represent the rest; thus, the primary cause serves as the general principle.
The heading: "Two people" is for the sake of clear distinction. Ānanda is the "intimate" one; Mādrī is the "causal" one. Regarding the phrase "attaining the bodhicitta," etc.:
this sutra cuts off craving and exhausts the root of the characteristics of views, tracing them back to the reason why mountains and rivers suddenly arise.
Therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi can be realized; from this point on, one enters the ocean of perfect and universal knowledge that illuminates the three realms through and through.
Thus, the function of this sutra is to reveal the truth by severing craving. Furthermore, the attainment of the bodhicitta may also be termed its "essence" (mūla).
Entering the ocean of universal knowledge may also be termed the "essence" (tattva); however, in contrast to the other two chapters, it here pertains solely to "function. Youxi said:
"Mañjuśrī’s exhortation and guidance is called 'rescue and protection' (trāṇa), while the Buddha’s revelation of the three *tathāgatagarbhas* is called 'deliverance' (vimokṣa).

Thus, while both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are fully encompassed, this specific name is entirely absent from the title of the sutra. Furthermore, regarding "rescuing and protecting one's own causes":
It derives its name from the parasol above. Attaining the bodhicitta comes from the Buddha’s crown; this is the cause.
Entering the ocean of universal knowledge comes from the pure ocean-eye; this is the fruit. III. The Essential Tenets of the Samādhi Sūtra.
It is also titled *The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization*.
The perfect cultivation of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) constitutes the secret cause.
Ānanda’s initial request for the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—the very method by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi—is precisely this secret cause. As it says:
