To explain the three Tathāgata-garbhas in response to this request: because those of the provisional vehicle do not recognize them, they are termed "esoteric" (*mi*).

Alternatively, they may be understood as "esoteric" in the sense of being distant versus proximate; that is, the single contemplation is "distant" while the three contemplations are "proximate. However, this is not necessarily so.
It is as clarified in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where it is stated that the Tathāgata first taught impermanence and subsequently taught permanence, using impermanence to conceal permanence.
Therefore, the eternally abiding is the secret treasury; there is nothing that is not thus regarding bliss, self, purity, and so forth.

Now, this sutra takes non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation. Although it employs the distinct teaching (biejiao) to manifest the perfect and eternal (yuanchang), is this not indeed "secret" (mi)?

Cultivating in reliance upon this constitutes cultivation of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), as exemplified by the singular selection of the faculty of hearing from among the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*viśuddhi*).
Realizing in reliance upon this constitutes realization of the definitive meaning, as exemplified by the sixty stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*).
However, while this sutra involves both provisional means (*upāya*) in its exegesis and the arousal of practice, its clear realization is exclusively perfect (*pariniṣpanna*).

This is because Ānanda’s initial request for the three contemplations included the phrase "the foremost provisional means"; thus, his understanding and practice were associated with the provisional, requiring considerable effort in discernment.

The subsequent clarification of the stages (*bhūmi*) as the ultimate goal is pure and perfect in meaning; yet, the inclusion of the distinct teaching while clarifying the perfect is intended to lead those of the distinct teaching [toward it].

Thus, it is clear that the core essence (*mūla*) of the Sūtra lies in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Based on the secret cause, there are three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which may also be distributed across the three chapters.
In contrast to the other two matters, this belongs exclusively to the core essence; this constitutes the opening and closing [of the exposition].
The meaning of this is as fully explained in the commentary on the title. ○ Fourth, the characteristics of the sūtra’s teaching:
it is also titled *The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*.
The term "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) appears similar to that of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet they are identical only in meaning.

When considered in terms of the chronological periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], it cannot be classified as belonging specifically to the *Avataṃsaka*; rather, it is most appropriately applied above the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
However, this title frequently appears among the sūtras of the Vaipulya period. Wuxing remarked: "Mahāvaipulya refers to the Dharma that is expounded."
"Great" (mahā) is its essence; "vast" (vaipulya) is its function. This refers to the empty *tathāgatagarbha* possessing the function of the non-empty.
Furthermore, "great" signifies constancy and pervasiveness; "direction" (*dharma*) signifies that which serves as a track and sustains; "vast" signifies that which encompasses and enriches.

These correspond respectively to the *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and *vimukti*. They are also the three virtues of the *tathāgatagarbha*. As stated in the *Zhongjing* (Sutra of the Middle), these three characters may be assigned to the essence.

The application of the school is threefold. When these three are combined, one may discuss the characteristics of the teachings (*jiaoxiang*). The name "Wondrous Lotus King" is identical to that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

From the fourth fascicle onward, this present sutra contains the most frequent expressions of "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*). For example, after each has explained their own perfect penetration, the Buddha says:
"In these practices, there is truly no superiority or inferiority. Is this not the bestowing of the great carriage upon each, as in the *Lotus Sutra*?
Is there no difference? That the provisional is identical to the real is the intended meaning of the metaphor of the lotus.

Because he possesses sovereign mastery over all provisional and real phenomena, he is called the "King. As for the phrase "Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," this is the name of the mantra.
As stated in the Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra: "This dhāraṇī mantra can serve as a father; it is..."
It may serve as the mother. Furthermore, it is said that the path of all Buddhas arises from this, making it the parents of the Buddhas;

the title [of this scripture] is now identical to that. Moreover, it should belong to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class. In general, this scripture must be a Vaipulya text that has been opened up to become the *tīrāma* (ghee) stage;
thus, it is its doctrinal characteristic (*jiaoxiang*). However, regarding how a single scripture constitutes two flavors: after the opening and manifestation [of the truth], the former...
The teachings of the four periods all enter the *t’i-mo* (Skt. *amṛta*, the "white nectar" stage). This present sutra is likewise so.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* differs from other sutras. In other sutras, each has its own specific audience; when they harbor doubts and approach the Buddha, the Buddha removes their doubts for them.

Second, distinguishing between the internal and external aspects. First, the internal aspect:
Ānanda, the internal aspect refers to the internal realm of sentient beings. Due to various attachments and defilements, deluded emotions are aroused;

as these emotions accumulate without ceasing, they can produce the water of craving. Therefore, when sentient beings think of delicacies, water flows from their mouths; when they think of... [text continues]
When a person feels pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes; when they greedily seek wealth and treasures, saliva of craving flows from their heart, making their entire body glossy;

when the mind is attached and they engage in sexual intercourse, fluids naturally flow from the two organs of male and female. Ānanda, although these various cravings differ, their resulting entanglements are the same:
moistened by them, one cannot ascend but naturally falls downward. This is called the "internal portion" (ādhyātmika-amśa).
Previously, because the two divisions were distinguished by means of "internal" and "external," it was said that there is an "internal division" and an "external division.
Now, the explanation states that the "internal division" refers to what is within the primary division; that is to say, one cannot transcend the bounds of ordinary sentiment. Jiaoguang says:
To be attached to one’s own natural inclinations is called "within the bounds" (*fennei*); that which is not one's natural inclination is termed "beyond the bounds" (*fengwai*).

Because craving is the root of emotional desire, craving is mentioned first. "Precious delicacies and wealth" refers to various objects of attachment, termed "various defilements of craving" (*zhū ài rǎn*).
"Delusive emotions" refers to affection, resentment, joy, anger, and so forth. Alternatively, it is said that they arise from attachment where there is nothing to be attached to.

"Name" refers to deluded emotion. "Emotion" (*qing*) refers to recollecting, clinging to, and greedily seeking; when this emotion accumulates without ceasing, water flows from the mouth—this is precisely the water of craving that arises.

Question: Since water is produced from the accumulation of emotion, why is it so difficult for water to arise? Answer: It is like human beings; unless one’s emotions are light and settled, one will not shed tears;
it is only when the emotion is heavy that tears flow. However, if one simply observes the water flowing from the mouth, [it is evident].
The human condition has accumulated for a long time. When the mind yearns for delicacies, is this not a deluded emotion arising from defiled attachment?

When water flows from the mouth, is this not the "water of craving" produced by the accumulation of such emotions? Because they greedily seek wealth and treasures, they must be people who possess riches;
therefore, their entire bodies are lustrous and moist. As for the similarity between flowing and congealing: that which flows moves downward.
When congealed, it becomes heavy and stagnant. It is like soil meeting water, which causes it to solidify and not disperse. II. External Factors.
Ānanda, external factors refer to that which lies beyond the sphere of sentient beings. Due to various forms of longing and aspiration, they give rise to empty imaginings (*vikalpa*).

When these imaginings accumulate without ceasing, they can produce a superior vital energy (*vāyu*). Therefore, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure. When the mind maintains [the precepts]...
With the majestic and resolute gaze of mantra-seals, the mind desires to be born in heaven, dreaming of soaring aloft; with the mind fixed on the Buddha-lands, sacred realms manifest in the darkness.
For the sake of serving spiritual friends, one regards one’s own body and life as light. Ānanda, although these various thoughts differ, their quality of being light and buoyant is the same.
Moving with flight-like agility, one naturally transcends without sinking; this is called the "external division" (*bāhyabhāga*).

Because it involves transcendence, it is termed the external division. Observing the precepts, being reborn in heaven, and so forth—these are not merely single matters, but are collectively termed "various aspirations."

"Empty visualization" refers to the visualization of clarity and emptiness; it specifically denotes the mind that upholds the precepts and recites mantras. To visualize continuously without ceasing is also a form of cultivation.
For instance, when one upholds the prohibitive precepts, this does not refer to a mere temporary period, but must span the long duration of months and years before it can truly be called "upholding.
"Superior qi" refers to transcendent and victorious energy; this qi necessarily moves upward, whereas the moisture of water flows downward.
On the contrary, the deluded emotions of those above are also the mind, and the empty imaginings of those today are also the mind. There are no separate phenomena within the three realms;
they are created solely by this one mind. This establishes the essential tenet of this sutra: that all is "mind-only.

Therefore, the text below cites wholesome dharmas to verify the signs of the superior energy that can be generated. Is it not the case that upholding the prohibitive precepts arises from a heart of yearning and aspiration?

Is this not the cultivation of the thought of emptiness and clarity? When the entire body becomes light and clear, is this not because the accumulation of such thoughts without ceasing gives rise to a superior vital energy (*vīrya*)?
As for *dhāraṇī* and *mudrā*, they are like the "Unsurpassed Jewel Seal" in the present sutra; they are also names for mantras.
*Vīrya* (毅) refers to the aspect of heroic vigor. *Xunwen* says: "The 'Mantra for Subduing Poisonous Harm' is the *dharani* of the Buddhas of the three ages."
This is the seal of the bhikṣuṇī. If one performs rites of incantation for dragons and other such malevolent disciplines, it is not its true meaning. The sacred realm manifests in the hidden;
that is, within the sphere of contemplation, one silently beholds the pure lands of the Buddhas, or this sign is secretly communicated within dreams.

Since thought is already flying and moving rather than sinking, sentient beings naturally transcend [suffering]. This refers to "transcendence" (chāoshèng) in the sense of not falling into the three miserable realms.
II. The retributive fruits thus summoned: A. Restating the two causes of habituation.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, birth and death continue in succession. Birth proceeds from habitual conformity; death proceeds from transformative flux.

At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and tactile sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously. Death is contrary and birth is conforming;
these two habits intersect.

To verify whether one ascends or falls, one must examine the cycle of birth and death. In life, one follows one's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); at death, one undergoes a transformation of one’s category of existence.
As the preceding text states: "Sentimental attachments accumulate without ceasing," and again: "Conceptualizations accumulate without ceasing.

Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it says that the active mind produced by past and present habits is itself the habituation. However, the essential crux lies simply in the moment of impending death.
At this moment, both good and evil manifest as karma. At death, one encounters one's habitual tendencies; at birth, one accords with them.

Thus it is said that "the two habits intersect. This single phrase, "the two habits intersect," encompasses in its entirety all subsequent phrases such as "the two habits mutually inflame" and "the two habits mutually devour.
Although various masters offer further interpretations of the subsequent text...
One should consider this accordingly. For instance, when a lustful person sees the instruments of suffering in hell as objects of desire, it accords with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
when they subsequently undergo the suffering of the iron bed and copper pillar, it opposes those habitual tendencies. Thus, it is said that "the two habits intersect. Question:
Although it is thus for those falling into hell, what is the case for those born in heaven? Answer: Based on the time of death, there must inevitably be attachment.
The thought that birth is evil and death is good is also a dualistic habit. Generally speaking, when interpreting the sutras, one must not be restricted to a single path.
The statement that "death is contrary [to the Way] while life is compliant" is said primarily with reference to those who undergo retribution for evil deeds. Youxi said:

"At the moment of death, as long as warmth and tactile sensation have not yet departed"—for a person, consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*) constitute the three factors of life—and at the time of birth, consciousness comes first.
Upon entering the womb, one takes the father’s semen and the mother’s blood as the seed. Thus, there is breath (*āśvāsa*) followed by warmth (*uṣman*).
When these three factors combine, there is birth; when these three factors separate, there is death. At the time of death, one first relinquishes warmth and subsequently relinquishes breath.
After relinquishing the breath, consciousness (*vijñāna*) departs. This is what is meant by the saying: "The one who comes later and goes first acts as the master."
It is so. II. The Five Fruits Attracted: 1. Pure Thought.

One whose thought is purely focused on flight will certainly be reborn in the heavens. If, within that mind of flight, there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, [the result will be even more sublime].
Spontaneously their minds opened and they beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions; all pure lands became accessible for rebirth according to their vows.
One should know that these instances are also cases where the active mind can summon the retribution of pure goodness.

They must be reborn in the heavens at a level above the Four Heavenly Kings. Since they dwell in celestial palaces, they differ from those who merely visit them as transient guests; therefore, in the heavens—
The phrase "the words encompass" refers to all the heavens of the three realms. What follows, stating that they "roam through the four heavens," refers to temporary excursions.

Although these—comprising merit, wisdom, and so forth—are outside the seven destinies, they nonetheless consist of the manifestation of wholesome minds and mental factors in conjunction with the performance of pure, wholesome karma.
This is capable of summoning pure and wholesome fruits. "Comprising merit" refers to the first five perfections. Comprising... [text truncated]
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is *prajñā* itself; pure vows are the mind of formal resolve. To be born in the Pure Land, these three are indispensable;
as Wu-xing said, because merit and wisdom are discussed alongside the "flying mind," they are both termed "concurrent.
You-xi said: "Within the category of 'pure thought' there are two paths: first, birth in the heavens; second, birth in the Pure Land. Regarding the thought of being born in the heavens..."
Taking the ten wholesome deeds of the highest grade as one's karma, one is born in the Pure Land where all four meanings are fully present.
As for the statement that one is "born according to one's vow," this is because the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land takes the three dharmas of faith, practice, and vow as its core;
furthermore, among these three, the pure vow serves as the guiding principle. These four meanings refer to pure thought, merit, wisdom, and the pure vow.
2. When emotion is slight and thought is predominant, one is buoyant and does not travel far; such individuals become flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, or flying yakṣas.
The earth-walking rākṣasas roam through the four continents without obstruction. Among them, there are those who possess virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma;
or those who protect the prohibitive precepts in accordance with those who observe the precepts; or those who protect the divine mantras in accordance with those who hold the mantras.
Some protect meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and preserve the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). These beings dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
There are three kinds of yakṣas: first, those on earth; second, those in the void; and third, those in heaven.
Earth yakṣas, who can only bestow material gifts (*āmiṣadāna*), cannot fly. Sky and heavenly yakṣas, because they bestow vehicles and horses, are able to fly.
The "wholesome vow" is the vow to protect the Dharma; the "wholesome mind" is the mind that turns toward the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Since the prohibitive precepts and the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*) are all the teachings of the Tathāgata, one dwells beneath the seat of the Tathāgata. The patience of the Dharma is necessarily attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Jiaoguang says: "That which is lightly raised does not go far" means that vertically it does not exceed the four heavens, and horizontally it does not exceed [the four continents].
The Cakravāḍa Mountains. Those who travel there merely arrive briefly; they are not like those born in the heavens who dwell there permanently.

"Going" means departing. "To preserve and soothe the patience of the Dharma" (*dharmakṣānti*): "soothe" (*sui*) has the meaning of "peace. The "patience of the Dharma" refers to categories such as the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
Zhenji said: "Sentiment is slight while thought is abundant"—this is a general statement. In principle, it is appropriate to categorize them by equally dividing them into four classes. First:
With nine thoughts of passion, one becomes an immortal who flies. With eight thoughts of passion, one becomes a powerful ghost-king.
With seven thoughts of passion, one becomes a flying yakṣa. With six thoughts of passion, one becomes a land-walking rākṣasa. Youyixi said:
"When passion is slight and thoughts are many, even within these four grades there are two further paths. First, those who lack virtuous vows or a virtuous mind..."

The practice consists of the ten wholesome actions of the lower grade. Second, those who possess wholesome vows and a wholesome mind are for the most part people whose aspiration for the Mahāyāna is urgent while their observance of the precepts is lax;
therefore, they are able to personally dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata to hear the Great Dharma. Third, their emotional attachments and conceptualizations are equalized.
When emotion (*qing*) and thought (*xiang*) are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans. When thought is clear, one is intelligent; when emotion is obscure, one is dull.
Not flying results in being a celestial immortal (*tianxian*); not falling results in being in the three miserable realms (*santuo*).

The five emotions and five thoughts are what is meant by "equality. Because thought is clear, human retribution is intelligent; because emotion is obscure, one is dull compared to celestial immortals. — *Gushan* (Solitary Mountain).
It is said: "The dullness or sharpness of one's faculties today is induced by the emotional attachments (*saṃjñā*) of the past.

Thus we know that what is called 'equality' refers to karma as a collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), while what is called 'the obscure and the luminous' refers to karma as individual retribution (*pratyeka-vipāka*).

Due to the varying strength or weakness of the emotional attachments one has cultivated, there arise differences such as dullness or sharpness. Youxi remarked: "Even within the category of equal emotional attachment, there are two paths. Although the attachment..."
The five faculties differ in their clarity and obscurity. Those with clarity are sharp-witted, and thus possess much wisdom. Although the emotions are likewise fivefold, they also differ in weight;
those that are heavy are dull, and thus are mostly ignorant and deluded. ○ When the four emotions are many and thought is few.

When emotion is excessive and thought is meager, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth; as a heavy being, one becomes part of the fur-bearing beasts, and as a light being, one becomes part of the feathered tribes.

When the seven emotions and three thoughts sink into the water-wheel, one is born at the boundary of fire, receiving breath from fierce flames and becoming a hungry ghost whose body is constantly consumed by burning.
Water can harm oneself; for a hundred thousand kalpas, one has neither food nor drink. With nine feelings and one thought, one descends through the wheel of fire.
The body enters the ground where wind and fire intersect, resulting in rebirth in either of two types of hells: the Intermittent (Sāntara) or the Uninterrupted (Avīci).

Changshui says: "Cross-born" refers to animals (tiryagyoni). Yet there are degrees of lightness and heaviness: if the emotional affliction is somewhat heavy, one is reborn as a running beast, hence they are called the "furry multitude";
if the conceptual thought is somewhat strong, one becomes a flying bird, hence they are called the "feathered tribes.
Regarding those who sink into the water-wheel and are born at the boundary of fire, the ancient interpretation holds that they are near to the hells; this explanation is most correct.
However, because there is fire within the water, the lower limit of the water wheel (*āpa-maṇḍala*) is the boundary of the fire wheel (*tejo-maṇḍala*). This is precisely what was stated previously:

"Because the light of fire rises upward as steam, there is a water wheel that contains the realms of the ten directions. Based on what was explained in the preceding text, it is beyond doubt that there is fire beneath the water.
Regarding the statement that "water can harm itself," the ancient commentary says: "Even if one were to obtain water to drink, it would transform into fire."

This is most so. For although ghosts receive their vital energy from fierce fire, taking fire as the cause of their birth, if one further assists them with fire, it will inevitably lead to great harm.
Thus, even that which they consume entirely becomes fierce fire.

It can be known that there is no food or drink there. "Pervasive" (dòng) means penetrating through. The lowest part of the dwelling place is called the Ground of the Convergence and Passage of Wind and Fire.
At the very bottom of the Great Earth is the wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Since this [fire] now penetrates the fire-wheel, it is close to the wind-wheel.
As the preceding text states: "Because the firm awareness is formed from jewels and the shaking radiance produces wind, there is the appearance of fire as a transformation."
Regarding the nature of transformation: based on this, wind and fire must necessarily meet.

It should be understood that this place is not yet the Wind Wheel (*vāyumaṇḍala*), but is called the "Ground of the Convergence and Passage of Wind and Fire," meaning that wind and fire intersect and pass through this location.

Those who suffer the harm of wind shall be reborn in the eight cold hells; those who suffer the harm of fire shall be reborn in the eight hot hells. One must know that although there are [other factors] within the hells...
Fierce winds and great fires likewise establish the hells according to the natural topography of the ground;

thus it is said that within the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings), there are also original lands. If those in cold hells obtain warmth and those in hot hells obtain coolness, this constitutes an "interval" (*sāntara*);
if one experiences suffering exclusively and continuously, this is "without interval" (*ānantarya*).孤山 (Gushan) says: "These are precisely the seven hot hells."
There are inherent degrees of gravity [in karmic offenses], yet this [present] Avīci is not one of the five *ānantarya* (immediate) hells;

it is only the eighth hot hell, Abhiṣaṇḍa, mentioned in the subsequent text that is designated as the "five *ānantarya*. Furthermore, ancient commentaries maintain that this is not among the three wheels beneath the earth, as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"At the very bottom of the great earth are the wheels of gold, water, and wind; there are eight cold and eight hot hells."
Regarding the phrase "above the three wheels": this text states that one sinks beneath the water, fire, and wind wheels, which suggests being below the three wheels as if in hell.
It is suspected that what is indicated here refers not to the three wheels beneath the earth, but rather to the three wheels of hell.
I have privately examined this passage. It accords with the preceding four fascicles regarding the rising of fiery light, the swaying of radiant wind, and so forth;
that is to say, the establishment of the world has always been thus. Why need it necessarily be the three wheels beneath the earth?
Moreover, since it already mentions the "three wheels of hell," why would hungry ghosts also be born therein? I fear this explanation may not be definitive.
If these do not accord with the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is because the Sautrāntika school follows different precedents in many such instances. Youxi said:

"When the mental factors (*caitta*) are predominant and the primary mind (*citta*) is subordinate, they are divided into four categories. However, regarding the realms of rebirth (*gati*), there are only three types.

Within these three, each is further divided into light and heavy degrees to explain the retribution received. Two of these clarify the opening [of the path], while one has a hidden meaning. If one were to analyze them..."
Thus, the light [offense] results in having wealth, while the heavy [offense] results in having no wealth. ○ Fifth, pure affliction:

if one sinks into the Avīci Hell due to pure affliction—specifically if, with a deeply submerged mind, one slanders the Mahāyāna, violates the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, speaks deceptive and false teachings, vainly covets offerings of faith, unworthily receives respect, or commits the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts—the retribution will extend throughout the ten directions.

Avīci Hell. Wēnlíng says: "Avīci" here means "without interval. This refers to the five things—receiving punishment, suffering, the physical form, the duration of the kalpa, and the lifespan—all of which lack any intervening gap;
hence it is called the "Five Uninterrupted [Sins]. Only those whose emotional karma is most grave fall into this realm.

One enters [the Avīci hell] and remains until the kalpa is destroyed before finally emerging. If one additionally commits the sin of slandering the Mahāyāna and so forth, then even when this kalpa is destroyed, one re-enters the Avīci hells of the ten directions with no prospect of release.
Master Yu said: "Those who slander the Dharma cause countless beings to give rise to false views;
those who destroy the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts include such as the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmā, who practiced deception and falsehood."
The Dharma is like those such as Sunakṣatra, who falsely preached that dharmas are empty;

they greedily accepted the faithful offerings of others without merit and received the veneration of others without virtue, even committing the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses—all of whom are destined for the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions.
Youyixi said: "Those of pure delusion in the uninterrupted hells are also divided into two categories: the first are those who do not slander the Mahāyāna."

The Avīci Hell of those who emerge after the kalpa’s destruction is exhaustible; however, the Avīci Hell of those who, for instance, slander the Mahāyāna and do not emerge even after the kalpa’s destruction is inexhaustible.
Slandering the Mahāyāna and committing the five heinous crimes or the ten grave offenses involve both monastics and laypeople;
whereas violating the Buddha’s prohibitions and so forth—these four types of offenses—reside solely within the monastic community. Therefore, for those who are practitioners of the Way...
If one has not yet emptied their thoughts, they should first empty their emotions. Once one is involved in emotion, it becomes a step toward losing one's footing;

how much more so when pure emotion reaches the point of the inexhaustible Avīci Hell? ○ Second, a detailed explanation of the sevenfold cause and effect of that which invites and that which is invited:

The ancient edition reads "yuan" (enmity) instead of "yuan" (resentment). Changshui says: "Yuan" means hatred; having anger as its precursor, it takes the nature of harboring malice without relinquishing it, thereby forming a grudge.

I now maintain that "yuan" carries the sense of an enemy with whom one cannot share the same sky—such as Yan Zhongzi’s stabbing of the Chancellor of Han, or Zi Xu’s flogging of King Ping’s corpse—which is precisely what is termed "the habituation of enmity. therefore, it is said to differ from the habitual practice of deception. "To add" (*jia*) means to inflict [punishment] upon a person. "Mounting together" (*he shan*) refers to seeing [the truth].

Two mountains come together so that the sinner has no place to flee; the closing of the rocks is like this. The grinding mill and the plowing and crushing are all manifestations of oppression and harm.
Because one desires at such times to reduce others to minced powder, one invites this retribution.
"Slanderers and thieves" refers to the principle that the fruit experienced corresponds to its cause. ○ Second, the state of the mutual intermingling of habitual tendencies.
Because the two habitual tendencies oppose one another, there arise various matters such as pressing down, crushing, squeezing, straining, weighing, and measuring.
"Opposing" means that contrary habits oppose favorable habits. "Pressing down" refers to the mind being unwilling to submit, so one forcibly presses it down and suppresses it.
"Crushing and pressing" refers to the will being dissatisfied, so one forcibly presses it down and strikes it with blows.
"Squeezing and filtering" (*cùlù*) refers to clenching the hands and feet and pressing them down to filter out the blood. *Suǒyǐn* (Sōuyǐn) states:

"Balancing and measuring" (*héngdù*) means balancing to weigh lightness and heaviness, and measuring to determine length and shortness; all these are for the purpose of determining the nature of the offense so that there is no room for evasion.
○ Thus, the Three Sages and Worthies rebuked and rejected [such punishments].

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate those who harbor malice and slander as "slanderous tigers" (*chán-hǔ*). When a Bodhisattva encounters such injustice, it is like being struck by a bolt of lightning.
To harm others through speech is called "slander" (*chán*); that which can injure others is called a "tiger" (*hǔ*). Not knowing where it originates, [this vice] is exceedingly grave.
The fearsome is like a thunderclap. ○ Tenth, the habit-energy of litigation: first, the habit-energy of compliance already contains the habit-energy of resistance.
"Tenth" means that the clamor of litigation arises from concealment within the storehouse-consciousness. Because it is thus, there is the illumination of clear discernment;
it is like being unable to hide one's shadow in the midst of the sun.
Since I conceal it, he will surely bring forth the dispute; therefore, concealment itself is the habituation of litigation.

I wish to hide it, yet others bring it forth, and thus it results in clamorous contention. This is a situation that runs contrary to one's own inclinations even while within the midst of those inclinations.

The mirror that reflects and illuminates—what is commonly called the "karmic mirror stand"—is precisely this. That one cannot hide one's shadow even in the midday sun merely serves as a metaphor for the objective realm experienced through one's karma.
[Section Two: The state of the mutual intermingling of the two habits.
Because the two habitual tendencies confront one another, there are "evil friends," the "karmic mirror," and the "fire-pearl" that reveal past karma and provide verification for various matters.
The two habitual tendencies confront one another in such a way that the contrary habits are laid bare by the favorable habits. "Evil friends" refers to those who act as witnesses.
Fellow wicked people testify to their litigation; the karma-mirror and fire-jewels can both illuminate their right and wrong.
Third, the sages and worthies censure and reject them.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize concealment as "hidden thieves" (śatru). When Bodhisattvas see concealment...
It is like carrying a high mountain while treading upon a vast ocean.
The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The 'hidden thief' refers to secret plotting and malicious injury.
To 'carry a high mountain' means that one’s intent to conceal [the evil] instead results in self-oppression; looking down upon a bottomless abyss, there is no ground left for standing. Wēnlíng says:
The ten habitual practices arise from the ten delusions, encompassing both the fundamental afflictions and their secondary derivatives. There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):

the first are anger, resentment, vexation, concealment, deception, flattery, arrogance, and injury. Here, "fraudulent practice" corresponds to flattery; "enmity" corresponds to resentment; "injustice" corresponds to injury;
and "litigation" corresponds to concealment. This is merely a brief illustration. Youxi said: "Since the ten habitual practices belong to the fundamental [afflictions]..."
Following [the primary afflictions], there are six roots of affliction, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view.

Alternatively, when expanded, there are twenty secondary afflictions: anger, enmity, resentment, concealment, deception, guile, arrogance, harmfulness, jealousy, stinginess, lack of shame, lack of dread, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, lethargy, restlessness, forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction. Now...
The habit of lust is the karma produced by it, which is fully endowed with greed and delusion. The habit of deceit is flattery. The habit of resentment is enmity. Views refer to the five views.
Oppression refers to the subjugation of the virtuous and is comprised within harm; it is also a category of anger.
Litigation refers to mutual dispute over gain and loss, as it corresponds to the nature of the single dharma of affliction preceded by resentment. These ten habits above are—

This is explained in terms of the conditions that attract retribution to clarify the stages of cultivation and realization. Although there are ten such states, they are merely the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of greed, anger, and delusion, differing only in their combinations and permutations.
When applying contemplation, one should rely on the "neither-walking-nor-sitting samādhi" from the fourth chapter of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
One should allow the three natures to operate freely while maintaining awareness within them; as long as the mind arises, one may immediately apply contemplation.
This serves to manifest the inconceivable realm; one need not fear its vastness. As it is said: "Provided there are fish, however large, they are all excellent.
This concludes the detailed answer regarding how the ten causes of habitual practice can summon their retributions. 2. The six types of intersecting retributions summoned [by those causes].
2-1. General explanation.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, all sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses; the evil retributions they thereby attract emerge from the six sense organs.

Regarding the active causes and habitual tendencies, according to the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), there are only the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The present mention of "six consciousnesses" does not contradict this.

The mind is the sovereign. That is to say, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the mental factors (*caitta*), as well as the minds of sensation, perception, and formation, are also capable of giving rise to evil.

As for those who commit transgressions in conjunction with the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*): since consciousness emerges from the organs, it is created by the organs and returns to the organs to receive [the results].
Wu Xing said: "In the creation of karma and the summoning of retribution, the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) must necessarily coexist.

That consciousness is now designated as the 'karma' while the retribution is attributed to the faculties is because karma generally arises from the mind, whereas retribution mostly pertains to form (*rūpa*). This is what is called the 'sixfold mutual retribution.'"
Master Jun said: "In that case, cause and effect intersect; now it is not so. Rather, it is simply that at the time of the fruit, the six faculties interact with the retribution for evil.
Youxi said: "The subsequent text clarifies each point individually:

that one faculty receives the retribution while the other five faculties receive it along with it, this is brought about by the six types of confused deluded thoughts. Did we not say previously? Therefore..."
In the world, sound exists because of movement; form exists because of sound; fragrance exists because of form; flavor exists because of fragrance; touch exists because of flavor;
and mental objects (*dharma*) are known because of touch. Because these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions [of existence] revolve from this.
Since that clarifies the root of the twelve classes of living beings, it is called "exhausting the twelve transformations."
This constitutes one cycle of retribution. Now, these six mutual retributions belong to the class of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

When they first created the ten causes of habituation, it was necessarily through a single faculty that they committed offenses, yet their six disordered delusions rushed outward in flight, creating them in concert with that [offense].
Therefore, while retribution is received by one faculty, the other five faculties receive it together with it; they merely alternate as host and guest.
This likewise clarifies the distinctions among the six intersections; this is precisely the retributive fruit that is summoned. ○ Second, specifically indicating [the source], part one:
the inquiry. It asks:
How is it that evil retribution issues forth from the six sense organs?

Previously it was stated that the evil retributions they attract emerge from the six sense organs; thus, because the organs and the retributions intersect, they are called the "sixfold intersecting retributions" (*ṣaḍ-vyāmiśra-vipāka*).
Now, he raises an inquiry: "How can evil retributions emerge from the six sense organs? This further clarifies the meaning of the "sixfold intersection.
Furthermore, it is said: "First, regarding the retribution of seeing which attracts and induces evil fruits—the fruit itself belongs to the retribution, and this too is an organ."

Regarding the meaning of the interaction between retribution and perception: although it is said that this "interaction of seeing and karma" refers to the interaction between karma and the sense organs, because karma transforms into retribution, it is further stated that "first one sees a fierce fire," which fundamentally refers to the interaction between retribution and the sense organs.

If one were to say it is an interaction between karma and its fruit, the meaning would seem inconsistent. Second, the indication of the six [aspects]: first, the retribution of seeing; second, the single heading.
First, seeing that retribution invites evil results.
Second, explaining the three types of visions at the time of death:
when one’s karma manifests, at the moment of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the worlds of the ten directions.
Wenling says: "Because seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, they evoke a fierce fire. Wuxing says: "First seeing the fierce fire is the retribution in the present life;
the deceased’s consciousness and so forth constitute the retribution upon rebirth. II. The initial signs of entering hell.
The consciousness of the deceased flies down and descends, riding upon smoke to enter the Avīci Hell.

Because the element of fire ascends first, it flies before it falls. Wēnlíng says: "The fact that all six modes of interaction enter directly into Avīci is stated for emphasis regarding the most serious cases.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because of extreme goodness or extreme evil, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Therefore...
Direct entry. ○ Third, the signs after entering hell; these are further divided into two: first, the manifestation, and second, the signs.
Regarding the manifestation of the two signs: the first is clear vision, by which one can see all manner of evil things everywhere, giving rise to immeasurable fear.
Second is seeing in darkness. Being silent and seeing nothing, one gives rise to immeasurable fear.
As previously explained in the section on "seeing," one sees both light and dark; now, entering hell is likewise so. Master Yu said:
"Because people in the human world commit various evil deeds with eyes wide open and hearts bared, possessing a mind entirely devoid of fear, they therefore see all manner of evils here within."
Beings give rise to immeasurable fear. What are called "evil things" include such entities as iron snakes, bronze dogs, sword-trees, knife-mountains, and the ox-headed *āpāpas*.

Because one committed various evil deeds while secretly deceiving others in the human realm, remaining complacent and unconcerned, one now finds oneself here in total silence with nothing to see, giving rise to immeasurable terror. Indeed, fear arises from objective conditions.
Yet one fears they may be hidden within the mind. ○ Second, the six sense organs interact:
such a vision of fire can burn hearing into boiling cauldrons and molten copper; it can burn the breath into black smoke and purple flames.
The burning of flavors can turn them into scorched balls of iron gruel; the burning of touch can turn it into hot ash, furnaces, and charcoal;
the burning of the mind can produce sparks that scatter upward and fan the expanse of space.
Wenling says: Hearing belongs to the element of water; therefore, when hearing is burned, it can become boiling cauldrons and molten copper. The nose governs the breath;
therefore, when the breath is burned, it can become black smoke and purple flames. The tongue governs taste; "wheels" and "porridge" represent the category of flavors. The body governs touch;
"ash" and "charcoal" represent the category of tactile sensations. The mind properly belongs to fire; when it is burned, it blazes even more fiercely, so that sparks fly and scatter into the void.
Regarding the element (*dhātu*): the text states that the mind fundamentally belongs to fire; when discursive thoughts proliferate and burn it, it becomes like sparks.

"To scatter" (*bèngsǎ*) means to scatter them all at once. A dictionary defines "to scatter" (*bèng*) as to run away or escape. One faculty (*indriya*) creates karma while the other six faculties assist it;
therefore, when one sees fire, it burns through all six faculties. 2. Hearing the Report: Part One, the Title.
Second, hearing reports that invite and draw forth evil retributions.
Regarding the second [section], the threefold explanation: first, the signs seen at the time of death.
When this karma of hearing intersects with other conditions, at the moment of death one first sees oneself submerged in waves, drowning in heaven and earth.
According to this, karma intersects with the faculties; when karma transforms into retribution, that retribution then intersects with the faculties.
○ Second, the initial signs of entering hell:
the deceased’s spirit-consciousness descends and flows into the Avīci Hell.
"Descending and pouring" refers to flowing downward. ○ Third, the two signs that appear after entering hell: first, the sign of manifestation; second, the sign of illumination.
Regarding the sign of manifestation, there are two: first, open hearing, wherein one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes confused and disordered; second, closed hearing.
In profound silence there is nothing heard, and the dark souls sink away. Tongzhou said:
"The two objects grasped by the faculty of hearing—movement and stillness—create all manner of karma; now one receives their retribution, which likewise depends on these two.
When the ears are open, it is movement; when they are closed, it is stillness. Xunwen said: "To be 'disturbed' means to be bewildered and confused. Above...

"Yin" (音) is read as "zhì" (質) in the second character; it means "foolishness. (Textual Note: Within the realm of darkness and obscurity, they appear to possess a physical form and undergo the suffering of drowning.
Hence it is said: "The dark souls are submerged. Second, the six sense organs interact.

Thus it is with the waves of hearing: when they enter through the ears, they can act as reproach and interrogation; when they enter through the eyes, they can act as thunder, roars, and poisonous vapors;
when they enter through the breath, they can act as rain and mist, drenching all venomous insects over the entire body.
If one focuses on flavor, it can manifest as pus, blood, and various kinds of filth; if one focuses on touch, it can manifest as animals, ghosts, excrement, or urine;
if one focuses on thought, it can manifest as lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.
Regarding the phrase "spraying poisonous insects," this refers to the scattering and spraying of poisonous insects within rain and mist.

Aquatic creatures such as fish, turtles, and the like, as well as ghosts that also exist within the water—all these undergo transformations according to their forms, and all constitute harmful contact (*duṣṭa-spraṣṭavya*). Wuxing remarked:
"The previous passage spoke of seeing fire, while this one speaks of hearing waves; various explanations have not clarified this. Now, I shall examine it in detail based on proximate meaning."
As the *I Ching* says: "Li represents the eye and fire; Kan represents the ear and water. It seems that seeing and hearing are fundamentally based on the natures of fire and water;
thus, they manifest as the phenomena of burning and pouring forth. Wénlǐng says: "Hearing belongs to water;
therefore, when the hearing is turned back through contemplation, water cannot drown one. Yet, if one relies upon it to create karma, one can be moved by waves and surges. (End of quotation)
Because hearing produces sound, it serves as the basis for censuring faults and interrogating circumstances. The commentary notes that being able to produce a thunderous roar refers to this.
Hearing belongs to the Yin, while seeing fire belongs to the Yang; because Yin and Yang clash with one another, thunder is formed.

The commentary notes that "stopping" (the faculty of smell) becomes rain and mist, for water changes according to the qi. The commentary notes that "taste" becomes pus and blood, for water changes according to the flavor. The commentary notes "touch."
For animals and ghosts, water transforms according to their form. For those with focused intent, thunder and hail arise from the mind; this is the mutual resonance of water and fire.
There is no physical phenomenon that does not undergo transformation by means of the five elements and the interaction of yin and yang.
Therefore, all matters concerning the transformation according to the faculties do not transcend these principles. [Section Three: Rebirth through Smell; Part One: The Heading.]
Third, the retribution of smelling invites and draws forth evil fruits.
○ Second, the explanation of the three [stages]: first, the signs seen at the time of death.
When this karma of smelling intersects with one's life, then at the moment of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.
Zizhong said: "The olfactory faculty creates karma by greedily inhaling various fragrances; thus, one summons poisonous vapors to undergo their retribution.
Second, the initial signs of entering hell:
the deceased’s consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell."
Those who emerge from the earth have nostrils that appear to have holes. Because their breath must ascend from below, they emerge from the earth;
furthermore, because it must descend from above, they enter the Avīci Hell. III. The Signs Following Entry into Hell, Part One:
The Manifestation of Two Signs.
This explains two types of symptoms: first, "open hearing," where the mind is extremely disturbed by being permeated by various noxious vapors;
second, "blocked hearing," where the vapors obstruct the channels so that one faints and falls to the ground.
II. Interacting with the Six Faculties:
When such odors strike the breath, they can become solid matter or a path; when they strike the eyes, they can become fire or a torch;
when they strike the ears, they can become submersion, drowning, melting, or boiling; when they strike the sense of taste, they can become hunger or refreshment.
If one collides with it, it can cause one to split open and rot; one becomes a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes, which insatiably devour one.
If one thinks of it, it can turn into ash and pestilence; it becomes flying sand and gravel that shatters the body.

"Abundant brine" refers to its appearance when it overflows. "Contacting the body" means that the body becomes a great mountain of flesh, wherein hundreds of thousands of pores are inhabited by immeasurable worms that gnaw and devour it.
"Becoming ash and so forth" means that when the mind is distracted and agitated, one contracts a toxic vapor and turns into ash and sand;
"miasma" (*jang*) is also a toxic vapor. Gushan says: "When fish spoil, they are called 'putrid' (*nai*); when soup spoils..."

It is said: "Slight" (*shuǎng*). Wēnlíng says: "Substantiality and obstruction. "Treading" (*lǚ*) means penetration. The basis upon which smelling depends does not depart from penetration and obstruction;
therefore, the energy of impact (*chōng*) can constitute substantiality and treading.

When the perception of sight becomes a torch, and the perception of hearing becomes drowning in a boiling ocean, it is clear that the faculty of seeing belongs to fire and the faculties of hearing and smelling belong to water. It becomes hunger and slightness, as flavor follows the breath.

It is transformation. The body, becoming frayed, torn, and decayed, follows the changes of the vital energies (*qi*). "The agitation of thought becomes ash and sand, depending on the earth" means that thought depends on the sensation of the earth element.
Wénlíng says: "Depending on the sensation of the earth" refers to the fact that the spleen governs thought, and the spleen belongs to the earth element.
[Section Four: The Retribution of the Four Flavors; Part One: The General Statement.]
Fourth, the retribution for flavors invites and draws forth evil fruits.
Changshui remarked: "The tongue-root commits the most extensive offenses. First, because of craving flavors, one commits the offense of slaughter, which is necessarily frequent;

second, because it initiates speech and creates karma, its offenses are again extensive. Now, since it is said that the 'retribution for flavors' is mostly the retribution for craving flavors," [it follows that this refers to the physical experience of taste].
Changshui’s citation of false speech and so forth is merely a secondary point; however, as they cannot be dispensed with, both should be employed.
II. Explanation of the Three: 1. Signs Seen at the Time of Death.
When this karmic retribution for the sense-object of taste intersects with other actions, at the time of death one first sees an iron net of fiercely blazing flames covering the entire world.
Because the tongue-root has committed transgressions that are like a snare, leaving nothing uncovered, one thus first sees the iron net at the moment of death.
Just as there is no one who is not burned by a great fire, they again behold fierce flames; this resembles the retribution for false speech.
Second, the initial signs of entering hell:
the deceased’s consciousness descends and passes through, becoming entangled in a net with its head hanging downward as it enters the Avīci Hell.
Dropped down through the hanging net, their heads hang upside down, as if their consciousness were submerged within the flavors;
this is also the retribution for speaking perversely. ○ Third, the signs after entering hell: Part One, the manifestation of the two signs.
It elucidates two aspects: first, the inhalation of breath, which forms freezing ice that cracks the flesh of the body;
second, the exhalation of breath, which flies forth as fierce fire that scorches and rots the marrow of the bones.
Changshui said: "Inhaling draws in flavors; exhaling results in the utterance of speech. I now say that one should not take this view exclusively.
Even the utterance of speech possesses a quality of being sometimes cold and sometimes hot.

Those who crave flavors may crave its coldness or crave its heat—just as one distinguishes between the taste of pickled fish, submerged plums, boiling soup, and hot broth, each bringing a different pleasure.
Therefore, inhaling the breath belongs to the Yin and is associated with cold ice; exhaling the breath belongs to the Yang and is like a fierce fire.
○ Second, traversing the six sense organs:
thus tasting flavors, if one traverses them through tasting, they can serve as support and endurance; if one traverses them through seeing, they can serve as burning gold and stone.
When experienced through hearing, it can become sharp weapons; when experienced through inhalation, it can become a great iron cage covering the entire land;
when experienced through touch, it can become bows, arrows, crossbows, and projectiles; and when experienced through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
"Enduring" (*kṣānti*) refers to receiving and enduring all foul odors; it is the perception that what belongs to fire is burning metal and stone.
As the saying goes, "The mouths of the multitude can melt gold"—this is the retribution for slandering others.
"Sharp weapons" refers to the sound of striking sharp blades together; the breath, originally empty and floating, becomes an iron net—this is the person who fabricates charges.

This is the retribution. It is also the retribution for capturing various flavors in a net. Wénlǐng says: "Because one harms creatures by touching their flavors, one feels the sensation of being wounded by bows and arrows oneself;
speaking is likewise so. A *nǔ* (crossbow) is also a type of bow. The Yellow Emperor first created the crossbow. *Nǔ* means "wrath" (*nù*). Its handle is called the *bì* (arm);

the hook that engages the string is called the *yá* (fang-tooth). Outside the *yá* is the *guō* (guard-rim); the lower part is called the *xuánlì* (suspended power). These names combined are as follows: [text continues].
It is said: "The mechanism. This refers to the skillfulness of a mechanical device. Just as an arrow shot from a crossbow flies forth, so too does the speech that issues from emptiness arise;
likewise, the thought that contemplates flavors also issues from emptiness. Therefore, it evokes the falling of flying iron from the sky like rain.

Fifth, the retribution of contact invites evil fruits.
[Section] Two: Explanation of the Three. First, the signs seen at the moment of death.
When this karma of contact intersects, then at the time of death, one first sees great mountains approaching from all four sides, closing in so that there is no way out.

The five objects of experience are all *niśrita-vipāka* (dependent retribution), yet among them, touch (*spraṣṭavya*) is the most prominent as dependent retribution. For example, palaces and dwellings are all touches of dependent retribution;

when they are cool or warm and agreeable to one's wishes, people collectively seek them. Because one creates karma based on these, at the moment of death one sees the four mountains closing in from all sides.
Is it not therefore true that the ancients took the physical bodies of men and women to illustrate the meaning of touch?
However, this is merely the very first stage of contact. For those with no way out, there is no escape. II.
The Initial Signs of Entering Hell:
The deceased’s consciousness perceives a great iron city, filled with fire-serpents, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, ox-headed hell-wardens, and other such beings.
Horse-headed rākṣasas, wielding spears and lances, drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell.
What the ancients called "contact with the foul and mixed sensations" refers to those who, while alive, sought the pleasures of dwelling and companionship, seeking out people to their liking.

Regarding objects of play and luxury: what is seen now upon entering hell is the initial sign. III. The signs after entering hell have two parts: A. The manifestation of the signs; B. The two types of tactile contact.
A. The manifestation of the two signs:
first is *saṃsparśa* (contact by union), where mountains press against the body until the flesh, bones, and blood are crushed; second is *viparīta-sparśa* (contact by separation).
"Swords and blades touch the body and mind, carving and tearing the liver.
Wénlíng says: "The basis of the karma of contact does not transcend separation and union; 'carving and tearing' refers precisely to the characteristic of separation.
○ Second, the six sense organs intersect.
Thus, when combined with touch, it can act as a path, a contemplation, a hammer, or a board; when applied to sight, it can act as a burner, a heater;
when applied to hearing, it can act as a striker, a blower, a thrusting spear, or an arrow;
when applied to the breath, it can act as a clamp, a bag, a torture, or a bond; and when applied to taste, it can act as a plow, a pincers, a hatchet, or a saw.
Reflecting upon this, one realizes that [the body] can fall or fly, and can be roasted or grilled.
Previously, one craved the tactile sensations of dwellings—whether cool or warm—to suit one's fancy; now, one sees the path leading to hell and the place where punishments are meted out.
Observing this text, it becomes clear that the dwellings and paths of the world are indeed nothing but tactile sensations. As Guxiang said: "In ancient times, whenever..."
The gates, trees, and two watchtowers stand before it to mark the palace; one may dwell upon them, and ascending them allows for a distant view, hence they are called *guān* (watchtowers).
When ministers are about to attend court, they reflect upon their deficiencies upon reaching this place, hence they are called *què* (gate-towers).
Burning constitutes the sensation of heat for the body; burning is what is seen by the eye, while heat is what is experienced by the body. To strike [the bell]...
Striking and the like constitute the tactile objects (*spraṣṭavya*) of the ear category. *Zì* (pronounced *zì*) means to stab a blade into the body; *shè* means to insert an arrow into the body.
Binding in a bag and the like constitute the tactile objects of the nose category. "Binding" (*kuò*) means to tie up; binding [the nose] in a bag prevents the passage of air.

The breath fundamentally depends upon the body; when it undergoes the most severe transformation, it becomes the "torture" (kāraṇā) bond. Plowing and tongs constitute the contact of the mouth-faculty (*mukha-āyatana*):

plowing refers to the tongue, while tongs refer to the cutting and severing of the teeth. Flying and falling constitute the contact of the mind-faculty (*manas-āyatana*), because through volition (*cetanā*) one either ascends or descends, or experiences feverish affliction.

When this karma of thought intermingles, then at the moment of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing and destroying the land.
When delusive thoughts stir within, the wind-wheel arises without; it is clear that such thinking can evoke an evil wind.
○ Second, the initial signs of entering hell:
the deceased’s consciousness is blown upward into the void, then whirled down and carried by the wind to fall into the Avīci Hell.
Whether ascending or descending, they are tossed about by the wind. III. The signs following entry into hell, which consist of two parts: first, the manifestation of the signs;
second, the clarification of the two signs. First is non-awakening: when delusion reaches its extreme, one wanders aimlessly and runs on without ceasing. Second is non-delusion.
When one becomes aware [of this], suffering is immeasurably scorching and its pain is so deep as to be difficult to endure.

Regarding the faculty of the mind (*manas*), there are two states: darkness and clarity. Lack of awareness is darkness; awareness is clarity. "Wasteland" (*huang*) refers to the disordered state of the spirit and thought.
It is a natural principle that from bewilderment and distress, one arrives at such wasteful disorder. Although it is the body that runs about, [the mind is what is truly in flight].
This is truly the image manifested within the mental faculty (*manas*). The preceding phrase reveals delusion through non-awakening; the subsequent phrase reveals awakening through non-delusion.
Since the mind can universally perceive the objects of the five faculties, its capacity for sensation is profound and exceeds that of the other faculties.
○ Second, the mutual interfusion of the six faculties.
Such are these perverse thoughts. When thought is bound, it can become a direction or a destination; when view is bound, it can become a mirror or a witness;
when hearing is bound, it can become a great clashing of rocks, ice, frost, earth, or mist;
when breath is bound, it can become a great fire-cart, a fire-boat, or a fire-cage; and when taste is bound, it can become great wailing, regret, and weeping.
When knots are tied, they can be made large or small; they may be formed a myriad times in a single day, sometimes face-up and sometimes face-down.

Changshui says that what is produced by evil habits is entirely due to perverse thinking. Thinking has "discrimination" as its essential meaning. Whatever phenomena appear within the mind are all produced through such knotting.

This knotting constitutes spatial location, which is established through discrimination. Spatial location and the mirror-like realization [of reality]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
Their connection likely represents the manner in which transgressions are created; thus, what follows is the testimony regarding those who commit such offenses.
As for "the great confluence of stones" and so forth, Wénlǐng considers this to be the mutual resonance of water and earth. The meaning is clear from the preceding text, which states:
"When mountain rocks are struck, they produce flames; when melted, they become water. It further states: "Fire ascends and water descends, mutually manifesting and establishing [their presence]."
Solidity and moisture form the great oceans; when dried, they become continents and sandbanks. As for ice and frost being of the same category as water, this is stated in reference to rain;
thus, they are equivalent to *mái* (haze). An alternative manuscript reads *méng* (dew) for "frost," which is identical to *móu*.

When the celestial qi descends but the earth does not respond, it is called *móu*. Because the breath circulates through inhalation and exhalation, [these elements] serve as fire-carts, ships, and railings for all movement.
The elephant’s crying out in lamentation and weeping must involve verbal expression; this, too, is a matter of the tongue-faculty.

Suddenly perceiving the body as large, suddenly perceiving the body as small—these states of lying down and rising in birth and death are all manifestations of suffering experienced through the contact of the body. Indeed, throughout myriad lifetimes one does not receive a myriad different forms;
rather, it is within a single body that one undergoes myriad births and deaths in a single day. This clearly demonstrates what is summoned [by one's karma].
The response is concluded. ○ Third, the general conclusion revealing the illusory nature, in two parts: (1) that which is produced by delusion; (2) that it is not the true original reality.
Furthermore, [the first part] has two sections: (1) the general conclusion on being produced by delusion.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six effects of the hells; they are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings. Question:
According to the "Sixfold Mutual Retribution," the hells into which one falls are all said to be "Avīci" (Uninterrupted).
Is it then the case that all ten habitual causes constitute the karma of Avīci? Answer: For example, the eight cold hells induced by the habit of greed are not Avīci.
Furthermore, even such things as the karmic mirror and the fire-pearl, which are induced by the habitual tendencies of litigation, are matters pertaining to the period prior to receiving retribution;
they also universally reflect those entering hell. The Sūtra’s mention of "Avīci" likely refers to those minor hells in contrast to them;
thus, all eight cold and eight hot hells may be termed "Avīci," and it does not necessarily refer exclusively to the Avīci [Hell] itself. However, the Avīci is also called the "Great... [Avīci].
There is no interval. If sentient beings were to awaken to their own minds, they would see that all retributions of suffering are identical to illusory transformations.

Because they are deluded regarding their own minds, they falsely perceive various sufferings; how could these truly exist? ○ Second, the specific conclusion on the causes and effects of the subjective and objective:
1. The causes and effects of the Avīci Hell.
If various sentient beings collectively commit evil karma, they enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.

"Collectively committing" refers to those who have jointly created the ten habitual causes (*daśa-ābhyāsa-hetu*). Because their malicious minds are grave, the duration of their suffering throughout the kalpas is extensive.
The ancients claimed that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the ten habits were created simultaneously; however, this is not so. It is simply one...
They are born with all manner of evils in their ears. ○ Second, regarding the causes and effects of the Eight Uninterrupted Hells:
if one commits offenses through each of the six sense organs, or performs such acts while involving both objects and organs, that person shall enter the Eight Uninterrupted Hells.

"Each is created by its own [faculty]" means that each of the six sense faculties creates its own; for example, the eye creates the evil belonging to the eye-faculty, and so on up to the mind creating the evil belonging to the mind-faculty.
"Inclusive of objects and so forth" refers to the matters created by the ten causes. Although the ten causes are inclusive, the faculties themselves are not inclusive;
thus it is called "inclusive of objects. Alternatively, at the time of creating evil, although the creating faculties may be inclusive, as for the objects—
When not combined, they are merely called "combined faculties. Combined objects occur within the ten causes, ranging from two or three up to eight or nine.
Combined faculties occur among the six faculties, ranging from two or three up to four or five. Each of these constitutes six combinations;
with combined objects, there are seven; with combined faculties, there are eight. Thus, there are eight causes capable of summoning the suffering of the eight Avīci hells. Eight.
Because they are named according to the causes that summoned them, the "Eight Uninterrupted Hells" (aṣṭāv avīcyaḥ) do not necessarily refer to specific individual hells.
Furthermore, as for the name "Uninterrupted Hell" (avīci), it does not necessarily refer to either a cold or a hot hell, nor does it definitively designate a particular one.

Nevertheless, even if one enters the Avīci hell due to these causes, one will not remain there for immeasurable kalpas. The mention here of "eight hells" likely refers to eight types of persons who enter them.
Appended here is a commentary on the name of the Avīci Hell.
According to the sutra: "With nine feelings and one thought, one descends through the wheel of fire; the body enters the ground where wind and fire intersect."

There are two kinds of hells: those with intervals (*sāntara*) for those who take life lightly, and the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) for those who commit it repeatedly. Those of pure emotion immediately sink into the Avīci hell;

thus, it appears that Avīci lies outside the Uninterrupted Hell. Furthermore, it is said that those who collectively commit evil deeds enter the Avīci hell to undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
This applies to those who have committed offenses through each of the six sense organs, as well as those who have engaged in such acts in combination.
If one who possesses both the sense objects and the faculties [commits such an act], they enter the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (*aṣṭāv avīcyaḥ*).

Thus, it appears that the "Uninterrupted" (*avīci*) is actually outside of these eight; however, among the eight hot hells, since ancient times the *Avīci* has been considered the eighth. As the verse says:
"The Reviving, the Black Rope, the Three Crushing, the Howling, the Great Howling, the Six Heats, the Seventh Intense Heat, and below that, the Eighth, the *Avīci*."
The nose. Regarding these eight fundamental hells of cold and heat, how are the two [conflicting] explanations to be reconciled?

Guishan’s commentary on the preceding section of the sutra states that those who die lightly are reborn in the *antarābhava* (intermediate state) while those who die heavily are reborn in the *avīci* (uninterrupted) hell; this simply means that within the previous seven hells themselves, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness.
It would be more appropriate to consider the sixth as having an interval (*sāntara*) and the seventh as being without an interval (*nirantara*).

However, there is no explanatory reconciliation for this in the latter part of the sutra. Since these verses originally derive from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Dīrgha Āgama*, they must not be contradicted.
If one were to claim that Avīci is definitely outside the eight *anantarya* [sins], it seems—based on the present sutra—that...

This conforms [to other teachings] yet contradicts the *Āgamas* and the *Abhidharmakośa*; I fear it is not a treatise that applies universally. ○ Regarding the causes and effects of the thirty-eight hells:
if one commits the three actions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through body, speech, and mind, such a person will enter the eighteen hells.

To speak of the three—body, speech, and mind—means that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not fully clear. To commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct means that the ten causes (*daśahetu*) are not fully clear.

One must know that while the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are frequently committed by worldly people, the ten habitual practices (*daśābhyāsa*) cannot be performed concurrently except by those who are not merely great evildoers.
Regarding the eighteen hells: the body commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the mouth commits killing and stealing...
Sexual misconduct. When one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the mental faculty, there are nine acts committed and nine agents of commission.
These two nines, totaling eighteen, serve as the causal conditions that attract retribution, resulting in the fruit of retribution experienced in the eighteen hells.

It is the natural law that for every cause there must be a corresponding result; there is no room for doubt. This refers to the "present activity" which attracts the name of the retribution it brings about.
The retribution is clearly explained and evident; by comparing it with preceding and succeeding cases, all can be understood.
○ Fourth, the causes and effects of the thirty-six hells:
if one does not commit all three karmas simultaneously but instead commits either one instance of killing or one instance of stealing, such a person will enter the thirty-six hells.
The three karmas not being combined constitutes "repetition" (*āvṛtti*). This consists of nine propositions and thirty-six causes: (1) performing killing and stealing with body and speech;
(2) performing killing and sexual misconduct with body and speech; (3) performing stealing and sexual misconduct with body and speech;

(4) committing killing and stealing with body and mind; (5) committing killing and sexual misconduct with body and mind; (6) committing stealing and sexual misconduct with body and mind; (7) committing killing with speech and mind.
Regarding theft: there are eight cases where one commits killing and sexual misconduct through speech and mind; nine cases where one commits theft and sexual misconduct through speech and mind.

Since there are thirty-six causes, they certainly lead to rebirth in thirty-six hells. As for the statement that "in the interim, one may commit a single act of killing or a single act of theft," these also consist of nine phrases and thirty-six causes:
first, performing killing through body and speech; second, performing theft through body and speech; third, performing [sexual misconduct] through body and speech...
1. Sexual misconduct through body and mind; 2. Killing through body and mind; 3. Theft through body and mind; 4. Sexual misconduct through body and mind;
5. Killing through speech and mind; 6. Theft through speech and mind; 7. Sexual misconduct through speech and mind.
Among these, there are eighteen types of active agents and likewise eighteen types of karmic actions performed; these thirty-six causes that attract [retribution] bring about three [results].

These are the fruits of the sixteen hells. Such persons are not limited to a single individual; for instance, if one commits the offenses of killing or stealing through body and speech, one will experience four hells.
The number of hells into which one enters depends solely on what the person has provoked. V. One hundred and eight hells:
the causes and effects.
When "seeing-seeing" occurs through a single faculty, one commits a single karma and enters one hundred and eight hells.

Regarding the term "seeing-seeing," ancient interpretations are not uniform; however, the *Zhong* (the *Zhonglun*) states that "seeing-seeing" can encompass all six faculties. This is evident from the mutual retributions of the first six faculties:
in the case of the hearing faculty, it is said that one first sees billowing waves; in the case of the nose faculty, one also first sees poisonous vapors. Thus, it is the same for the others.

For the faculties (*indriya*) to receive retribution, there must first be the presence of views (*dṛṣṭi*). The number of afflictions (*kleśa*) is one hundred and eight, and the hells are likewise so numbered.
Although the specific enumeration may not be detailed, the underlying principle can be inferred from this. However, when a faculty and its object (*viṣaya*) correspond, two hells are formed.

At present, we are considering only the transgression of the faculty itself, which has not yet involved the object—for example, when one utters false speech or slanders another, but the person has not yet suffered harm; or when one hatches a plot to kill someone.
A person is not killed; however, because the eyes and ears commit transgressions by going to look and listen, one falls into one of the hells from among the one hundred and eight.
○ Second, they are not truly inherently existent.
By this, sentient beings separately act and separately create, entering the stage of homogeneity within the world. These delusive thoughts arise;
they do not exist from the beginning.
To "separately act and separately create" means to separately perform these karmas and separately fashion these fruits. Xunwen says: Previously, Ānanda...
Question: Do these various hells have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously? Since each person generates their own karma and experiences it individually, the answer is now given:
they enter the common ground (*sabhāga-bhūmi*) within the world-system.

Furthermore, as to the previous question—whether this path exists inherently from the beginning or arises from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings—the answer is now given: it is produced by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Birth does not exist from the beginning. Now, since the nature of sentient beings is endowed with the ten realms, hell is likewise inherently present within that nature.
However, because the phenomena inherent in nature are fused into a single principle where no marks can be apprehended, this constitutes the three truths being complete within a single mind.
How, then, could one say that hell exists as a substantial reality? Therefore, it is said that it does not exist from the beginning. This is due to the [sentient beings...]
