II. Investigating the Origin and Developing Vision. A. General Exposition:

One investigates the root of all living beings, observing that source which is profoundly pure yet constantly subject to agitation. Thereafter, there arise various conceptual calculations and speculations.
Such a person falls into the doctrine of five nirvāṇas, with the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) being the last.
Because they reckon nirvāṇa to occur within that final body, it is called "subsequent existence" (*paścāt-bhava*).
II. Specific Explanation, Part One: The Direct Clarification.
Either the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is taken as the primary basis of transformation (*āśraya-parivṛtti*), because one perceives its perfect luminosity and gives rise to longing for it;

or the first dhyāna is chosen because its nature is free from sorrow (*daurmanasya*); or the second dhyāna is chosen because the mind is free from suffering (*duḥkha*); or the third dhyāna is chosen because of the presence of extreme bliss (*sukha*).

Alternatively, because both suffering and pleasure have perished in the four dhyānas and one does not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, one becomes deluded regarding the contaminated heavens and conceives the notion that they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Taking these five abodes as secure and supreme pure refuges, one thus cycles through them until reaching their ultimate limit.
The preceding fascicle explained that one in the first dhyāna is not oppressed by suffering and affliction, while one in the second dhyāna cannot be oppressed by any anxieties or distresses.

Now, it is stated that the first dhyāna is without anxiety and the second dhyāna is without suffering; this is merely a stylistic variation in the presentation of the text. Because the first dhyāna is free from desire, there is no anxiety;
because the second dhyāna is characterized by supreme joy, there is no suffering. Regarding the phrase "supreme bliss followed" in the third dhyāna, the previous text states:
Attaining great conformity, one’s body and mind become tranquil and secure, obtaining immeasurable bliss.
In the second dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is countered by sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and thus constitutes suffering; in the third dhyāna, the absence of both sorrow and joy constitutes bliss.

Those who conceptualize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) falsely reckon it to be the fruit of liberation and sovereignty—namely, "my own virtue," "tranquility and bliss," "supreme purity," "purity as a basis," and "ultimate permanence."

This refers to the four inversions of ordinary beings. The *Supplement* states: "Alternatively, taking the desire realm as the primary basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) precisely clarifies the characteristics of meditative concentration within the desire realm.
This is because when such concentration is accomplished, one no longer perceives the obstacles of physical objects, such as beds and mats."

This is precisely because the direct retribution (*vipāka*) of the concentrated mind can transform the circumstantial retribution (*adhipatiphala*); therefore, the text below states, "one perceives the perfect clarity.

Regarding the interpretation of "transforming the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), Master Jiaoguang follows the commentary of Master Wenling. Furthermore, it is said that one "perceives the perfect clarity" because this is the initial attainment of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Master Youxi stated: "Regarding the reckoning of five locations in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the human realm of the desire world (*kāmadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are excluded."
The realms. One does not reckon the human realm because those currently dwelling therein are within the cycle of birth and death.
One does not reckon the formless realm because [some] take the heaven of non-conception in the four dhyānas to be nirvāṇa. ○ Second, the summary of faults.
Based on this conceptualization, they fall into the ranks of external paths by mistaking the five states of present nirvana for the nature of Bodhi.
Having been born in those heavens through the power of meditative concentration, they do not necessarily attain ultimate peace and bliss immediately upon casting off their bodies;
hence they are called the "five states of present nirvana. Furthermore, because the five aggregates still persist while they nonetheless conceive of nirvana, it is termed "present nirvana."
This is demonstrated by the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This is called the tenth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of those who establish nirvāṇa within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) based on the five manifestations.
It is truly because the five aggregates do not perish that they take the five heavens to be eternally abiding. Thus, Wu Xing said: "From..."
The sixth [view] flows from the externalists. The previous sixth [view] stated: "Some, firmly clinging to the body, say that form (*rūpa*) is the self (*ātman*), etc.

Because this present [view] flows from that, it belongs to the same category. Regarding why the five [attainments of] nirvāṇa do not reach the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is fully explained in the Tongzhou commentary.
○ Second, the conclusion of the faults and the exhortation to show the way.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of delusory insights arising from *dhyāna* all manifest as such awakenings because the mind is applied to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) in a state of mutual conflict.
Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When these states appear before them, they mistake their confusion for awakening.
Claiming for themselves that they have attained the ranks of the Sages, they commit a great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata to me [as your guide].
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit this teaching to the age of the final dharma (mappō), causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.

Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamities within themselves; maintain and protect them so that they may suppress false views. Teach their bodies and minds to open to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter bypaths on the unsurpassed path.
Do not let them pray for the heart's desires and consider a small attainment sufficient; [thereby] act as a Great Awakened King to purify [them].
The pointing finger and the holding of the phrase:
"Ming" (冥) maintains the breath and wards off the heterodox; "Jiao" (教) teaches the phrase and reveals the teaching that returns to the orthodox.

From "At the bottom of non-existence" (*wu-xia*) onwards, this generally clarifies the maintenance of good and the warding off of evil. All ten demons arise from taking little as sufficient; this points out the root of their ailment so that they may return to the ultimate.

The fruit must surely take the present text as the definitive pointer to purity. Changshui said: "When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is not yet exhausted, one is still led by external māras.

Now that the aggregate of perception is exhausted and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is clearly revealed, one merely gives rise to divergent views regarding the objects of awareness, grasping at them as being correct;
therefore, it is called the 'mind-māra'. Xunwen said: "The words 'birds, beasts, and insects' refer to..."

The anomaly of locusts is called an "evil omen" (*niè*). Now it is said that the mental demon (*xin mó*) harms oneself just like that anomaly; "message" (*xiāo xī*) here refers to its elimination and extinction.
Wēn-líng says: What was previously stated—that the manifestation of realms during *zhēnā* (dhyāna) is when the celestial māra seizes the opportunity—is precisely this.
This so-called "mad understanding" (*cīna-kṣānti*) arises as a deep affliction from the mind itself.

Generally, when one's realization of the Way is not true, various divergent paths and false reckonings are all instances of mad understanding; this is what is called the "mind-demon," which must be guarded against most deeply. Wuxing said:

Previously, it was stated that at the conclusion of the aggregates of form, sensation, and perception, all are "non-existent," lest the celestial Māras find an opportunity to exploit them; here, it is called the "demon of the mind" (*citta-māra*).

Later, regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it is called the "demon of views" (*dṛṣṭi-māra*). These "mind" and "views" do not transcend the two delusions of view and craving; they are precisely the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).
Within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the fifth [aggregate] gives rise to inexhaustible sorrow and a desire not to live, which is like the Māra of Death.
Furthermore, the five aggregates that are observed constitute the Māra of the Aggregates (*skandha-māra*). Thus, the four Māras are complete. Youyixi said:

"The Master of Wenling stated, 'Those whose vision of the Path is not true engage in false calculations regarding many divergent paths. These words deeply strike at the vital organ of scholars. Indeed, in this world..."
In their practice, they frequently fall into two kinds of errors. First, they follow their own minds and establish themselves without a lineage of teachers.

In vain, they admire the lofty character of ancient virtuous ones and enter deep into the remote seclusion of forest hermitages (*araṇya*). Through perverse reasoning and arbitrary fabrication, their minds suddenly become empty;
like a fish caught between ice, they mistake this for the true Way. Consequently, they give rise to biased views and fall into heterodox schools. They establish...
At their gates and in their courtyards, they cite the ancestral teachings as proof, yet they compare brass to gold and confuse jade with white jade.
Having brought ruin upon themselves and others, they ultimately fall into the ranks of Māra. Having received the transmission for but a short time, their study and contemplation lack refinement.
Eager to act as teachers to others, they establish their own rules; being unwilling to yield to others in terms of rank and position, they further seek to pull them up [to their own level].

All streams flow back to their source; yet those who shoulder the Chan tradition stand alone as its sole upholder, their heads held even higher. Having never studied the categories of medicinal substances, they have no connection to the legacy of Shennong;
nor can their dispensing of decoctions compare to that of Zhang Zhongjing. Their medicines do not correspond to the ailment, and their prescriptions do not fit the disease.

They indiscriminately administer drugs at random, regarding the people as mere grass. While there may be slight benefit at first, it ultimately leads to great harm, causing them to enter into the realm of the heterodox.

Beholding them within the thickets of the forest, they have fallen into the net of Pāpīyān. They establish doctrines and set forth treatises to serve as models for future generations, yet the Master himself loses his footing and enters a pit of fire without realizing it;
his disciples follow blindly, falling onto perilous paths without being aware of it.
This is entirely because they have not yet seen the Way and yet hastily attempt to cultivate it; by relying on deviant paths, they erroneously claim to have realized the fruit.
○ Fifth, the Aggregate of Consciousness (vijñāna-skandha): 3. A general demonstration of its beginning and end; 3. A conclusion regarding the exhaustion of the preceding practices.

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle and pure natures of all worldly phenomena, along with the stirring commonality of the generative impulse, suddenly fall apart.
The deep-seated cords of the subtle and the latent tendencies of the *pudgala* that repay karma are severed;
the resonance between cause and effect is suspended.

This clarifies the characteristics of the cessation of formations (*saṃskāra*). Changshui says: "The nature of the world" means that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the very essence of the world.
There are three meanings of "the world": first, it possesses arising and ceasing; second, its nature is outflowing (*sāsrava*); third, it is subject to destruction.

Since one has fallen into the world, one shares with it the nature of the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations. Regarding "the generative mechanism of the homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*):
The life-force (*jī-mi*) common to all twelve classes of beings is likewise so. Its sudden shattering is precisely the mark of exhaustion.

Because the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* illuminates and breaks through this life-force, it is called "shattered. Although it is said that the common lot is shattered, in reality, it occurs within a single person.
The terms "deeply subtle" and "heavy and low" explain the meaning of exhaustion. Both Wēnlíng and Jiāoguāng take "deeply subtle" as the basis for their interpretation.

The phrase "suddenly collapsing the coarse and sinking the fine cords and ties" (*shūrán huīliè chénxì gāngniǔ*) is read as connected to the preceding clause. However, it is now said that such a syntactic structure does not exist here;
it should likely be read as connected to the following clause. The large ropes on a net are called *gāng* (cords), and the knots at the collar of a garment are called *niǔ* (ties);
both serve as metaphors for what is essential. The twelve classes of living beings are like a net or a garment, and the binding essence of the *xing-yin* (aggregate of formations) is like the cords.
Like a knot, its substance consists of the seven consciousnesses; thus it is said to be "deep and subtle. *Pudgala* means "one who repeatedly takes up existence";
herein lies the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) capable of repaying prior karma. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the deep channel.

It is called "deep" because it is formed by obscure and hidden delusive thoughts. Karma is the stimulus, and retribution is the response. Because the channels are severed and no longer intersect, it is said to be "suspended and cut off. This refers to the stimulus.

This should be understood as being identical in meaning to the "suspended" [state] described for the lower categories. For the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is pervasive:

first, it extends to both self and others; second, it extends to both the sentient and the insentient. Within the three realms, beings of various classes evoke this and that response because the aggregate of formations serves as the channel through which they communicate.
Thus, when formations are exhausted, the interaction between stimulus and response ceases. Alternatively, the term "deep" may refer to the profound channel.
The "Fine Net-Knot. As it is said: "What is the 'sinking fine net-knot'? It is the deep channel through which the *pudgala* reaps the results of its karma.
[Section Two: A Preliminary Indication of the Beginning and End. Part One: The Characteristics of the Beginning Not Being Exhausted.]
Regarding the near dawn of awakening to the heaven of Nirvana: it is like the crowing of a rooster at daybreak, when one looks toward the east and already perceives a subtle radiance.
The six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipated; internally and externally, they are profoundly clear and luminous, entering a state of non-entry.

One deeply penetrates the fundamental source from which the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions receive their lives. By observing that the source arises from grasping, one sees that none of these various classes can summon it back; thus, within the realms of the ten directions...
Having already attained this sameness, the refined essence does not sink, but reveals what was hidden and secret; this is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

Below the section on Nirvāṇa, there is a combination of Dharma and analogy to clarify that as the True Principle is about to be revealed, the *vijñāna-skandha* will manifest accordingly. The first two lines constitute the Dharma.
Since the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* has been eliminated, the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing is about to appear before one.

Therefore, it is said that "one is about to greatly awaken. Gu Shan states: "The Nirvana of the Three Virtues is called the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"This refers to when the preceding hindrance of the mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is broken, one enters the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*) and is about to ascend to the heaven of the Middle Way of true reality;
therein, at the breaking of dawn, one perceives the semblance of the three truths. This is like the metaphor of the rooster reaching its peak color."
The fact that the rooster crows later simply indicates that it is the time for dawn to break;

why must the three cries at the fifth watch be correlated with the five aggregates (skandhas) and the number of sensation, perception, and mental formations (vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra)? "Pure color" is the sign of the eastern sky approaching dawn;

because the light has not yet been mixed with other colors, it is called "pure color," which is a metaphor for the three truths in their mutual correspondence. This refers to the six sense faculties merging downward.
From the state where the six sense faculties are empty and still up to the manifestation of the profound and secret, all resemble the atmosphere of a clear dawn;

thus, the appropriateness of this analogy is evident. Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has been shattered, the six sense faculties before one no longer run toward sounds and forms.

This is the uprooting of the "floating dust" faculties (*bhrānti-indriya*). As the subsequent scripture states: "Because they do not emerge from the body as seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing," it is thus designated.

The six sense organs (ṣaḍāyatana) are empty because they lack the first four aggregates; they are still because they are free from agitation. The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is called "profoundly pure.
Now, by eliminating even this aggregate of formations, is it not indeed empty and still? Internally there is the essence of consciousness, and externally there are the six sense organs.

There is only a single body of profound clarity, with no further subject that enters nor object entered. This is because within the aggregate of formations, the nails grow, the hair develops, and vital energy arises.
The smoothing of wrinkles was never perceived as awakening; yet now that one is free from these signs, how could it not be profoundly clear?

It is for this reason that the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (Paramārtha-dhātu) is about to shine forth. "Deeply penetrating" and below refers to the manifestation of the consciousness-body (vijñāna-kāya).
Not only does one see sentient beings dying here and being born there, but one also sees that the seeds within consciousness are the fundamental source of receiving life. This is universal knowledge.
It is also another matter. Furthermore, the meanings of the two characters "yuan" (origin) and "you" (source) differ. "You" refers to the seeds which have now become capable of observation;
"yuan" refers to the portion of consciousness that enters the womb and has now become capable of grasping. Because it is capable of observation, the view of causelessness is eliminated.

Because one maintains and guards [this realization], there is no karma for rebirth; thus, exhausting the twelve categories of beings, none can drag one into further birth—this is the matter of self-benefit.

The term "the ten directions" encompasses both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as self and others; all are manifestations of consciousness, sharing the same single essence of consciousness.
Regarding the statement that "refined color does not sink, but reveals the profound and secret," an ancient said: "These two phrases alone [suffice]."

This is the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The preceding passage regarding the "exhaustion of formations" (*saṃskāra-kṣaya*) specifically refers to the person who has severed the aggregate of formations;
because the aggregate of formations has been severed, the aggregate of consciousness is subsequently severed as well, and thus there follows the statement about "transcending the turbidity of life.
The two phrases concerning "purity" and "form" refer instead to those who have suppressed the formations but have not yet severed them, along with what precedes them.

Sensation, perception, and form are all merely temporarily suppressed. Now, as we advance to contemplate consciousness, because the mind is luminous and tranquil, the refined essence does not sink away, and its profound secrets manifest.
Thus, the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle) states that the doctrine of "suppressing and severing" most accurately captures the core intent of the sutra.

Nevertheless, the current division of the text seems somewhat inconsistent; it is likely that the two phrases concerning the "refined essence" follow from the preceding passage regarding the emptiness of the six sense organs.

When stillness reaches the point of entering that which has no entry, is this not the essence of refinement remaining unsubmerged? This non-submersion is the departure from the ailment of concealment.
Next, it says one deeply penetrates the ten directions and the fundamental source of receiving life; is this not the manifestation of the profound and secret?
This means that the seeds within consciousness, which had been hidden and secret, have now manifested. Because the refined essence does not sink away, it manifests as something hidden and secret;
this place of secrecy is called the domain of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṣetra*).

When one practices until consciousness manifests, for the practitioner who has severed [the fetters], the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) merely appears and is then able to be severed. Therefore, the subsequent passage in the sutra explains the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness.
Regarding the signs: when one who is practicing subduing falls into the realm of consciousness, ten kinds of demonic activities arise.

The sūtra contains two meanings which fundamentally do not contradict one another; the opening passage on the preceding aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is also like this. 2. The signs of the ultimate end of [the aggregates].

If, amidst the various calls [of sensory objects], one has already attained sameness within them and dissolved the six gates; if the union and opening are perfected, such that seeing, hearing, and the other faculties interpenetrate and function with mutual purity;

and if the ten directions, the world, as well as body and mind, are as clear and transparent inside and out as lapis lazuli—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
The first phrase points to being within the *vijñāna-skandha*. Although the various summoning [of the faculties] differs, the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) is the same.

Being the same, it is empty, still, and profoundly unified; thus, the summoning cannot move it. At this time, through the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the obstructions of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are worn away.

Previously, there was only the emptiness and stillness of the six faculties; now, even the appearance of the six faculties no longer exists. Regarding "the achievement of merging and opening": merging...

The single consciousness opens and forms the six faculties. Furthermore, when these are merged back into one while the six functions remain distinct and manifold, it is called "accomplishment through opening.

When they are opened into six while the one mind remains sovereign, it is called "accomplishment through merging. Moreover, the mutual penetration of seeing and hearing is accomplishment through opening;
the purity of their reciprocal functioning is accomplishment through merging. Regarding the term "mutual penetration," it refers to the six functions...

There is no separation between them, like the mutual communication between neighbors. Changshui said: "The body and mind are internal, while the world is external; both are manifestations of consciousness alone.
Now that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, there remains only the essence of awakening. This essence of awakening is luminous and wondrous, like pure lapis lazuli.
Previously, it was merely a refined color that did not sink; now, like lapis lazuli, it is transparent and penetrating—this is great enlightened realization. Thus he spoke.

Regarding those who transcend the turbidity of life: while consciousness abides and life remains, consciousness perishes as life departs. Now that consciousness has been shattered, there is certainly no doubt that one has transcended the turbidity of life.
Having privately investigated the domain of the five aggregates, I shall now continue to clarify the ultimate nature of the exhaustion of the five aggregates.
This is because for a person of sharp faculties, when the preceding aggregate is severed and the subsequent aggregate manifests, a wondrous awakening may arise.
This means that one breaks through the subsequent aggregates (skandhas) without waiting for further contemplation after encountering the demonic realms before attaining awakening.

Therefore, it is clarified here that the characteristic of the exhaustion of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is described as "wearing away the six gates" and "attaining mastery over their opening and closing," which occurs prior to the ten realms.

Furthermore, the cloth and knots are again raised as a metaphor for the delusion of the aggregates. The Tathāgata’s skillful exposition makes it clear and readily intelligible. Therein lie the dharmas of the six sense faculties.
By this analogy, the number of the six sense organs is not in vain; and by this analogy of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the words regarding their sequence are further validated.
Neither the sense organs nor the aggregates alone, taken in pairs, would suffice to exhaust the metaphor of the single cloth. II. Concluding Exhortation to Transmit and Demonstrate.
You should thoroughly investigate the root source of these deluded thoughts so that your mind may attain clarity.

Transmit this teaching to all practitioners of future ages during the Dharma-ending period, causing them to recognize the profound unreality of their own arising, to develop deep weariness with it, and to know of nirvana so as not to cling to the triple world.
The opening and penetration of one’s own mind is self-awakening; transmitting this to those who come after is awakening others.

Previously, Ānanda requested [instruction on] the "initial expedient means," and later, when the Buddha asked the various sages about their perfect penetrations, he again spoke of the "initial arousal of the mind.
The intent of this sutra is simply to enable ordinary beings to cultivate the Way so that they may swiftly realize the perfect principle. Within this context, it says "transmitting."

This indicates what will come in the future age of the Dharma (mofa) to correspond with the preceding text. "Causing them to recognize" means causing them to recognize that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are all produced by false conceptualization (parikalpita);
thus, they will naturally grow weary of these five aggregates. Recognizing their falsity is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).

Deep weariness is the abandonment of the origin [of suffering] (samudaya-prahāṇa). Nirvāṇa corresponds to cessation (nirodha). Not being attached corresponds to the path (mārga). The main body of the teaching is concluded.

III. The Section on Dissemination (Parīndanā) has two parts: 1. The conclusion and exhortation for dissemination; 2. [The specific exhortations]. Regarding the first, there are two: 1. Exhortation by comparing it with the merit of giving; 2.

Direct exhortation regarding the attainment of Buddhahood. The first [of these] also has two: 1. Comparing and manifesting it in relation to the merit of giving. Regarding this, the first is the question.

Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a heart that never wasted its intent. What do you think?
Would this person, by virtue of these causes and conditions of giving to the Buddhas, obtain much merit?
Regarding "pervading and so forth": the upper instance of the character *man* (滿) refers to filling space;

the lower instance of the character *man* refers to filling with the seven treasures—that is, the seven treasures fill the void until no space remains. Regarding "serving and making offerings": this refers to serving the seat below and making offerings of body and mind.
*Xunwen* says: "In the question, there are three points: first, 'pervading' [refers to] the lower part, which raises the abundance of seeds; second..."
The first [section] below shows that the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is great; the second shows that the mind of reverence is great. These three "greats" serve as the basis for comparison.
Specifically, the middle [passage] states: first, it cites the abundance of the seven treasures; second, it cites the abundance of the Buddhas.
By offering such treasures to the Buddhas, one’s mind naturally does not pass in vain. Therefore, within this passage, there are only two [points].
The intention corresponds with the answer below. Second, the answer: "The precious jewels filling the void" answers the previous point regarding the abundance of jewels;
"the Buddha-lands being filled" answers the previous point regarding the abundance of Buddhas.
Ānanda replied: "The void is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to a Buddha."

If even by sacrificing one's body one may obtain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, how much more so when one actually presents precious jewels that fill the entirety of the Buddha-fields throughout space?
Even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, it could not be fully grasped; how, then, could there be any limit to such merit?
To say that "empty space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless" clarifies that these can be offered to all Buddhas.

Furthermore, the latter phrase arises from the former: since empty space is inexhaustible, precious jewels are boundless. The passage beginning with "In the past... cites the inferior to illustrate the superior;
seven coins are extremely few, which serves as a contrast to show that the seven treasures are exceedingly many. By giving so little, one still attains the [Wheel-Turning] King.
Regarding the royal throne, because the Buddha-field is supreme, the merit of a Wheel-Turning King—complete with the seven treasures and surrounded by a thousand sons—is surpassed;
how much more so the merit of one who offers all the jewels filling space to Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust?
To say "space is exhausted" means that its extent has been reached. To say that the Buddha-fields are filled and one offers precious jewels therein means that one is making offerings to the Buddhas.
At that time, throughout the entire land, all were composed of precious jewels; because every Buddha was likewise so, it is said that "all were bestowed. Part Two:
Exalting Merit to Encourage Practice, which has two sections. First, the merit of extinguishing transgressions.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The speech of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is without falsehood.

If there should be a person whose body has committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājikas, they will in an instant pass through this world and other worlds, through the Avīci hells, until they have exhausted their passage through the uninterrupted hells of the ten directions, experiencing them all.
Yet, if such a person can, with a single thought, uphold this Dharma-gate during the final kalpa..."

This is revealed for the sake of those who have not yet studied. The karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished upon mere recollection; the causes for the suffering of hell they are destined to undergo will be transformed into a land of peace and bliss.

*Pārājika* is translated here as "abandonment" (*qi*) and also as "that which is not to be enjoyed. Because one has abandoned [the precepts], one immediately ceases to function as a member of the Saṃgha. Not...
Those who find pleasure [in such acts] shall immediately enter hell. Regarding the ten things to be abandoned in the Mahāyāna:

in addition to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, one further adds the six [sins] such as selling alcohol and so forth. Since these are grave offenses, how could they possess this Dharma-gate?

It is merely used for the purpose of comparing merits. "In a flash" refers to the speed with which one falls into hell; when the hells of this region are destroyed, one proceeds to other regions, and so on.
It pervades the ten directions without interval. The "Dharma-gate" refers to the Śūraṅgama Dharma-gate. The "final kalpa" is a time when the Dharma is difficult to propagate.

"Those who have not yet studied" refers to those who have nothing by which they may be enlightened. "A single thought-moment" is that single thought-moment in which the faculty and the teaching correspond.

Although a single thought-moment is but brief, when the capacity of the transformer and the recipient, as well as the teaching and the recipient, are brought into harmony, then self-benefit and benefit for others are fully realized.
To accomplish such a difficult task during the final age is truly rare.

When it is said that he establishes the Land of Peace and Bliss, this reveals the cause through its fruit. Previously, even the Avīci hells of the ten directions were born from his [vows]; now, they are all...
Since the lands of the ten directions are all Pure Lands of Peace and Bliss, it is said that they are "transformed. Second, regarding the generation of merit:

the merit obtained here surpasses that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million, a billionfold, and so on, even to the point that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Regarding the phrase "a hundredfold, etc.": the merit of the previous giving was merely a single unit, whereas this [merit] surpasses that by hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of times.
Because the fruit of happiness from such excessive meritorious giving is inexhaustible, it conversely becomes an obstacle to attaining Buddhahood.

Now, since both oneself and others attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and directly achieve the fruit of Buddhahood, this [merit] is able to surpass that [previous merit]. Furthermore, the giving of jewels merely fills...
The void arises within the Great Awakening like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.

Now that both self and others have realized this Great Awakening, its capacity to encompass the void makes the bestowal of blessings beyond description. ○ Second, the formal exhortation to attain Buddhahood.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra— as I have extensively explained, which would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon—
and who follow my instructions and practice according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic interference.

The preceding text states: "To reveal this to those who have not yet studied, lest they doubt that the merit of benefiting others is what one obtains, I shall again clarify, based on both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, the profundity of the merit of self-benefit.
Regarding the phrase "as I have explained extensively," it means that I have explained the nature of its karmic rewards at length.
Next, based on my [teaching], following the previous section, it is clarified that reciting sutras and maintaining mantras may not yet be fully endowed with the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Now, by further possessing both the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), one will certainly lack nothing in terms of benefiting oneself and others. "Reflecting" means relying on my words and teachings;

"cultivating" means practicing the path according to those teachings. When the three types of wisdom are complete, one swiftly attains *bodhi*. As for "directly attaining," this refers to the aforementioned "direct" [path].
The mind responds to my words: from the initial aspiration until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is forever no trace of crookedness;
how, then, could there be any demonic interference? Since what is taught in this section encompasses the entire purport of the sutra, it serves as the concluding text. II.
Conclusion on Benefits and Circulation.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās,
as well as all those in the world— gods, humans, asuras, and the bodhisattvas from other directions, the followers of the two vehicles, the holy seers and youths,
along with the powerful spirits who had first resolved their minds toward enlightenment— all were greatly rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
"That they all rejoiced greatly" constitutes the section on the benefits (*anuśaṃsā*). "They paid homage and departed" constitutes the section on the dissemination (*pravartana*). Changshui said:
"Although the twenty-five sages and Mañjuśrī each have their own explanations, the merit ultimately returns to the Buddha; thus, all are termed 'the Buddha’s teaching'. Xingfu said:
"Those who listen to the Dharma with joy can be enumerated as the thirty-six assemblies. This is stated in the *Zhongjing* (Collection of Scriptures).
Each of the three wholesome paths has four groups, such as bhikṣus, totaling twelve assemblies. When these are traversed through the three vehicles, they become thirty-six assemblies.
Although this world possesses the three vehicles, other realms likewise possess the four groups; these are merely skillful explanations that mutually illustrate one another.
Since the great power of the noble ṛṣis transcends that of humans, they are subsumed under the celestial realm; therefore, there are only thirty-six assemblies.
Regarding the term "holy seer youth" (*ṛṣikumāra*): he has attained the fruit of holiness through the path of a seer and is also a youth in his true nature (*kumārabhūta*).
The three characters for "initially generating the mind" (*prathamacittotpāda*) indicate that the intent of this sūtra is directed toward ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) practicing the Way.

There is the generation of the mind at the stage of true attainment (*bhūtasthāna*), and there is the generation of the mind at the stage of semblance (*pratirūpasthāna*); here, it refers merely to the generation of the mind by those at the stages of the outer and inner ordinary persons. [He possesses] the great power of a holy seer.
All these are the spiritual capacities (*indriya*) of this land; ghosts and spirits are most numerous, and they are governed by the manifestation of great power.

All rejoice greatly, encompassing both ordinary beings and sages. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three reasons for their joy: first, the purity of the person who preaches; second, the purity of the Dharma preached;
and third, the purity of attaining the fruit by relying on that Dharma. Based on this, the former two belong to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The latter one pertains to the capacity [of the audience]. Youxi said: "If we discuss the sūtra’s account that after the Buddha had finished preaching this sūtra, all were greatly delighted, it depends solely upon the Dharma preached.
However, this Dharma cannot be struck unless there is a capacity, nor can it be preached unless there is a response.

Because the resonance and the response are manifested together, it possesses these three meanings. That is to say, the *Zhonglun* states that the meaning of the three phrases encompasses the four *siddhāntas*.
The three meanings constitute the world; the person who can expound them constitutes the person; the Dharma being expounded constitutes the remedy;

and attaining the fruit by relying on the Dharma constitutes the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, this sutra upholds the Vinaya while discussing the eternal, and incorporates provisional teachings while expounding the real.

Because it provides the wondrous benefit of the perfect [teaching] to those with partial understanding, they experience great joy. Those who prostrate themselves do so to receive the Great Dharma upon their heads and then depart.
In this land and in other lands, they shall propagate the sutra according to their capacity; these so-called twenty-five persons are those to whom one hundred pieces of gold may be entrusted.
Therefore, the four characters "Thus, having paid homage, he departed" constitute the very essence of the circulation [of the teaching].

Lingyao reflects that he is mediocre and unworthy, possessing no capacity for such tasks; he has merely silently and diligently cultivated the vow to repent his transgressions and attain rebirth before the Great Being.
On the Bingwu year, he was humbly entrusted with the robe and whisk by the Elder Tianxi, who further commanded him to provide commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, saying:
"If the *Śūraṅgama* does not encounter a wise person to judge and explain it, it will remain unresolved for a thousand autumns."
This is a case of doubt. Although various masters have provided commentaries and sub-commentaries, they have not yet revealed the essential intent of the contemplation of the mind.

You should devote your whole heart to composing an exposition that will enlighten future generations; you will not only be a meritorious contributor to our mountain school, but will truly be repaying the Buddha’s profound kindness.

As for me, Yaosim, my attempt to peer at the heavens through a mere inch-long tube finds it utterly impossible to capture even a faint resemblance. Yet, as I cannot disobey the Master’s command, I can do nothing but accept it with shame and trepidation.
In the autumn of the Gui-chou year, I responded to the request for a lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at Haitao Temple.

As I proceeded to analyze the matter, I considered that since this sutra is fundamentally the method of both general and specific contemplation of the mind according to the principles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the task of the scribe lies solely in identifying the subtle harmony between the minds of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
it is not appropriate to further append extraneous discourses. The two major sections of the work form a single, continuous thread from beginning to end.

Just as the sun and moon are so radiant that all people in heaven and earth can see them, when it comes to dissolving the texts and explaining the phrases while extensively gathering various merits, my adherence to and employment of the profound teachings of Youxi Zhizhou’s *Jijie* (Collected Commentaries) predominate. It is like a painter:
once the spirit and likeness are captured and the outlines are complete, there is no hindrance to borrowing the hands of others for filling in the colors and applying the pigments. —Spring of Wumu.
The carving of the woodblocks was undertaken at the outset. In the winter of the Gengshen year, the work was completed.
In total, twelve volumes were published, including ten volumes of definitive commentary (*nirnaya*), one volume of the general outline, and one volume of topical headings.

While I dare not claim that this reveals what was previously unrevealed by the former sages as a definitive interpretation for all time, it is my hope that it accords with the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so that they may be invited to witness and certify it.
This is merely for those with true knowledge of the Way. I reflect deeply that Lingyao is a common person caught in the cycle of birth and death, transmigrating in the lower realms.

The poisons of greed, anger, and delusion manifest in his conduct, and both their seeds and their active expressions remain present. Through delusions, karma, and afflictions, he must repay his debts in this life and in future incarnations.

While diligently applying right mindfulness, one is suddenly entangled in the bonds of craving; though a gateway to merit may briefly arise, it is difficult to escape the mutual confusion of its application.
Bound by the ropes of attachment, one enters the *piṅgala* (the "golden" or "frivolous") state of a *pudgala* without cause, like a moth heedlessly casting itself into a flame.
If there is a vow for rebirth, when will the guidance be received? I only pray that you exhaust this worldly consciousness to repay the Buddha’s kindness and bring all causes to their ultimate end.
May these merits universally benefit all sentient beings. From this day forth until the attainment of Buddhahood, may their delusions, karma, suffering, and obstacles be entirely eliminated;
and from now until they achieve enlightenment, may their categories of precepts, concentration, and wisdom constantly increase in clarity.
May they be reborn in the Pure Land to behold Amitābha face-to-face, and only then return to the Sahā world to extensively deliver all sentient beings. (Geng)
On a day in the eleventh month of winter, the bhikṣu Lingyao, who dwells at Lengyan Jangsi in Jiahe as the fifth-generation successor in the transmission of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations,
wrote this at the quarters of Dashi, following the conditions of his life.
